en: Preface to the Supplementary Notes on the Three Great Works of Tiantai Although our Buddha appeared in the world and extensively expounded various sūtras, his fundamental intention was fully realized only in the *Lotus Sūtra*.
Since the time Ānanda compiled the teachings in the Western Regions, only the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu composed a treatise to elucidate it; however, that work alone...

I shall now explain the meaning based on the text, providing a general outline; yet the great matters of this sutra—the beginning and end of its transformative teaching—remain obscure and unclarified.
Since the time of Kumārajīva’s translation in the Land of the East, those who have composed commentaries and explanations have spread in all directions, and their divergent views are manifold.
Only the Master Zhizhe of Tiantai, who served as the teacher to the two emperors of the Chen and Sui dynasties, formerly at Ling... [text continues].

Having personally received the transmission from the Buddha on Mount [Wutai], he subsequently realized enlightenment at the Great Suo Dharma-assembly and expounded its wondrous purport, providing profound assistance to the Supreme Vehicle.
Thus, he explained the title through five meanings and the textual passages through four sections;

for ninety days he proclaimed and performed the teachings, clarifying the dharma-gate of tranquility and presenting both understanding and practice together, while simultaneously elevating both meaning and contemplation. Truly, this may be called a heart-mirror for practitioners and a bright lamp in the great night.
Even the great treatises of India do not yet equal its kind, let alone the teachers of China being able to hope to reach its heights.
Thus, Master Zhān'ān sighed, saying: "If these teachings were to fall into ruin, the future would be lamentable. Thereupon, he followed the sacred scriptures and recorded these virtuous words;
the *Xuánwén* (Profound Text) and *Zhǐguān* (Stopping and Contemplation) together comprise thirty fascicles. People of the time called them the "Three Greats" (*Sāndà*).
The "sections" (bù) refer precisely to this. Their literary intent is lofty and remote, and their underlying principles are vast and expansive;

were it not for the talent of one nearly equal to a sage, who could have fathomed the depths, analyzed the layers, and dissected the nuances? How else could the profound meanings of the three sections be understood?
Only Master Jingxi was able to shoulder this Way, drawing it out and extending it, pushing it forward and broadening it; thus, there came to be these annotations and records.
As for the *Fuxing* (Subcommentary), its language values essential substance over ornate carving;
its intent is simply to cause every person ten thousand generations hence to awaken to the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision, and for every thing to realize the nature of the secret treasury.
Liang Jingmei, a Hanlin Scholar of the Great Tang, said: "To expand the primary truth (*paramārtha-satya*) by means of words and letters..."

Is it not the case that verbal explanations serve to elucidate liberation? For this reason, throughout antiquity and the present, those who study the Buddha and seek out its profound depths and hidden mysteries have all revered these works as great precepts. Allow me to attempt a discussion of them:
the texts of the three sections transmitted by one school, along with their annotations and records, do not merely encompass the three studies of the Sage’s single lifetime; rather, they...
The Dharma further serves as a cage for the doctrines of the two schools of *dharmatā* and *lakṣaṇa*, and the teachings of the hundred masters;

were it not for one who has accumulated learning, penetrated the subtle, and possesses extensive knowledge and far-reaching vision, such a person could not hastily transmit this to others based on superficial practice.

Having been unworthily exposed to these teachings through my own ignorance, I have spent many years poring over, admiring, and studying them from beginning to end. As for the source of the Sage’s transformation—

The fundamental principles of the Dharma have already been explained in detail by the Patriarchs in their commentaries on the textual meaning; how could there be anything further to supplement them now?
Nevertheless, regarding the Chinese and Sanskrit glosses of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, there may be instances where the Great Master has omitted certain explanations;
furthermore, within the *Fahua Xuanyi* and *Mohe Zhiguan*, there are historical accounts and causal circumstances that Jingxi also left only briefly mentioned.

To speak further, regarding the mutual references and citations found in the *Zhēnjì* and the *Fǔxíng*, as well as the discrepancies between the nature (*xìng*) and characteristics (*xiàng*), and the gains and losses of past and present masters—from the time of Zhāng'ān and Jīngxī onwards, the years have been vast and distant;

among those who propagate and transmit the teachings, who has been able to investigate these matters with such precision as to remain free from obstruction? For this reason, I have not measured my own shallow [understanding].

I have extracted the essential passages from the extensive scriptures and extensively consulted various other works to supplement their omissions and deficiencies, annotating them to clarify their meaning.
This has been compiled into a single volume consisting of fourteen fascicles. It is intended for my own use when lecturing on the Way or encountering the texts;

thus, it will both save the trouble of searching through vast sources and prevent errors and confusion. Should this work provide even a slight benefit to the writings of the former sages, it may yet be circulated.
This work serves as an auxiliary to the Way of our school as it circulates in the world;
were it otherwise, I leave it for future sages to judge.
*Supplementary Notes on the Three Great Works of Tiantai*, Fascicle Upper.

Volume One: Chapter on Matters Concerning Mount Tai and the Vidyāmātra School; matters concerning Zhǎng Ān; matters such as Emperor Míng’s nocturnal dream; matters concerning the Emperor’s governance of the realm;
matters concerning his miraculous birth; matters concerning the translation [of scriptures]; and all movements and actions were recorded by the left official and established therein.

The matter of compiling the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (Gaoseng zhuan) by Dharma Master Huijiao; the matter of the Great Master receiving the Dharma Master’s lectures on the *Golden Letter Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* in succession;
the matter of the three concentrations and three wisdoms, which are identical to the three cessations and three contemplations; the matter of the three peaks of Mount Tiantai;

the matters of the two imperial edicts from the Chen and Sui dynasties inviting the Great Master; and the matters concerning the four types of discernment. This is the first [section] concerning the Great Master.

Matters of rare and extraordinary events; matters of indistinct and obscure occurrences; matters concerning the Crane Grove (*Kalandakanivāpa*); matters regarding the *Śikṣānanda-śamatha-vipaśyanā-dhyāna-mukha* and the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra-ṭīkā*;

matters concerning the classification of "having a remainder" (*sa-upadhiśeṣa*); matters concerning inquiries into the meanings of characters; matters such as the youth on the Snowy Mountain hearing half a verse;
and matters concerning differing accounts of the timing of the Buddha’s renunciation and attainment of enlightenment—[these are] *nayuta*s [in number].

The matters of his fundamental and manifested traces (*honji-suijaku*) are the matter of the ten meanings; the matters of the three faculties transforming into one another and attaining sharpness or dullness are the matters of names;
the matters of the "head and horns" *śrāvakas* are the matters of Mañjuśrī’s transformation of names;

the matters of accumulation, essential accumulation, and the accumulation of characters are the matters of the eight aspects of the Great and Small Vehicles; and the five hundred *yojanas* have three meanings.
The matters concerning the Jewels and their locations; the various matters regarding the jewels; the orderly matters;
the general sequence of five, six, or seven matters; the four kinds of Ānanda; the matters of the three locations; the translation of the name *Srotāpanna* and related matters;
the essential meanings and etymological definitions of characters such as "ritual" (*li*); and the matters concerning the Buddha’s profound subtlety as expounded by Vajragarbha.
The matter of the identity of essence and function; the matter of the *cintāmaṇi* (wish-fulfilling jewel); the matter of the translation of the name "Siddhārtha";

the matter of the translation of the name "Devadatta"; the matter of the translation of the name "Gopī"; the matter of the three similes in the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*; the matter of the translation of the name "campaka";
the matter of which section of the canon the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* belongs to; and the matter of the four times for eating.

Matters concerning the *zhiguī* (earth-measuring rod) and the observation of the sun’s shadow; matters concerning the suddenness of the *Avataṃsaka* and the gradual-perfection of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*;
matters concerning the establishment of the teaching site; matters concerning the gathering of scattered teachings; matters concerning Śunakṣatra and the icchantika;

matters concerning the immovable place of tranquility (*acalā-pratisthāna*) and other matters with many meanings held by the ancients; matters concerning Jambudvīpa; matters concerning the ten jewel mountains; and the matter of Master Sengzhao.

Regarding the various matters mentioned above: the new physician and the old physician; the two types of Bodhisattvas—first, those who practice seated meditation, and second, those who recite the sutras;
the four-line evaluation concerning the wisdom derived from hearing; the matters concerning Mouzi; the terminology of India;
the matters of the Hu (foreigners) and Han (Chinese); the matter of Pūṇa; the matter of the four horses; and the eyes of Śāriputra.
The matter of the successive manifestations and the teaching of the Dharma; the matters of the *Avataṃsaka* regarding worlds facing upward and downward;
the matter of Mañjuśrī’s silent response; the matter of Maitreya; the matter of Śāriputra; the matter of Harivarman;
the matter of Kṣudraka; the matter of Kātyāyana; the matter of Nāgārjuna; and the matter of Asaṅga.
The account of serving five hundred arhats to compose the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra*; the account of Cunda; the account of Kauśika;
the account of Aśvaghoṣa; the account of Kaśmīra; the account of the eighty thousand dharma-treasuries and their various differing characteristics;
the account of Pūrṇa converting non-Buddhists for ninety days; and the account of the *Kaṭhina* robe.
The story of Śāriputra not crossing over; the matter of the increase of merit and so forth;
the second volume of the *Xuán* (Mysterious); the matters concerning Guṇavarman; the Buddha acting for the Four Heavenly Kings by means of four phrases; and the *Fǎyún* (Dharmamegha) of Guāngzhái.
The account of Master Zhigong; the account of the events in Guanzhong; the account of Kumārajīva; the account of Dharma Master Daosheng;
the account of Jetavana; the account of the contradiction; the account of Aṅgulimāla and the five faculties of the śrāvakas;
the account of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* on all dharmas tending toward the one dharma; the account of shattering the subtle dust of the mind; the three turnings.
Reading the text concerns the matters of the Ten Dharma Realms according to the Tiantai school, including the meanings of their names, the causes and fruits of habituation,
and the account of the Buddha showing five skulls to Jīvaka; it also covers the two types of causes and conditions— those that are favorable and those that are adverse—
as well as the seven kinds of birth and death according to the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, and the encounter between Prajñācakṣus Bodhisattva and Mañjuśrī.
The questions and answers concerning the Buddha’s marks and signs (lakṣaṇa-vyañjana) and whether they are retributive or non-retributive; the matter of those below not seeing those above;

the matter of attaining the extinction of ambrosia (amṛta-nirvāṇa) and the realization of the path; the matter of the five aggregates arising and ceasing; the matter of the three provisional designations (tri-vidhā prajñapti);
the matter of the three seers and two devas; the matter of the twenty-five truths (pañcaviṃśati-tattva); and the matter of the twelve links of dependent origination (dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda).
The summary of results and the summary of causes; the matters concerning the five stages within the womb; the matters concerning the four types of twelvefold dependent origination;

the matters concerning the increased enumerations in the Mahāyāna Sūtras; the matters concerning the investigation of dreams through the four propositions; and the matters concerning the three kinds of mind-made bodies.
Volume Two: Matters concerning the *Ratnakaraṇḍa Sūtra* and matters concerning the *Vyākaraṇa* (Abhidharma). *Xuán* 3b.
The fourfold establishment of the Four Noble Truths; the account of the Great Dogchira; the matter of the four nutriments; the matter of the dhūtas;
the matter of two truths falling together into hell; the matter of the five obstacles to be abandoned by a Bodhisattva;
the matter of the fruit of Buddhahood transcending the two truths; and the twenty-three schools of antiquity clarifying the two truths.
The matter of meaning; the matter of five hundred lifetimes of causes; the five kinds of worldly dharmas; the matter of the meeting and connection of similarities and differences;
the matter of the introductory prelude; the matter of perverse attachments that cause the root of the tongue to rot;
the matter of destroying the Dharma and destroying the Buddha as being equal; the eight matters of impurity; and the matter of China: one cessation, three cessations, and one.

Contemplation and the like; the distinct matters of the Separate Teaching (*prātibhedika-śāsana*); matters concerning practice (*caryā*); matters concerning the teaching and realization (*deśanā-adhigama*);

the five practices possessing the five dharmas; (and) matters such as the three substances; the meanings of names and terms according to the *Erya*; the matter of Zhang Kai creating mist and Luan Ba spitting out clouds;
the matter of Ge Xian casting coins into a well and causing them to fly out by incantation; the matter of "feeling and modeling" (*momen*); and the matters of the Vinaya.

The four evaluations of household affairs in the *Vibhāṣā*; the three types of Tripitaka Buddhas; the matter of severing fetters through thirty-four moments of mind; the fourfold propositions regarding objects and knowledge;
the matter of the five eyes which do not follow a sequential order; the matter of the *vyutkrāntakasamādhi* (leap-over samādhi);
the stage of firmness in the power of faith; the analogy of the *kalaviṅka* bird; and the matter of the Tripitaka Bodhisattva being like a vessel of poison.
The matters of the afflictive hindrances and the cognitive hindrances;
the matters of the solitary and the widowed; the matters concerning the five divisions of the Vinaya; and the matters regarding the unattainability of the four great elements and the four natures.

The five practices of heat (*pañca-ūṣmagata*), the practice of falling away (*parihāṇi*), the matters of *koṭi*, the matters of *nayuta*, the matters of fixing the mind on a single object through one-pointed contemplation,
the matters of the fourfold *jñapti-caturtha-karman*, the matters of natural precepts (*prakṛti-śīla*) and prohibitive precepts (*pratikṣepaṇa-śīla*),

The matters of the eight noble lineages; the thirty-six types of impurity; the matters concerning the specific excellence of the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*);
the matters concerning the definitions of names and meanings; the matter of a single body possessing heaven and earth, etc.; the matters of the six desire realms;

The matters of the soil on a fingernail from the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*; the matter of the Bodhisattva purifying Buddha-lands; the three kinds of compassionate deeds;
the matter of the withering and flourishing of the twin trees; the matter of the *Śūraṅgama Samādhi*; the reason why Vāsava fell into hell;
the causal conditions of the eighty thousand devas; and how Śākyamuni Bodhisattva was once a six-tusked white elephant.
1. The matter of successive inference as the supreme matter; 2. The seven matters of goodness; 3. The matter of "looking up and grasping" (*yangpan*); 4.
The matter of "three in the morning and four in the evening"; 5. The matter of *Lokāyata* and its inverse;
6. The matter of the *caṇḍāla*; 7. The matter of the eighteen emptinesses; 8. The matter of the Dharma-body saving sentient beings, like the lute of the asuras; 9. The third [matter].
The matters of *samādhi*; the names and meanings of the Hall of Wholesome Dharmas; the nine types of matters concerning the four fruits of Arhatship;

the matters of karma to be experienced in the present life and so forth; the matters of the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*); the matters of sporting with supernatural powers (*abhijñā*); and the matters of the six stages (*vihāra*) within the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*.
Section Five, Part Two:
The *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* on the three types of giving, such as the field of compassion (*karuṇā-kṣetra*) and the field of reverence (*guru-kṣetra*);
the matter of *sarvajñā* (translated here as "all-knowing wisdom"); the ten practices of the Brahmā-kings; and the matters concerning the wheelwright and others. [Opening]

Regarding the contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*), it clarifies the matters of the five heinous crimes (*pañcānantarya*) as being like saving one's head from fire; this concerns the causal conditions [found in] *Xuán* (玄) 7, lower section.
Regarding the color of the rice in the vessels of the heavens, there are ten distinctions when comparing the four lands (*caturdhātu*). Regarding the Licchavis, there are ten [sections].

and the matter of the Buddha-nature existing within delusion being like the medicinal herbs of the Snowy Mountains— these are from the eighth fascicle of the *Xuanyuan*.
The matters of *nāmakāya*, *padakāya*, and *vyañjanakāya*; the errors found in the translation of scriptures; the three difficulties [of translation];

the matters of the five classics and the six, seven, and nine classics of non-Buddhist texts; the matters of the Three Tombs and Five Canons; the matters of bamboo slips, wooden tablets, and bound volumes;

(Xuánshí, Scroll 10, Part B).

The *Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Great Song* states: "It is like translating brocade or fine silk; although the front and back are different, the flowers [the patterns] are one and the same.
Thus, although the languages of India and this land differ, the intent of the Buddha remains without distinction. Translation means to change; it is a process of transformation.

"Brahman" (梵) refers to making [foreign] speech conform to the language of China (華語). Furthermore, "translation" (譯) denotes the act of transmitting words. The *Liji* (Book of Rites), in the section on the "Regulations for Kings" (*Wangzhi*), states: "The people of the five regions have unintelligible languages and differing desires; one must convey their intentions and facilitate their needs. Those from the east are called *ji*; those from the south are called *xiang*; those from the west are called *didi*; and those from the north are called *yi*. To trace the origin of this: [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The following is a continuation of the thought based on the context of the cited passage. ...it was originally intended that these officials should interpret the speech of the various peoples so as to ensure mutual understanding and the fulfillment of their needs. It was through such interpretation that the diverse voices of the world were brought into harmony with the central culture. Thus, the term "translation" (*yi*) carries with it the profound significance of bridging linguistic and cultural divides to achieve universal communication. Regarding the term "Brahman" (*fan*): while it is a transliteration of the Sanskrit *brahman*, in this context it serves to denote the sacred language of India, which was used to transmit the Buddha's teachings. By employing this term, the translators sought to preserve the authenticity of the original terminology while simultaneously adapting it to the phonetic and semantic conventions of the Chinese language. This dual function—faithfulness to the source and intelligibility for the recipient—is the very essence of the art of translation.

Thus, when we speak of translating the "Brahman" [teachings], we are engaging in a process that requires both scholarly precision and cultural sensitivity, ensuring that the profound meaning of the original is conveyed clearly and accurately to the Chinese-speaking world. This is why the work of the translators is described as "transmitting the words" (*chuanyan*); they serve as the vital link between the wisdom of the distant lands and the civilization of the Middle Kingdom.
The Buddha-dharma came from the West; its proper term is *dikṣi*, yet it is called "translation" (*yi*).

This is because during the Han dynasty, affairs were many and the translators from the north were also proficient in Western languages, hence the term "translation" was used. Subsequent generations have all followed this precedent.

Regarding the "preparatory practices (*pūrvayoga*) prior to the Lotus Sutra," Nanyue said: "The samādhi you have entered is the preparatory practice for the Lotus Samādhi;

The *nirveśa-samādhi* is the dharani of concentration; this is the dharani of wisdom.
Since there are three kinds of wisdom, how could the concentration of samādhi not also be threefold? It is simply that they are omitted and not enumerated in the sutra.
Since the *āvartana-dhāraṇī* is called the first and foremost samādhi, is it not the preceding one? The Dharma-sound of the Middle Way is named...

These are the actualities; the preceding hundred thousand [names] are collectively termed "expedient means" (*upāya*), for by means of these two expedients one enters the Middle Way, and thus they are called the "expedient means of the Dharma-sound.
Since the former is named the "ear-rotation," it logically follows that the latter should be named the "principle-rotation.

Furthermore, since concentration and wisdom (*samādhi-prajñā*) are simply stillness and contemplation (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*), and since there are three types of wisdom-contemplation, how could there not be three types of concentration-stillness?
Therefore, within the context of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, three names for *śamatha* are established by reflecting upon the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*).

Furthermore, since the names and meanings of these three *śamathas* and three contemplations accord perfectly with those of the three *dhāraṇīs*, one can truly trust that the concentration of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi* does not transcend the meaning of the three *śamathas*.

To the north of the temple where the Great Master Tangxi resided was a separate peak called Huading; from its heights, one could not see the surrounding mountains, and its climate remained forever distinct from other places.
It was here that the Great Master subdued the heavenly demons and māras. This was located to the southwest of Mount Tiantai.
A peak on one corner is named Fulong (Buddha’s Mound); those who travel upon this mountain frequently see Buddha images, hence its name.

The eloquence of joyful exposition (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*) is as explained in the first commentary on *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*:

Unimpeded eloquence of joyful exposition (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*). A Bodhisattva is able to expound all syllables within a single syllable, and expound all speech within a single utterance.

thus, once the temple was completed, the country became pure, which is the origin of the name Guoqing Temple (National Purity Temple). This is the account of its establishment.

In the *Mohe Zhiguan*, ten major chapters are listed: first, the general meaning; second, the explanation of names; third, the essential nature and characteristics; fourth, the inclusion [of all dharmas].

Regarding the Dharma, there are ten points: first, the partial; second, the complete; third, the six expedient means; fourth, correct cultivation; fifth, the retribution of the fruit; sixth, the arising of the teaching; seventh, the pointing to the ultimate goal;

eighth, [the stages]; ninth, [the practice]; and tenth, [the realization]. Within "correct cultivation" (*samyak-bhāvanā*), there are ten kinds of objects, namely the aggregates (*skandha*), sense bases (*āyatana*), and so forth.

As soon as these objects are perceived, the wheel of the Dharma ceases its turning, and the latter portion is not proclaimed. This is truly because it is the end of the summer retreat, which is why the chanting is suspended. The Chan school follows immediately after this.

"I shall now go myself to test him. He then transformed his body into the form of a rākṣasa and proclaimed what had been spoken by the Buddhas of the past.
Regarding this half-verse, "All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; they are the nature of arising and ceasing," at that time, having heard this half-verse, my heart was filled with joy.
Looking in the four directions, I saw only the rākṣasa, and I spoke these words: "Excellent, Great Being!
From where did you obtain such a half-jewel of wish-fulfillment? At that time, the rākṣasa said: "You now do not..."
I should have asked him about this matter: "It has already been many days since I last ate. I then said to him, "Excellent, Great Being!
If you can proclaim for me even half of such a verse as this, I shall become your disciple for as long as I live.
The rākṣasa replied, "I am currently suffering from hunger; how indeed could I [speak]? I then asked him:
"What do you eat? The rākṣasa replied, "That which I eat is nothing but human flesh and blood.
I then said to him, "Simply speak it, and I shall offer my own body as a gift to the Great Being. Thereupon, the rākṣasa recited half a verse:
"When birth and death have ceased, the cessation of extinction is bliss. At that time, having heard this verse, I...
Whenever he saw a rock, a wall, a tree, or a path, he would write this verse upon it;
immediately thereafter, he would climb to the top of a tall tree and cast himself down. Before he had even reached the ground, the rākṣasa would assume the form of Śakra and catch him.
The five bhikṣus were:
first, Cunda; second, Kāśyapa; third, Aśvajit; fourth, Bhadrika; and fifth, Kauṇḍinya.
Nineteen years after leaving the city.
The *Wenju ji* (Record of Explanations of the Text) states: "If he left home at nineteen, he attained enlightenment at twenty-four;
if he attained enlightenment at thirty, he left home at twenty-five. These differing views need not be reconciled. The *Tazong zhangji* (Record of Chapters on Other Schools) states:
"The *Dvādaśavyākaraṇa*, the *Ekottarika-āgama*, and the *Dīrgha-āgama* all state that he left home at twenty-nine and attained enlightenment at thirty-five."

the *Benqi yinguo jing* says nineteen years; the *Sishou wuxiang sanmei jing* says thirty years until his attainment of enlightenment;
and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* records that when the Buddha was approaching his parinirvāṇa, he told Subhadra: "I left home at nineteen to seek Buddhahood."
Since leaving home to enter the religious life, more than fifty years have passed, yet the time of his attainment of the Way has not been stated.
Some interpretations say that after leaving home at nineteen, he served the sages for five years, practiced the "joyful conduct" for six years, and attained the Way at thirty.
Bodhiruci, however, says that eight years were spent as an infant and seven years as a youth.
He studied the five sciences for four years, indulged in the five desires for ten years, and practiced austerities for six years.

A note on the *Sutra in Forty-two Sections* states: "At nineteen he left the city; five years were spent traveling, and six years were spent in ascetic practice. The *Tongyuan ji* (Record of the Source) says:
"According to the *Lalitavistara Sūtra*, he left home at nineteen and attained enlightenment at thirty; therefore, these [periods] total eleven years, both before and after [the renunciation]."
Regarding the remainder of this section: the differences between the sutras and śāstras are due to variations in the capacities and perspectives of the audiences.
As for the interpretations of various masters, please determine their errors by relying on the *Wenjuji* (Record of Textual Phrases).
The *Miaoxuan* (Profound Meaning) states: "nayuta."

It is also called *nayuta* and *ayuta*; this is translated as "ten billion. Among the fifty-two numerical units, this corresponds to the tenth number. The *Shiqian* (Exegesis on the Profound Meaning) states:
"As detailed below in the section on the functions of the fundamental and trace [teachings], each possesses ten meanings."
The ten meanings within the traces (*vyañjana*) are: (1) destroying three to reveal one; (2) abolishing three to reveal one;
(3) opening up three to reveal one; (4) harmonizing three to reveal one; (5) abiding in one to reveal one; (6) abiding in three to reveal one;
(7) abiding in that which is neither three nor one to reveal one; (8) concealing three to reveal one; (9) abiding in the function of three to reveal one; (10) abiding in one.

Based on the ten meanings within the three versions: first, destroying the traces to reveal the fundamental; second, abolishing the traces to reveal the fundamental; third, opening the traces to reveal the fundamental;
fourth, harmonizing the traces to reveal the fundamental; fifth, abiding in the fundamental to reveal the fundamental; sixth, abiding in the traces to reveal the fundamental;

seventh, abiding in that which is neither trace nor fundamental to reveal the fundamental; eighth, concealing the traces to reveal the fundamental; ninth, abiding in the traces while employing the fundamental; tenth, abiding in the fundamental.

Regarding the application of these traces, it is fully detailed in the commentary (*śāstra*). As for the three faculties (*indriya*) transforming into one another and receiving the designations of "sharp" or "dull," this is fully explained in the tenth section of the fourth fascicle of the commentary.

Regarding the mutual transformation of the three faculties: transforming the lower and middle [faculties] into the superior, one attains awakening during the section on the "Exposition of the Dharma" (dharmadeśanā);

transforming the lower into the middle, one attains awakening during the section on the "Exposition by Analogy" (avadānadeśanā). Those with inferior faculties do not transform; they only reach full understanding after all three cycles.

The tenfold explanation consists of: first, that which is common and that which is specific; second, that which includes śrāvakas and that which excludes them; third, the thickness or thinness of delusions; and fourth, the faculties.
1. Transformation versus non-transformation; 2. The five faculties having realization versus non-realization; 3. The six [faculties] having comprehension versus non-comprehension;

The eight phases are: first, birth in Tuṣita Heaven; second, entering the womb; third, dwelling in the womb; fourth, emerging from the womb; fifth, leaving home; sixth, [attaining enlightenment]; seventh, [turning the wheel of Dharma]; eighth, [entering parinirvāṇa].

[The distance is] five hundred yojanas.
*Yojana*, *yojana*, *yu-zhun*, or *yushanjna*—this is translated as "conjunction" (*he*) or "appropriateness" (*ying*).

It refers to a measurement calculated as being appropriate for such a distance. Since ancient times, it has been the distance traveled by a sage-king (*cakravartin*) in one day, equivalent to a postal relay station (*yi*) in this region.
Depending on whether one follows the Mahāyāna or Hīnayāna, it is either sixteen *li* or forty *li*.

This is because what is taught therein differs [from other contexts]. Regarding the statement "five hundred," there are three meanings: first, in terms of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), the three realms constitute three hundred;
the land of skillful means (*upāya-bhūmi*) constitutes four hundred; and the land of true retribution (*vipāka-bhūmi*) constitutes five hundred.

Second, in terms of delusions, the delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) constitute one hundred; the upper division of the five [categories of] afflictions constitutes two hundred and five; and the lower division constitutes three hundred.

The "dust-sands" constitute four hundred; ignorance constitutes five hundred. Thirdly, regarding the three contemplations: the contemplation of emptiness knows three hundred; the contemplation of the provisional knows four hundred;

and the contemplation of the middle knows five hundred. The *Miaoxuan* (Exquisite Profundity) refers to this as the "Jewel Place" (*ratnasthāna*), while the *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary on the Profound Meaning) refers to it as the "Jewel Island" (*ratnadvīpa*).

The name "Jewel Place" (ratnasthāna) derives from the designation "Jewel Island" (ratnadvīpa) found in the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*; as it is fully described in that Great Scripture, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* states:

"Having traveled five hundred yojanas, one arrives at the place of precious jewels. Since the true reality (*dharmatā*) is worthy of veneration, it is metaphorically termed a "jewel," and this jewel is located beyond five hundred yojanas. As the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "It is like a merchant..."

When a person desires to reach an island of treasures but does not know the way, if someone shows it to them, they will immediately arrive at the treasure island and obtain all manner of precious things.
The Great Parinirvāṇa is metaphorically likened to such a treasure. The *Erya* states: "A place in the water where one may dwell is called a *zhou* (island);
a small island is called a *zhu*; now, that which is at the edge of the land and the limit of the water is named a *zhu*. Thus, it is a treasure-place and a treasure itself.
Although the names "Island" (*dvīpa*) and "Treasure Island" (*ratnadvīpa*) differ slightly, their essential meaning is no different; therefore, various texts cite one another.

It is known through personal realization because it arises in dependence upon that [path]. Within this, the wise perceive the meaning of the true reality (*satyārtha*).
Thus it is said: "This wisdom does not abide in either nirvāṇa or the world. Such contemplative practice is extremely subtle.

Because it relies upon a samādhi that is extremely subtle, pure, extremely subtle in its meritorious qualities, extremely subtle in its supremacy, and extremely subtle in its transcendence of the world—thus, the second [point] differs from the self-proclaimed venerables of the non-Buddhists; and the fourth differs from the followers of the two vehicles.
Furthermore, what are the characteristics of this extremely subtle wisdom? A verse says: "Its own essence is originally empty."
There is that which is non-dual, inexhaustible, and far removed from all realms of existence, possessing a character identical to nirvāṇa;
it is neither beginning, middle, nor end, is not something expressed by words, and transcends the three periods of time. Its character is like space. As the Treatise says:
"The self-nature is originally empty because wisdom itself is empty; thus, that which is empty in its own nature should be understood as being like a rabbit's horn."
Is it not so that one cannot grasp [it] in such a way? Is there something other than this wisdom of emptiness, or is there something else that is empty? Is it not so?
Can it be grasped in such a way that there is a self-nature of "this" and "that," or that "this" and "that" undergo mutual extinction? Is it not so? How then can it be grasped?
This self-nature is empty, non-dual, and inexhaustible; it is in this way that it is grasped. This phrase reveals the departure from the three types of emptiness.
First, the inclusion of being free from slander; second, the inclusion of being free from difference; third, the inclusion of being free from exhaustion and cessation.

There are two verses on this: "Existence, non-duality, and non-exhaustion; certainty, non-duality, and non-exhaustion. Although these verses differ, they equally clarify that [the object] truly exists.
If it were not truly existent, one could not say it is "certain. Why is it certain? Because this certainty is able to extinguish all afflictions (*kleśa*).
Master Qingliang Guanding said: "The meaning is that because 'concentration' (samādhi) is itself existent, it is able to extinguish delusions.

Now, since the text of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* lacks the word 'existent,' how can this be reconciled? There are two points of view: first, it is not fully subsumed [by the term], meaning that because its essence is existent, it is not fully exhausted by the term;
second, the Indian manuscripts of the sūtra themselves exist in two versions, as the treatise states: 'there are two.'"

Regarding the verses cited here, although they do not appear in the current *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, their meaning is identical to the definitive version; that is to say, "definitive" refers to the non-duality of existence and non-existence.
Students of our school must understand that following the treatise, one should comprehend the intent behind Tiantai’s adaptation:
while the verse in the treatise contains only three lines and lacks the line on "non-differentiation," although the text is missing, its meaning is not.
What is deficient? Since there is already "non-duality," how could there not be "non-difference"? Thus, the four propositions are complete and the general principle is fully realized;
this is why Tiantai borrowed [the formula] and further added the term "non-difference. Furthermore, as the *Śāstra* states: "The two [dualities] are subsumed under difference;
since they are already separated from difference, it is clearly known that 'non-difference' [is established]. It is precisely for this reason that the term was added.
The "Dust-Clothed Body" within is in fact the Elder;
the *Xuanji* (Profound Commentary) states that opening the "dust-clothed body of sixteen feet" signifies the identity of provisional and real aspects (*tongti-quanshi*).

Regarding the "Jewel-Necklace Elder," the *Xuanji* clarifies the essence of the sutra; one should know that the "inner body" is thus the "inner essence. This inner essence is none other than the true reality (*shixiang*).

Since the Dharma-body is inherently internal, how could it not be external? Thus we know that the robes and necklaces represent the superior and inferior retributions, which are precisely the external functions.
Prior to the *Lotus Sūtra*, the three Buddhas were distinct and separated from the partial and limited teachings; therefore, their superior and inferior functions were termed "separate bodies.
Now, in the *Lotus Sūtra*, the sixteen-foot inferior response-body and its soiled robes are revealed to be the internal body.
Because this is the Dharma-body of true reality (*bhūtatathatā*), it is identical to the "excellent and extraordinary" (*prativiśiṣṭa*) necklaces and ornaments;

since their substance as the Dharma-body of true reality is the same, whether superior or inferior, the phenomena of the Dharma-body of true reality and those of the recompense and response bodies are spontaneously identical in their external manifestations.
If they were not thus identical, they would contradict the essence of the Dharma; therefore, the Dharma-body of true reality, being of one substance, constitutes the body of the sutra.

This is precisely the correct meaning of the *Xuánqiān* (Profound Commentary). Therefore, the tenth fascicle of the *Shìqiān* (Commentary on the Profound) clarifies that although the presiding masters of the two assemblies in the *Avataṃsaka* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* differ—being Vairocana and Śākyamuni respectively—their distinction lies merely in the slight difference of their robes and necklaces; their inner bodies are not distinct.

Is this not because the majestic and sublime response-body (*vairocanavigraha*) of Vairocana in the *Avataṃsaka* wears necklaces, while [the corresponding form] in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is Śākyamuni?

Although the two functions of the *kāya* of six *cubits* (the *hīna-nirmāṇa-kāya*) and the one clad in soiled robes (the *saṃbhoga-kāya*) differ slightly, there is fundamentally no distinction in their single *dharmakāya* body.
The *Wenju ji* states: "If one grasps the true meaning, one will know that the bodies of the four Buddhas are identical while their functions differ.

Those who lecture on the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* speak only of 'my Buddha'; how could they know the differences between the past and present, or that although the robes and necklaces differ, what is within is the same?"

Since the physical body, its substance, and so forth are without distinction, how much more so for the phrases [of scripture]? It is said that while the conditions and suitability differ, they are briefly categorized as ten types of differences.
Since the *dharmadhātu* and the wisdom of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) are without distinction and constitute a single essence, yet possess two functions, what hindrance is there?

In the *Avataṃsaka*, the Honored One with the Distinctive Mark (the *vairocana-kāya*), and in the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda*, the [body] adorned with necklaces; in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the six-foot inferior response-body wearing soiled robes—their substance is the *dharmakāya*, and there is no difference.
Although these distinctions are merely the mutual functioning of characteristics, they establish a hierarchy of differences; how could they possibly be conflated?

Were it not so, since the *Xuánqiān* (Profound Commentary) already states that the "defiled robe" is the inner body which is itself the "necklace," why would the *Wénjù* (Textual Passages) and its *Jì* (Record/Commentary) then say that the Master and Disciple of the *Fǎhuá* [Sūtra] concealed the practice of patience (*kṣānti*) and manifested the provisional body of coarse and inferior clothing?

All these base and perverse people claim that [the *Jūryō-hon*] was not written by my ancestor, while those who claim it was written by [Hui-]k'ai argue that the *Kai* and the *Chō* differ, thus forming a grave and heterodox slander.

Alas! Those of the past did not understand the reason for the various texts concerning the *jūryō* (life-span), and they vainly engaged in refutation and establishment, misleading immeasurable people and turning them into enemies because of the Dharma.
It is feared that the merit of transmitting the Dharma and benefiting others will not compensate for this.

One should know that the fault of using unrighteousness to disparage others is addressed by the *Xuánqiān* (Profound Commentary), which explains that the "body within the soiled garment" is identical to the "necklace-wearing elder.

This discussion of the identity of essence and form serves to clarify the meaning of the sūtra’s essence. If one were not internally embodied in this oneness, how could one externally employ the identity of essence and form?
Although essence is form and form is essence, their mutual manifestation is self-evident; it is not merely a matter of being internally embodied.

though the inferior response-body is manifest, its essence within the soiled garment is eternally that of the jeweled necklace—its substance is identical while its functions differ. These words have a basis in reality.

It clarifies that in the two assemblies of the *Avataṃsaka*, the two periods of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*, and the four instances of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the Buddha manifested supreme bodily radiance and immeasurable verbal teachings of the true reality (*dharmatā*). Quoting the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* as proof, it says: "I adorn myself with marks."

The radiance of his body illuminates the world as he expounds the Seal of the True Mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇamudrā*). he gathers the superior back into the inferior, and the humble and small appear perfectly as they were. Thus, the *Miaoxuanming* (Sublime and Profound Elucidation) states:

"Śākyamuni dwells in a birth-body (*janmakāya*) to manifest the One—how could this be a birth-body of a different substance belonging to the *xiang* (Shared) or *tong* (Distinct) vehicles? This is indeed so.

The *Wenju* (Textual Explanations) clarifies that the Dharma Flower Sūtra conceals the supreme response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) and manifests the real body (*dharmakāya*), while bestowing the inferior response-body as a provisional manifestation;

furthermore, the *Jingming shu* (Vimalakīrti Commentary) states that from Śākyamuni’s inferior manifestation, the venerable and supreme [body] appears, possessing boundless radiance—this refers to the function of the superior and inferior.
If one cites the function to clarify the essence, one must point to the *Xuanshan* (Profound Notes), which states that within the soiled raiment, the inner body is identical in nature.
That is to say, if the superior and the inferior were not of the same substance, how could the superior be concealed and the inferior manifested?
How could the *zhàng-lù* (six-foot) form be perfectly manifest from the inferior state to manifest the superior and serve as a representation?

Therefore, in this passage of the *Xuánqǐn*, as well as in the *Jìngmíng shū* and the *Wénjù jì*, one must distinguish between essence (*tǐ*) and function (*yòng*); they must not be confused or conflated. Furthermore, it must be understood that the *Xuánqǐn* clarifies the opening [of the teaching].
The body within the soiled garment is itself the necklace-garment; while the necklace and the garment differ slightly, the body within them is not distinct.
This clarifies that although the *Avataṃsaka* and *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* differ in their superior or inferior applications, they are identical in their single substantial reality.

If the text says, "the garments and necklaces differ while the person is one, distinguished only by what is hidden or manifest," how could this concern a difference in substance? This is precisely to clarify the [identity of] the *Avataṃsaka*.

If the "adornment" (of the Deer Park) and the "superiority-inferiority" function differ while the single substantial entity remains the same, then even though the temporal periods of the present and the past are distinct, since the functions differ while the entity remains the same, what further distinction could there be?
Thus, the *Xuánqiān* clarifies that within the opening of the defiled garment, the internal body is precisely the case where "the function differs while the entity remains the same";
this is the trans-temporal opening of the provisional (*kua-jie kai-quan*). This specific textual passage, however, clarifies the *Huáyán*.
At the Deer Park, the robes and necklaces were hidden or manifest; that people are one body and identical is precisely what clarifies the Buddha’s intention.

If it were not the Buddha’s intention, then even with the arising of responsive capacity (*nenggen*), there would still be a separation; how could one know that people are one body and identical regardless of whether [the truth] is hidden or manifest?

Therefore, the Buddha’s intention transcends the stages and opens up the provisional means (*upāya*); although the present and the past are divided, their essence is identical while their functions differ. Because they are non-dual and without distinction, one attains the profound mystery (*xuan*).

That is to say: (1) sitting is itself walking, standing, and so forth; (2) being here is itself being there; (3) the seventh [gate] is the gate of mutual dependence through dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*);

(6) the tenth is the gate of accomplishing the great assembly of the *dharmadhātu*. I maintain that within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), even "one" is not obtainable—how then could there be the confusion of ten meanings?
How manifold are the conventional truths (*saṃvṛti-satya*) according to conditions; their principles and meanings are immeasurable—how could they be fixed by ten meanings alone?
Therefore, one must employ the principle of non-arising (*anutpāda*) to sweep away all conceptualizations before one can discern the great function of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
It is from this that our school’s profound intent regarding affirmation and negation arises. If it were otherwise, attachments and calculations would be difficult to abandon.

In the *Jīngāngbēi*, this view is correctly refuted; even when verified by present-day standards, the same remains true. Furthermore, the *Huá...* [text fragment].

The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "For example, just as True Suchness (*tathatā*) cannot be corrupted or disturbed by even the slightest dharma such that it would not be awakening, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness for awakening;

it causes all dharmas to be universally awakened, its mind being immeasurable and pervading the entire Dharma-realm. Master Qingliang’s commentary (*śāstra*) states: "As for 'pervasive,' it is not..."

Sentient beings possess only a partial degree of awakening; how much less so for that which is not sentient? Furthermore, the Sūtra states that "Buddha-nature excludes tiles and stones," and the Treatise states that when it exists within the category of non-sentient things, it is called "Dharmatā," whereas when it exists within the category of sentient beings, it is called "Buddha-nature.

It is therefore clearly evident that non-sentient things do not possess the nature of awakening. Thus, one should explain that while the nature follows conditions, [in the case of] sentient beings, it is not [merely] non-sentient.

Sentient and insentient beings differ in their conditions, and thus their natures are also distinct—just as in the case of *nirvāṇa* and so forth. When one eliminates conditions to follow the nature, it is neither awakening nor non-awakening;
fundamentally, it transcends the hundred negations and words fail at the four propositions. If these two natures are mutually fused, there is nothing that is not awakening.
The *Yanyi chao* states: "This passage of the commentary is intended to refute the false attachment that all insentient things possess Buddha-nature."

Regarding the interpretation of this meaning, there are naturally varying depths. First, it is said that spirit transforms into plants and trees, and that emotion changes into non-emotion, and so forth.

Second, it is said that the insentient share a single nature. This latter explanation is excessive in its error; it destroys the distinction between the characteristics of the sentient and the insentient.
If one were to encompass both mind and objects within the ultimate emptiness of Nirvāṇa, then what would Nirvāṇa itself be?

If you say that "insentient" (wuqing) refers to the removal of rubble and debris, I would say that the meaning of the sutra text is simply to discuss *tathatā* (true suchness), which is nothing other than awakening.
How could there be even the slightest dharma that could destroy it and cause this *tathatā* not to be awakening?

The intent of the sutra is clear; yet, in the *Qingliang Shuji*, it is treated as if *tathatā* pervades non-sentient things, thereby implying that there is a slight portion [of it] that is not awakening.

If one is not an awakened commentator, how could such a view be correct? Moreover, the claim that *nirvāṇa* and clods of earth lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is merely a provisional teaching concerning the non-universality of the conditions and causes for enlightenment.
As for the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, its text states that the *tathatā* within insentient things is fundamentally non-existent;

how then can it be cited as evidence? Therefore, one should know that the passage in the commentary beginning from "following the universality of *tathatā* in insentient things" and below is likely incomplete.
If one accepts that the two natures are mutually fused as described below, this meaning contradicts what was stated previously;
