Furthermore, Siming stated that the physical marks and signs (lakṣaṇa-vyañjana) filling the dust-motes are the thousands of myriads of koṭis of Śākyamunis, and he further maintained that the Buddha-body of the *Avataṃsaka*—when discussed in detail regarding the eight phases of manifestation—is called the "Exalted Body" (zunte).
This is truly because he did not read the two versions of the *Fanwang jiejing shu* (Commentary on the Brahmajāla Sūtra Precepts).

Consequently, the traces [of later commentators] have erroneously judged that the Vairocana with the *zhunti* (extraordinary) mark possesses an immeasurable and eternal lifespan, while Śākyamuni is a lesser, impermanent response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*).

Since these two functions have thus become confused and indistinguishable, if one were to take Śākyamuni as Vairocana and Vairocana as Vairocana of the *Vairocanābhisambodhi*, would this not be a matter of rectifying names? One must reflect upon this; it is essential to understand the *Avataṃsaka*.

The marks and signs that adorn the body like a treasury of dust are the manifestation of the *Sāmbhogakāya* (Śānta), the *Nirmāṇakāya* (Buddha-dharma), and the exalted, special, and eternal *Mahāpuruṣa* with immeasurable lifespan;

these are definitively without before or after, and are spoken of as the state of the "Successor to the Throne. As for the *Nirmāṇakāya* Śākyamuni within the realm—sixteen feet in height, subject to measure and impermanence, who practiced under the Bodhi tree for seven years, left home at thirty, and attained enlightenment—it is only in reference to this that one discusses "the former" [stages].
The doctrine of the "Successor" (Avalokiteśvara) is therefore ascended to the palaces of the various heavens, where it is said that a former Buddha once came to this place;
for this reason, it is the most auspicious. All such statements are made in reference to the six-foot *saṃbhoga-kāya* within the realm [of the Sahā world].

Zhiyi of Siming did not understand that the *nirmāṇa-kāya* and *saṃbhoga-kāya* are distinct, and because he confused the arising of dharmas, he indiscriminately took the Lotus [to refer to the *saṃbhoga-kāya*].

That a lotus pedestal equipped with a treasury of marks and signs as numerous as motes of dust was established for the sake of a thousand billion Śākyamunis as a matter of succession to the position of a future Buddha—this has been widely circulated throughout the world;
yet to insist on correcting it [as false] is surely not a case of extreme obscuration by Māra?

Reclining on his side with back pain, as recorded in the eighth fascicle of the *Zhiguan* (Mo-ho chih-kuan), the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, "Chapter on Manifesting Illness," states: Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying, "The Buddha has already transcended all illness;
for what reason do you now say that you have an illness? Why do you lie in silence without preaching the Mahāyāna sūtras, nor treating [your ailment]?"
"How do various wicked bhikṣus lie silently on their right sides? Thus began the *Caryā-pravartana-sūtra*. The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"In the past, there were two wrestlers—one of the Kṣatriya caste and the other of the Brāhmaṇa caste—who were competing in a wrestling match.

At that time, the one of the Kṣatriya caste seized his opponent’s waist with his left hand and pressed down on his head with his right hand, breaking the spine by crushing it; he was thrown to the ground and died immediately."
The Kṣatriya caste was my own body, while the Brāhmaṇa caste was Devadatta;
for this reason, although I have now attained Buddhahood, I still suffer from back pain. This refers to manifesting physical traces to transform others through illness.
To write "yi" (倚) here instead of "bing" (病) is an error.

Regarding the practice of lying with the head toward the north and so forth, as recorded in the first commentary on the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* and the seventh commentary: as for "lying with the head toward the north," the *Ekottarika Āgama* states that this signifies the long endurance of the Buddha-dharma in Northern India.
Furthermore, according to the *Dīrgha Āgama*, the Buddha told Ānanda: "Place my head to the south and face toward the north."
To ensure that the Buddha-dharma remains long in the Northern Heaven, it is unnecessary to reconcile differences in perspective, as the capacities of those there differ.
In the city of Pāpā, at the Jeta Grove, there was an elder named Cunda;
Cunda is likely the same as *Cūḍa*, differing only in the Sanskrit pronunciation. As for "Pāpā" and "Jeta," their translations remain unknown.
Furthermore, the statement in the later text, "In the answer below, such as the analogy of the entrusted gold in the *Dīrghāyuṣka-parivarta*," is an error.
This is not the text of the Buddha’s response; rather, it is the speech of the bhikṣus addressed to the Buddha prior to Kāśyapa’s formulation of the thirty-six questions.
As for the Buddha’s response to Kāśyapa’s question regarding long life, it is as follows:

This is from the "Chapter on the Vajra Body. Furthermore, the *Miaoxuan* states: "Although that sutra mentions this in only one or two places, according to Zhiyi’s (Zhang’an) interpretation of the Buddha’s praise of Kāśyapa regarding the thirty-six questions, it says:

'When I first sat at the site of enlightenment, there were also bodhisattvas who came to ask about these meanings. This refers to the original, perfect initial sitting, not the site of enlightenment as a path of expedient means."
Furthermore, it cites the second fascicle, which says: "I have already attained Buddhahood for immeasurable kalpas;
this is also like the attainment of Buddhahood after a long duration as described in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Is this not a clarification within the Great Sūtra that the past is eternal?

Moreover, regarding the two or three instances in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* where the future is said to be eternal, these refer to the provisional reliance on permanence within the prose section of the "Life Span" chapter (*Nidāna-parivarta*).
Regarding the four characters for "non-extinction" (*amṛta*), since they do not perish, their influence extends further into the future;
this is precisely what is meant in the "Chapter on Future Buddhas" within the "Expedient Means" (*Upāya*) chapter: "The characteristics of the world are eternally abiding.

Furthermore, the passage below stating that "the mouth proclaims the Great Dharma of True Purity" appears in the "Tathāgata’s Supernatural Power" (*Tathāgata-ṛddhi*) chapter; it was merely chanted by the bodhisattvas who emerged from the earth, and is not [the Buddha's own teaching].
"Much Treasure, Much Treasure," it says; "it is thus, it is thus," he says, meaning that all that Śākyamuni has spoken is nothing but the truth.
Although the meaning of "truth" does not differ from the Great Dharma of True Purity, the phrasing must be distinguished;

therefore, we know that the citation in the *Xuánzhǎn* (Profound Commentary) contains an error. Furthermore, the *Shìqiǎn* (Commentary on the Profound Meaning), in its explanation of the benefits of the circulation [of the sutra], states: "The Gate of Traces..."
The "hidden benefit" (mingli) refers only to bestowing predictions (jù) and does not speak of entering the stages (rùwèi); this is clearly shown in the "Chapter on the Distinction of Merit.
As for the claim that "the bodhisattvas of the Trace Gate (jìmén) receive further benefit upon reaching this point, as do those newly attained in the Root Gate (běnmén)," this is likely an error.
This is because the *Miaoxuan* explains it as the benefit of circulating [the teaching] to others, whereas the *Shiqian* interprets it as the self-benefit of the Correct Teaching (zhèngzōng).
Furthermore, this does not accord with the principle of attributing the merit of transformation to oneself; please reflect on this further.

Moreover, regarding the passage in the subsequent text which says, "As stated in the commentary [Sū]: 'May I quickly attain the state of a Tathāgata, like the Buddha, like the Tathāgata,'" there are three characters in error therein:
first, the character "sū" (疏) should be "guān" (觀); second, the character "sù" (速) should be "yì" (亦); third, [the character "rú" (如) should be "zhǐ" (止)].
The character "de" (得) should be read as "su" (速); please compare it with the following text and you will see its error for yourself.
The *Miaoxuan* states: "Abhibhūti is translated here as 'non-retrogression' (*avaivartika*).
Furthermore, the following text says: "'Floating raft' (*fu cha*): the character 'cha' is pronounced with the *chu* and *jia* initials; it is a raft floating upon the water."

Regarding the statement that "wood [was used] and bird tracks formed patterns to create writing," this refers to Cang Jie’s initial observation of bird tracks and his subsequent creation of characters.
Cang Jie was the Grand Historian during the era of Emperor Huangdi (the Yellow Emperor). Furthermore, it is held that written characters already existed during the time of Fuxi.

As for the spider’s web drawing out its silk and so forth, these are explained as they appear in the *Xuan Yi* (Profound Meaning) of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*. However, there is an explanation of the names [of these phenomena] therein.
The five [aspects]—the initial general and specific [titles], up to the title as the essence itself—are likewise present here.

Why? Because the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* possesses both the general and the specific. "Saddharma" and so forth in Sanskrit correspond to "Miaofa" (Wondrous Dharma) and so forth in Chinese; thus the translation is clear.
By using the metaphor of a lotus flower made of grass, the analogy for the Wondrous Dharma is made manifest. Within this, I shall further refute the views of Guangzhai and others.

Masters, do you not thereby refute the ancient analogy as being incomplete? Yet, when one correctly analyzes the ten mysteries of the fundamental and the trace, is it not the case that they likewise possess the completeness of both horizontal and vertical analogies?

Furthermore, when citing the scripture’s description of the udumbara flower as a rare and auspicious omen resembling a lotus, is this not merely an adherence to the literal text? If one were strictly adhering to the scriptural text, it would simply say "lotus."
It is stated that the names "Saddharmapuṇḍarīka" and "Ratnapuṇḍarīka," among others, are even more credible as designations because they are literal names;

furthermore, it is said that the lotus is not a mere metaphor but receives its name from its actual substance (*dharmatā*), and that even such statements as "all are established as phenomena based on principle" do not fail to refer to the actual substance.
Furthermore, a question is raised: is it certain that this is the *Dharmapuṇḍarīka* (Lotus of the Dharma), or is it certain that it is merely a grass?

Lianhua replies: "The *Dingyi fahua jing* (Sutra on the Meaning of the Lotus) surely serves as an illustration for the subsequent 'Examination' section following the 'Chapter on the Essential Substance.

Yet, while that text speaks of the coexistence of the two capacities—sharp and dull—this [text] speaks of being directed toward those of superior, middling, and inferior faculties; how have they ever differed?

Furthermore, while that text states that the name is established based on the Dharma and does not borrow worldly gold to serve as a metaphor for the Dharma and so forth, this [text] speaks of 'benefiting'..."
Is it not likewise the case that the faculties themselves are called "understanding the principle" (*dharmatā*) and do not depend on metaphors and the like?

However, the title of this work is "The Sublime Dharma" (*Saddharma*), which is the Lotus of the Dharma; this is a metaphor. Furthermore, this metaphor applies both to the essence itself and to the essence as a metaphor for the Dharma.
The principle of the Dharma governs phenomena such that they do not require metaphors to be modeled after the Dharma; this refers to those of sharp faculties and superior capacity.
If one takes the lotus flower to represent the tenfold "wondrous Dharma" of the original and the trace, this refers to those of dull faculties, the middle and lower capacities.

Now, in explaining the lotus, since there is both the "Dharma-lotus" and the "grass-lotus," that interpretation of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* also employs the Dharma itself as a metaphor to illustrate the Dharma; however, in that case, the "Dharma" simply refers back to the text of the sūtra itself.
The title "Dharmatā-śrotra" (The Ear of the Nature of Phenomena) indicates that there is no dharma that can be pointed out;
thus, the entire *dharmatā* constitutes the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*, which is the analogy for the Dharma itself. Now, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* establishes its principles through phenomena.
Therefore, just as the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama* uses the *dharmatā* as an analogy, the present lotus plant serves as a metaphor for the Wondrous Dharma; thus, the meaning may also be applied here.
Regarding these two approaches, both must be preserved; there are indeed precedents for treating what is near as distant.

Is it not the case that although the *Lotus Sūtra* and the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* admit of both interpretations, they constitute a single metaphor? Although it is a single matter, one must distinguish between the sharp and the dull:
taking the Dharma itself as the metaphor to approximate the Dharma. However, those [other texts] rely on the literal phrasing, taking the substance itself as "near. This is excellent.
Since that sutra does not employ the metaphor of light to illustrate the *dharmatā*, it is merely our own school’s inference based on its meaning.
Although this [sutra] is definitively the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the text here states it is "like the *udumbara* flower";
this is an analogy used to approximate the Dharma as something proximate. This is truly because the titles of these two differ in their singular or plural forms.

This is because of the differences between the near and the distant. Worldly people, failing to understand this, speak at length in vain. *Pārijāta* is translated here as "Garden-Born Tree" (*yuánshēng shù*);
it is also written with the characters for "round" (*yuán*) or "circular" (*yuán*). Thus, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states:

"The roots of the Circular-Born Tree (*yuánshēng shù*) are five *yojanas* deep and wide; its fragrance is exquisite and wonderful, and its branches extend horizontally to a height and breadth of one hundred *yojanas*."
Its fragrance also pervades one hundred *yojanas*. In reality, this refers to the *Pārijāta* tree;
some say it means "interspersed adornment," meaning that this tree is adorned all around with flowers of various colors; others say it means "perfectly wondrous adornment.

Regarding the "partial analogy" and the "complete analogy" as found in the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*, there are two passages in the sutra: the first is in the fifth [chapter], and the second is in the second.

Seventeenth, it is said that there are eight parables, with some minor parables existing outside of these eight; the eight parables are fully contained within the *Fire-House Parable*, as cited in the *Wenju Buzhu* (Supplementary Notes on the Words and Phrases).
The *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary) states: "Fuxi created the Eight Trigrams."
"Fu" (伏) means that he subdued all things through his sagely virtue. "Xi" (犧) refers to teaching people to take sacrificial victims;
it is also called "Baohu Xi" (包犧), meaning he took the victims and wrapped them [in grass]; it is further called "Pao Xi" (庖犧), meaning he took those sacrificial victims to provide for the kitchen.
The Eight Trigrams are Qian, Kun, Zhen, Xun, Gen, Kan, Li, and Dui. As stated in the Preface to the Book of Documents:
In ancient times, when Fuxi reigned over the world, he first drew the eight trigrams and created writing and seals to replace the administration of knotted cords;
from this, written records came into being.
Shennong cultivated the five grains;
his mother was named Nü Deng. A divine dragon with a human head and a serpent’s tail (or a dragon-headed serpent) moved her heart, and she gave birth to Yan Di, who had a human body and an ox’s head.
Ban Gu stated that because he taught people farming, he was called Shennong. As for the "five grains," they are the fruits of the grain plants.
The five kinds that form the grain are called *gǔ*, *qǐ*, *jì*, *mài*, and *dào*; hemp is the fifth.
Regarding the creation of boats, the *Shìběn* states that Gònggǔ and Huòdí created them; both were ministers of the Yellow Emperor. Mòzǐ says: [text continues].
Gong Chui made boats; the *Lüshi Chunqiu* states that Yu Xu made boats. Weifa created mortars and pestles, as recorded in the *Shiben*;
Zhongshuo says Luo Fu created mortars and pestles.
The character for "Fu" (父) is pronounced like "Fu" (甫); thus, names such as Nifu (尼父) and Shangfu (尚父) are all [derived from this].
"Man" (*nanzi*) is an honorific designation for a male.
Regarding *Chiyou* (Cai You), Ying Shao states that he was an ancient Son of Heaven; Wang Zan states that the *Kongzi Sanzhao Ji* (The Record of Confucius on the Three Courts) speaks of Cai You.
Among the common people, there were those who were greedy; Chiyou incited rebellion and did not obey the Emperor’s commands.
Thereupon, the Yellow Emperor summoned his armies from the feudal lords and fought Chiyou at the wilds of Zhuolu, where he slew him.
The Yellow Emperor created the *guān* and *miǎn*.
The Yellow Emperor was the son of Shàodi; his surname was Gōngsūn and his name Xuányuán. *Guān* means "to thread through"; it is used to thread and contain the hair.
Regarding the Yellow Emperor’s crown, the *Huángguān* (Yellow Crown) and *Miǎn* (Tiara), the *Báihùtōng* states: "The word 'biàn' (tiara) signifies 'fénchí' (encircling and supporting)."
The *fayi* (hair-band) is made of dark-red deerskin; as stated in the *Fuzhi*, the "dark-red differentiator" (*juebian*) is also called *yuan*;
it is eight inches wide and two inches long.
Rongcheng created the calendar.
The *Shiben* states that Rongcheng created the calendar; the "Treatise on Pitch Pipes and Calendrical Calculations" (*Lüli zhi*) in the *Hanshu* states that the Yellow Emperor created the calendar;
and the *Shizi* states that Xihе created the calendar.
Qibo created medicine.
The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that Wu Peng was the first to practice medicine.
Li Shou created the art of calculation;

the *Rites of Zhou* lists nine types of calculation: *fangtian* (square fields), *sumi* (grain and millet), *chabian* (proportional division), *shaoguang* (square roots), *shangjue* (commercial interest), and *junshu* (equalization).
Regarding the calculation of deficits and surpluses and the auxiliary methods, the *Shiben* (Book of Origins) states that Lei Shou invented numbers.
Gao Yao established the legal system;
there is a chapter titled "Gao Yao's Counsel" (*Gao Yao Mo*) in the *Shangshu* (Book of Documents), and Gao Yao was a minister of Shun.
Xi Zhongzao’s *Cheyou Shiji* states:
"The Yellow Emperor fashioned the chariot; during the time of Shaohao, oxen were added; during the time of Yu, Xi Zhong added horses;
and the Duke of Zhou fashioned the south-pointing chariot."
Bo Yi invented the well;
the *Shuowen Jiezi* states that eight households constitute one well, and the character for "well" (井) must be written as such, for it was created by Bo Yi in ancient times.
Meng Tian invented the brush.
Meng Tian, the general of Qin, was originally from Qi. "Bi" (pen) refers to recording; it means recording events through speech.
According to the *Shangshu Zhonghou*, when the mystic tortoise emerged bearing the diagrams, the Duke of Zhou took up his pen and transcribed the patterns according to the seasons.
The *Qu Li* states: "The scribe carries the pen, and the scholar carries the tablets. This indicates that pens already existed prior to the Qin dynasty, likely among the various states.
Before its name was established, Qin alone obtained it; Tian merely made further adjustments to it. The *Shuowen* says:
"In Chu it is called *yù*, in Wu it is called *bùlǜ*, in Yan it is called *fú*, and in Qin it is called *bǐ* (pen)."
Cai Lun invented paper during the Later Han dynasty;
his courtesy name was Jingzhong. He used tree bark, rags, and fish nets to make paper, which he presented to the Emperor;
consequently, it became renowned throughout the world.
Although the person who first fashioned the net has not been seen, one may understand it by analogy.
The *Appended Statements* of the lower section of the *Book of Changes* (*Zhou Yi*) says: "In ancient times, when Bao Xi ruled over the world, he looked up and observed the patterns in the heavens;
he looked down and observed the laws on the earth; he observed the markings of birds and beasts and the suitability of the terrain."

He took from his own person and took from external things; it was then that he first created the Eight Trigrams to communicate the virtue of the spiritual intelligences and to categorize the conditions of the myriad things.
He made knotted cords to form nets and snares for hunting and fishing; this was likely derived from the hexagram Li. The commentary states: "Li means 'to cling.
In the use of nets and snares, one must carefully examine where things cling. Fish [cling to their environment].
"Adorning the water-beasts; adorning the mountain-beasts. The *Shiben* (Book of Origins) states that this was composed by Mang, a minister of Baoxi.

Furthermore, regarding the "lotus pods" mentioned below, the *Erya* says: "The *he*, *fuqu*, and *lianhua* are names for the lotus plant. Its stem is called *qia*; its leaf is called *xia*; its root is called *mi*;

its flower is called *han dan*; its seed-pod is called *lian*; its root is called *ou*; the core within it is called *zhi*; and the seeds within the core are called *yi*. The commentary notes: [text follows].
The "yi" (薏) refers to the bitter seeds within the lotus; "di" (的) refers to the seeds within the lotus; "lian" (蓮) refers to the pod;
the white rhizomes below the stem that grow in the mud have the alternative name *fúróng* (芙蓉); in Jiangdong they are called *hé* (荷). The character for "yi" (薏) is pronounced *yì* (憶);

"huá" (華) is pronounced *hù zhuǎo* (戶爪); "mì" (蔤) is pronounced *mì* (密); "xiá" (蕸) is pronounced *xiá* (遐); "qié" (茄) is pronounced *jiā* (加); "ruò" (蒻) is pronounced *ér zhuó* (而灼). This refers to the portion of the lotus stem that enters the mud.
"Coiled lotus in the heart" means that the *yì* (fruit) is coiled within. "Rounded and coiled" means being coiled like a lotus in the heart.

Regarding the phrase "outside the *guǒ* shell," it is likely an error; one should instead say "outside the *pí* shell. However, this character *guǒ* is polytonic, read as *kōng*, *gǔ*, *kǔ*, *jiǎo*, or *kǔ*, *hòu*, *sān*, *qiè*.
If it were made a level tone (*rùshēng*), it would result in a redundant repetition of two characters.
If it were read with the departing tone (qùshēng), it would not mean "a fledgling that must be fed," from which we know it should instead be read as "the shell" (*píkào*).
*Yǎn* (魚檢切) and *yóng* (魚容切) describe the appearance of fish opening and closing their mouths.
To explain the meaning of the Great Sūtra as recorded in the first commentary on the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*, the Sūtra says:
"For example, on the Snowy Mountains there is a medicinal herb of a single flavor situated beneath dense thickets; no one is able to see it.
In the past, there was a king who fashioned a wooden tube to receive this medicine; the medicine then flowed from the earth and collected in the wood."
After the king had passed away, that medicine subsequently became sour, salty, sweet, bitter, pungent, or bland;
yet the true flavor of the medicine remained on the mountain like the full moon.

Ordinary people of meager merit were unable to obtain it, but when another holy king appeared in the world, by virtue of his meritorious causes and conditions, he immediately obtained the true flavor of that medicine.
The *Zhengzhīwèijīng* (Sūtra on the Flavor of Rectification) provides a combined analogy, stating: "The secret treasury of the Tathāgata is likewise in its flavor;
though covered by the thickets of various afflictions (*kleśa*), sentient beings of ignorance are unable to perceive it. That 'one flavor' is analogous to the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*);
because of the afflictions, it manifests various flavors, namely from those in the hells up to the *piśācas*."
The Buddha-nature is heroic and fierce, difficult to obstruct or destroy. The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) states: "True flavor" refers to the ultimate principle (*li*).
Its presence "in the mountains" is a metaphor for the principle being present within the aggregates (*skandha*). This concerns the householder Ugra.
Ugra is translated here as "Majestic Power" (Weide).

When Brahmā first descended [to earth], it was as described in the *Shu* (Commentary) and the seventh fascicle of the *Zhiguan* (Mohe Zhiguan), where the general meaning has already been extensively cited and annotated; one can understand this by looking it up, so there is no need to say more.

In the *Gantong zhuan* (Biographies of Spiritual Resonance), it is recorded that because the practice of the Nanshan Vinaya was so pure and refined, it moved the various devas to discuss this matter together; the details are contained within that biography.
Furthermore, the phrase "first, the fundamental dharma" (*chū fǎběn*) in the following text is an error; it should read "first, the exegesis of the scattered [sections]" (*chū sànshì*). Again.
Second, regarding the "phrase-body" (*pada-kāya*) and "syllable-body" (*vyañjana-kāya*): when ancient translators rendered the scriptures into Chinese, they translated the text as "flavor" (*rasa*).
This "flavor" refers to the "syllable" (*vyañjana*), for just as flavor can manifest the saltiness or blandness of food, so too can the syllable manifest the name and phrase.

The *Bai fa shu* (Commentary on the Hundred Dharmas) states: "One name or many names are called the 'name-body' (*nāma-kāya*); one phrase or many phrases are called the 'phrase-body' (*pada-kāya*); one character or many characters [are called the 'syllable-body']."

This is called the "body of phonemes" (*vyañjana-kāya*). Regarding the term "body of phonemes," it serves as the basis for names and phrases to manifest what is signified. There are four meanings [of what is manifested]: first, fanning;

second, physical marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*); third, the faculties and form; and fourth, flavor (*rasa*). These respectively manifest wind, coolness, a great person, male and female, and taste.
Therefore, the body of phonemes is used as a metaphor for its ability to manifest principles. The ancients took "phonemes" (*vyañjana*) to mean "flavor" (*rasa*).
However, that which is manifested is not the manifester. The *Vibhāṣā* asks: "What is meant by 'many-word-group' (*nāmakāya*)?
It is answered: "Because it is a collection of many names. Is this not explaining 'group' (*kāya*) as a 'collection' (*caya*)?
*Vatsa* means "well-adorned"; *Maghavat* means "unconquered"; and *Indra* means "thousand-eyed radiance."
"At one time, knowing a thousand meanings and severing a thousand matters" refers to the "Vajra-body," which signifies a body of firm solidity.

Furthermore, regarding the statement that "the five aggregates (pañca-skandha) are also called 'inversion' (viparyāsa)," Zhan'an says: "The five aggregates are called inversion because they are with outflows (sāsrava);

they are called the Truth of Suffering (duḥkha-satya) because they are the objective realm of the Truth of Suffering; and they are called 'mindfulness' (smṛti) because they are what is observed by the foundations of mindfulness (smṛty-upasthāna)."

Excluding the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), the remaining four aggregates (*skandha*) constitute the four stations of consciousness (*vijñāna-sthiti*). These aggregates, encompassing both the internal and external, are called the four nutriments (*āhāra*);

this is omitted in the present text. That which enables passage [to liberation] is called the Path (*mārga*). Because the real dharmas (*dravyadharma*) of the aggregates exist, there are provisional names for time and sentient beings;

their essence is signless (*animitta*), and this is called the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). The three cultivations of body, mind, and wisdom constitute the conditioned liberation (*saṃskṛta-vimukti*). Ten.

The second [point] concerns the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) as the substance of the two causes and conditions; these five aggregates are capable of forming the bodies of the three vehicles (*tri-yāna*).

The remainder of the text is visible [in the source]. Regarding the four nutriments (*catvāra āhārāḥ*): edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*) refers to present-day meals, as they can be divided into portions;

contact-nutriment (*sparśa-āhāra*) refers to clothing, bedding, and the like derived from external conditions; thought-nutriment (*manaḥsañcetanā-āhāra*) refers to karmic nutriment; and consciousness-nutriment (*vijñāna-āhāra*) refers to the mind (*manas*). These names are expressive designations.
The phrases concerning intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) that express distinctions are as shown in the *Wenju Buzhu* (Supplementary Notes on the Text).

Furthermore, regarding the passage in the *Miaoxuan* (Profound Meaning) stating "arising from the tip of a hair" and so forth, the *Laozi*, in the "Dejing" (Chapter on Virtue), says: "A tree with a trunk large enough to embrace by both arms grows from the tip of a hair;
a nine-story terrace begins with a pile of earth; a journey of a thousand li starts from beneath one's feet. This is also as stated in the *Wenju*.
In the Supplementary Notes (*Bǔzhù*), the commentary on the *Shìqiàn* (Exegesis on the Profound Meaning) below states: "Why not rely exclusively on a single principle?

Regarding the character "why" (*hé*), I request that it be determined as "should" (*kě*) according to the original text. Furthermore, the phrase "first merely accumulate" (*xiān qiě jī*) in the text below is likely an error;

it should read "first correctly borrow" (*xiān zhèng jiè*). As for the twelve characters of the Sanskrit script, I once inquired with those of the Buddhist studies community in the capital regarding their calligraphy.
Although he transcribed those twelve characters, he was still not certain of their authenticity; therefore, they are not recorded here, but are left for later scholars to investigate.
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "that is, it possesses the ten wonders" (*ji jù shí miào*) found in the text below, the character *jí* (即) should be *sè* (色).
Also, regarding the phrase "because it universally encompasses, nothing is discarded," it should instead read "because it universally encompasses, what is there to discard? (*biàn shè gù hé suǒ*).

"Because there is nothing that is not included within what is abandoned, what is there that is not abandoned? Regarding the phrase "as stated in the citation," the character "yuè" (云) is likely superfluous.
Thus, Master Dao’an said: "There are five losses and three difficulties in translating scriptures. To translate from Sanskrit into the Qin language is like chewing food for someone else;
it causes the person to vomit."
Dharma Master Dao’an of the Fu Qin dynasty was a native of Fuliu in Changshan; his surname was Wei, and his family had been distinguished scholars for generations.

Master An often remarked that there are five losses and three difficulties in translating scriptures. First, changing the phonetic sounds—whether they differ in tone or even in the *qie* system—is one difficulty.

Second, the language of the Hu (Indians) is entirely inverted, yet it must be made to conform to the Qin (Chinese) style; this is the first loss regarding the original text. Second... [text continues].

First, the Hu scriptures value simplicity while the people of Qin prefer literary elegance; to transmit [the teachings] so as to accord with the minds of the masses, they must not lack literary refinement—this is the first loss of the original.

Second, the Hu scriptures are exhaustive in detail; when it comes to eulogies, exhortations, and repetitions, occurring three or four times, they do not disdain textual prolixity, yet now these have been excised—this is the third loss of the original. Fourth, the Hu [scriptures] possess... [text fragment].
In terms of meaning, the current discourse closely resembles the confused expressions of the original;
as for the phrasing, it differs from the preceding text, whether by a thousand or five hundred characters, yet these have been excised and not preserved—this is the fourth loss of the original.

Fifth, when a matter is composed of various elements and the discussion shifts to collateral points, the preceding words are reversed and restated only after the digression, and all of this is removed—this is the fifth loss of the original. However...
Thus, the intellect traverses the path of the threefold penetration, and what is set forth before one’s face must necessarily accord with the times;

for as the customs of the age change, the refined and ancient must be edited to suit the present—this is the first difficulty. The gap between the ignorant and the wise is as vast as heaven and earth, yet the Sage is difficult to approach;
how then can one wish to transmit the subtle words from a thousand years past so that they harmonize with the final ages of a hundred kings? This is the second difficulty.

This is the second of the two things that must not be altered: Ānanda compiled the scriptures not long after the Buddha’s passing, and Mahākāśyapa commanded five hundred arhats possessing the six supernatural powers to examine and record them one by another. Now, more than a thousand years have elapsed;

yet while those arhats who performed the compilation were as cautious and reverent as this, the ordinary people of these later ages are as complacent and indifferent as such. How could this not lead to error?
One who knows the Dharma finds these three difficulties formidable; traversing these five losses and three hardships, why should the translation not be treated with great care?
Master Kumārajīva said: "The customs of the country of India place great value on literary elegance.
To change the Sanskrit into the Chinese, though one may capture the general meaning, the literary style is utterly transformed—resembling nothing more than chewing food for another."
It is not merely that people lose their sense of taste; it even causes them to retch and belch. *Yuei* (嘔) is pronounced *wu* (烏) and *hou* (后); *yuei* (噦) is pronounced *yi* (乙) and *lüe* (劣).
A single speck of dust contains a thousand-world sūtra scroll, as recorded in the third fascicle of the *Zhiguan*;
this was previously pointed out, and here it is emphasized once more.
Regarding "absence of narrowness" and so forth, as recorded in the sixth fascicle of the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* commentary, the Sūtra states:
"Furthermore, liberation is without narrowness; it is like a narrow path that cannot even accommodate two people walking abreast.
Liberation is not otherwise. Such liberation is precisely the Tathāgata’s contemplation of the objects of the Tripiṭaka."
Because one cannot immediately take this matter to mean a narrow path, the Great Sūtra states: "Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are like a narrow path where two people cannot travel side by side.
Since form and emptiness are mutually identical, they are said to be "side by side"; because form is extinguished while emptiness remains, it is said they are not "side by side.
The emptiness that does not extinguish form is called a narrow path. According to the old text, this is in the [relevant] section.
In the fifth record, the *Miaoxuan* (The Profound Meaning) further states: "What does it mean to use the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*) to certify cause and effect?

This refers to how ancient masters interpreted the essence of the vehicle as pervading both cause and effect, citing the *Puxian guan jing* (Sutra on the Contemplation of Samantabhadra)—which states that cause and effect are the true reality—as their proof.
However, Zhanran (Zhang’an) criticized these ancients for improperly citing that passage concerning "cause and effect being the true reality" [as a general principle].

Regarding the statement that "the realization of the vehicle's essence (zhèngchéng tǐ) pervades both cause and effect," the *Shìqiǎn* (Sub-commentary on the Profound Meaning) explains this, but it is likely erroneous.
Furthermore, the subsequent passage stating "compassion is the carriage" (*xuān*) is an abbreviation; it should read "it is the canopy" (*xiàngài*).
Moreover, regarding the term "network-governance" (*wǎngjǐ*) in the following text, the *Báihùtōng* states: "Great... [The text here appears to be truncated].
The "great" refers to the main cords (*gang*), and the "small" refers to the subsidiary cords (*ji*). "Gang" means to stretch out; "ji" means to regulate.

These are the means by which the order between high and low is established and human relations are brought into harmony. "Zi" (子) means compassion (*ci*); "ci" should be written as *zi* (孳), which signifies diligence. "Zi" refers to the act of showing concern for those below.
The character *bu* (哺) simply denotes the hour of Shen (the third watch), whereas the character *pu* (餔) specifically denotes eating at that time.
"Qī Huán was upright and not deceitful.
In the *Lúnyǔ*, Chapter 14, "Xiàn Wèn," it says: "Jìn Wén Gōng was deceitful and not upright; Qī Huán Gōng was upright and not deceitful. The *Zhèngyì* states:
"This chapter discusses the affairs of the two Hegemons. 'Jué' (譎) means guile or deception. Jìn Wén..."
To summon the Son of Heaven and require the feudal lords to pay court to him is deceptive and improper.
When Duke Huan of Qi attacked Chu, he did so by first invading Cai and then proceeding to supplant Chu;

yet he used public righteousness to demand that the tribute of *baomao* grass not be withheld and to inquire why King Zhao had not returned from his southern expedition—this was upright and not deceptive.
The Duke of Zhou established the rites;

both the *Rituals of Zhou* (*Zhouli*) and the *Ceremonial Rites* (*Yili*) were composed by the Duke of Zhou. The *Classic of Ritual* (*Lijing*) comprises three hundred articles of ritual and three thousand points of decorum.
The *Commentary on the Rituals* (*Liji*) was originally compiled by the disciples of Confucius based on what they had heard. Later scholars each made their own deletions and additions, as did Zisi.
The *Zhongyong* was composed by Gongsun Nizi; the *Ziyi* was composed by the Han Wendi’s *boshi*; and the *Wangzhi* was composed by the *boshi*.
Although there were many ancient poems, Confucius selected from them; taking from the Shang and down to the Lu, he compiled a total of three hundred and eleven.
During the reign of the First Emperor of Qin, the books were burned and six of these [poems] were lost; what remains today consists of three hundred and five.
When Master Mao composed his commentary, it was called the *Mao Shi*.
As for the "Classics," they refer to the Five Classics, the Seven, and the Nine.
The *Baïhù tōng* states: "The *Yì*, *Shū*, *Shī*, *Lǐ*, and *Yuè* are called the Five Classics (*wǔjīng*).
In antiquity, the *Yì*, *Shū*, *Shī*, *Lǐ*, *Yuè*, and *Chūnqiū* constituted the Six Classics; however, when the books were burned during the Qin dynasty, the *Yuèjīng* was lost.
Thus, today the *Yì*, *Shū*, *Shī*, *Lǐ*, and *Chūnqiū* are regarded as the Five Classics. This is also noted by Prince Zhānghuái of the Táng dynasty in his commentary on the *Hòuhànshū*.

The Book of Documents, the Book of Rites, the Book of Music, the Book of Changes, the Book of Poetry, the Spring and Autumn Annals, and the Analects constitute the Seven Classics. When the *Liji* (Book of Rites) is divided into the *Zhouli* (Rites of Zhou),

the *Yili* (Ceremonial Rites), and the *Liji* (Record of Rites), and the *Chunqiu* (Spring and Autumn Annals) is combined with the *Zuo zhuan*, the *Gongyang zhuan*, and the *Guliang zhuan*, along with the *Yi*, *Shu*, and *Shi*, they are collectively termed the Nine Classics.
The *Sanfen* (Three Mounds) signifies "greatness. The preface to the *Shangshu* states: "The books of Fuxi, Shennong, and Huangdi are called the Three Mounds;
they speak of the Great Way."
The "Five Canons" (Wǔdiǎn) signify the constancy of the classics. The Preface to the *Shūjìng* states that the records of Shàohào, Zhuānxù, Gāoxīn, Táng, and Yú are called the Five Canons,
meaning they represent the constant Way.
Regarding the "writing on bamboo slips" and so forth of the ancients:

in antiquity, bamboo was treated with fire to remove its sap (the process known as *shāqīng*) to serve as slips, which were then bound together with leather thongs (*wéi*). These bound slips constituted a chapter, much like the way paper is joined today to form a scroll.
As the Preface to the *Zuǒzhuan* of the *Chūnqiū* states: "Matters of great importance were recorded on *cè* [strips of silk], while minor matters were recorded on slips and tablets."
The *Wenxuan* commentary states: "Large bamboo is called *ce*; small bamboo is called *jian*; wooden boards are called *du*.

Furthermore, it says that the *Liutao* (Six Tactics) is a chapter title from the *Zhou Shu* (Book of Zhou), or alternatively, it refers to secret prophecies. Because they consist of the Wen (Civil) and Wu (Military), the Hu (Tiger), Pi (Bear), Long (Dragon), and Quan (Dog), they are called 'six.
Regarding *Tianwen* (Celestial Patterns): Heaven possesses the sun, moon, and stars, thereby forming patterns. [The text continues with] Earth...

As for "principle" (*li*), it refers to the earth having rivers, plains, and marshes as its structural order. Regarding "East [is] *Zhen*," etc., these are fully explained in the "Explanation of the Trigrams" (*Shuogua*) chapter of the *Zhouyi*.
As for "one hexagram generating seven," this is like *Kan* and *Zhen* forming *Zhun*, or *Gen* and *Kan* forming *Meng*, and so forth.
*Kan* is water, *Liang* is mountain, and *Zhen* is thunder. As for the "eight pure" hexagrams, they are the *Qian* and [the others]; as for the names of the hexagrams, there are six.
The "Fourteen" refers to the names of the hexagrams, such as Qian (Heaven) and Kun (Earth).
"Hexagram Affiliations" (*xi*)—the character *xi* being pronounced *hu jì* (with the correct form being *xì*)—refers to the "Affiliations" (*Xici*) of the upper and lower sections of the *Yi*.

"Images" (*xiàng*) and "Judgments" (*tuàn*)—the character *tuàn* being pronounced *tù luàn* and meaning "to decide" or "to determine"—are present in all sixty-four hexagrams; they provide a comprehensive discussion of the structure of each hexagram to clarify its essential nature.
It is called the *tuan* (judgment) because it is the master of the hexagram; the *xiang* (images) refers to the subtle images and the modeled images, which express the underlying intention.
The *yan* (words) clarify these images; nothing is better than the images for exhausting the intention, and nothing is better than the words for exhausting the images.
The Five Elements are as recorded in the sixth fascicle of the *Zhiguan*:
the five are metal, wood, water, fire, and earth. "Element" (*xing*) refers to the movement of the celestial qi.

The earth receives from heaven just as a wife serves her husband or a minister serves his sovereign. This originated when the Yellow Emperor was moved by the constellation of the Woman of the Dark Void (*Xuan’v*).
To explain this in detail: Wood is minor Yang and presides over the East; Fire is Yang and honored, presiding over the South;
Metal is minor Yin and presides over the West; Water is Yin and humble, presiding over the North;
Earth is great and pervasive, presiding over the Center and reigning during the four seasons.
"Shè" (She) refers to Hòutǔ (Lord Earth), and "Jì" (Ji) refers to Hòují (Lord Millet). This is roughly as recorded in the sixth and tenth fascicles of the *Zhíguān* (Stopping and Contemplation).
The *Báihùtōng* (White Tiger General Discourse) asks: "Why does a king possess Shè and Jì? It is because he seeks blessings for the world and recompenses merit.
Man cannot stand without earth, nor can he eat without grain; yet the land is so vast that it is impossible to pay reverence to it all."

Therefore, earth was raised and altars were established for the She (Earth) to signify the veneration of those who possess land; because the various grains are too numerous to be sacrificed to individually, Millet (Ji) was enshrined and sacrificed to instead.
The *Zhouli* commentary states: "She and Ji are the spirits of Earth and Grain; those who possessed virtue are paired with them in the sacrificial feasts.

Furthermore, each is represented by the trees native to its territory: the Great She altar uses only pines, while the Eastern She altar uses only cypresses, and the Southern [altar] uses only... [cypress].

The eastern altar is made of catalpa wood; the western altar is made of chestnut wood; the northern altar is made of locust wood. This is recorded in the fourth section of the *Liji* (Book of Rites), in the "Institutes of the King" (*Wangzhi*), which states:

"Only after the otters present their offerings of fish do the marsh-keepers enter the wetlands with nets and beams; only after the jackals present their offerings of beasts does one engage in hunting.
When Jie of Xia was unrighteous, he cast his nets in all four directions; when Tang of Yin became a sage ruler, he removed the nets from three sides, as can be seen in the texts.
It is recorded that Zhang Ling was swallowed by a giant python and Xi Kang was slandered by Zhong Hui; thus, the accounts claiming they attained immortality are erroneous.
Li Ying’s *Shu Ji* states that Zhang Ling lived during the reign of Emperor Shun of the Later Han dynasty and traveled to study in Shu, whereupon he entered [Mount Chengdu].
Mount Huming is located within Yizhou, to the west of Jinyuan County. [Zhang Lu] styled himself the Heavenly Master;
he treated humans and spirits with contempt and was immediately retributed by his own body. At the end of the Jiaping era of the Han dynasty, he was swallowed by a giant python.

His son, Zhang Heng, fled out in haste, yet [Lu] remained unperturbed. Having incurred the censure of the "pure reputation" (qingyi), he then devised expedient means to manifest his spiritual transformations.
The traces of this were as follows: he bound the legs of a crane and placed it atop a stone cliff; once his plans were finalized, he set a date for its release.
In the first year of the Jian'an era, he dispatched an envoy to announce: "On the seventh day of the first month, the Celestial Master ascended to Mount Dongmin in the Eastern Capital.
The local tribes (lao) gathered like ants outside the pass, and the people of the Yuntai Commandery prostrated themselves twice, saying: 'We have humbly heard of the Sage...'"

"The Sovereign of the Mysterious Metropolis has departed; we, your subjects, bid him a long farewell from beneath his shade. As we dwell amidst the dust of the corpse, we shall enjoy the darkness of the Nine Netherworlds.
After a long time, he entered through the gate of night and emerged; yet he falsely claimed, 'I have returned my carriage to the Radiance of Dawn, and you each return to your respective domains.

Maintain a pure mind and uphold your practice; preserve the Master and keep the Way in mind. At this, Heng secretly withdrew from the entanglements of the world and soared directly into the void like a wild goose. The people [were amazed].
The Liao people were foolish and dull-witted, and all claimed he had ascended as an immortal. The *Wei Zhi* states that Zhang Lu, whose courtesy name was Gongqi, was the grandson of Zhang Ling.
Ling was a traveler in Shu who studied the Dao in Mount Guoming; he composed Daoist scriptures to delude the common people.

Those who received the Dao from Ling were required to provide five *dou* of rice, and thus he was popularly known as the "Rice Bandit. After Ling died, his son Heng inherited the teachings; after Heng died, it was passed on to Lu.

Furthermore, it was transmitted to Ling, who served as the Celestial Master; the biography of Liu Yan states that Ling was bitten by a python, and his disciples followed one after another in being devoured by snakes, yet they claimed he ascended to heaven in broad daylight—a matter clearly revealed in records as fraudulent, demonic, and delusional.
The *Book of Jin* states that Xi Kang, styled Shuye, was a native of Qiaoguo; from his youth he possessed rare talent and was widely learned.
According to the *Weizhi* (History of Wei), Zhong Hui, styled Shixiu, was a native of Changshe in Yingchuan and the youngest son of Zhong You.
He was precocious and attained maturity early; he served as a Librarian and was subsequently promoted to General of the West.
At that time, Zhong Hui harbored a grudge against Ji Kang. Meanwhile, Lü An’s elder brother, Lü Xun, had committed adultery with An’s wife; Lü Xun was... [text fragment ends]
The Chief Secretary of the Grand General then fabricated a false accusation to harm Ji An. Zhong Hui was favored by the Grand General;
consequently, he urged the Grand General to execute Kang Senghui on the same charges as Lü An. He further slandered him, saying, "Ji Kang is a 'sleeping dragon.
Subsequently, both Ji Kang and Lü An were executed in the Eastern Market. This account is found in the *Shenxian zhuan* (Biographies of Divine Transcendents).
To say that he attained the state of an immortal (*ṛṣi*) would not be an error.

Regarding the account of Dīrghanakha, as recorded in the fifth fascicle of the *Zhiguan* (Calming and Contemplation), the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "There was a brahmin named Dīrghanakha, also called Śreṇika, and also named Vatsa."

He was also named Satyaka and also named Māgandika. Because he claimed that all treatises could be refuted, all speech could be destroyed, and all attachments could be overturned, there was no true dharma in him worthy of trust or respect.
When the World-Honored One rebuked him for asserting that all treatises could be refuted, the Buddha challenged him with a single sentence: "Do you see this patience? Do you not reflect upon it?"
After a long while, he could not find a single dharma to enter his mind, and so he said: "The śramaṇa has placed me within the gate of two-fold defeat (*dvividha-parājayamukha*).
If I answer 'I endure,' this is a coarse gate of defeat that everyone knows; how can he say for himself that I do not endure, yet now claim that I do?
If I answer that I see my own lack of endurance, this is a subtle gate of defeat that no one would know."
He replied to the Buddha, "I do not even tolerate this view. The Buddha said, "If you do not tolerate this view, with what will you refute the views of others?
At that, Dīrghanakha attained the pure eye of Dharma; because he was so diligent in his studies that he had no leisure to trim his nails, they were long, hence he was called Dīrghanakha (Long-Nail).
This passage and the commentary are concise and difficult to discern; the text states: Dīrghanakha spoke to the Buddha, saying, "One..."
"All dharmas are 'not-enduring'; 'endurance' means 'peace. This means that regarding all dharmas, I am able to shatter them so that they are not at peace.
The Buddha asked, "Do you see this endurance? The remainder is as can be seen in the current text. Furthermore, the preceding text states: "The one who discusses power is a Brahmin.
The character *ruò* (若) is a gloss for *rǔ* (汝), or it may have been intended as the character *gè* (各).

Furthermore, the *Miaoxuan* (Profound Mystery) states: "That which is 'neither existence nor non-existence' as existence corresponds to the fourth phrase within the fourfold set of propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) in the *Zhi guan* (Stop and Contemplation);
it is simply the fourth phrase of the 'existence' category. That which is 'neither existence nor non-existence' as non-existence is simply the fourth phrase of the 'non-existence' category.
It further states: "Because these are immeasurable characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), they are called 'characteristics.'"
As for the entry [into the meaning], I fear it may be erroneous or abbreviated; please examine it further in detail.

Regarding the "one finger" and "two fingers," as recorded in the fifth commentary on the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*, the eighth fascicle of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* records Kāśyapa asking the Buddha: "How is it that the Buddha-nature is difficult to see and difficult to enter? The Buddha replied with a parable:
It is like a hundred blind men who, for the sake of treating their eyesight, go to a skilled physician.
At that time, the physician uses a golden probe to incise the film over their eyes and points with one finger, asking, "Do you see? They reply, "I do not see.

He asks with two fingers, and they likewise say they do not see. When he asks with three fingers, they reply, "I see a little. The sutra provides a metaphor for this, stating that [the vision] is non-existent.
Although a practitioner of the *liang* (measuring) Bodhisattva path may practice the six perfections and even reach the ten stages (*bhūmi*), they are still unable to see the Tathāgata;
only after the Tathāgata has preached does one then see him slightly. This is why, in the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*), those in the ten stages do not yet see [the Buddha].

Zhanran’s *Shu* (Commentary) states: "The three truths themselves serve as the three fingers. The first finger represents the Truth of Ultimate Reality (*paramārtha-satya*); because one does not yet see the nature [of reality], it is said 'no'."
Seeing two fingers is used as an analogy for the two truths—the ultimate and the conventional—because their true nature (dharmatā) is not seen; hence it is said that "one does not see.
Pointing with three fingers is used as an analogy for the one truth or the three truths, which is called "seeing the nature"; hence it is said that "even a slight seeing is perfect" (*daśabhūmi*).
This is stated in the *Jinbi* (The Golden Needle), following the teachings. Therefore, it is so said.

The texts concerning Zhang Yi and others appear in the "Biographies" (Liezhuan) of the *Shiji*; the claim that they appear in the "Hereditary Houses" (Jiaoshi) is an error. Guiguzi resided in Yangcheng, Yingchuan;
because he lived among the people there, he was called the "Master of Guigu. He was a master of the School of Vertical and Horizontal Alliances (Zonghengjia) during the era of the Six States.
Regarding the phrase "Qin bound him and admonished": this refers to admonishing his disciples not to act as intermediaries and ensuring he could not leave.
A few days later, he was seen sitting beneath the hall. As for "Huiwang" (慧王), "Hui" should be written as "Hui" (惠);

it refers to a *hu-xi* (檄)—a formal document or writ, a two-foot-long letter—used here to mean that he caused the messenger to become clearly enlightened (*jiao*). [The character] "Pei" (背) signifies the back.

As for Zōng (Zǐzōng), King Āi betrayed the treaty and, following the ritual protocols, requested peace from Qin. Zhāng Yí returned to serve as Chancellor of Qin; after three years, King Āi again turned his back on Qin.

The records concerning Fàn Lĩ are found in the *Shìjì* (Records of the Grand Historian) in the "Biographies of Feudal Lords" (*Shìjiā*), not the "General Biographies" (*Lièzhuàn*)—to say it is in the latter is an error.
A "Feudal Lord" (*shìjiā*) refers to one whose descendants receive hereditary stipends and rank. Initially, Goujian’s army...

"Defeated and taking refuge at Kuaiji—this was a disgrace. Later, when Wu was destroyed and Fuxi was captured, he requested execution because, in the past, when the army was defeated at Kuaiji, Goujian had suffered humiliation there;
thus, he requested execution for himself. Regarding the character "jian" (間) in "jianxingzhe" (間行者), it is pronounced with the departing tone (*qiàn*).
Yan Shigū’s commentary on the *Hánshū* states: "Jian means 'emptiness' (*kōng*); one proceeds through an opening or gap rather than in public view."
"Taking advantage of intervals" (*jiāndào*) means to travel in secret; it refers to taking advantage of gaps and empty spaces to go out privately.

Because these people were lowly and humble, it is called "traveling in secret" (*wéixíng*). The *Hòuhànshū* states, "private conversation," and the commentary notes that "private" (*sì*) is the meaning.
"Zhèngyú Táo" should likely be read as "zhǐyú Táo"; "Táo" refers to Dìngtáo. "Before long" (*jù wú hé*) means before much time had passed.
Why is this? Yan Shiguo’s commentary on the *Hanshu* states that "not long" (*wu jihe*) means not much time has passed.
*Ji* (幾) is pronounced as *ju* or *qi*. Regarding Xiongqu and the *Cifei* (Falconers):

the *Hanshu* mentions the *Cifei* archers, and its commentary notes that the *Cifei* office had one *ling* (Commandant) and nine *cheng* (Deputies) stationed within the Shanglin Park, where they would tie on feathered arrows and nets to hunt wild ducks and geese every year.
Ten thousand heads were provided for sacrifices in the ancestral temples. Furthermore, ancient brave men were selected to name official posts, such as the class of the Xiongqu (Bear Channel).
As for the Cifei (Convenient Fly), they were taken because of their agility and swiftness, like birds in flight; hence they were called Cifei.
The office of Zuoyi (Left Hunt) under the Qin was renamed Cifei by Emperor Wu. "Ci" may also be written as "Ci," and "fei" may also be written as "fei."
The *Lüshi Chunqiu* states that there was a brave warrior in Jing named Cifei; "Zhongshuren" (中庶人) should be read as "Zhongshuzu" (忠恕者).

The *Lunyu* says, "The Way of the Master consists simply of loyalty (*zhong*) and reciprocity (*shu*). Regarding the study of numbers, it refers to the study of the Abhidharma (*śāstra*) of the Hīnayāna.
As for "skillful ground," it means hitting the mark when shooting; regarding people, it means hitting the mark in evaluating them. The *Lun* (Discourse) follows this principle.
