Regarding the phrase "the followers of the Faxiang school" (Faxiang zongtu), the character *tu* (徒) should be read as *tú* (途). Thus, the *Jinbi* states:

"The school’s path (*zongtu*). This refers to the general approach (*datú*) of the Faxiang tenets employed by this particular school, which for the most part relies upon the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
The *Miaoxuan* states: "Master Yiji of Mount Huqiu;
Mount Huqiu is located in Suzhou. Master Yiji’s clan and lineage are unknown.
[He was a disciple of] Dharma Master Zong’ai."
His clan and lineage are unknown.
Master Zhuangyan Min was the Dharma Master Sengmin of Zhuangyan Temple in Yangdu during the Liang dynasty; his surname was Sun, and he was a native of Fuchun in Wu Commandery. (7)
In his youth, he left home at Mount Huqiu to become a monk under Senghui; as a disciple of Senghui, he received the Five Classics and was able to memorize them upon hearing them once.
Content with poverty and fond of learning, he studied under the two masters Rouru and Fazhi alongside Fayun, Fakai, and others.

At night, he would sleep wrapped in his patched robe, and during the day, he would travel in borrowed clothes. He thoroughly investigated the *Mahāyāna-saṃparigraha-śāstra* and the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra*, as well as the sūtras and vinaya.
The two masters Rouru and Cizi together lectured on the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* at Puhong Monastery. Daomin sat in the rear row of the assembly;
his discourse was characterized by clear eloquence and profound, far-reaching expression. As he spoke, Cizi set down his fly-whisk and sighed, saying:

"I have studied under the master of Pengcheng and have reflected deeply upon these five aggregates (*skandha*). I have identified fifteen points that I consider to be difficult cruxes, and I have always regretted [not being able to resolve them]."
"Having never encountered a formidable opponent, he was determined to exhaust his own depths; it has been several years since we arrived in Jinling, yet today at last we have seen him utterly spent.

Furthermore, when I reflect upon this, I recall that during the evening lecture, I was about to respond, but as soon as we had exchanged a few words, his arguments became so dense that Master Ci (Cizong) shifted his expression and looked around at the assembly, saying, 'The youth are to be feared—these words are indeed true.'"
At that time, Daochao of Linggen Monastery applied himself diligently to his studies with the aspiration to emulate Master Sengmin.
He suddenly dreamed of a person who said, "Dharma Master Sengmin was already able to lecture on the scriptures during the time of Vipaśyin Buddha; how can you say you are only now beginning to study?
He authored more than one hundred volumes of treatises and commentaries. At the age of sixty-one, he passed away in the second month of the eighth year of the Datong era.
The two masters Rou and Ci of Dinglin:
Master Rou of Dinglin Temple was surnamed Tao and was a native of Danyang. He applied himself with diligence to the precepts and devoted himself deeply to dhyāna and wisdom.
He thoroughly mastered all the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna scriptures of the Vaipulya class. He passed away in the capital at the age of sixty-four.
The Master [Seng]xie took leave of the Dharma Master Huiji of the temple; his surname was Yin and he was a native of Jizhou.

He followed the will of Faxian of Xuzhou with tireless devotion, rising far above his contemporaries in solitary excellence. Zangzhi, Sengmin, and others all requested instruction from him, and he passed away at the age of fifty-seven.
Kaishan refers to Kaishan Temple.
[This was written by] the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhata, the Guangtong.
Dharma Master Huiguang was surnamed Yang and was a native of Dingzhou. At the age of thirteen, he received the Three Refuges from Chan Master Fotuo.
Fotuo marveled at how his eyes emitted light outward; he subsequently ordained him as a monk and gave him the name Huiguang.
He first studied the Vinaya and later propagated the Sūtras and Śāstras. He served as the State Preceptor (Guōsēngdū) and was later appointed State Overseer (Guōtǒng); thus, he is known as Kuàngtǒng.
Also: Master Anlin of Qishu Temple on Mount Qi, whose secular surname was Qin; he left home at twenty-five and studied under [Master] Song.
Gong Guang of Shao Temple on Mount Gao attained realization upon hearing the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra* once; he comprehended it entirely beyond words.

He further received the dharma of Chan and thoroughly investigated the profound gates. By imperial decree during the Yongding era of the Chen dynasty, he was appointed to reside at Qisheshan Temple. At the age of seventy-seven, he passed away in the first year of the Zhide era.

The Chan Master of Beidi once said to Kumārajīva: "The Buddha’s single perfect sound is equal and without duality; it is without thought, yet universally responds to the hearing of those according to their capacities.
It is not that the original utterance of his speech was divided into Great and Small [vehicles]. Later, Bodhiruci of the Northern Wei stated: "The Tathāgata..."
With a single sound, he simultaneously responded to ten thousand beings, great and small, presented together.

Although various interpretations have emerged since my own patriarch, there are further differing systems of doctrinal classification (*panjiao*) by various schools; I shall now briefly record these, as set forth by Paramārtha.
The Tripitaka Master established two teachings: first, the Gradual, and second, the Sudden. The Gradual is defined by gradual awakening;

for Bodhisattvas who arise from the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) through the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna), it possesses the teachings of the Three Vehicles and is thus termed "Gradual," such as the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* and others. The Sudden is for those with direct, sudden capacity;
they do not arise from the Small Vehicle but proceed solely through the Bodhisattva Vehicle, such as the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*. [Compiled] in Tang China by Haidong Xinxila.

The National Master Wonhyo composed a commentary on the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* establishing four teachings: (1) the Separate Teaching of the Three Vehicles, such as the Four Noble Truths and the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*;
(2) the Common Teaching of the Three Vehicles, such as the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*; (3) the Distinctive Teaching of the Three Vehicles, such as the *Ratnakaraṇḍa-avadāna* and the *Brahmajāla-sūtra*;
and (4) the Perfect Teaching of the One Vehicle, such as the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*. — Recorded by Jizang of the Tang Dynasty.
The Master [Wonhyo] established three teachings: first, the Dharma-wheel of the Single Root, which is the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*;

second, the Dharma-wheel of the Branches and Endings, which refers to the Three Vehicles and so forth as explained later; and third, the Dharma-wheel of Gathering the Endings Back to the Root, which is the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
The Dharma Master Yin of Jiangnan during the Tang dynasty established two teachings: the first is the *Śākyamuni Sūtra*, termed the "Teaching of Crookedness."
Because it pursues the capacities of the faculties (*indriya*) to refute attachments according to their conceptual reckonings, the second is the Path of Equality, namely the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*.

Because it teaches with sovereign freedom according to the capacities of the faculties, the Tripiṭaka Master Amoghavajra of the Tang established five teachings: first, the Teaching of the Four Truths, namely the four *Āgamas*;
second, the Teaching of Signlessness, such as the *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtras; third, the Teaching of Contemplative Practice, namely the *Avataṃsaka*.
The *Sūtra on the Four Teachings of Peace and Bliss* is the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*; the fifth, the "Teaching of Protection," is the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*, so called because it protects the True Dharma.
The Tripiṭaka Master of the Tang Dynasty and the Dharma Master Ci'en Ji, relying on the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra*, established the doctrine of the three periods of teaching.
As that sūtra states: "The Bodhisattva Paramārthasamudgata addressed the Buddha, saying: 'World-Honored One, at one time in the beginning...'"
In the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana near Vārāṇasī, for the sake of those setting out upon the Śrāvaka vehicle alone, the Wheel of Dharma was turned by means of the characteristics of the Four Noble Truths;
although this was most wonderful and exceedingly rare, it was nonetheless surpassed and not of definitive meaning.
During the second period, it was turned solely for the sake of those setting out upon the practice of the Mahāyāna.
Although the turning of the wheel of the Dharma based on the fact that all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature and are without arising or cessation—
by means of the hidden mode of expression— is even more marvelous, it still has something superior to it and is of provisional meaning; whereas now, during this third period,
the Bhagavat has universally taught for the sake of those setting out upon all vehicles, based on the fact that all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature from the very beginning.
The turning of the wheel of Dharma that reveals the characteristics of coming-to-rest is most rare and is known as the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).

According to this scriptural passage, the Āgamas and other such sūtras constitute the first period, which generally and secretly teaches existence without clarifying what the nature of that existence is.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* and other such sūtras constitute the second period, which generally and secretly teaches emptiness without clarifying it.

That which is empty is also empty; what nature [remains]? In the *Avataṃsaka* and other sūtras, the third period of teaching is the explicit exposition of existence—the dependent and the perfected natures—and the explicit exposition of emptiness—the imagined nature. Furthermore, in the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*, there are three wheels of Dharma:
namely, turning, maintaining, and illuminating. Moreover, in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, it is said that when a physician administers milk, there are likewise three stages. Now, based on these...

The *New Sūtra* (the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*) states that the Mahāyāna of the sudden teaching (*tun-jiao*) is but a single period; however, because it is categorized according to gradual stages, these three periods exist.

It further says that teachings are judged according to the capacities of sentient beings (*sui-ji pan-jiao*), and so forth. The Tang dynasty master Xianshou Fazang established the Five Teachings (*wu-jiao*):

first, the Teaching of the Dull-Witted Hīnayāna; second, the Initial Teaching of the Mahāyāna; third, the Final Teaching; fourth, the Sudden Teaching; and fifth, the Perfect Teaching. Small... [text fragment].
The "Initial Teaching" (shijiao), which refers to scriptures such as the *Āgamas*, is also called the "Partial Teaching" (fenjiao).
This is because, during the second and third periods of the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra*, it is uniformly admitted that those of fixed nature among the two vehicles will both fail to attain Buddhahood;

therefore, these are combined into a single teaching. Since this does not yet exhaust the principles of the Mahāyāna Dharma, it is established as the "Initial [Teaching]" where some do not attain Buddhahood.
The Final Teaching (*niṣṭhā-naya*) is established as such because it is also called the "Teaching of Reality" (*tattva-naya*);

since it teaches that those of fixed nature among the two vehicles (*dviyāna*), as well as those without nature (*agotra*) such as the icchantikas, shall all eventually attain Buddhahood, it represents the ultimate discourse of the Mahāyāna. Thus, it is established as "Final" to accord with the principle of reality, and is further termed "Real.
The Sudden Teaching (*tada-naya*) holds that the mere non-arising of a single thought is itself called "Buddha," without relying on the gradual progression through stages (*bhūmi*).
Next, it is taught according to the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra* that those who have attained the true nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena do not proceed from one stage to another.
The *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* also states: "In the tranquil, true suchness (*tathatā*), what sequential order can there be?

The Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) clarifies that one stage is all stages, and all stages are one stage, according to the infinitely interpenetrating net of Indra within the Dharma-realm of Samantabhadra.

Regarding the aforementioned masters who established the classification of the teachings (*panjiao*) based on the complete assembly of primary and secondary elements, none of their systems are adopted according to the Tiantai school.
In the present age, those that are widely disseminated are only the two traditions of Cien and Xianshou.

To trace the origins of these two schools, the Dharma-character (*Faxiang*) and the Nature-realm (*Xingzong*), they both originally arose from Nālandā Monastery in the Western Regions; at that time, there were two masters of śāstras, one named Śīlabhadra...

The second [lineage] of the Venerable Ones is known as the "Wisdom-Light" (Jñānaprabha) and "Virtue-Light" (Śīlaprabha). They inherited the tradition from afar from Maitreya and Asaṅga, and followed closely upon Dharmapāla and Sthiramati.
Relying on the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, and other treatises, they established the doctrine of the Three Periods of Teaching;

this is precisely the system employed by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang of the Tang Dynasty and the Master Ci'en Ji. The second, Master Jñānaprabha, inherited the tradition from afar from Mañjuśrī and Nāgārjuna.

The master Qingmu (Sthiramati), who resided near the tree, and the master Qingbian (Bhāviveka), following treatises such as the *Prajñāpradīpa* and the *Madhyamakahṛdaya*, also established a system of three periods of teaching based on the *Prajñāpāramitā*.

They maintain that the Mahāyāna of signlessness (*animitta*) constitutes the true definitive meaning (*nītārtha*). They assert that the Buddha first taught the Hīnayāna at the Deer Park, clarifying that both mind and objects are existent;
subsequently, during the middle period, he taught the *Dharmalakṣaṇa* Mahāyāna for those of middling faculties, concerning the nature of objects.
The principle of "emptiness of mind" and "mere consciousness" has not yet fully entered into the equal, true emptiness;
it is during the third period that the Mahāyāna of signlessness is taught, wherein both mind and objects are empty, and this single flavor of equality constitutes the definitive meaning.

Master Qingliang (Xuanzang) said: "Thus, while these two schools clarify the teachings of the three periods, neither is able to exhaustively encompass the entirety of the Buddha’s lifetime teachings."
Because each [system] has its own basis yet they contradict one another; because scriptures such as the *Saṃdhinirmocana* have not yet reached their final position;

and because [the classification] is made merely according to the meaning of a single category, there are only three periods. If one examines the teachings of the three periods according to the two aforementioned schools through the perspective of Tiantai, there are three [deficiencies]:
first, the timing is incomplete; second, the judgment of the teachings is not exhaustive; third, it is fixed [and lacks flexibility].

To cling to a single sutra while disregarding the various Mahāyāna teachings—let alone the purport of an entire era, the meaning of the five periods, and the principles of bestowing, opening, and setting aside—is surely not the way for one who has set their heart upon these matters.

Master Qingliang (Zhiyan) originally lectured on Tiantai, but later followed Xianshou (Fazang), harmonizing the latter’s five teachings with the four teachings of Tiantai, stating: "The 'Dull-Witted' Hīnayāna is precisely the Tiantai Tripiṭaka."
The beginning corresponds to the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao) and the end corresponds to the Distinct Teaching (Biejiao); the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) is identical to both.
Furthermore, it is said that Tiantai did not establish a "Sudden Teaching" (Dunjiao) because within each of the four teachings there is already an ineffable aspect.

That which is now opened up—the sudden revelation of the ineffable as a distinct category—is precisely in accord with the Chan school. I, however, ask: how could Xianshou’s Five Teachings (Wujiao) possibly... [be compared]?

Is it the same as the Four Teachings of Tiantai? For instance, when the Sanzang (Tripitaka) Teaching points to the Deer Park and the *Vaipulya* (fangdeng) scriptures as containing the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) and so forth, how could this be the same as Xianshou (Fazang), who uniquely points to the four Āgamas?
Furthermore, while that [teaching] speaks only of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), this [teaching] possesses both the emptiness of persons and phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*);
how then could they be the same? If you claim that the "ineffability" (*anabhilāpya*) of the Four Teachings constitutes the Sudden Teaching (*dun*), this is utterly unacceptable.
What is the principle that transcends words in the Four Teachings? That principle fully encompasses the True and the Middle, as well as the Expedient and the Real.

Since they establish their own "Sudden Teaching" (Dun-jiao) as being inherently Mahāyāna, how can it be the same [as ours]? Furthermore, their own Perfect Teaching (Yuan-jiao) points directly to the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*;

how could it be the same as the Tiantai system of the Five Periods, which—excluding only the Deer Park period—manifests only the Exoteric and lacks the Perfect? Their "wonderful" and our "wonderful" are not the same.
Are there no differences between these two? Yet, although Xianshou (Fazang) employed the Five Teachings in his practice, when it came to his formal compositions, he praised Tiantai most highly.
He was truly one who had "ascended the hall and entered the inner chamber," and his status and rank were clearly established; he never offered even a subtle criticism [of Zhiyi].
This was simply because Master Guan (Zhanran) established the *Avataṃsaka* as the "Sudden-Sudden" and took the *Lotus Sūtra* as the "Gradual-Round," and furthermore—
The Huayan teachings on the non-duality of perfect interfusion (*yuanrong*) and sequential arrangement (*xingbu*) merely contradict the doctrines established by Tiantai;

yet, they fully employ the profound meanings of Tiantai, such as the ritual for seated meditation, the methods for settling the mind (*anxin*), the discourse on the three truths and three knowledges (*sandi sanzhi*), and the exposition of the three virtues and three contemplations (*sande sanguan*).
Furthermore, they speak of the Buddhas not severing their inherent evil (*xing'e*) and sentient beings not severing theirs.

The principle that nature is inherently good, the possession of all virtues, the profound logic of the mutual penetration of *tathatā*, the doctrine that taking one entails the three and the three constitute the one,
the mutual fusion of body and land, the non-duality of the environment and its inhabitants, and the significance of the Great Matter (*mahā-kāraṇa-pratyaya*)—

there is no such meaning that he did not cite as the essential core of his thought. As for Guifeng, he did not take Chan Master Yuanzhao of Canyuan as his fundamental teacher, nor did he rely on his various commentaries.
The *Chao* (Commentary) recklessly generates refutations and critiques; when those with discernment examine the Tiantai school, can they not feel compassion?

Those who study our present school fail to grasp its intent, yet instead claim that the "Ultimate Teaching" (*zhongjiao*) is the conventional aspect of our present Perfect [Teaching], the "Sudden Teaching" (*dunjiao*) is the true aspect of our present Perfect [Teaching], and the "Perfect Teaching" (*yuanjiao*) is the middle aspect of our present Perfect [Teaching].
Alas, how erroneous this is! How can one take these three truths of the present school and equate them to those?

Regarding the "Three Teachings," those who possess true knowledge know that they cannot be refuted. The *Song Gaoseng Zhuan* (Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Great Song) and the *Senglu* (Monastic Records) establish three wheels of teaching:
First, the Wheel of Exoteric Teaching (*xianjiao lun*), which refers to the various vehicles of the sūtras, vinayas, and śāstras; its founding patriarch is taken to be Kāśyapa Mātanga.

Second, the Wheel of Esoteric Teaching (*mijiao lun*), which refers to the Yoga system of consecration (*abhiṣeka*), the five families (*pañcakula*), homa fire rituals, and the three secrets of the maṇḍala.

The Dharma of Vinaya takes Vajragñāna as its progenitor; the Dharma of Chan takes Bodhidharma as its progenitor, teaching the wheel of the three minds to point directly to the human mind and see one's nature to achieve Buddhahood—this is the transmission of mind by mind.
Now, if this were the case, why have the various Mahāyāna sūtras such as the *Avataṃsaka* never failed to point directly [to the nature]?
"Does the human mind see its nature and thereby attain Buddhahood? Ning Gong’s understanding is far too superficial; I hope that those of later virtue will examine this in detail.
This [point regarding] old age and death is as explained in the sixth fascicle of the *Zhiguan*.
This was already cited previously.
As stated in the "Chapter on Eating Tandu" (Tandu-ear Soup), Zhǎn'ān said: "If one sees the Buddha personally begging for food and arriving at Cūḍa’s house to eat the tandu-ear soup..."
Entering extinction at night, he proceeded toward the Twin Śāla Trees, cremated his body with fire, and entered nirvana; this is what was perceived by those of limited capacity,
such as Kālodāyin.

This refers to the account of the origin of the precept (*śikṣāpada*) regarding coarse black [robes] and entering a village at improper times, wherein [a monk] was beaten to death by a layperson and buried in horse dung;
subsequently, he reappeared and passed away, leading to the establishment of the rule.
The five names for Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*) are as explained in the third fascicle of the *Mohe Zhiguan* (Great Calming and Contemplation), though with slight differences in detail.
The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*, fascicle twenty-five, states: "All sentient beings possess the Śūraṅgama Samādhi;
it is also called Prajñā, also called Vajrasamādhi, also called Siṃhanāda, and also called Buddha-nature.
Because its realization of śamatha and vipaśyanā encompasses the three virtues (triguṇa), it is said that its meaning remains somewhat distinct [from other texts].
Regarding the physical body, up to the nine types of grievance, the *Mahā-śāstra* states: first, the Brahmin woman Sundarī slandered five hundred arhats and was herself slandered;
second, the Brahmin woman Ciñcā-Mānavikā tied a large piece of rotting wood to her belly and slandered [the Buddha]; third, Devadatta pushed down a mountain.
1. A stone was thrown at the Buddha, striking his big toe and causing it to split into four pieces; 2. A wooden splinter pierced his foot; 3. King Virūḍhaka raised an army and slaughtered the Śākyas;
4. The Buddha suffered from a headache; 5. He accepted an invitation from the Brahmin Aṅgada and ate horse-gram;
6. Due to a cold wind, he suffered back pain; 7. He practiced austerities for six years; 8. He entered a Brahmin village.

When going out for alms, he might return with an empty bowl; furthermore, during the eight nights before and after the winter solstice, there are cold winds that pierce through bamboo, requiring him to wear the three robes to ward off the chill. Moreover, he suffers from heat. According to the *Udāyin-sūtra*, there are ten afflictions:
first, the slander of Sundarī; second, the slander of Cīrṇa-vāsas; third, headaches; and fourth, pain in the joints and bones.
1. Suffering from back pain; 2. Being struck by a wooden wedge; 3. Datta throwing a stone; 4. The Brahmin woman Ciñcā’s slander; 5.
Eating horse- oats for sixteen years; 6. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* commentary states that *gan*, *wu*, and *tan* are all incorrect characters;
they should be *yu* (bowl) and *pen* (basin).

Regarding the record concerning the novice Cūḍapanthaka, following the fourth record on *śamatha-vipaśyanā*, a later person sought out the ninth record, which states: "Among the three trainings, it is not only the path of wisdom (*prajñā-mārga*) that is not lost through successive births;

the same applies to morality (*śīla*) and meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Why is this? Morality is a conditioned dharma of form (*rūpa-dharma*), while meditative concentration is a conditioned dharma of mind (*citta-dharma*)."

At the time when life decays, the physical form ceases to act; although the substance of the precept (*śīla-dravya*) has passed away, the non-informative karma (*avijñapti-karma*) of the precept is attained and does not perish, because it follows the path of karma into the future. Even the substantial dharmas (*vastu-dharma*) of the Hīnayāna reach into the future.

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "milk and *tuṇḍa*" etc. in the text below: *tuṇḍa* should be written as *tuṇḍa* (pronounced with the initial *zhú* [cut] and the final *duō* [gòng] tones), meaning breast-milk.
*Yě* (也): Pronounced *gǔ hòu* (古候切); it means to take milk. Regarding the phrase "to provide you with the seed of milk," one should say "you give me milk" (*rǔ yǔ wǒ rùn*).
*Yuān* (蜎): Pronounced *kuáng yuǎn* (狂兗切). The *Erya* states: "The *yuān* and *xuān* are small insects in a well; the *qì* and *áo* are red insects. *Xuān* (蠉): Pronounced *xiāng yuǎn* (香兗切).
*Yuān* should be written as *xuān* (翾), which is also written as *xuān* (蠉) with the phonetic *xǔ yuán* (許緣切); it means to fly lightly. *Rěn* (蠕): To wriggle or crawl.

"Yǔn" (允) and "yǎn" (兗)—the latter being pronounced with the *qiè* (切) [rhyme] of *dòng* (動)—mean "to move. One who is fond of lending money out of a desire for profit, and having finished repaying the principal, again offends others;
one who constantly delights in lending money to outsiders, and when the agreed period for repayment arrives, immediately demands interest while others are still settling their debts;

one who, after the repayment is complete, again falsely accuses others by saying it is not yet finished—one who commits such acts is called a "sitter" (*zuò*). The character for "sitter" (*zuò*) is pronounced with the *cí* (慈) [rhyme].

The term "wo" (臥) means to be afflicted by transgression. Regarding the phrase "exhalation" (*chū-xī*): it is like "offspring" (*zǐ-xī*). Offspring refers to the vital breath (*qi*) received at birth that resides within the human body.
This is why people today say that when one lends money and receives interest, it is also called "interest" (*xī*); this follows that same analogy.
Furthermore, the following passage clarifies the "dirt on the nails," citing the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, fascicle 31, which states: "The Flower Ornament" (*Huá-yán*).
Since within this [text] a small amount of soil is compared with the soil of the great earth, we know that the dharmas of a Bodhisattva of the Ten Stages cannot be compared to those of a Buddha.
Furthermore, it says that the *Avataṃsaka* is profound only as its introduction;
one should rather say that the *Anantamukha-dhāraṇī* (or *Anantārtha*) is profound.
Eight thousand śrāvakas received their individual predictions of enlightenment, as recorded in the seventh fascicle of the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*.
The *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* states: "For example, in the darkness of night, all manual labor comes to a halt; those tasks not yet completed must wait for the light of day.
Likewise, those who study the Mahāyāna must wait for the sun of the unsurpassed Great Parinirvāṇa"—this refers to this sutra.
The supramundane [teaching] is like that fruit which brings great benefit and peace and happiness to all, enabling sentient beings to perceive the Tathāgata-nature;

it is just as the eight thousand śrāvakas who received their predictions in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, namely those mentioned in the "Chapter on the Encouragement of Devotion" (*Anuparīndanā-parivarta*).
Piśāca; here translated as "Consumer of Vital Essence," meaning one who consumes the vital essence of humans and the five grains; also called Piśāca. Pūtanā.
This is called the "Superior among Foul-Smelling Ghosts" and is also known as the "Ghost that Governs Fever Diseases.
As previously indicated in the seventh fascicle of the *Zhiguan* (Calming and Contemplation) by the Tathāgatas,
it has been cited there before.
The eight great śrāvakas—
Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, Kāśyapa, Ākāśagarbha, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, Revata, Aniruddha, and Ānanda—
and the eight great bodhisattvas.
Mañjuśrī, Avitathadarśana, Ratnaśrī, Sarvapāpagati-vivarjita, Chāyāvaraṇa-vivarjita, Lokendrarāja, Pratibhānasaṃcaya,
Abhyudgata-taraṇa, Avitatha-padakrama, and Trapuṣa.
All masters have claimed that this is a spurious sutra; however, one must consider that Tiantai personally received it at Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa—how could he have cited a spurious sutra to mislead others?
The *Sanbao lu* states: "The old catalog records the *Tiwèi jīng* (Sutra of Tiwei) as a separate volume;
its language is identical to that of various other sutras, but Tanjing added five lines of verse and described the use of stone and gold for the five directions."

This has merely given rise to doubt; now, taking the single fascicle as established as the definitive version, we find that Tánjìng composed the *Tíwèi bōlì jīng* (Sūtra of Trapuṣa and Bhallika) in two fascicles at the Northern Terrace.
Its text states: "In the east is Mount Tài, which in Han language is called Mount Dài; because yin and yang alternate there, it is called Mount Dài.
This was produced during the Wèi dynasty, so it should have been said "in Wèi language," yet it says "Han language"—this is a failure to distinguish [the periods].
The character "dai" (代) here is a false [transliteration]; "Taishan" (太山) is simply a local dialectal term used to translate the name of that mountain.
These two terms are mutually interchangeable, yet one fails to recognize that both the Sanskrit and the Wei (Chinese) versions contain errors.

Regarding the six causes and four conditions, as recorded in the eighth fascicle of the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* (Cessation and Contemplation), the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states: "The efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*), the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*), the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*), and the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*)—these are accepted as the only six kinds of causes.

The *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "The six causes are the acting cause (*kāraka-hetu*), the common cause (*sādhāraṇa-hetu*), the cause of one's own seeds (*svabīja-hetu*), the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*),..."

Regarding the four conditions (*pratyaya*)—the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), the sequential condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*):

the new translation renders *samanantara-pratyaya* as "equal-and-immediate condition" (*tingxianglian yuan*) and *ālambana-pratyaya* as "object-condition" (*suoyuan yuan*). The other two names remain the same.

Furthermore, it is said that if the *Abhidharmakośa* states that the causal condition consists of five types of causes (*hetu*), the *Kośa* indeed says that the causal condition comprises five causes.
Regarding "the nature of cause" (*hetutva*), this "nature" refers to the category of conditions;
among the six causes, excluding the efficient cause (*kāraṇahetu*), the remaining five causes constitute the nature of the causal condition (*hetupratyayatā*). The six causes are as listed above.

Regarding the ten similes in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, as recorded in the fifth note of the *Zhiguan* (Calming and Contemplation), the seventh fascicle of the *Great Treatise* states: first, like a magical illusion; second, like a mirage; third, like the moon in water;

fourth, like space; fifth, like an echo; sixth, like a city [of the gandharvas]; seventh, like a dream; eighth, like a shadow; ninth, like a reflected image; tenth, like a transformation. Furthermore...
The subsequent text states that there are twenty-one characters, but there are actually only twenty.
That "all dharmas tend toward suchness" is as previously cited in the second record of the *Zhiguan* (Mohe Zhiguan).
In the Buddha’s response at the end, it is stated once again that a bodhisattva should not eat meat; thus, we know that [the allowance for meat] still exists within the Hīnayāna teachings.
I fear this judgment may be erroneous. Why? Because the text of that sūtra, in the Buddha’s response, states in full:
"All meats have immeasurable causes and conditions; therein, a bodhisattva should give rise to compassion and must not eat them—namely, those that are the flesh of sentient beings."
Since beginningless time, within the cycle of birth and death, we have repeatedly been each other’s parents, brothers, and kinsmen;

how, then, could one take them as food? Even to say, "If I were to permit the śrāvakas to eat meat, I would not be called one who dwells in a mind of loving-kindness," and my teaching in various places that ten types of meat are forbidden while three types are permitted, was intended as a gradual approach.

I have prohibited [the eating of meat] so that they may practice and study; within this very sutra, I have completely forbidden all meat, whether from animals that died naturally or were killed by others.
Mahāmati, I have never permitted my disciples to eat meat, nor do I permit it now, nor shall I ever permit it.
Mahāmati, all meat is impure for those who have left the household life; if there is any delusion [regarding this], [it must be abandoned].

If people slander [me], saying that the Tathāgata permits the eating of meat and even eats it himself, you should know that such people are shrouded by evil karma and will inevitably fall forever into states that are not beneficial.
Mahāmati, since even those of the Two Vehicles and Bodhisattvas subsist solely on the food of Dharma, how much more so the Tathāgata?
Furthermore, as stated in the verses: "Those who eat meat without shame and remorse shall always be reborn in a state of perpetual delusion."

The various Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, as well as those of the Two Vehicles, all loathe [the eating of meat]. In the *Gaja-pāda*, the *Mahāmegha*, the *Nirvāṇa*, the *Śrīmālā*, and this *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, I have all prohibited the eating of meat.
Having previously taught that meat is forbidden upon seeing, hearing, or suspecting [its origin], I have thus severed the consumption of all meat.
The general meaning of the texts in the four-fascicle and ten-fascicle versions of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* is the same; it is only the wording that differs.
There is only a difference of detail; therefore, we know that both the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* and the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* equally prohibit the three vehicles from eating meat.
It is not the case that the *Laṅkāvatāra* merely restricts bodhisattvas while failing to forbid the two [lower] vehicles.

Thus, it is an error to claim that the present [text] preserves the Hinayana teachings by permitting [meat-eating]. This is because all Mahayana scriptures unanimously do not allow the three vehicles to eat meat.

Furthermore, the subsequent passage states, "excluding the Heaven of Delighting in Transformations. This is because, according to the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*, when preaching up to the Heaven of Delighting in Transformations, one teaches the ten dhyānas as well as all four dhyānas.
Furthermore, regarding the "eight arts," as recorded in the eighth fascicle of the *Zhiguan*:

the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states, "Moreover, there is a skilled physician who understands eight kinds of arts; he comes from a distant land. Zhanran (Zhang'an) comments: "There are ten kinds of physicians:

namely, the Bodhisattvas of the Perfect Teaching at the initial, middle, and final stages of the mind; the Bodhisattvas of the Three Teachings; and the practitioners of the Two Vehicles of the two [lower] teachings."
The eight arts of the *prahāṇika* (those who sever bonds), the *tapasvin* (ascetics), and the *śūnyadṛṣṭika* (those with views of emptiness) are: first, treating the body; second, treating the eyes;
third, treating the womb; fourth, treating children; fifth, treating sores; sixth, treating poisons; seventh, treating demonic afflictions; and eighth, knowing the stars.

Internally, these correspond to the Buddha’s knowledge of the Eightfold Noble Path, which is able to cure the diseases of the eight inversions. Furthermore, there are the three types of penetration and the five [powers].

Regarding the statement that "the eye is called the eight arts," or alternatively that "the four such as permanence and bliss, together with the four such as neither impermanent nor non-impermanent, collectively constitute the eight arts"—this is likely an error.
It should rather state: "the four such as impermanence and so forth, together with the four such as permanence and so forth.

Because the Middle Way negates both extremes and thus destroys all eight inversions, it is said to be "neither permanent nor impermanent" and so on; furthermore, it is able to negate both simultaneously.
Because the two modes of illumination function distinctly, it is said that they can be both permanent and impermanent.

Now, to clarify that they illuminate both simultaneously, it is called the "eight methods" (*aṣṭavidha*). If one points to their simultaneous non-duality, this is simply the essence of the eight methods.

Regarding "practicing together with the sages," the current text says "the two interpretations are not distinguished," which should rather be "not clearly differentiated.
Regarding "phenomena and principle are mutually identical," the current text should rather say "identical with phenomena as principle, and identical with principle as phenomena.

Regarding "ordinary beings practicing together with sages, etc., as in the previous three phrases," the current text should rather say "ordinary beings practicing with ordinary beings, and ordinary beings practicing with sages."
The "common practice" that is neither extraordinary nor noble, when analyzed in terms of both persons and dharmas, constitutes both [the bondage of wisdom and the bondage of skillful means].
This is thus slightly different from the preceding three phrases. Furthermore, citing the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, it says: "Wisdom without skillful means is bondage;
this is called the compassion of craving and views. According to that sutra, "skillful means without wisdom is bondage," which refers precisely to craving and views.

If one accomplishes the welfare of sentient beings with the mind alone, yet lacks the skillful means of wisdom, one is bound; this is merely planting the roots of virtue while remaining within the three poisons.
Conversely, if one possesses the liberation of wisdom through skillful means, or the liberation of skillful means through wisdom, the opposite should be understood to apply.

In the *Miaoxuan* (Exquisite Profundity), citing the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*’s account of the initial attainment of enlightenment, the *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary) states: "For now, we borrow from the secret [teachings].

I have previously read the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* commentary (*Niepan shu*), which differs greatly from this. That commentary says: 'The old interpretation holds that [the Buddha] sat at the site of enlightenment and was also questioned;
some say this is from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, where the translation was incomplete and the text had not yet arrived,' or they say it is..."

The texts of the provisional and indeterminate teachings have likewise not yet arrived; furthermore, the claim that these belong to the secret teachings rather than being included within the revealed teachings is incorrect.
Herein it is clarified that "sitting at the site of enlightenment" (bodhimaṇḍa) refers to the primordial, perfect initial sitting, not a site of enlightenment attained through expedient means.
This directly addresses the question posed in the past and does not mark the beginning of a single period of transformation. The above constitutes the commentary (*śāstra*).
If that is so, does it not also contradict [the claim] that this is now "secret"? It does not.

Generally speaking, when interpreting the scriptural text, the primary citations are considered the main authority, while the commentary (*shu-wen*) serves as the secondary support; the *Xuan-qián* frequently employs such analogies as its secondary support, and there is no great fault in this.

Regarding the three versions of the *Nāga Palace* [Sūtra], Master Guan says: First, the "Abridged Version" refers to the eighty-fascicle edition currently transmitted and the sixty-fascicle edition of the old translation;
these are abridged translations from among the one hundred thousand verses and are therefore incomplete. Second, the "Lower Version Sūtra" refers to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.
The Mahāyāna Piṭaka is this sūtra which Mañjuśrī and Ānanda compiled together at the Iron Ring Mountains (Cakravāḍa).
It was stored within the Dragon Palace. When the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna went to the Dragon Palace, he saw this Great and Inconceivable Sūtra in three versions;
the abbreviated version consisted of one hundred thousand verses and forty-eight chapters. Nāgārjuna recited it from memory and transmitted it to the world.
The *Xiyuji* (Records of the Western Regions) states that the *Zhajupan* (Cakravāḍa) country possesses this complete version;
among the three versions, this middle version consists of 498,800 verses and 1,200 chapters.

The four superior versions contain as many verses as there are atoms in thirteen thousand great thousandfold world systems, and as many chapters as there are atoms in one four-continent world system (*cāturdvīpaka*).
The two aforementioned texts are not sustained by the mental power of ordinary humans, and therefore they have not been transmitted. The *Five Universal Eye Sūtras* are sustained by Sāgaramegha;

even if one were to use ink equal in volume to the great ocean and a pen as large as Mount Sumeru, one could not exhaustively record this Dharma-gate of the Universal Eye—even within a single chapter, a single section, a single teaching, a single meaning, or a single phrase.
A small portion of this sutra is missing; of the three translations, the first and third are complete as they appear in the present text,

The body of a syllable (*vyañjana*) lacks intrinsic nature and is conventionally established based on phonemes (*akṣara*). If it possesses no sense of modification or transition, it is merely called a "phoneme.
When there is modification beyond a single phoneme, such that distinctions can be expressed, it is called a "phrase" (*pada*).
This is because, at the time of expressing the distinctions of intrinsic nature through this [phrase], it serves as the basis for both names (*nāman*) and phrases.

That which is called "syllable" (*vyañjana*)—although its essence is identical to that of a "letter" (*akṣara*)—is designated as a syllable only when it serves as the basis for the other two [names and phrases] and possesses the sense of modification.
If it does not serve as the basis for the other two and lacks the sense of modification, it is merely called a letter.
Regarding the statement that "name expresses intrinsic nature," this refers to the intrinsic nature of all phenomena; that is, the intrinsic nature of all conditioned and unconditioned things.

Whether they are contaminated (*sāsrava*) or uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), whether they are form (*rūpa*) or mind (*citta*), whether they are provisional (*prajñapti*) or substantial (*dravya*), and whether they are localized or attached to their own essence—all such things are termed "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*).
That which designates this intrinsic nature is called a "name" (*nāman*). It is not restricted to a single syllable or two syllables;

rather, whatever expresses intrinsic nature is collectively designated as a "name. For example, a single syllable may constitute a name, such as "eye," "ear," "nose," "tongue," "earth," "water," "fire," or "wind."
When two characters form a name, such as *adhimukti* (resolute belief) or *vīrya* (diligence);
when three characters form a name, such as *Vaiśālī*—these phrases that express distinctions refer to the meaning of difference inherent within the very essence (*svabhāva*) of phenomena.
This "difference" applies to both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*). That is to say, from two characters upward, they merely express [such distinctions].
Distinctions are all termed "phrases" (*pada*). Furthermore, a two-syllable phrase that expresses a distinction is, for example, "Buddha-eye.
If one were to speak merely of "eye," it would express only the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the eye;
however, since the word "Buddha" is added before "eye," it expresses the specific distinction of the eye. If one says "defiled eye," then three syllables constitute a phrase expressing a distinction.

Furthermore, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states, "As it is said in the *Ṣaṭpādābhidharma*," because that treatise says, regarding karma that results in retribution in the hells, "as explained in detail in the *Lòuchán* [Saṃgītiparyāya] within the *Ṣaṭpādābhidharma*.
Here, the text concerning hellish karma is not employed; rather, only the *Ṣaṭpādābhidharma* is cited.
Regarding King Aśoka, the *Xiyu ji* states that "Aśoka" is translated here as "Wuyou" (Sorrowless); formerly it was called "King A-yu.
The *Wenju* states: "The remaining chapters each have their own specific allocation."
The end of the treatise states: "As previously assigned; 'as previously' means as before; 'place' (處) means location;
'assigned' (分) is read with the level tone, meaning as previously assigned. Therefore, the treatise says:
"From here below, for the sake of sentient beings who possess seven kinds of afflictions, metaphors are taught as antidotes for the seven kinds of *adhimāna* (conceit). The first is seeking..."
1. Those with power; 2. those seeking the liberation of a śrāvaka; 3. those of the Mahāyāna; 4. those with fixed resolve; 5.
those without fixed resolve; 6. those who accumulate merit; and 7. those who do not accumulate merit.
These seven types of arrogant inversion seek merit through arrogance, for the various worldly afflictions are burning intensely.
However, because seeking the retributive fruits of the sublime realms of devas and humans serves as an antidote to this, the Parable of the Burning House is taught;
because the conceit of those in the Śrāvaka vehicle that "my vehicle is no different from the Tathāgata’s vehicle" serves as an antidote to this, the Parable of the Poor Son is taught;

and because the conceit of those in the Mahāyāna that "there is no distinction between the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha vehicles" serves as an antidote to this, [the Parable of the Rich Man and His Poor Son is taught].

Therefore, the parable of the clouds and rain is taught: although it does not truly exist, those with overweening pride conceive of worldly samādhis as real and give rise to the notion that nirvāṇa exists where there is no nirvāṇa; to counteract this, the parable of the conjured city is taught.

Furthermore, although a chaotic mind lacks true concentration and one has great roots of merit from the Mahāyāna in the past yet remains unaware of them, to counteract this, [the parable of the poor man] is taught.
The parable of the tied jewel illustrates that those who possess merit preach the Mahāyāna Dharma yet do not adopt it as the Mahāyāna;
to counteract this, the parable of the crest-jewel is taught. Those who lack merit do not accumulate roots of goodness regarding the Supreme Vehicle and do not accept the Supreme Vehicle as supreme;
to counteract this, the parable of the physician is taught, and so on, up to the point where it says "oneself."
From this point onward, there is a manifestation through five gates of the power of the Dharma and the power of practice: first, realization; second, faith;
third, making offerings; fourth, hearing the Dharma; and fifth, reading, reciting, upholding, and explaining.
These four gates are manifested in the "Maitreya" chapter, while the "Constant Diligence" chapter manifests the first gate, realization, as stated in the sutra: "The lifespan of this Tathāgata..."
The two types of faith regarding the long duration of life and so forth are as described in the sutra: "Sentient beings in eight worlds attain the mind of *samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The three types of offerings are as described in the sutra: "These bodhisattvas obtain great benefit from the Dharma, and a rain of *māndārava* flowers falls.

Regarding "hearing the Dharma," it is as explained in the Chapter on Rejoicing (*Anumodanā-parivarta*). Regarding "manifesting a single dharma-gate" in the Chapter on Constant Diligence (*Sadā-vīrya-parivarta*), it means:

Regarding those who engage in recitation, copying, and meditative concentration (*samādhi*), there are three dharma-gates, as extensively explained in the "Dharma-Teacher" chapter, the "Peaceful Conduct" chapter, and the "Encouragement to Maintain" chapter, which describe the power of the Dharma.
Regarding the power of manifestation, there are three dharma-gates: the chapter on Supernatural Powers describes first, the manifestation of the broad and long tongue;
second, the sound of clearing the throat; and third, the snapping of fingers, so that practitioners may attain awakening.
Therefore, the power of practicing asceticism is manifested in the "Medicine King" chapter; the teaching of sentient beings who practice asceticism is manifested in the "Wonderful Sound" chapter;
the protection against various difficulties is manifested in the "Avalokiteśvara" chapter and the "Dhāraṇī" chapter;
the superior power of merit is manifested in the "King Adorned with Virtue" chapter; and the power of protecting the Dharma is manifested by Samantabhadra.
This is demonstrated in this chapter and the subsequent chapters.
The commentary states that within the accomplishment of the introduction, there are two further types:
first, the demonstration of the accomplishment of sovereign power (*vaśitā-guṇa-sampad*), as in the sūtra passage: "The city of Rājagṛha excels all others."
Because the city and the old Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain are superior to all other mountains, this Dharma is revealed as being superior.
In the six subsequent sections of accomplishment, each has its own division.
Second, regarding the accomplishment of the assembly, there are four parts: first, number, meaning that the great assembly is infinite; second, conduct, meaning the śrāvakas...

1. The cultivation of the practices of the Śrāvaka-vehicle; 2. The cultivation of the practices of the Bodhisattva-vehicle; 3. The three types of Bodhisattvas manifesting according to the occasion; 4.
The accomplishment of the fixed majestic deportment of renunciants, all of whom are Arhats; 5. The third [section], on the arrival of the time to preach the Dharma;
6. The accomplishment of the enumeration of seventeen distinct names; 7. The accomplishment of abiding in majestic deportment, extending up to the seventh [point].
The answers to these questions regarding the accomplishment [of qualities] are explained at length in the treatise.
The section on praising the merits of the Dharma-preacher (*dharmabhāṇaka*) in the *Śāstra* states: "Because the Tathāgata has accomplished the merits of a Dharma-preacher."
The *Jñānasārasamuccaya-nibandhana* states:
From this point onward, it is demonstrated based on three meanings: first, the meaning of certainty; second, the meaning of doubt;
and third, the basis upon which the doubt arises, as in the sūtra passage beginning with "At that time, the great assembly... and so forth.
The *Discourse on Resolving Doubts* states that there are four kinds of doubts to be severed. First, the doubt concerning "at what time [the teaching] was spoken":
namely, at what time did the Buddha-Tathāgata arise various skillful means to sever this doubt? Therefore, the Sūtra says: "The Buddhas appear in the five turbidities," and so forth.

Regarding Hexi, as recorded in his own biography and in the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*, Daoping was likewise a master of the Dharma of his time; however, because he was rigid by nature and antagonistic toward others, those who debated with him held him in low regard.
Fayao of Xiaoshan in Wuxing of the Song dynasty, known as Jiangdong Yao, was surnamed Yang and was a native of Hedong. From his youth, he was fond of learning;
he traveled ten thousand *li* to seek out teachers and composed commentaries on the *Nirvāṇa*, *Lotus*, and *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* (Dapin) Sutras. He was seventy-six years old at that time.
There was also the Dharma Master Tanyao,
who lectured on the Three Treatises: the Madhyamaka-śāstra, the Śata-śāstra, and the Dvādaśamukha-śāstra.

The details regarding Dharma Master Faying of Guangzhai Temple during the Liang dynasty are fully explained in the *Xuanqiān Bùzhù* (Supplementary Notes on the Profound Commentary); they are all identical.
The *Book of Rites* (*Liji*) states: "Do not be like the 'lei-tong' (the simultaneous response to thunder). The commentary notes: "When thunder sounds, all things respond at the same time;
it is not so with human speech, which ought to proceed from each individual. Mencius says: "A person who lacks the heart of right and wrong is not a human being."
In his deep veneration of the *Analects*, Yan Hui praised Zhongni, saying: "I look up to him and he seems ever higher; I drill into him and he seems ever firmer.
The Master leads us on step by step, skillfully guiding others."
Regarding the "Questioning at the Ford" (*Wenjin*): The *Lunyu* states that when Confucius passed by Chang Ju and Jie Ni while they were plowing, he sent Zi Lu to ask for the ford.
The commentary notes that a "ford" (*jin*) is a place where one crosses a river.

The *Erya* states regarding "diverging roads": "A road with one branch is called a *dao*; a road with two branches is called a *qi*. The commentary notes: "A diverging road (*qi dao*) is one that extends out from the side."
Regarding "kui-jing" (crossroads), the *Erya* states: "That which has nine thoroughfares is called a kui. The commentary notes: "Four roads intersect, with further lateral passages.
Tánluán was a person of the Northern Qi dynasty.

There were the Northern Qi and the Southern Qi; the region south of the Yangtze River was the Southern Qi, and the region north of the Yellow River was the Northern Qi. [The character] Luán (鸞) is sometimes written as Luán (巒);
his clan and lineage are unknown. He was a native of Yanmen and died at the age of sixty-seven in the fourth year of the Xinghe era of the Wei dynasty.
The *Wenju* states: "Whether exceeding or falling short. The *Lunyu* records:
"Zi Gong asked, 'Which of these two was more virtuous, Zigong or Shang? The Master said, 'Zigong exceeded the mark; Shang fell short.
Zi Gong said, 'In that case, is Zigong the better? The Master replied, 'Exceeding is just like falling short. The commentary notes: "Both fail to attain the Mean."
Now, borrowing their own words to refute these two schools:
Long of Mount Lu and Yìn of Zhongxīng Temple in the Qi dynasty.
Master Yìn of Zhongxīng Temple was surnamed Zhū; he was a native of Shòuchūn who studied under Huìlong of Mount Lu.
Master Yiliang of the Fahua school was renowned in his time for propagating the tenets of the Lotus Sūtra.
Although Master Yin had studied a wide range of scriptures, he was particularly famous for his expertise in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, having lectured on it two hundred and fifty-two times.
Mount Lu is located in Nankang Commandery in Jiangnan; the *Record of Mount Lu* states that Kuang Yu appeared during the reign of King Wei of the Zhou dynasty.
He was born at that time, and his spiritual essence remained hidden and submerged; he dwelt in seclusion upon this mountain, which the common people called "Lord Lu" (Lujun).
For this reason, the mountain took this as its name.
— Xuan Chang.
During the Qi dynasty, there was the Dharma Master Xuanchang, surnamed Zhao, a native of Jincheng in Hexi. He left home to become a monk in Liangzhou;
his original name was Huizhi, but later, upon meeting Xuangao, he became his disciple and changed his name to Xuanchang.

He thoroughly understood the sutras and vinaya and had deeply penetrated the essentials of dhyāna. He was most proficient in the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* and the Three Treatises (*Sanlun*), and for this reason, he attracted many students.
He was widely revered and honored.
A record states: "The *Yi* says, 'Its fragrance is like that of orchids.
The *Commentary on the Attached Verbs of the Upper Part* of the *Zhou Yi* says: "The way of the gentleman may consist in going forth or remaining at home, or in silence or in speech. (2)
"When people are of one mind, their sharpness can cut through metal; when they speak with one mind, the fragrance of their words is like that of orchids. The *Yi Zheng* (Correct Meaning) states:
"This means that when two people align their minds and utter words together, the vaporous essence is dense and the fragrant scent is as rich as that of orchids.
*Duàn* (cut) is pronounced *dīng luàn qiè*; *chòu* (fragrance) is pronounced *chāng yòu qiè*.
Regarding the name "Tiantai": "Tian" means the summit;
"Tai" is the name of a constellation. The celestial division (*fenyue*) of that region corresponds to the Three Terrace Stars (*santai*), as commonly explained.

Regarding the locations and assemblies, as cited in the *Śīkṣānanda-śāstra* (Shiqian), the old translation of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* contains seven locations and eight assemblies, while the new translation adds one further assembly at the Universal Radiance Hall (*Samantaprabhā-maṇḍala*).
First is the Aranya of Magadha; second is the bend of the Kṣīranadī River in Magadha and the Universal Radiance Hall.
The third was in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; the fourth, in the Yāma Heaven; the fifth, in the Tuṣita Heaven;
the sixth, in the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven; the seventh, again in the Universal Radiance Hall; the eighth, once more in the Universal Radiance Hall;
and the ninth, while wandering in the Jeta Grove.

The term "pian" (chapter/section) signifies the abundance of sections. "Pian" takes the meaning of binding together bamboo slips (*pianjian*). In antiquity, bamboo was treated with fire to remove its sap (*shaqing*) to serve as slips, which were then bound together with leather (*wei*) to form a "pian.
This is similar to how paper is joined together today to form a scroll (*juan*). Thus, Du Yuankai said: "Great..."

Matters are recorded on *ce* (strips); minor matters are merely on *jian* (slips) and *du* (wooden tablets). Large bamboo is called *ce*, small bamboo is called *jian*, and wooden boards are called *du*.
This is as in the case of the "Ten Wondrousnesses" and so forth, which fully possess the four meanings.

Regarding the objects such as the twelve links of dependent origination and the four noble truths, there are four sections: first, the correct explanation; second, the judgment of the coarse and the subtle; third, the opening of the coarse to reveal the subtle;
and fourth, the contemplation of the mind.
This is like staying for two nights.
In the *Mao Shih*, within the *Zhou Song*, the poem "You Ke" states: "The guest has stayed one night; the guest has stayed two nights. The commentary notes:
"One night is called *su* (stayed); two nights are called *xin* (trusted). The text of the *Erya*, in the "Shixun" section, says: "'The guest has stayed one night' means he has stayed two nights;
'the guest has stayed two nights' means he has stayed four nights. Guo's commentary states: "Two nights constitute *xin*."

Regarding the stubborn adherence to old ways, Master Han [Yü] said: "In Song there was a farmer who, while plowing in the fields, saw a rabbit strike a tree stump and die; he subsequently caught the rabbit.
Thereafter, he ceased plowing and constantly sat by that stump, hoping another rabbit would come along. A bystander tried to advise him, but he would not listen."
Because of this state of cessation (*śamatha*), popular tradition refers to those who remain mired in delusion as "those who guard the stump.

Thus it is said that because contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) accords with the sūtras, the eighth fascicle of the *Śikṣāsamuccaya* (or relevant commentary), in the section on "Knowing the Successive Stages," states: "Each and every phrase and verse is practiced in accordance with what has been heard, leading to entry [into realization]."

When the mind forms contemplation, that contemplation accords with the sūtra; thus, contemplation possesses the seal (*mudrā*), and the seal causes the mind to perform contemplation—this is not like counting another's treasures.
As for the character "釋" (shì), the old editions read "釋" (shì, to explain), which is incorrect; the new edition from Yuèzhōu reads "擇" (zé, to choose), which is correct.
The details of this matter are roughly as explained in the *Zhiguan ji*.

This "unconditioned compassion" (*nirālamba-maitrī*) is precisely the compassion of the Tathāgata; it is of one essence with the Treasure-store Samādhi (*ratna-kūṭa-samādhi*), and because it is not empty quiescence, it is not the compassion directed toward phenomena (*dharma-ālambana-maitrī*).

Because it is free from attachment and views, it is not the compassion directed toward sentient beings (*sattva-ālambana-maitrī*). The two aforementioned types of compassion [are distinct] from bodhi...
Because the Great Compassion that is without conditions belongs solely to the Tathāgata, the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*, in the "Chapter on Brahma-conduct," states:
"If compassion exists, it neither exists nor does not exist; such compassion is not the domain of Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, yet it is not different from that of the partial Bodhisattvas.
However, for partial Bodhisattvas, hearing the Dharma is easily transformed, though they still possess only a small portion of it."

Because the two vehicles are entirely deficient in this regard, it is addressed to them alone. Furthermore, from the twelve links of dependent origination, the seven factors of enlightenment, the eightfold noble path, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and all the supernatural powers of the Buddhas, there is not one that does not take loving-kindness as its root.

For example, when Devadatta instructed King Ajātaśatru to release his intoxicated elephant in an attempt to harm the Tathāgata, the Tathāgata immediately entered into a state of loving-kindness at that moment.
When he extended his hand and pointed toward them, five lions and elephants appeared at his five fingers; seeing this, they were struck with fear.
One should know that these were all the power of the roots of goodness and compassion. [This was recorded by] Sengzhao, using the style of Master Daorong.
Master Zhaolun was like a profound commentary that supplements the Way of the past;

Dharma Master Rong of Jijun and Linlü was a man of exceptional talent whose understanding was peerless, both within and without, as he roamed through the depths of the inner and outer scriptures. When Kumārajīva entered Guanzhong, Rong went there to seek instruction.

Master Śrīmitra marveled at him and ordered him to lecture on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Śrīmitra himself listened to it and sighed in praise, saying: "The flourishing of the Buddha-dharma depends upon Rong."

As for this person, he initially followed the "Nine Paths" (Jiuzhe) of Master Daorong; the eighth record therein states that after Master Kumārajīva completed the translation, Master Rui lectured upon it and expanded it into nine paths.
At that time, people called him the Dharma Master of the Nine Paths: First, the Path of the Sage’s Manifestation and Response;
Second, the Path of Entering the Teachings and Returning to the True; Third, the Path of the Flourishing and the Latent Manifestation; Fourth... [and so forth].

1. The Chapter on Describing the Circumstances of Success and Failure; 2. The Chapter on Manifesting the Causes through Advancement and Realization; 3. The Chapter on Praising Conduct and Learning; 4. The Chapter on the Non-arising of Essence and Trace; 5.
The Chapter on Raising the Cause to Illustrate the Subtlety of the Fruit; 6. The Chapter on Praising the Far-reaching Salvation. The first is the Introductory Chapter (*Nidāna-parivarta*);
the next seven constitute the Main Body (*Śarīra*); and the last one is the Dissemination (*Pariṇāmanā*). The titles are most beautiful, yet the essence of the doctrine—
I fear that what is currently [stated] may be based on Master Rong’s interpretation of Master Rui’s *Jiuzhe yi* (The Meaning of the Nine Paths), or perhaps it uses what Master Rong himself employed;
for this reason, it was stated thus. Otherwise, the current character "Rong" (融) must be changed to the character "Rui" (叡).
As stated in the verses of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and explained in the *Shiqian*:
"For example, a poor man spends all day counting the treasures of others, yet he himself possesses not even half a coin.
Likewise, it is the same with much learning if one does not practice the Dharma."
Zhuangzi says, "Obtaining the rabbit," etc.
In the twenty-sixth chapter of the *Zhuangzi*, "Waiwu" (External Things), it is said: "The trap is for the sake of the fish;
once the fish is caught, one forgets the trap. The snare is for the sake of the rabbit; once the rabbit is caught, one forgets the snare. Words are for the sake of..."
"When one has attained the meaning, one forgets the words; how could I find someone who has forgotten the words and converse with them?

The commentary states: "The trap for fish is merely a means. It is made of bamboo, hence the character contains the radical for 'bamboo' (艸), though there are also versions with the radical for 'grass' (艹).
Fragrant grass can be used as bait for fish; one places fragrant grass within a wooden frame to catch fish."
The term *tí* (蹄) refers to a rabbit snare; it is also a rabbit trap used to bind and tether the legs of a rabbit.

Now, the author of this record follows the *Shuowen Jiezi*, which states that the character must be written as *dí* (罤), meaning a rabbit net; whereas the character *zhào* (罩)—specifically *zhì* (罣)—refers to the cord of the rabbit net.
The text quotes from a sūtra stating that after departing the palace of the Śākyas, he attained bodhi not far from the city of Gayā.
The *Xiyuji* (Records of the Western Regions) states that the country of Kanyākubja is the former name for Kapilavastu.
To the southwest of the monastery of the master Śīlabhadra in the kingdom of Magadha, one travels four or five li and crosses the Nirañjanā River.

Following the river, one arrives at the city of Gayā. This city is险固 (xian gu—precipitous and fortified), with no inhabitants other than some one thousand households of Brahmins who do not acknowledge the King as their sovereign;
all people revere and honor them. Traveling west from the city for five or six *li*, one reaches Mount Gayā, where the valleys and gullies are fragrant and serene.
According to the local customs of India, it is called the "Numinous Mountain" (*Lingshan*). To the southeast is the [site of] Gayā...

From the place where Yaśodīpa (Yana-ti-er) of the Kāśyapa clan practiced fire-worship, one crosses a great river to the east and arrives at Mount Prāgbodhi (Bō-lu-jí pútí shān), which in the language of Táng means "Mountain of Prior Perfect Enlightenment. Fourteen or fifteen *li* to the southwest of this mountain is a Pippala tree;
when the Buddha was in the world, it stood several hundred feet high, and it was beneath it that he sat and attained enlightenment.
Because the Samyaksaṃbuddha attained enlightenment there, it is called the Bodhi Tree.
As for the phrase "not far," it means that the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) is approximately twenty *li* from the city of Gayā.
The *Ji* (Commentary) says: "As if observing one's fingers and palm.
The *Analects* says: "Regarding the *Di* sacrifice, from the point after the libation has been poured, I do not wish to observe it.
Someone asked about the principles of the *Di* sacrifice, and the Master said, "I do not know them. One who knows its principles would handle the affairs of the world as if pointing at his own palm."
Since the passage concerning "ripening subsequent to the fruit" states that the past constitutes ripening, I suspect the character "near" (近) should be changed to "past" (過).
If one were to speak of it as "near," then one would be referring to the past as being near.
Regarding the phrase "適過世脫" (shì guò shì tuō),
since it is stated that "recently" (jìn shì) has been altered to "escaped" (tuō), I fear the character "guò" (over/erroneous) must be changed to "jìn" (recent). However,
if one intends to point to the recent as being erroneous, then there is no need for such a change.
The character "jin" (near) in the phrase "jinri" (near today) is an error; it should read "jinsi" (recent times).
Regarding the three periods and nine periods, see the *Zhiguan ji* and other such works.
The text of the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) contains some slight errors and omissions; I shall now cite it in full.
Both the old *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, fascicle 31, and the new *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, fascicle 53, state that there are ten ways of explaining the three periods of time:
namely, explaining the past within the past, explaining the future within the past, and explaining the present within the past.
To speak of the future world in terms of the past world; to speak of the future world in terms of the present world; to speak of the future world in terms of the inexhaustible;
to speak of the present world in terms of the past world; to speak of the present world in terms of the future world; to speak of the present world in terms of equality;
and to speak of the three periods of time as being a single thought-moment—these are the ten. Furthermore, the *Ratnavyuha Sūtra* (瓔珞經) states:
The Devaputra Ubhayatovimukta asked the Buddha, "Are there Buddhas in all three periods of time? The Buddha said, "What three periods of time do you ask about?
The past? The present? Or the future? You should know that this also refers to the meaning of the nine periods."
The *Wenju* (Exegesis on the Text) states:

"Regarding 'the lion’s vigorous display' (*siṃhavijṛmbhita*), Master [Daoxuan] says that both 'lion's yawn' (*siṃhavijṛmbha*) and 'vigorous display' (*vijṛmbhita*) describe the state of stretching out the four limbs to achieve thorough relaxation.

Furthermore, it notes: "In the phrase 'the Buddha responds to the capacity' (*fo cheng ji*), the character '承' (*cheng*) is an error; it should be '乘' (*cheng'), as found in the *Amitāyurdhyāna Sūtra*."
The *Śū* (Commentary) states: "The Great Sage bestows compassion and expounds the Dharma according to the capacities [of beings]. The *Jì* (Record) states:

"Some, based on the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra* and others, provide this explanation within the *Fahua xuanzan* (Profound Commentary on the Lotus Sutra) by Ci'en; if one discusses the five hundred [disciples] alone, they are still within the period of the True Dharma (*saddharma*)."
Regarding the Dharma, it is said that there are five periods of five hundred years each; let us follow one perspective regarding the beginning of the Final Dharma (mofa).
The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra-śāstra* states that the scriptures present differing accounts: some say that the True Dharma (zhengfa) and the Semblance Dharma (xiangfa) each last for one thousand years;

some say each lasts for five hundred years; some say the True Dharma lasts five hundred years and the Semblance Dharma lasts one thousand years; others say the True Dharma lasts one hundred years; or others say... [text ends].
The eighty [intermediate kalpas] are said to be "brief" or "prolonged" merely because the conditions for their existence vary in intensity.

Furthermore, it is said that the True Dharma (saddharma) would have lasted for a thousand years, but because women were permitted to go forth [into the monastic order], it was reduced by five hundred years.
I shall now briefly record the passage from the *Mahāvaipulya-sūtra* concerning the infant. The sūtra states: "An infant is unable to arise, stand, come, go, or speak; the Tathāgata is likewise.
Because he does not give rise to the marks of dharmas, he is called 'non-arising'; because he does not cling to any dharmas, he is called 'non-abiding'; his conduct is without..."

Because it is subject to movement and fluctuation, it is called "not coming"; because it has already reached nirvāṇa, it is called "not going. What is spoken is non-speaking, which is called the absence of speech.
Furthermore, just as an infant can utter great words, the Tathāgata is likewise; he speaks of "great words," namely *bha* and *ja*.
*Bha* refers to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and *ja* refers to the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). Moreover, an infant does not know suffering.

Just as one delights in day and night, so too does the Bodhisattva for the sake of sentient beings; because his mind is impartial, he perceives neither suffering nor pleasure, nor the characteristics of day or night.
Furthermore, because there are no distinctions such as parent or relative, nor near or distant, he is like an infant who cannot perform great or small deeds;
likewise, the Bodhisattva does not commit the five heinous crimes, and thus does not perform great [evil].
Because they lack the mind of the two vehicles, they do not engage in the small [vehicle].
Furthermore, when an infant cries, the parents immediately stop it with yellow leaves from a *śiṃśapā* tree, saying, "Do not cry, do not cry; I will give you gold.
Upon seeing this, the infant forms the perception that it is real gold and stops crying; yet these yellow leaves are in reality neither gold nor wood.
When people see ox-wood, horse-wood, male-wood, female-wood, or infant-wood, they likewise give rise to the perceptions of "male" or "female";
the Tathāgata is also like this. When he sees those who commit evil deeds, he speaks to them of the pleasures of the five desires in the celestial palaces.
Upon hearing this, sentient beings, desiring to be born in heaven, cease their evil actions; yet this is actually nothing but the impermanence of birth and death. Furthermore, as for infants...
