Regarding the fourteen transformations:
there are two transformations in the first dhyāna, three in the second, four in the third, and five in the fourth.
A detailed explanation is provided in the *Fajie Cidi* (The Sequential Order of the Dharma Realm).

Next, one contemplates those who possess both [insight and concentration] and are liberated from both sides; it is only when these are fully present that one possesses "contemplative dhyāna" (*vipaśyanā-dhyāna*). One who possesses contemplative dhyāna will necessarily attain the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha-samāpatti*), the eight liberations (*aṣṭa-vimokṣa*), and so forth—these are called contemplative dhyāna.
The nine successive attainments (*navānupūrva-vihāra-samāpatti*) are called "refined dhyāna" (*pariśuddha-dhyāna*). Thus spoke the Son of the Teacher.
The swift [attainment] is called the "perfuming meditation" (vāsanā-dhyāna), while the transcendent samādhi is called the "cultivation meditation" (bhāvanā-dhyāna).

According to the Abhidharma, one who attains the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) is called "liberated in both ways" (ubhayatobhāga-vimukta); one who does not attain this single absorption is merely called "liberated by wisdom" (prajñā-vimukta).
Next, the ten *kṛtsnāyatana*s—
blue, yellow, red, white, earth, water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness— all pervade every location.

In the *Miaoxuan* (The Profound Meaning), the "Saintly Practices" (*ārya-caryā*) and the "Dhyāna Section" clarify two types of dhyāna:

first, contaminated (*sāsrava*) dharmas, which refer to the four fundamental dhyānas, the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), and the four formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*); second, uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) dharmas, which refer to the nine notions (*navasaṃjñā*), the eight recollections (*aṣṭānusmṛti*), the ten notions (*daśasaṃjñā*), and so forth, as fully detailed in those texts.
The eighteen transformations are as recorded in the tenth fascicle of the *Zhiguan*:
now, to summarize them in verse: (1) water issues from the right side; (2) fire issues from the left side; (3) water issues from the left side; (4) fire issues from the right side;
(5–8) water and fire issue from above and below the body, making four [transformations], which together with the preceding ones total eight; (9) walking on water as if on land; (10) walking on land.
11. Like water, he disappears from mid-air and reappears on the ground; 12. he disappears from the ground and reappears in mid-air.

again, he manifests a small body (19). Regarding the "trembling": 1. because he moves the various elements through mastery over meditative concentration (*samādhi*); 2. blazing.
1. Emission from all parts of the body: emitting fire and pouring forth water; 2. Various colors: because the light is distributed throughout all worlds; 3. Threefold distribution:

The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "When the śramaṇa Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa had not yet left the household life, he entered the sea to seek jewels; he lost his companions and was alone."
While traveling, he saw a tree named Pāriyātra and stayed overnight beneath it.
As evening fell and night set in, a grove appeared from within it, and men and women of exquisite beauty, wearing celestial jewel crowns, emerged and enjoyed themselves together.
When the night passed and day broke, they instantly vanished. Then a pack of dogs came and devoured the flesh of those men until only their bones remained.

Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa then regretted not having asked that person what karma he had previously performed to now receive such retribution—being good by night and evil by day—and thought, "I should stay here and wait to ask him. When night fell, it was once again as before:
the man and woman were handsome and enjoyed themselves together. Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa asked, "What conduct did you practice to now receive this retribution—being [good] by night..."
The wicked man named Śubhadivasa replied: "In the country of Aśmaka-āpade, there was a certain butcher.
At that time, the Elder Mahākātyāyana would come and go to my house, and I constantly provided him with clothing and food.
He always told me, 'Do not commit various evils, lest you later undergo great suffering. When I heard this, I did not [heed it]."
At that time, Kātyāyana spoke to me again, saying, "You have committed this evil; is it more frequent by day or by night? I replied, "It is more frequent by day.
He then said to me, "You should now receive the five precepts at night; you may thereby obtain a small measure of merit. I immediately accepted them.
By reason of these causes and conditions, I have now obtained this retribution: good at night and evil by day. Thus it was with Akṣobhya.
Proceeding further, he again saw two trees named Pāru; he stayed beneath them to rest for the night until daybreak.
Therein appeared a man and a woman of handsome appearance, wearing celestial jewel crowns, who took pleasure together.
When day turned to night, they both vanished, and centipedes emerged to devour the man.
When the flesh was consumed and only the bones remained, the night passed into day, and as before, he indulged in pleasures.
Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa asked him, "What practice did you perform to obtain this retribution—good by day but evil by night?
The man replied, "In the country of Aśmaka-āpajjāla, a certain man committed adultery with another's wife; Mahākātyāyana would frequently enter and leave my house."
He instructed me, saying, "Do not commit evil deeds, lest you suffer great misery hereafter. I did not follow his advice.
He spoke to me again, saying, "Regarding this matter, do you commit it more by day or more by night? I replied, "More by night.
Then Kātyāyana said to me, "You should now receive the five precepts during the day; thus you may obtain some slight merit. At that time, following his instruction, I immediately received them.
"By reason of these five precepts, one now receives this retribution: good by day and evil by night.
The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śūtra* (Sapoduo lun) states that Kātyāyana manifested this event through transformation in order to deliver Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa, but it was not actually so.
Cūḍapanthaka and others were also called Cūḍapanthaka, which means "born by the side of a small path," or alternatively "snake-slave" because he was born on a road; he was by nature very dull-witted.
In the past, he was a Dharma Master who was well-versed in the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Abhidharma, and had five hundred disciples.
Because he was stingy with the Buddha-dharma and did not teach others, he now receives this retribution of folly.
Kātyāyana heard this with his divine ear;
according to the sūtra, it was actually Śāriputra who heard it with his divine ear. Please verify this further.
The commentary states: "The four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) are:

first, the unimpeded knowledge of the ultimate meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*), which is like the dharma-realm; second, the unimpeded knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*); third, the unimpeded knowledge of language (*niruktipratisaṃvid*); and fourth, the unimpeded knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhānapratisaṃvid*). A detailed explanation is provided therein."
All take the delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) as their object.

As stated in the tenth fascicle of the *Zhiguan* (Calming and Contemplation), these delusions of views are one [in nature] yet can treat four [different types of practitioners], which differs from the various preceding texts where the persons of the four teachings all treat the delusions of views—this is precisely that meaning.
Although there are four teachings, if one examines the initial mind, it does not exceed two [categories]. First...

Regarding this, there are two points: first, those of the three preceding vehicles who treat views as the entry into emptiness; second, those of the Perfect Vehicle for whom views are the Dharma-realm.
These two meanings are self-evident;
do not conceive of them as divergent paths. As the Sūtra says: "Ānanda..."
Regarding the character *ā* (阿), the *Ētù* (遏兔) is pronounced with the *nǎihóu* (乃侯) rhyme; Cien (慈恩) states it should instead be written as *róu* (羺).
The *Jì* (記) says that while the characteristics of giving (*dāna*) are explained extensively here, this is not urgent for the present context;
since the commentaries (*zhāngshù*) of other schools mostly discuss this matter, [the author] has rejected them.
"Grass" (cao) in "grass-draft" (caochuang) also signifies "initial.
The *Zhouyi* states, "Heaven creates in the chaotic obscurity," and the *Lunyu* says, "Regarding the formulation of mandates, Bi Shen drafted the initial version.
The *Zhengyi* explains that "drafting" (chuang) carries the meaning of the very beginning.
As for Zhu Daosheng, he was originally not surnamed Zhu;
the Dharma Master’s original surname was Wei, and he was a native of Julu. From his youth, he was exceptionally brilliant and possessed a spiritual wisdom that seemed divine.
Later, encountering the śramaṇa Zhu Fatai, he took refuge in him and adopted the teacher’s surname. He devoted himself to his studies under the master and subsequently received full instruction.
Upon entering Chang’an, he again studied under Kumārajīva.
Regarding the phrase "Fuṣa Buddha," it is also called Tiṣya, which is translated as "Luminous. Furthermore, the preceding passage states that the Duke of Zhou sighed, saying, "I am Wen."
Regarding the phrase "the sons of the king" and so forth, the text is derived from the *Shiji*, in the "Genealogy of the Duke of Zhou.

"Washing three times and grasping [the hair]" means washing the hair three times and grasping it each time. "Eating three times and spitting out the food" means eating three times and spitting out the food each time.

Washing the hair three times and grasping it, and eating three times and spitting out the food, he would rise to wait upon scholars even while doing so; he did this because he feared losing the worthy men of the world. Therefore, it is so stated.
The honoring of the worthy is such as this.
His parents wished to test him, so they went with empty vessels; upon opening them one after another, they found a hundred flavors fully provided.
Nalada thought to himself: "In the past, during the ninety-first kalpa, when the world was suffering from famine, I sold firewood."
When a Pratyekabuddha went begging for alms and was invited into my home, I offered him a gruel made of millet seeds;
immediately in this present life, I obtained immeasurable merit. From that time until now, throughout ninety-one kalpas, whether in the heavens or among humans, I have lacked for nothing.
Even until this present life, while I was still living as a householder, I always lived in leisure and did not take pleasure in worldly affairs.
My elder brother Mahānāma was always speaking resentful words about my mother, saying, "My son possesses great merit.
Mahānāma said, "I alone toil and worry over the household and its fields and business, while he merely lies in leisure, eating and sleeping; how can you say he has merit?
My mother, wishing to test me, sent me to the fields to supervise the work and instructed that no food be sent to me. I grew suspicious regarding the food.
When it was late, I sent someone to my mother to ask for food. My mother then sent someone to tell me, "There is nothing to give.
I returned and reported this, saying, "I pray only that you send me 'nothing at all'.
Once my mother heard this, she immediately took a precious vessel, adorned its contents, covered them with a cloth, and sent it to me, saying, "Mahānāma."
Following him to observe, he had already arrived at my location; I removed his cloth bundle, and the table was completely filled with food and drink of a hundred flavors.
The Record states: "Sleep is the food of the eyes," as noted in the fourth commentary on *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*.
The *Ekottarika-āgama* states: While the Buddha was preaching the Dharma for the sake of Anāthapiṇḍada, Aniruddha fell asleep with his eyes open during the discourse.
The Buddha then rebuked him. Aniruddha said to the Buddha, "From this day forward, even if my body were to dissolve and my flesh rot away, I shall never again sleep with my eyes open.
Because of this, he remained awake until dawn; consequently, his faculty of sight was lost. The Buddha said, "For one who exerts diligent effort, it is like restlessness and frivolity."
Regarding those associated with indolence, they are associated with the fetters and latent tendencies. In your practice of the Middle Way, everything exists by means of nutriment:
the eye has sleep as its nutriment, and so on, until the mind has mental phenomena as its nutriment.
In the *Kathina-saṃgraha*, nineteen Buddhas told Nanda: "Nanda, you should act as a bhikṣu and explain the *kathina*.

Thereupon, Nanda recounted his own account of leaving the household life to seek the Way, his weariness with the world, his study of the Dharma, and how he distanced himself from the ten unwholesome actions while guarding the sense faculties.
One must uphold the prohibitive precepts and cultivate meditative concentration to attain supernormal powers before one may receive the *kāṭhina* robe and so forth.

The *Nanshan lüchao* (Commentary on the Nanshan Vinaya) quotes the *Vidyāmātra-siddhi-śāstra* (or *Abhidharma-vibhāṣā-śāstra*), which translates it as "firm and solid" (*kaṭhina*), because it enables one to obtain many robes and ensures that the robes do not fall into decay.
It is also called "difficult to live by" (*dullabha-jīvita*), for it is difficult for the poor to sustain their lives; by relinquishing these meager resources, one enters into the merit of this robe.
Its virtue is as supreme as the great mountain Sumeru; it is also called "solid" (*khaṭhinī*) or "sheltering" (*chādanī*).

Translated into Chinese as "the robe for rewarding the good and punishing the evil," it was granted to those who completed the *pūrvavārṣika* (first) retreat, while those who completed the *paścimavārṣika* (second) retreat did not receive it.
It is also termed the "robe of merit" (*guṇavastra*), because by the Saṃgha collectively receiving this robe, one invokes five kinds of beneficial merits.
The *Caturvargika-vinaya* states that there are five matters by which one receives the *kaṭhina* robe:

namely, possessing extra robes, not losing the [status of] robes, eating in a separate group, eating in succession, and entering a village without informing a bhikṣu. Having received the *kaṭhina* robe, one obtains these five matters:
namely, one may keep extra robes, stay apart from one’s robes overnight, eat in a separate group, eat in succession, and enter a village without informing [a bhikṣu].
[The section on] "Falling" [is concluded]. Regarding the sequential and non-sequential [practices], as recorded in the third commentary on *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*:

the three types of *śamatha* and the three types of *vipaśyanā* serve as the causes, while the three types of wisdom (*jñāna*) and the three types of vision (*cakṣus*) obtained thereby constitute the fruits; this is what is termed "sequential."
In this context, cessation (śamatha) is itself insight (vipaśyanā), and insight is itself cessation; the eye is itself wisdom (jñāna), and wisdom is itself the eye.
Because it is the eye, it is discussed as seeing; because it is wisdom, it is discussed as knowing. The Buddha’s eye possesses the five eyes, and the Buddha’s wisdom possesses the three knowledges;
this is what is meant by "non-sequential."
The *Wenju* (Textual Commentary) states: "The trace [of his attainment] is shown as the 'half-head' divine eye (*divyacakṣus*).

The *Jingming Guangshu* (Extensive Commentary on the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*) states: "Nanda practiced dhyāna and attained the pure derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) of the four great elements known as the 'half-head' divine eye;
from the upper half of his head, he was able to see all forms, observing the trichiliocosm as if it were an *āmala* fruit."
According to the *Tripiṭaka*, when a Buddha attains the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), his entire head becomes pure in color, allowing him to see all things without obstruction.
The *Mahā-śāstra* states that the divine eye obtained as a karmic reward (*vipākaja*) resides within the physical eye; it is the divine eye that opens up so that the physical eye may perceive forms.
This is because, since the divinely rewarded eye already exists within the physical eye, we know that the cultivated divine eye (*bhāvanā-maya*) must likewise be present there.
Because it must exist outside of the fleshly eye, when Aniruddha’s fleshly eye was lost, his *divyacakṣus* (heavenly eye) became pure over half of his head.
Although the Buddha’s fleshly eye is clear according to the Tripiṭaka teaching, his *divyacakṣus* is pure throughout his entire head;
thus we know that "half" is designated in contrast to "whole. Since the heavenly eye is located above, it is said to be on the head, whether it occupies half the head or the whole.

Regarding the "head" and "ear," some have used the character for "head" (*mūrdhan*) to calculate the number of heads; this is likely due to not having read the *Guangshu* (Extensive Commentary), resulting in such forced interpretation.
The wording can be verified in the Āgamas.
The Madhyama Āgama, fascicle 42, states: "The Buddha was traveling through the kingdom of Magadha and arrived at Rājagṛha.
At that time, the World-Honored One went to the house of a potter and said to him, 'I wish to stay overnight;
will you grant me leave? The potter replied, 'I have no objection, but there is already a bhikṣu staying here. If he permits it, you may do so.'"
While he was staying there at his pleasure, the bhikṣu Vakkali had already been inside that potter’s workshop.
The Blessed One said to him: "I wish to stay overnight here; will you grant me permission? The bhikṣu replied: "Sir, I have no objection.
A grass mat has already been spread out in this potter’s workshop; if you wish to stay, you may do as you please."

At that time, the World-Honored One spread out his sitting mat (*niṣīdana*) upon the seat of grass and sat cross-legged, remaining in silent meditative concentration throughout the night. The bhikṣu likewise remained in quietude throughout the night.
Then the World-Honored One thought to himself, "This bhikṣu is truly marvelous and extraordinary," and he asked him: "Who is your teacher? Upon whom do you rely?"

“Who has gone forth to study the Way and received the Dharma? A bhikṣu replied: “The śramaṇa Gautama, a scion of the Śākyas, out of supreme faith has left his home for the homeless life to study the Way.
Having shaved off his hair and beard and donned the saffron robes, he has attained unsurpassed enlightenment;
he is my teacher. Relying upon him, I have gone forth to study the Way. The World-Honored One asked: “Have you seen him?”
The monk replied, "No, World-Honored One, I have never seen him. The World-Honored One asked again, "If you were to see your teacher, would you recognize him?

The monk replied, "Even if I were to see him, I would not recognize him; I have only heard that he is one who possesses the ten titles of a Tathāgata, and it was upon hearing this that I went forth into homelessness.
The World-Honored One said, "I shall preach the Dharma for you; you should listen attentively."
The bhikṣu replied, “Yes, indeed. The Buddha said to the bhikṣu: “A person consists of six elements, six bases of contact, eighteen mental explorations, and four abodes.
As for the six elements, they are earth, water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness.
Because of these six, there are the six bases of contact, namely: eye-contact seeing forms, ear-contact hearing sounds, nose-contact [smelling odors]...”

Through smelling odors, tasting flavors with the tongue, feeling tangibles with the body-faculty, and cognizing mental objects through mind-contact—due to these six, there are eighteen mental explorations (*manopavicāra*).
That is to say: when the eye sees a form, one dwells contemplating the form with joy, one dwells contemplating the form with sorrow, or one dwells contemplating the form with equanimity.
It is the same for the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. Because of this, there are four [categories].
The abodes are as follows: the abode of ultimate truth, the abode of wisdom, the abode of generosity, and the abode of tranquility.
It is for this reason that it is said that one possesses heedfulness and wisdom. If a bhikṣu discerns the element of the body, he reflects:
"In this body of mine there is the internal earth element which undergoes birth, namely hair, body hair, nails, teeth, and so forth, as well as the external earth element."
"None of these are mine; I do not belong to them, nor do they belong to a self, nor are they a deity.
Observing with wisdom in this way, one knows it as it truly is and does not become stained by or attached to it. This is called the heedful wisdom of a bhikṣu.

In this manner, one should likewise observe fire, water, wind, space, and consciousness—both internally and externally—one by one, as explained at length in the Sūtras. Having taught this Dharma, [the Buddha said: "Bhikṣus..."
When the bhikṣu Kālasiri had distanced himself from dust and removed defilement, and the Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena had arisen, he dwelt in the realization of the fruit.
He immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and said: “Please allow me to repent. Because of my ignorance, I did not recognize the Tathāgata;
instead, I addressed the World-Honored One as ‘Your Majesty. I only pray that the Tathāgata will grant me permission to repent of my transgression.”
He addressed the bhikṣus, saying, "I permit you to repent your transgressions.
The record states that if one were to follow the lunar mansions (nakṣatras) of the Western regions, they would likewise be indeterminate;

as noted in the tenth fascicle of the *Zhiguan* commentary regarding the lunar mansions of this region: "The seven stars of the west are Kui, Lou, Wei, Mao, Bi, Zi, and Shen; the seven stars of the south are..."
The seven stars of the East are Jing, Gui, Liu, Xing, Zhang, Yi, and Zhen; the seven stars of the North are Jiao, Kang, Di, Fang, Xin, Wei, and Ji;
the seven stars of the West are Dou, Niu, Nu, Xu, Wei, Shi, and Bi; and those stars of that region [the South] are Mao, Wei, Shi, Yi, Zui, Kou, and Liu.
Thus they shift in succession, with seven stars for each quarter; this is due to the differences in the terrestrial regions.
Therefore, regarding the shifting of the three seats of the stars, if one were to follow what the Rishi Prabhāsa said to the Buddha in the Mahāsannipāta Sūtra—
that the twenty-eight lunar mansions originally began from the eastern asterisms of Ārdrā and Kṛttikā— then this would not account for the shifting of the three seats of the stars.
The *Wenju* (Textual Explanations) states: "The Buddha accepted the invitation of King Ajātaśatru... until they all ate horse barley.
The *Sapoduo* (Sarvāstivāda) school says it was called Ajātaśatru because he made offerings to the fire. The *Sifenlü* (Dharmaguptaka Vinaya) states:
"When the Buddha was in the country of Surāṣṭra and had traveled to the foot of a bilva tree, a brāhmaṇa immediately went there to invite the Buddha."

When the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus had accepted the invitation for the three-month summer retreat, this brāhmaṇa failed to provide any offerings. Why was this? It was the work of Māra Pāpīyān.
At that time, in the country of Vārāṇasī, there was a horse merchant who drove five hundred horses and stayed at the Piḷandhana forest for ninety days during the summer retreat.

At that time, grain was expensive and it was difficult to obtain through begging. When the bhikṣus went to beg, they were given five *sheng* (升) for each bhikṣu, while the Buddha received one *dou* (斗).

This continued daily. [The term] *chí* (呞)—the character is pronounced with the initial *qù* (切) and means to regurgitate and chew; [the character] *qiào* (哨)—pronounced with the initials *jiǎo* (且) and *zhào* (醮)—is an error;
it should be written as *jiào* (噍), pronounced with the initials *cái* (才) and *xiào* (笑), meaning to chew. [The term] *yí* (夷) means to eliminate; "not yet *yí*" (*wèiyí*) means not yet eliminated.
"Zhe" (者) means not yet extinguished. "Shà" (唼) is pronounced with the initial *suo* and *he* (合), or *suǒ* and *jiǎ* (甲). "Zhì" (摘) is pronounced *zhé* (陟革切); it means to take with the hand.
"Śrīṣa" (尸利沙) is the *śirīṣa* tree, which in this region is the *héshèn* (合棔) tree. There are two kinds; if it is named Śrīṣa, both its leaves and fruit [are so].

The tree called *śirīṣa* is large, while its leaves and fruits are all small; this tree occasionally grows in the low-lying villages east of the human realm, where it is mistakenly named the *sāla* tree.
Master Yijing states that this tree exists in the south of the Lingnan region.
Many texts claim that Śāriputra alone accepted the invitation from the Heavenly King, which differs from the present text.
The Sūtra states that in the name Revata,
the character "li" (離) is pronounced with a level tone (*ping sheng*).
The Commentary (*Ji*) states that the account of the two ghosts contending over a corpse is found in the seventh fascicle of the *Zhi guan* (止觀).
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 13, states: "It is like a person traveling far who stays alone overnight in an empty pavilion.
In the night, one ghost arrives carrying a corpse and places it before him. Then another ghost comes from behind and angrily reviles the first ghost, saying:
'This is my corpse; why have you brought it here? The first ghost replies: 'It was originally my property. Each of the two ghosts then..."
One hand grasped him from the front as the first ghost said, "You may ask this man.
The second ghost then asked, "Whose corpse is this? Who brought it here? The man reflected, "Both of these ghosts possess great power;
whether my words are true or false, neither will escape death. I shall speak the truth. He then answered the ghosts, "The one in front brought it here."
The great demon grew furious and tore out his hands and feet, casting them onto the ground. The first demon felt ashamed of this and took the corpse to replace them;
as soon as they were joined, the arms, hands, feet, and so forth were restored, and his entire body was transformed.
Thereupon, the two demons together devoured the newly acquired living body, each wiping their mouths and departing with their respective heads. The man then reflected upon his parents.
With his physical eyes, he saw that the food had been consumed; "Now this body of mine is entirely other people's flesh—is there a body, or is there no body?
As dawn broke, he sought the path and departed, whereupon he encountered a community of monks. He immediately asked them, "Is my body existent or non-existent?
The monks replied, "Your body is fundamentally and eternally non-existent; it is merely by means of the four [great elements]..."
Through this great harmony, he left the household life and attained the fruit of Arhatship.

Regarding the *Jinzang jing* (Sutra of the Golden Treasury), which was compiled by the Master of Discourse during the time when Yuwen Yong was cruelly persecuting the followers of Śākyamuni: there was a certain oral error in its transmission. It is said that at that time, when the teachings of the Buddha were being suppressed, a master of discourse collected [the fragments].

The essential meaning of the various sutras has been disseminated in the world and is titled the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* (Golden Treasury). This particular episode originally derives from the *Saṃyukta-ratnapiṭaka-sūtra*.
The sutra states: "In the past, in the kingdom of Kaśmīra, there was an Arhat named Revata who sat in meditation upon a mountain.
A certain person lost his ox and, following its tracks, arrived at that place. At that time, Revata was boiling grass, intending to dye [his robes]."
Suddenly, that grass transformed into beef, and the alms bowl he held turned into a cow's head. When the owner of the cow saw this, he seized him and took him before the king;
the king committed him to prison for twelve years, where he was constantly made to serve as a jailer’s cook, eating horses' fodder and clearing away dung.
After his karmic conditions were nearly exhausted, a disciple of Lyue who had attained Arhatship sought his teacher but could not find him.
He then saw him inside a prison in Kaśmīra. Thereupon, he went to the king and asked, "My teacher is in prison.
The king immediately issued an order for Revata to leave the prison; he rose into the air and performed the eighteen transformations.
When the king witnessed this, he sought his mercy and repented his transgression. The king then asked, "By what karmic conditions are you in this prison? Revata replied:
In the past, I also once lost my ox and followed its tracks to a mountain, where I saw a Pratyekabuddha sitting alone in meditation;

I immediately slandered him for a full day and night. Due to these causes and conditions, I fell into the three miserable realms, and as the remaining retribution was not yet exhausted, I became an Arhat and am still subjected to slander. Furthermore, the *Prajñāpradīpa-śāstra* also states that "Bhadraka..."
The statement that the bhikṣu was confined by King Brahmā for twelve years has this very meaning.
One should cite at length from the *Pratyutpanna-samādhi* (the *Banzhou sanmei*).

"Pratyutpanna" here is translated as "Buddha-standing. There are three meanings to "standing": first, the power of the Buddha; second, the power of samādhi; and third, [the power of] the practitioner.

By the power of the practitioner’s original merit, they are able to see the Buddhas of the ten directions appearing before them within meditative concentration (*samādhi*), just as a person with clear vision observes the stars on a clear night;
seeing the Buddhas of the ten directions is likewise manifold. Therefore, it is said that "the Buddhas stand [before them].
For a detailed account, one should refer to the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* (Cessation and Contemplation), though I cannot cite it here in full detail.
The extensive explanation of the conditions for pride is recorded in the second note of the *Zhiguan* (Cessation and Contemplation).
Regarding his crossing of a river where the current was so swift that it was difficult to cross, he rebuked it, saying, "You little slave, stop flowing!

The river deity became enraged and went to the Buddha to complain, saying, "Pilindavatsa has insulted me. The Buddha then commanded Pilindavatsa to perform a repentance before the river deity; thus Pilindavatsa repented.
He called out, "Little maid, come here; I shall perform repentance for you! The crowd laughed and said, "To repent and yet still revile [us]!
The Buddha asked the River God, "Did you see Piṅgala joining his palms? He replied, "I saw him.

The Buddha said, "Since he has already repented and is no longer arrogant, yet still speaks these words, you should know that this person acted as a Brahmin for five hundred lifetimes. Furthermore, I have seen..."
In a previous life, the River Deity had been her own servant; she was habitually arrogant and used to deriding others with mere words, as was her natural practice.
The text states that she would even "sell her nature."
In the *Yinyi* (Phonetics and Meanings) of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, it states that *Luti* is a personal name; this is translated as "the surname of the seller.

*Ti* is pronounced with the two phonetic components *tu* and *di* (or *chì-xì*). It is also written as *Sajulu-ti*. The *Wubai dizi benqi jing* (Sutra on the Original Arisings of the Five Hundred Disciples) states it is the surname *Xiong*;
the *Yinyi* says "Xiong" is incorrect; it should be written as *Xiong* with the phonetic component *xiu* and the radical *zheng* (i.e., *xióng*), and it is also permitted to be read as *Xuán*.

he is so named because he is able to courageously bestow the Dharma-treasure of the true reality (*dharmatā*) of both the mundane and supramundane realms, by means of seeking [enlightenment] above and transforming [beings] below, based upon the realm of the unconditioned truth (*anabhisaṃskāra-satya*).

Therefore, "Precious Moon" (*ratnacandra*) refers to that which is realized—the three truths (*trisatya*), perfect and subtle, venerable like a treasure, and capable of illuminating all things perfectly, lovely like the moon.
"Moonlight" (*candraprabhā*) refers to the nature of the four virtues (*caturguṇa*); being free from all feverish afflictions, it is cool like moonlight and destroys darkness.
"Full Moon" (*pūrṇacandra*) refers to the perfect realization of the three bodies (*trikāya*), which is without deficiency or diminution. It is called "Great" (*mahā-*)...

"Power" (*bala*) refers to the great functional efficacy arising from the profound union of object and wisdom. "Infinite power" (*ananta-bala*) means that this great functional efficacy pervades the entire *dharmadhātu* without limit.

"Transcending the three realms" (*traidhātuka-vyatīta*) means that through the wondrous realization of the true and eternal, one transcends both the *pariccheda* (segmented) and *pariṇāma* (evolutionary) forms of birth-and-death.
"Jewel-accumulation" (*ratna-koṭi*) means that the three virtues (*triguṇa*), being like jewels, do not disperse; thus they are called "accumulation. Because they are vast, they are called "Great."

28. The Gaṇakāra devas; 29. The Cakravartana devas; 30. The Urdhvasrotas devas; 31.
The Tejaḥprabhāsa devas; 32. The Tejoraśmicakra devas; 3. [The third group].
The thirteen Śuddhāvāsa devas. The Bhadrakalpa is also called the Bhadrakalpa;
the Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra states that within this single kalpa, one thousand Buddhas appear, and these are the Śuddhāvāsa devas.
Because seeing this brings joy, it is called "Good" (*śubha*); it is also called "Worthy" (*bhadra*) because a thousand sages appear in the world. Question:
How do the gods of the Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*) know that there will be a thousand Buddhas in this kalpa? Answer:

After the previous kalpa had already been destroyed and everything was utterly empty, a great flood arose; from the bottom of the water, a thousand lotuses made of the seven precious jewels emerged, radiating light.
This is precisely the sign of the thousand Buddhas; thus, when the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens perceive it, they know that the thousand Buddhas are appearing in the world.
The Record states that this surpasses the Bhadrakalpa, as detailed in the Prajñāpāramitā.
The passage originates from the *Ratnavyuha-sūtra* (瓔珞經). Within its prose, it states "two thousand twenty-four kalpas," which I suspect is an error;
it should simply read "twenty-four. Thus, the *Ratnavyuha* says:

"O Śakra, Lord of Devas, as for the multitude of your meritorious practices, they have passed beyond the brothers of a thousand Buddhas and no longer bear the name of the Bhadrakalpa; the interval between them is forever vast."
After twenty-four intermediate kalpas have passed, a Buddha shall appear in a land named Universal Endurance (*Sarvakṣānti*).
That Buddha’s lifespan shall be seven kalpas, and his Dharma shall remain for another seven kalpas. Once that Dharma has completely vanished, a vast void shall endure for five kalpas.
You shall then succeed to the rank of Tathāgata in that buddha-field, with the name Honored One Without Attachment (*Asaṅga*), and you shall teach and transform an incalculable number of beings.
Having gauged the capacities of sentient beings, I have further examined various repositories and compiled two thousand characters to clarify the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
I request that you seek this out to distinguish errors from the correct text.
As the text states: "gandharva."
This refers to the celestial deity who seeks fragrance through conduct (*gandharva*), a god of worldly pleasures.
*Pūtana* means a preeminent among the stinking hungry ghosts (*preta*).
Pretas— translated here as "ancestral hungry ghosts"— are the lowest among [the classes of] hungry ghosts.
Kumbhāṇḍas...
This is called the "jar-shaped" [demon], which somewhat resembles a winter melon.
*Piśāca* means "one who devours vital essence"; it refers to one who devours the vital essence of humans and the five grains. It is also called "the madman."
They are ghosts (*piśāca*).
*Rākṣasa* is translated here as "the Terrifying" or also as "the Violent and Evil."
*Yakṣa* is translated here as "light and swift" (*qīngjié*); the new translation renders it *yàochā*.
The *Record* states that according to the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra*, each of the four tiers has ten dwelling places, as described in the *Xuánwén* (Explanatory Text).

The *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra* states that sixty thousand mountains surround Mount Sumeru. On the four terraces of Mount Sumeru dwell the Mālādhāra devas, who have ten abodes, each measuring one thousand yojanas.
To the north are four [terraces], and the others [the other three directions] each have two.
Of the four northern ones, the first is named Kāmadhara; continuing eastward, the second is named Cāraṇa; the third is the Kālotpala devas.
Furthermore, the first of the ten abodes of the Trāyastriṃśa gods is named Caru-padmaka, and so on, up to the tenth, named Samtuṣita;
the third, the Tuṣita gods, also has ten abodes, the first of which is named Nandana and the tenth is named Nitya-vihāra;
the fourth, the Nirmanarati gods, also has ten abodes, the first of which is named Gandharva and the tenth is named Samyak-caryā.
It is twenty-four thousand *li* wide; its origin is unknown.

The third fascicle of the *Loutan jing* (Ratnakūṭa-sūtra) states: "To the east of Mount Sumeru, the King of Mountains, forty thousand *li* away, lies the city of the Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra named Xiánshàngwángchù (Worthy Superior King’s Abode), which is twenty-four thousand *li* in both width and length."
The villages were adorned with sevenfold railings made of the seven treasures; the same was true for the south, west, and north, as fully described in the sutra.

I am unable to cite the passage in full here; regarding the statement in the current record that "the source is unknown," Master Jingxi searched the entire Tripitaka extensively, and while his interpretations of the meanings were profound, his admission of not knowing this particular matter is truly due to the vastness of the underlying causes and conditions.
The deeds of the Master are vast and numerous; although I have read them, it is ultimately difficult to record them all completely.
At the time of this composition, some may have been forgotten. One must not, on account of this, harbor doubts regarding his Great Way.
The *Twenty-eight Sections of the Mahāmāyūrī-vidyārājñī Sūtra* states: "In each of the four directions there are four sections; in the six directions, this constitutes twenty-four sections.
With one section in each of the four intermediate directions, they total twenty-eight sections. Furthermore, another explanation says that there are five sections in each direction. That is to say:
Earth, water, fire, wind, space, and the four directions constitute twenty divisions; together with the eight classes led by the Four Great Kings, they form twenty-eight divisions.
[The distance is] one *krośa*.

According to the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, this is two *li*; the claim that each of the four parts increases by one is likely an error, and it should rather be stated that each part of the four increases by one.
Regarding the question posed by Kokālika to the Brahmā King, "Why have you come here having attained the state of an Anāgāmin? and so forth:
The *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra* states that Kokālika is translated as "one of evil times.
The *Ratnarāśi Sūtra* clarifies that this merely means he does not come to receive birth within the Desire Realm; it does not mean he cannot descend from the heavens.
Thus, we know that "coming temporarily from the heavens" is distinct in meaning from "receiving birth [there]. This applies to those such as Kokālika and his peers.
To raise objections against the Brahma King without yet having mastered this principle is to incur the reproach of that very Brahma King.

Furthermore, according to the various scriptures of our own school, one who has first attained the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*) and has not yet completed the fourteen rebirths, upon encountering a Buddha, immediately becomes an Arhat;
the same applies by analogy to those in the second and third fruits. Thus, these individuals of the third fruit descend from heaven out of a wish to behold the Buddha.
This is fully as recorded in the *Myōgen* (Excellence of the Profound) and in the *Kugi* (Phrase Commentary) on the "Chapter on Expedient Means.

The Sūtra states that the Brahmā King, Lord of the Sahā World, specifically refers to the Great Brahmā of the First Dhyāna; however, according to the *Yingluo Jing* (Sūtra of the Necklaces), there is a Brahmā King in each and every dhyāna.
The *Brahmajāla-sūtra* also speaks of the "Eighteen Brahmās" and so forth. Zhanran said that the Lord of the Sahā World is precisely Maheśvara;

he further stated that although the Lord of the World actually governs only a small chiliocosm, he is called the "Lord of the World" because his family’s excellence has been praised. Jingxi remarked that this is [the case] within the great trichiliocosm.
As the Lord of the Great Trichiliocosm, one cannot descend [to lower realms].
The *Wenju* (Textual Explanations) states that they dwell together with those of the nine paths;

it is also called the "dwellings of the nine existences" (*navabhavasthāna*), and further referred to as the "dwellings of the nine sentient beings. The *Ekottarika Āgama* asks: "What are the nine? If...
There are sentient beings with various kinds of bodies, namely the gods and humans;

or there are sentient beings with various kinds of bodies but a single perception, namely the Brahmakāyika gods; or there are sentient beings with a single perception and a single body, namely the Ābhāsvara gods;
or there are sentient beings with a single body but various perceptions, namely the Śubhakṛtsna gods.
There are sentient beings who are infinite in the sphere of infinite space, namely the gods of the sphere of infinite space;

there are sentient beings who are infinite in the sphere of infinite consciousness, namely the gods of the sphere of infinite consciousness; there are sentient beings who are infinite in the sphere of nothingness, namely the gods of the sphere of nothingness;
and there are sentient beings who are infinite in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, namely [the gods of] neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

The nine [abodes] consist of the realms of perception (*saṃjñin*), the realm of non-perception (*asaṃjñin*), and all other classes of beings that are born. The *Abhidharma-jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* states:
"Humans, the gods of the desire realm, the Brahmakāyika, the Ābhāsvara, the Śubhakṛtsna, the non-percipient gods, and the four formless [realms]—these constitute the nine existences.
The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra-ṭīkā* states: "The eight dhyānas together with the desire realm constitute the nine abodes of sentient beings (*sattvāvāsa*)."
The Dharma Master Guānyīn states that this heaven is called "Light-Sound" (Ābhāsvara) because when its inhabitants speak, pure light issues from their mouths;

it is also said that since these beings lack discursive thought (*vitarka*) and investigation (*vicāra*), they have no verbal speech at all, but communicate solely by means of light, and are thus called "Light-Sound."
Furthermore, the Āgamas state that when the flames of the fire calamity reach the celestial realm, the gods newly born there all feel fear.
The elder gods say to them, "Do not be afraid; by recollecting the light of the flames, you shall be named the Heaven of Light-Sound (Ābhāsvara). Thus it is called the Heaven of Light-Sound.
Furthermore, there is no obstruction;
"guà" (挂) should be read as "guà" (罣, hù guà qiè).
It derives its name from the ocean.
It is because *Sāgara* is translated here as "the Salt Sea" (*xián-hǎi*). It refers to the vast ocean;
Xi Kang said it is so called because it is "mysterious and boundless" (*míng-mò wú-yá*). Emperor Jianwen of the Liang dynasty said: "Profound..."
"Ming" (Ming) signifies the Infinite. The *Shishouji* (Record of the Ten Continents) by Dongfang Shuo states that water of black color is called "Ming.
In the Ming Sea, there is no wind, yet the great waves reach a height of a hundred zhang;
this is what is meant by "many heads."
Dharma Master Shen Kai said that these are nine-headed dragons.
The Sūtra states "several" (*ruo gan*);

here, "ruo" means "like" or "such as," while "gan" refers to a number. Whether they be a thousand or ten thousand, it is impossible to list them all exhaustively; thus, they are indicated collectively by this term.
It is merely a matter of a few words.

The record states that the four great rivers are fully present in that sutra, as seen in the commentary (*śāstra*) on the phrases of the current text; however, they are not mentioned here. That sutra, however, says: "At the summit of the Snowy Mountains is Anavatapta..."
The pond is fifty yojanas in length and breadth; its waters are clear and cool, and it is composed of the seven precious gems.
To the east of the pond, the Gaṅgā River flows from the Ox Mouth and enters the eastern ocean via five hundred tributary rivers.

To the south of the pond, the Sindhu River flows from the Lion Mouth and enters the southern ocean via five hundred tributary rivers. To the west of the pond, the Vaksu River flows from the Horse [Mouth]...

From his mouth issues the Sītā River, which flows through five hundred tributaries into the Western Sea; from his elephantine trunk issues the Hiraṇyavatī River, which flows through five hundred tributaries into the Northern Sea.
The *Wénjù* (Textual Commentary) states: "Fánshā" [is the name of the river].
Regarding the character *zha* (唼): the *Shìqiàn* (釋籤) transcribes it as "suō xiá" (所狹切), while the *Yùpiān* (玉篇) transcribes it as "zǐ hé" (子合切).

The *Chǔcí* (楚辭) states, "The ducks and geese all *zha* upon the aquatic plants of the bridge," and it is also transcribed as "suǒ jiǎ" (所甲切); this is correctly written as *chì* (啑), meaning the sound of a duck eating.
*Dié* (喋) is transcribed as "zhàng jiǎ" (丈甲切); *chì* (啑) is also written as *zha* (唼).
Pañcavārṣika is also transliterated as Pañca-yu-se; this means "a gathering once every five years.
In Western India (Indraprastha), all great dāna assemblies are termed pañcavārṣika. Various sūtras also refer to it as Pañcavārṣika. This is because...
In that [text], the lute song praises the Buddha’s virtues; "Pañcaśikha" refers to one who possesses the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijña*).

It may be doubted that the current term "Pañcaśīrṣa" (Five-Headed) should instead be rendered as "Pañcaśikha," for the latter meaning would be much more convenient. Future scholars should further examine and distinguish this matter in detail.

The *Ji* (Commentary) states: "The ten jewel mountains are as recorded in the fifth fascicle of the *Zhiguan" and in the twenty-second fascicle of the *Huayan*, which says there are ten jewel mountains—namely, Snowy, Fragrant, Kailāsa, Rishya, Gandhamādana, Aśvakarṇa, Nimindhara, Cakravāḍa, Yugandhara, and Sumeru. Each one...
All say "Rāja," and they also say "Sumeru," which is Mount Sumeru. Regarding "Yugandhara" and so forth:
"Yugandhara" means "Double-Track. Because there are two ridges on the peaks of this mountain, it is called "Double";
because they resemble the tracks of a chariot, they are called "Tracks. "Īṣādhāra" means "Axle-Bearer. This mountain...
Its shape is like the axle of a chariot. Kailāsa—translated as "Carrying Wood"—is so named because this mountain resembles a tree of that name.
Sudarśana—translated as "Good to Behold"—is so named because this mountain is so wondrous and beautiful that all who see it praise it as excellent. Aṭavīkaṇa—translated as "Horse Ear"—this...

The shape of this mountain resembles that [previous one]. Vimalagiri (Vimākha), translated here as "Obstructing Deity," refers to a deity in human form who obstructs anyone with business whenever they approach; the shape of this mountain now resembles that deity.
Nimindhara, translated here as "Earth-Supporter," refers to a fish in the ocean; the shape of this mountain now resembles that fish.

Therefore, this concludes [the section]. The above are the names of the seven golden mountains; they are recorded here for the sake of showing them to those who do not yet know them. The *Wénjù* (Textual Commentary) states: "Dhāraṇa" (*dǎngdào*);

the *Āhan Yìnyì* (The Meaning and Pronunciation of the Āgamas) states: "To grasp by the banner" (*yuánzhāng*) means to grasp an object with the hand and lift it up. A "banner" (*zhāng*) is a soft pole, used for play.

The flexible pole used within the arena is what serves as the "supporting pillar" (*yuan-zhu*). Furthermore, "to support" (*yuan*) means to seek or follow; "banner" (*zhang*) refers to a pillar or a performance pole.
The character "banner" (*zhang*) is an error and should be "tall pole" (*chong*). People of other schools say that in the Western Regions, performers of secular music are called *gandharva*.
There are two types of these: the first are those who do not use stringed or wind instruments, such as drums and stone chimes.
The second category refers to stringed and wind instruments, such as the *xiao* and *di*. That which is inferior to stringed and wind instruments is called "music" (*yue*);
that which is superior to stringed and wind instruments is called "musical sound" (*yinyue*). That which is inferior to stringed and wind instruments is called "beauty" (*mei*);

that which is superior to stringed and wind instruments is called "beautiful sound" (*meiyin*). Others also read the character "music" (*yue*) with the phonetic transcription *wǔxiào*, explaining its meaning as follows:
This means "to cause others to love and delight in. According to the intention of the present school, it is pronounced as *wǔjiǎo* (五角).

When Master Tanyan met Xi Zaochi of Xiangyang for the first time, Xi Zaochi said, "Xi Zaochi from the Four Seas," to which Master An replied: [The text continues with the dialogue between Master An and Xi Zaochi.]
Shi Dao’an of Miti was called "The One Who Answers All" by his contemporaries.

A high official of the Qin state submitted a memorial stating that a virtuous star had appeared in the celestial division corresponding to foreign lands, signifying that a sage would enter to assist the Middle Kingdom; whoever obtained him would rule.
The Lord of Qin thereupon launched a campaign against Xiangyang to bring back Master Dao’an and Xi Zuochi. The Lord of Qin said: "I have employed..."
Among ten thousand teachers, one and a half were found; the "one" was Master An, and the "half-person" was Xi Zuochi.

When the ruler of Qin wished to tour the Eastern Garden, he ordered Master An to share the same carriage with him. The Left Vice Director remonstrated, saying: "Your servant has heard that for the imperial carriage of the Son of Heaven, the Zhongzhong (Attendant-in-Ordinary) accompanies the ride.
Dao’an is a lowly man who has discarded his physical form; how can he be forced to participate in such a journey alongside the imperial vehicle? The Qin ruler [relented].
Emperor Fu Jian, his expression turning stern with indignation, said: "Master Dao’an’s Way reaches the ultimate realm and his virtue is honored as supreme by the age.
The weight of the entire empire cannot compare to him; this is not your honor, but rather my own honor.
He then ordered the Left Vice Director to assist Master Dao’an in ascending the palanquin. Cien criticized this, saying: "Dao’an and the Sovereign..."
In former times, sharing a carriage was the pinnacle of worldly honor; Kumārajīva, however, lived separately from the Qin princess for a thousand years, enduring disgrace.
I maintain that Dao’an and Kumārajīva were bodhisattva-monks—their depths are unfathomable to those of inferior stream; therefore, one must not criticize them with a single-minded bias.
The *Book of Jin* records that Kumārajīva once lectured on the sutras at Caotang Temple, where Yao Xing and his [ministers]...
More than a thousand high-ranking virtuous śramaṇas and others listened with solemn countenances.
Suddenly, Kumārajīva descended from his high seat and said to Yao Xing, "Two small children have climbed onto my shoulders; they wish for a woman to shield them.
Xing then summoned a palace lady to approach him, and upon a single encounter, two sons were born. Xing then addressed Kumārajīva again, saying, "Great Master..."
His intelligence and transcendent realization were such that none in the world could equal him; how could he be made to have few heirs to the Dharma-seed?
Consequently, ten female entertainers were coerced into being accepted by him. Thereafter, Kumārajīva no longer resided in the monastic quarters but established a separate residence.
Many monks followed his example, whereupon Kumārajīva gathered a bowl full of needles and led the monks before it, saying to them: "If you can see [the needles]..."

"If those who wish to emulate his eating habits were to maintain a separate chamber, they might do so," he said, and then he presented the seven needles, which were no different from his ordinary food.

The monks were filled with shame and submission, and thus [the practice] ceased. Therefore, in the *Nanshan Gantong Zhuan* (Record of Miraculous Responses from Mount Nanshan), when asked about the Master’s matter of having a separate chamber, a celestial being replied: "This is not something for those of ordinary, worldly disposition."

I consider that now Master Shi occupies the rank of one of the Three Sages, and it is further said that Master An was a manifestation of the inconceivable traces of the Bodhisattva Ratnamudrāhasta, as described in detail therein. The *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* speaks of four kinds of asuras:
first, those who belong to the realm of ghosts yet achieve supernatural powers through the power of protecting the Dharma and enter into emptiness; these asuras are born from eggs and are ghosts.
The first two types are subsumed within the realm of gods; they descend from heaven and fall due to the loss of their merit, dwelling in places adjacent to the sun and moon.

These asuras are born from a womb and are subsumed within the realm of humans. The third type sustains the power of the world, possesses penetrating fearlessness, and is able to contend for victory with Brahmā and the various devas; these asuras are born through transformation in the celestial realms.
Regarding the four [categories] included therein, there is separately a class of inferior asuras born from the heart of the great ocean;
these asuras are born from moisture and are categorized within the realm of animals (*tiryagyoni*).
As the Sūtra says: "Kharaskandha..."
*Duó* (馱) is pronounced with the *táng* (唐) and *hè* (賀) initials.
The Record states: "The five fetters bind Māra," as explained in the fifth fascicle of the *Zhǐguān* (止觀).
In the "Four Reliances" chapter (*Sìyīpǐn*) of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, it says that the four types of reliance bodhisattvas expel Māra, referring to him as "Māra, the Heavenly Demon" (*Tiānmó*).
"If you come again within ten days, I shall bind you with the five fetters. Zhan’an’s commentary explains: "There are two kinds of binding:

first, the binding of the five corpses; second, the binding of the five locations. The binding of the five corpses refers to using the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) to subdue the demon of craving (*tṛṣṇā-māra*).
The binding of the five locations refers to using principle (*yukti*) to subdue the demon of views (*dṛṣṭi-māra*). As for the 'five corpses,' they are [the corpses of] death..."
This refers to humans, snakes, dogs, and so forth. Regarding the "five locations," the *Śūraṅgama Samādhi Sūtra* states:
"The two hands, the two feet, and the neck are called the five locations where one is bound by Māra."
The Five-Nature School posits five categories:
first, the bodhisattva nature; second, the pratyekabuddha nature; third, the śrāvaka nature; fourth, the indeterminate nature; and fifth, the natureless icchantika.
They establish two fixed natures—the two vehicles and the natureless icchantikas—asserting that these cannot attain Buddhahood; this is their dogmatic adherence.

To provisionally posit [the existence of seeds] without knowing that they are actually present, as cited previously—merely adding the term "seeds" and so forth—is the position established by the sūtras and śāstras of the Path of Teaching (śikṣāmārga).

This reflects their failure to understand the meaning of the new perfuming (*navavāsanā*) and the original presence (*mūlataḥ sattva*). Therefore, such seeds are identical to the primordial darkness (*ādikāra*);
how could they know that the True Principle (*tattva*) is inherently complete? Thus, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, citing the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, states:
Within the cycle of birth and death across the six destinies, for those various sentient beings born from eggs, wombs, moisture, or by transformation,
the mind-consciousness (*citta-vijñāna*) containing all seeds initially matures, undergoes successive integration, and increases and expands therein. Furthermore,
it is said that these afflictions are drawn forth by the seeds of the *ālaya-vijñāna* and operate spontaneously at all times.
Thus, while there is the arising of [the seeds], within the Perfect and Sudden teaching it is not that the meanings of planting seeds and forming karmic connections are absent;

rather, one must simply know that they are inherently possessed. The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) states: "Furthermore, regarding the defilement of one's own practice, there is the internal and the external.

'Internal' refers to ignorance (*avidyā*), and 'external' refers to the objects of others. Because the internal is possessed and because external objects can act as perfumers (*vāsana*), when observing what is perfumed, one sees only..."

Regarding "inherent in principle" (*liju*): if one contemplates what is inherent in principle, one realizes that True Suchness (*tathatā*) constantly perfuses and internally contains the hundred dharmas.
In the *Treatise on the Hundred Dharmas*, there are six root afflictions (*mūlakleśa*), namely: greed, anger, pride, ignorance, doubt, and false view.
As for the mention of the seeds of view, doubt, and ignorance, it likely refers to the seeds of the six afflictions—false view, doubt, and ignorance, etc.
The meaning of "seed" (bīja), as well as the perfuming agent (vāsaka) and the perfumed object (vāsyamāna), is as explained in the *Bǎifǎ shùchāo* (Commentary on the Hundred Dharmas).
Regarding the phrase "then he took her as his consort," the four characters [in the original text] are erroneous;

they should instead follow the *Zhǐguān dìsì jì* (Record of the Fourth [Volume] of the Stopping and Contemplation). Furthermore, the *Fēnbié gōngdé lùn* (Treatise on the Differentiation of Merits) states in its tenth record: "In the past, there was an elder who..."
The girl was named Shan-shi (Good Giver); before she had married, she felt the warmth of a fire and became pregnant.
Her parents rebuked her, and the matter reached the King’s daughter. The girl’s words remained unchanged, and the King granted her request on the condition that she would face death.
The girl said, "Now there is this unrighteous king who will falsely execute an innocent person; if I am not virtuous, he may keep his word."
The King immediately tested him, and the result was exactly as he had said. The King spoke to his parents, saying, "I wish to marry this girl.
The parents replied, "What use have we for this dead girl? Subsequently, she entered the inner palace, where she gave birth to a son who later left the household life and became an Arhat.
If one were to treat sentient beings as being like crystal water, it would be as previously cited from the *Buddha-darśana-sūtra*, which states that beings are born from the Ābhāsvara Heaven.
In this stage, when those who possess desire enter the sea to wash away impurities, the vital essence (*mahābhūta-sāra*) immediately enters their bodies;
because the body experiences pleasure through contact, the essence flows into the water.
The *Wenju* (Explanatory Text) states that there are twenty-four heads.
The scripture merely states "nine heads," which I suspect is an error in the text.

Regarding solar eclipses, the *Hanshu* (Book of Han) states: "The sun and moon eclipse each other. Wei Zhao explains: "Because the vapors advance and press against one another, it is called 'bo' (broad/pressing). Furthermore...
It gradually diminishes and erodes, like insects eating the leaves of trees and grass; therefore, it is called "eclipsing" (*śīla-śaithilya*). Regarding various heterodox teachings:

as stated in the tenth precept of the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* against slandering the Triple Gem, if one claims that non-Buddhist deities possess supernatural power and subsequently submits petitions to them or offers prayers for their release, or if one encourages others to do so, all constitute the offense of a minor defilement (*mṛdu-mala-pāpa*).
The *Jì* (Commentary) states: "The sequential arrangement of military equipment is as listed here now;
it should rather be stated that they are 'fully as listed in the Sūtra.
The *Wénjù* (Textual Commentary) states: "Zhuangzi calls it the Páng [Penglai] and so forth."
In the "Xiaoyao You" chapter of the *Inner Chapters* of the *Zhuangzi*, it says: "In the Northern Ocean there is a fish, its name is Kūn.

The size of the Kūn is such that one does not know how many thousands of li it measures. It transforms into a Páng; the back of the Páng is such that one does not know how many thousands of li it measures.

In the *Cí'ēn Sū* (Compassionate Teacher’s Commentary), the sentient beings of the six destinies (*ṣadgati*) are analyzed through six gates:

first, explaining the names; second, identifying their essence (*svabhāva*); third, opening and combining [the categories]; fourth, their locations; fifth, their lifespan; and sixth, cause and effect. Within the gate of opening and combining, they are treated as one in general.

This refers to birth and death (*saṃsāra*). Next, it is divided into two: the happy destinies (*sugati*) and the miserable destinies (*durgati*). It is further divided into three, namely the three realms (*tridhātu*).

Divided again, there are four, which are the four modes of birth (*catur-yoni*). Further divided, there are five, namely the five destinies (*pañca-gati*). Or it is divided into six, namely the six paths (*ṣaḍ-gati*).
Again, it is divided into seven, namely the seven existences (*sapta-bhava*), including the existence of karma (*karma-bhava*) and the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*).
The five destinies (*pañca-gati*) are further expanded into nine, namely the nine abodes of existence (*nava-bhava-sthāna*), up to the twenty-five existences (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*).
Regarding the "seven stations of consciousness" (*sapta-vijñāna-sthiti*), both the four-fascicle *Abhidharma* and the six-fascicle *Abhidharma* state that there are seven stations of consciousness:

the humans and devas of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) constitute one; the first three stages of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) constitute the next three; and the first three stages of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) constitute the final three.
It is sevenfold. The four evil destinies, the fourth dhyāna, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception are excluded.

This is because consciousness does not delight in dwelling within the four evil destinies due to the oppression of suffering; it does not delight in dwelling in the fourth dhyāna because the meditative attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) would destroy it;

and it does not delight in dwelling in the Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*) because those who enter them attain nirvāṇa; furthermore, it ceases in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception because it is without mind.

Because all meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) are subject to destruction, consciousness does not delight in dwelling there. Furthermore, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-ṭīkā* quotes Master Kumārajīva’s explanation of the seven stations of consciousness (*vijñāna-sthiti*), which is largely identical to this [view].

There is no need to cite it here at length. As for the nine abodes of beings (*navasattvāvāsāḥ*), they consist of the seven stations of consciousness with the addition of the sphere of non-perception (*asaṃjñisattva*) and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*); these are called the nine abodes of sentient beings because sentient beings dwell therein. Therefore, it is so stated.
The sutra says, "All who practice loving-kindness" (諸修行慈).
The character "xing" (行) is read with the departing tone (去聲) here; however, according to the meaning, it should instead be read with the level tone (平聲).
The record states: "Others divide this into three sections.

hence this statement was made. Since these are no longer extant today, it is difficult to consult them. Furthermore, the subsequent text contains many references to other works."
Based on this, one may discern the merits and defects when compared with Ci'en [Kuiji]. I shall cite and demonstrate each point in the relevant passages.
The text states: "Each explains the cause of the body," which is precisely its meaning.
The character "ge" (各) should be read as "gong" (共); please examine the reason for this.
The Sūtra says: "One erects a stūpa for the Buddha’s śarīra.
*Śarīra* is also called *śarīra*, which is translated as "bone-body" (*kushin*).
A stūpa is also called *stūpa*, or *tāpa*, or *tōba*, or again *thūpa*, or *sutūpa*, or it is also called *zhi*.
*Difu-du* (帝浮都) is sometimes called *zhiti* (支提), or *futuo* (浮圖), or *sudubuo* (窣堵波).
This is translated as "temple" (*miao*), or "square mound" (*fangfen*), or "great accumulation" (*daju*), or "accumulated form" (*zuxiang*), or "lofty and prominent" (*gaoxian*).
The commentary states: "All are called 'spiritual transformations' (*ṛddhi-prātihārya*).

As recorded in the first commentary on the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*, when the Buddha had finished manifesting the eighteen transformations in the *Maharddhiprātihārya-sūtra*, a son of heaven asked the Buddha:
"Are there any spiritual transformations that surpass these? The Buddha then instructed Mañjuśrī to explain the manifestations in detail, to which the son of heaven replied: "If it is so..."
"All dharmas are called spiritual transformations (*ṛddhi-prātihārya*). Śāriputra asked, "Do you not feel fear upon hearing of spiritual transformations?
The devaputra replied, "I am myself a spiritual transformation; why should I fear?"

The *Sūtra on the Great Treatise of the Dharma Prince* (Fawangzi dalun), fascicle 32, states: "Because the Buddha is the Dharma King and Bodhisattvas have entered the correct position of the Dharma up to the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*), they are all called 'Princes';
they are all capable of becoming Buddhas, just like Mañjuśrī."
The text states: *Vibhāṣā*, which means "Extensive Exposition.
This concludes the postscript.
Regarding the inscription, the *Shiming* (Explanation of Names) states that it is a "name" (*ming*), recording his name and his merits.
The *Sūtra* says [it was made of] sandalwood.
The *Fayuan* (Garden of the Dharma) records that Zhu Fanzhen ascended Mount Luo. The commentary (*shu*) states: "It originated from a foreign country at the end of the Yuanjia era; a monk..."
Chengfeng saw a great tree on the mountain that provided a circular shade covering several mu; it was over three zhang in circumference, its fragrance pungent and intense.
It is either sandalwood, or it is said that because this region lacks it, the name was not translated; alternatively, based on its meaning, it is translated as "that which bestows joy."
The Record states: "The Lion is fully described in the Mahāvaipulya Sūtras and the Mahā-śāstras.

Regarding the 'Lion's Roar,' the *Mahā-śāstra* says: 'It is like a lion king born from a pure lineage, dwelling in deep mountains and vast valleys, with square jaws, large bones, a body full of flesh, a large head, long eyes, and a lustrous, clear brilliance.'"
His eyebrows are high and broad; his teeth are sharp, white, and clean; his mouth and nose are square, large, thick, solid, and full;
his teeth are dense, even, and sharp; he protrudes a red-and-white tongue; his two ears are high; his mane is lustrous and smooth;

his upper body is expansive; his skin and flesh are firm and well-adhered; his spine is long and his waist is slender; his belly does not protrude; he has a long tail and sharp claws; and his feet stand firmly established.
With great physical strength, he emerges from his dwelling, arching his back and stretching with a yawn; he strikes the earth with his mouth, manifesting great majestic power.

He does not let the time for eating pass, displaying the signs of early morning. He demonstrates the power of the lion king to intimidate the deer, bears, brown bears, tigers, leopards, wild boars, and their ilk.
He awakens those who have long been asleep and subdues those who are haughty, powerful, and influential.
Opening the path of practice, he lets out a great roar. When he roars thus, those who hear it are either filled with joy or struck with fear:
those dwelling in burrows hide away; those living in the water plunge deep; those hidden in the mountains crouch in concealment;
the elephants in the stables shake their chains and flee wildly; and birds flying in the air soar high and far away. The lion’s roar of the Buddha is likewise.
Born from the six *pāramitās* and the four ancient noble lineages, he dwells within the deep and precipitous valley of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) that is the great mountain of *nirvāṇa*.

He possesses the head of all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), with all roots of goodness gathered as his cheeks; his pure right view is his nose, and the luster of his eyes consists of the practices of concentration and wisdom.
His high and broad eyebrows are the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), and his white, sharp, and unimpeded fangs are the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).
The four right efforts are his lips; the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are his teeth, closely set and even;
the meditation on impurity is his tongue, which he extends to the red and white [parts of the mouth]; mindfulness and wisdom are his ears, elevated by the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
the hair of his body is glossy, radiant, and pure white; his upper body is firm with flesh, and his spine is straightened through the three manifestations.

His belly is not protruding as he is perfected in knowledge and conduct; his waist is slender as he possesses patience; his tail is long as he practices the ascetic virtues; he is established in the four bases of power;
his claws are sharp as he possesses the five faculties of one beyond training; his strength is that of the ten powers; he is fully endowed with immeasurable, untainted qualities;
his body is the dwelling place of the Samādhirāja and other samādhis of all Buddhas; from him issue the four unhindered knowledges; and he stretches his limbs with grace.
Within the ground of all dharmas, through attachment to the unimpeded analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) and relying upon these ten powers and great majesty,
when delivering sentient beings, he does not fail to manifest the signs of the morning to all the worlds of gods and humans, revealing the majestic virtue of the Dharma King.
He awakens all classes of heterodox teachers, disputants, and those with false views, as well as all sentient beings, to the Four Noble Truths.
He subdues those who sleep within [saṃsāra] and are attached to the five aggregates; he dispels the power of indolence and pride; he opens the way for debate on the treatises of heterodox schools;
he causes those who practice paths of wrong views to feel fear, while those who believe in right view rejoice;

he sharpens the dull-witted; he comforts his disciples; he destroys the non-Buddhists; and he causes the long-lived devas to realize that even after enjoying celestial pleasures for a long time, they are impermanent.
When sentient beings constantly hear such a lion’s roar of the Four Noble Truths, they all give rise to a mind of revulsion; because of this revulsion, they attain detachment;
because of this detachment, they enter *nirvāṇa*. This is called the lion’s roar among the masses. As the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* says:
"Just as the lion king, knowing his own physical strength, with teeth sharp and jagged, plants his four paws firmly upon the ground and dwells securely in his mountain cave, shaking [the earth]..."
If a tail emits a sound and one possesses all such characteristics as these, it should be known that this is indeed the lion’s roar of a true lion king.
In the early morning, emerging from his lair, yawning and stretching, looking toward the four quarters, and emitting a thundering roar—these constitute eleven matters.
The first is for the purpose of destroying those who are not truly lions but falsely pretend to be lions, and so forth.
The eleventh is for the purpose of adorning one’s own retinue, as it says:
"Just as that jackal, though it may follow a lion for a hundred years, can never produce the lion's roar; yet when a lion cub reaches the age of three years, it can roar like the lion king.
Thus, the Tathāgata, the Perfectly Awakened One, possesses the tusks of wisdom.
From the "Four Bases of Psychic Power" (ṛddhipāda) up to the "Lion's Roar," it is definitively taught that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature,
that the Tathāgata is eternally abiding and undergoes no change, as fully described in the sūtras; I shall not trouble you by recording them here in detail.
