The *Jì* (Commentary) states: "That which is produced by the primary elements (*mahābhūta*). All newly translated treatises state that "the primary elements" refers precisely to the four great elements. This is why it says here that sound is the primary element of form (*rūpa-mahābhūta*).
It is also as stated in the *Abhidharma-jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* of the Hīnayāna: "The subtle [sound] of the Tathāgata’s throat..."
From these sublime great elements (*mahābhūta*), sublime speech and sounds can be produced. The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* asks: "What is meant by 'great element'? It answers:

"Because they are great and yet are elements, they are called 'great elements. Just as one speaks of the 'great earth' or a 'great king,' [these elements] are so called because they can diminish or increase, and can cause loss or benefit;
this is the meaning of 'element' (*bhūta*). Their substance, characteristics, forms, and dimensions pervade all regions."
To accomplish great matters is the Great Purpose; the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* also speaks of the time when the elements of water, fire, and wind disperse, perish, and are destroyed.
Regarding Nanda’s observance of the precepts, see the fourth note on *śamatha-vipaśyanā*.
That which was previously indicated is not further discussed here.
The Sūtra says, "exhausting the limit of all suffering" (*sarva-duḥkha-anta*).
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* asks: "Does this 'limit of suffering' exist within suffering or outside of suffering? If it were within suffering, it would not [be the limit]."
One should say that the limit of suffering (*duḥkhānta*) exists outside of suffering. How then can worldly metaphors be reconciled with this?
For example, just as a golden tally is gold throughout its beginning, middle, and end, so too is suffering: it is suffering throughout its beginning, middle, and end.
What, then, is called the "limit of suffering"? Some answer: it is the final aggregate (*skandha*) of an Arhat.
"This is the limit of suffering," or as it is said, "Nirvana, which is the extinction [of suffering], is the limit of suffering.
Because the final aggregates are the limit of suffering, suffering will not arise again, there will be no further continuity with suffering, and no causes of suffering will be created.
As for the claim that Nirvana, which is extinction, contradicts the present metaphor, this does not require further explanation, because it is not mentioned in the Tripiṭaka.

The Record states: "If one follows the analogy of the śrāvakas, one must clarify the modes of activity—whether contrary or conformable—and the inference regarding the twelve links of dependent origination based on views and craving, as detailed in the *Catuḥsmṛtyupasthāna*.
This is because within the Hīnayāna, there are no Buddhas of the ten directions."

If one follows the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, which cites the Āgamas stating that there are immeasurable worlds in the eastern direction, then even the Hīnayāna does not say that [the Buddha] exists, nor does it say that he does not exist.
If it were said that he exists, sentient beings would become indolent and fail to seek deliverance.
Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that while Śrāvakas perceive the body and mind of only a single Buddha, they see the Buddhas of the ten directions.
Sāṃprata [the author] then considers whether there are Buddhas in the ten directions within immeasurable Buddha-fields. If one follows the Sarvāstivāda, there are no Buddhas in the ten directions;

if one follows what is taught in the *Saṃghīti*, there are Buddhas in the ten directions; and if one follows the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, it says that there are none in a single world-system but many in multiple world-systems.
One should know that these are merely differences in their respective tenets. Now, they are contrasted according to the Great and Small Vehicles.
To distinguish between them: [the former] is absent in the Hīnayāna but present in the Mahāyāna.
Furthermore, because one sees the sons of the Buddha, it is said "to see";
according to the sutras, this should properly be stated as "seeing all of these therein," and because one beholds the Buddhas, it is called "seeing."
The Gaṅgā River (pronounced *qíng* with the *shēng* tone; the *Xiǎngyīng* [Sūtra] calls it the *Héngshā*, or the *Héngjiā Hé*, or the *Qiángjiā Hé*;
here it is translated as "Coming from Heaven"). According to non-Buddhist texts from Western India, it originally entered the crown of the head of Maheśvara.
The sound flowed forth from within his ears upon the ground because this celestial being had manifested a transformation body atop the Snowy Mountains;
thus, seeing it come from a high place, they said it came from heaven. For now, I shall follow that explanation, and therefore I say so.
The Sindhu River is also called the Xintou (辛頭) River; this is translated as the "River of Verification.
The Vakṣu River.
The Vaksu River is also called the Shengdan (生丹) River;
the Sītā River is also called the Siduo, Xiduo, or Sida River, which means the "Cold River."
The Sūtra states: "Gold, silver, and coral.
The *Mahā-śāstra* states: "Gold comes from mountain sands, stones, and red copper; silver comes from scorched stones;
'coral' is the name for a pearl. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "It grows in the sea, and its color is red."

The *Mahāratnakūṭa-sūtra* (Great Treatise on Pearls and Maṇis) states: "Pearls are produced from within the bellies of fish, from within bamboo, and from within the brains of snakes. Maṇi is also called *maṇi*;
this is translated as 'free from defilement' (*vimala*)."
Tridacna shell and agate:
tridacna shell is bluish-white, while agate is either white or blue; it is so named because its color resembles the brain of a horse.
Later generations sometimes added stone or jade to imitate these materials.
Vajra is among the precious substances of India;
it is produced from gold and, though refined a hundred times, does not melt away, and can be used to cut jade. It is used for vehicles.
The character "chéng" (乘) is pronounced with the departing tone; it was originally created by Xi Zhòng of the Xia Hou clan and is the general name for a carriage.
"Chì" (齒) is pronounced as *yé* (邪); it means a dwelling, referring to the place where a traveler stays. It is also pronounced as *jū* (居), meaning that which houses people.
"Chéng" (乘) means to mount, to drive, or to carry.

Regarding the term *lǎn* (palanquin): the *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it is a wheeled vehicle drawn by people leading it from the front. In ancient times, it was the vehicle used by high officials (*qīng dàfū*);
since the Han dynasty, the Son of Heaven has also used it. A carriage used by the Son of Heaven or the Empress is called a *lǎn*.
*Yǔ* (輿) and *shù* (庶): both pronounced with the second tone. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "The carriage and the platform. That which has wheels is called a *che* (carriage);

that which lacks wheels is called a *yǔ* (platform). Today, the distinct forms of carriages and platforms are regulated by ancient precedent. Some say the *Yupian* defines it as "the multitude," "that which carries," "that which lifts," or "much."
"Lan-shun" (欄楯) means "lan" (欄), which signifies to block or to screen; "shun" (楯) refers to a railing. When vertical, it is called "lan"; when horizontal, it is called "shun.
It is a flower-canopy.

"Hua" (華) is pronounced with the "hu" and "gua" finals. When the Yellow Emperor was battling Chiyou on the plains of Zhuolu, five-colored cloud-gas with golden branches and jade leaves settled above the Emperor, bearing the appearance of blossoming flowers; thus, he fashioned the *huagai* (canopy).
"Hua" is also pronounced with the "gua" final. In the hot lands of Western India, many people carry canopies, all of which are made of flowers.
Various sutras describe adorning [the vehicle] with banners, flags, flowers, and canopies; this is what is meant by that.
A "xuán" (chariot) is a decorated carriage, which is adorned with leather and other materials; such is the "xuán-chē" (decorated carriage).
The Record states that the specific characteristics are fully set forth as in the second record of the *Zhiguan* (Mohe Zhiguan).
Various Mahāyāna sūtras, as well as the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*, the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā*, and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, all clarify the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*).
As stated in the "Chapter on Mutual Inclusion" of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*: Pūrṇa addressed the Buddha, saying, "I now wish to speak of the conduct of a bodhisattva. The Buddha said, "Go ahead."
In your view, it is said that Rāhuṇa extensively clarifies here how the six perfections mutually encompass one another— namely, the thirty-six perfections resulting from this mutual inclusion—
such that one may speak of the various pāramitās by using "giving" as the name, or even speak of the various pāramitās by using "prajñā" as the name. Furthermore,
this is also found in the chapter on Mutual Manifestation (*anyonyaprabhāvana*) of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* and the *Mahāvaipulya-mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra*.
The "Adornments" and the "Uninterrupted Chapter" share the same intent as the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*.
The sutra states: "Donning the dharma-robe.
"Donning" (bei) is pronounced with the level tone; it means to cover.

The Record states: When a dragon obtained a single thread and a bull made a single touch, the Dragon King of the Ocean Sūtra records that the Dragon King addressed the Buddha: "In this ocean there are countless species of dragons, yet four *garuḍas* constantly come to devour them.
I pray that the Buddha will protect them so that they may attain peace and security. Thereupon, the World-Honored One removed [a portion of] his own body.
The one in black robes addressed the Dragon King, saying: "Take these garments and distribute them among all the dragons, ensuring they reach everyone.
Should anyone encounter even a single thread of them, the Golden-Winged Bird King shall be unable to harm them. Those who uphold the precepts will surely obtain their aspirations.
The *Dharmayuan* (Garden of Dharma) cites a passage from the *Karunapundarika Sutra* (Pity Lotus Sutra) stating that in the past, Shakyamuni Tathagata was at the [Palace of] Treasure...
The *Zangfo suoyuan* states that at the time of attaining Buddhahood, the five kinds of meritorious qualities induced by the *kāṣāya* are roughly the same as those cited in the current record.
The *Wenju* states: "From the first dhyāna, one grade, up to nine grades."

Regarding the dhyāna-pāramitā: when practicing the various meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), there are three grades—lower, middle, and upper—which, when divided, become nine grades according to their depth.
If discussed in detail, there are immeasurable grades; this is true for every level of dhyāna.

The *Xiuluo Qin Dalun* (Treatise on the Asura Lute) states: "Dharmakāya Bodhisattvas manifest infinite bodies to deliver sentient beings and preach the Dharma, yet the Bodhisattva's mind remains free from discrimination.
It is like the Asura lute, which constantly produces sound spontaneously according to the will, such that no one is able to play it."
Furthermore, the lute played by the kinnaras is adorned with petals of Jambūnada gold and is fashioned from the retribution of excellent,
pure karma; when played, its sound pervades the trichiliocosm, proclaiming the Dharma of non-arising and quiescent extinction.

The record states that the four signs of subduing Māra, as well as the eight and ten Māras, are as explained in the eighth fascicle of the *Zhi guan* (Mo-ho chih-kuan). Regarding the Three Treasuries (*piṭaka*), first one subdues the four Māras;
sitting at the site of enlightenment, one destroys the Māra of afflictions (*kleśa-māra*). Furthermore, by attaining the Dharma-nature body, one destroys the Māra of the aggregates (*skandha-māra*).

These two together destroy the Māra of death (*mṛtyu-māra*). Beneath the tree, one attains the Samādhi of Immovability (*akampya-samādhi*) and thereby destroys the Māra of the devaputras (*devaputra-māra*).
In the Shared Teaching (*pāryāyika-yāna*), one first attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and reaches the path of Bodhi at the sixth stage;

as previously mentioned, the simultaneous flow of the Path and Contemplation constitutes the Immovable Samādhi (*acala-samādhi*), whereby one destroys the Māra of the devaputras. In both instances, the Śrāvakas destroy only three Māras.

In the Distinct Teaching (*vaiśeṣika-yāna*), the four Māras within the realm of desire are destroyed from the Ten Abodes (*daśa-vihāra*); at the first stage (*prathamā-bhūmi*), one partially attains Bodhi and destroys the afflictions (*kleśa*).
By overcoming the demon of affliction (*kleśamāra*), one attains a portion of the *dharmakāya*; by overcoming the demon of the aggregates (*skandhamāra*), one attains the crimson samādhi;

by overcoming the demon of the devaputra, the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*) of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) simultaneously overcomes the eight demons and attains the path of Bodhi. This includes the overcoming of the demon of afflictions up until the stage of Wondrous Enlightenment (*samyaksaṃbodhi*), where they are forever exhausted.
Regarding the four demons: the demon of afflictions, the demon of the aggregates, the demon of death, and the demon of the devaputra—this is the classification based on...

If one speaks in terms of being within the realm (*dhātu*), as for those outside the realm, all segmented demons (*māra*) have been transcended; there remain only the four inversions, such as impermanence and so forth.

These are the affliction-demons (*kleśa-māra*) of the realm outside [the mundane]. Because they are affliction-demons, there exist the "unequalled and equal" forms, which are the aggregate-demons (*skandha-māra*) of the realm outside.
Because they are aggregate-demons, there exists the death-demon (*mṛtyu-māra*). The three levels of worthiness (*tri-kṣānti*) and the ten stages of sagehood (*daśārya-bhūmi*) abide therein.

In terms of retribution, there is no sixth "Heavenly Son Māra"; rather, it is only because the red-colored samādhi has not yet reached its ultimate consummation that he is designated as the "Heavenly Son Māra.
All designations from within the realm of ordinary beings (the *dhātu*) to those outside the realm are established based on their meaning;

thus, the contemplation of the red-colored samādhi regarding the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven is so named because there are still three afflictions (*kleśa*) remaining that have not been exhausted, which can destroy that heaven.
Taken together, these constitute the Māra of the Son of Heaven; these are called the eight māras. Regarding the ten māras, the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* states:

first, the māra of the aggregates (*skandha-māra*), because they give rise to various grasping; second, the māra of afflictions (*kleśa-māra*), because they produce defilement; third, the māra of karma (*karma-māra*), because it is capable of creating obstacles;

fourth, the māra of the mind (*citta-māra*), because it gives rise to arrogance; fifth, the māra of death (*mṛtyu-māra*), because it causes one to abandon the place of birth; sixth, the māra of devas (*deva-māra*), because of its own pride.
Ninth, the demon of negligence, because the seven roots of goodness are constantly seized by Māra; tenth, the demon of samādhi, because one long relishes its flavor;
eleventh, the demon of spiritual friends, because one gives rise to a mind of attachment; twelfth, the demon of the wisdom of the bodhi-dharmas, because one never relinquishes it.
The Sūtra states: "Dwelling in the forest, emitting light;

'dwelling' (chù) is pronounced with the upper tone. This applies to "dwelling alone in leisure and stillness" and "constantly dwelling in empty seclusion," where "dwelling" (chù) is always pronounced with the upper tone.
One should apply this principle to subsequent passages as well.

Our school refutes this, calling it "shutting one's eyes to engage in forced interpretation.
It further states that although the intention behind bestowing predictions upon the śrāvakas lies in a different time, our school’s...
Since the mind has already attained the opening of the provisional means (*upāya*), why would it instead be relegated to a "different time"?
Furthermore, if one were to claim that the single thought-moment of making a vow constitutes a "different time," this is certainly impossible;

thus, to say that the fierce and sharp wholesome practice of ten recitations at the moment of death belongs to a "different time"—how great a mistake this is! Moreover, to claim that the traces and the origin are separated by vast distances [is likewise erroneous].
Regarding the fact that the underlying intention (*āśaya*) and purpose (*abhiprāya*) may be either extensive or concise, our own school does not yet accept this.
Below, in the *Vyākhyāyukti*, there are two or three places where it speaks of the "four intentions" (*catur-abhiprāya*); therefore, I have cited them here in detail.
When you reach those passages later on, do not be confused by this explanation, for I am concerned that students often become bewildered when encountering the text.
Therefore, it is truly lamentable that those who have not yet understood the various texts I have extensively cited to demonstrate [the truth] instead give rise to derision and ridicule.
For this reason, the texts of the Three Great Works of one school are not easily propagated; how can one of shallow learning discard the fruits of extensive study?

As explained extensively in the "Analysis of the Four Gates" within the *Mohe Zhiguan*, where each gate establishes its own illustrations of phenomena and the universal refutation of dharmas (*pó fǎ biàn*), the text is very voluminous; here I shall provide only the general outline.

The Tripiṭaka teaching uses the hair of a tortoise and the horns of a rabbit as metaphors; the Shared Teaching uses metaphors such as illusions; and the Distinct Teaching uses the metaphor of gold wrapped in silk cloth.

Are such maxims as "the true void is dark and tranquil" not the nihilistic views of externalists (*tīrthika*)? Could they possibly be the stubborn emptiness of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*)?
Furthermore, Jiaxiang [Jingying Huiyuan] stated: "First, the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*) is called 'immeasurable';

How many sighs! Why do you falsely recognize what the Wise One of Jingxi refuted as being correct? Alas, O Fourfold Equality!

Loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity are called the four immeasurables (*catur-apramāṇa*); they are also called the four equalities (*catvāri samatāni*) in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

The "equalities" derive from the mind, while the "immeasurables" derive from the object. Since the objects are immeasurable, the loving-kindness is likewise without distinction or limit. Because the mind is directed toward these four [objects], they are called the four equalities.

The record states: "The eight qualities of voice and the four kinds of analytical eloquence, along with the powers and fearlessnesses, are as described in the *Fajie Cidi* (Gradual Order of the Dharma Realm) and other texts:

1. Unimpeded eloquence regarding phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*); 2. Unimpeded eloquence regarding meanings (*artha-pratisaṃvid*); 3. Unimpeded eloquence regarding linguistic expression (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*); 4. Unimpeded eloquence regarding inspired speech (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*). The ten powers (*daśabala*): 1.

The four fearlessnesses are: first, the fearlessness regarding the realization of all-encompassing knowledge; second, the fearlessness regarding the exhaustion of the outflows; third, the fearlessness regarding the proclamation of the obstacles to the path;

and fourth, the fearlessness regarding the proclamation of the path leading to the end of suffering. Above, I have merely cited their titles; for a detailed explanation of the terms and their meanings, one must consult that source.

Furthermore, one exhaustively investigates the source and causes of the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*). According to the time [of their attainment], they are termed "reversals" (*prātikūlya-vimokṣa*) as causes, and "liberations" (*vimukti*) as fruits. Regarding what are called the eight:

first, possessing the perception of internal forms while observing external forms; second, being without the perception of internal forms while observing external forms; third, the pure reversal, personally realized through the body; fourth...
1. The liberation of the sphere of infinite space; 2. the liberation of the sphere of infinite consciousness; 3. the liberation of the sphere of nothingness; 4.
the liberation of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; 5. the liberation of the cessation of feeling and perception.

If one explains this "Middle" [Vehicle] through the three fundamental samādhis and so forth, it is said that "dhyāna" refers to the four dhyānas of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), "samāpatti" refers to the four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), and "vimokṣa" refers to the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*).
Regarding the "three samādhis": first is the samādhi with both vitarka and vicāra; second is the samādhi without vitarka... [and so on].
There is the samādhi with vitarka and vicāra, and the three types of samādhi without vitarka and without vicāra.
Since recent times, this doctrine has been entirely discarded;
since the Tang dynasty, masters such as those of the Ci'en school have not distinguished between the One Vehicle of the Bodhisattvas and the Small and Great Vehicles—this is the fifth [point].

If such is the nature of the Great [Vehicle], as the Sūtra says that "when Bodhisattvas hear the Dharma, the net of their doubts is entirely removed," how then should one understand the passage which states that they still harbor notions of arising and ceasing upon hearing it?

The Record states: "This shows that those who discourse on the Dharma-realm have not yet exhausted its subtlety; consequently, they become confused regarding the phenomena of the fruit while remaining deluded about the principle of the cause.
This passage criticizes masters who propagate the *Avataṃsaka* but do not properly understand the *Avataṃsaka*'s Dharma-realm, for those various masters—[the text continues that] they... [do not].

One knows that because the principle of the causes of sentient beings inherently possesses all dharmas, it is sufficient to speak only of the mutual identity of the various dharmas on the level of the fruit;

for if one does not discuss this inherent possession (*ju*), how could there be mutual identity? Thus, we know that the interpenetration of the environment and its inhabitants on the level of the fruit is entirely due to the fundamental nature of sentient beings.
This being so, the first of the Dharma-gates discussed by our school is called "the Essential Nature" (*xingti*); this is what it refers to.

The primary cause has two aspects: first, the nature-as-capacity (*xing-liang*), which corresponds to the "revealing cause" (*liao-yin*); second, the nature-as-endowment (*xing-ju*), which corresponds to the "conditioning cause" (*yuan-yin*).
This endowment is precisely the provisional (*jia*); the provisional is itself the empty-and-middle (*kong-zhong*). Thus, within this single Dharma-nature there are these three meanings.

Although there are three meanings, when they are synthesized they are ever more distinct, yet when divided they are always unified. Though each one is all-pervasive, it has no fixed location; you should know this.
The school’s discourse on *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena) is likewise similar to our own school’s [discourse on] the substance and magnitude of the nature;

for they both state that *dharmatā*, *tathatā* (suchness), and empty space are equal. However, they merely lack the third meaning—the doctrine of the inherent inclusion (*xingju*)—and it is for this reason that our school’s various texts refute them.
Those who study our school either speak only of "inclusion" or investigate only "emptiness and quiescence"; this, then, regarding that...

The Complete Teaching (Yuanzong) treats these three dharmas as a whole, whereas [other schools] grasp only one corner of them. Therefore, one should know that the essence of nature possesses these three meanings;

only when they are presented together is the single meaning of the mind-nature fully revealed. While one meaning may be hidden in other systems, it is only in the Perfect and Sudden Teaching that it is fully manifest. For those who comprehend this principle, all disputes shall cease.

we only pray that the World-Honored One will explain this incomplete meaning so that all bodhisattvas may gain deep faith and understanding. This principle applies to the treatises as well; therefore, they are said to be "incomplete."

As soon as Śāriputra heard this—as recorded in the sixth fascicle of the *Zhíguān* (Calming and Contemplation)—it is said that when he first met Aśvajit, the latter spoke: "All phenomena arise from causes; these phenomena are explained by their causes and conditions;
such is their cessation; this is what my Teacher has taught. Upon hearing this, Śāriputra immediately attained the first fruit [of the path] and became [his disciple].

Maudgalyāyana preached the Dharma as described above; it was only upon hearing it a second time that he attained the first fruit of the path. The first phrase refers to the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*);

the second phrase refers to the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*); and the third phrase refers to the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*). Because Śāriputra’s faculties were so sharp, the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*) was not explicitly mentioned.

The characteristics of the dharma of faith and so forth are fully detailed in the sixty-four sections of the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* within the third of the ten vehicles, "Settling the Mind. This section discusses śamatha and vipaśyanā according to each of the four *siddhāntas* for faith, dharma, practice, and so forth, respectively;

these mutually support one another through their reciprocal application in both self-cultivation and the transformation of others, thus forming sixty-four sections. For instance, for a person of faith-practice, they employ śamatha...
The practice of settling the mind (*anxin*) has four *siddhāntas*, and the contemplation of settling the mind likewise has four *siddhāntas*.

When the four *siddhāntas* of calming and contemplation are combined, they constitute eight stages of faith-practice (*śraddhā-caryā*). Since the dharma-practice (*dharma-caryā*) is likewise the same, there are sixteen stages of faith-practice;
those who advance from faith-practice to dharma-practice also have eight stages, and those who advance from dharma-practice to faith-practice likewise have eight stages.
Furthermore, there are eight stages for a person; doubling these twice results in sixteen stages, which, when combined with the previous, total thirty-two stages.
By further combining self-practice and the transformation of others, this constitutes sixty-four stages.
According to that system, there are also one hundred and twenty-eight stages, and so forth.

Because it is able to grasp the physical bases of the sense organs (*rūpīndriya*) and is also able to grasp the continuity of rebirth (*pratisaṃdhi*), this consciousness is called *ādāna*.
Because its nature is unfathomable for sentient beings, it is said to be "profound" (*gambhīra*).

Because those of a lineage inclined toward tranquility (*śamaikāyana-gotra*) cannot penetrate it, it is called "extremely subtle" (*sūkṣma*). It is the true seed of all phenomena and the condition for their connection.

The evolving consciousnesses arise as waves that are constant and uninterrupted, like a violent torrent. "Ordinary" (vāna) refers to the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), while "foolish" (*mūḍha*) refers to those who have entered into tranquility (*śānti*).

Fearing that they might give rise to conceptual attachment toward this [state] and thereby fall into the evil destinies (*apāya*), obstructing the arising of the Noble Path (*āryamārga*), our World-Honored One did not expound upon it.

The term "dùn" (shield) in the *Wenju* (Textual Commentary) is an error for "shùn" (parapet). In the state of Chu, there was a man who sold both spears and shields;

A man came to buy a spear, and while he was still there, another came to buy a shield. The buyer of the spear said to the seller, "Give me back your spear and break your shield;

Furthermore, in accordance with the polemical passages of the Great Sūtra, that sūtra consistently states, "They do not understand my intention.

Within that sūtra, in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, twenty-three pairs of [opposing views] are presented, wherein the Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the World-Honored One, saying: "After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, sentient beings will..."
Thus it is said that the Tathāgata either ultimately enters parinirvāṇa or does not ultimately enter parinirvāṇa;
or he is said to have a self, or he is said to be without a self; or he is said to have an intermediate state (*antarābhava*), or he is said to be without an intermediate state;

The body is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Some say that the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) are conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), while others say they are unconditioned.
Some say that the mind is eternal, while others say the mind is impermanent.

Some say that the enjoyment of the five sensual pleasures (*pañcakāmaguṇa*) can obstruct the Noble Path, while others say it does not obstruct it. Some say that the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*) is... [only]... [the first dhyāna].
This [realm] is the desire realm; some say it consists of the three realms, while others say that giving is mental action (*manas-karma*);

some say there is derived matter (*bhautika-rūpa*), while others say there is no such derived matter.
Some say that there is unmanifest form (*avijñapti-rūpa*), while others say that there is no such thing as unmanifest form;
some say that there are mental factors (*caitta-dharma*), while others say that there are no mental factors;
some say that there are five kinds of existence (*bhava*), while others say that there are six kinds of existence; and some speak of the eightfold precepts of the lay follower (*upāsaka*).
Regarding the full observance of the precepts, some say it is obtained through incomplete observance;
some say that even after a bhikṣu has committed the four grave offenses, the bhikṣu-precepts still remain, while others say they no longer remain;
some say that those from the stage of srotāpanna up to arhat all attain the Buddha-way, while others say they do not; and some speak of the buddha-nature.
Regarding whether sentient beings exist, some say that Buddha-nature is apart from the existence of sentient beings;
others say that even those who have committed the four grave offenses, the five heinous crimes, or the icchantikas all possess Buddha-nature;
some say it does not exist; and some say that there are Buddhas of the ten directions, while others say there are no Buddhas of the ten directions. Having been asked such questions, the Buddha—
They all replied, one by one, saying they did not understand my meaning, as follows:
"In the sutras, I have told the bhikṣus that there is one vehicle, one path, one practice, and one object.
In this way, this single vehicle up to this single object can bring great tranquility to sentient beings and forever sever all bonds, sorrows, sufferings, and the causes of suffering."

I cause all the multitudes to arrive at the single truth of selfhood; yet my disciples, failing to understand my intention, proclaim that the Tathāgata has said that those from the stage of *srotāpanna* up to the *arhat* shall all attain the path of Buddhahood.
In my sutras, I have stated that the *srotāpanna* returns seven times between the human and celestial realms before attaining parinirvāṇa, and so forth—this is what I, my disciples, [have taught].
Not understanding my intention, he proclaimed that the Tathāgata taught that from the stage of *srotāpanna* up to the *arhat*, one does not attain the Buddha-way;
he even concluded by stating that such disputes constitute the realm of the Buddhas and are not known by *śrāvakas* or *pratyekabuddhas*.

Refuting the various non-Buddhist schools regarding whether the intermediate state (antarābhava) exists as being identical to or distinct from the aggregates (*skandha*):

The *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* cites the statement of Upatissa that there is definitely an intermediate state for those born in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*). The *Vibhajyavādins* say there is no intermediate state, while the Sarvāstivādins also maintain that there is definitely an intermediate state.
The masters of the treatises likewise agree; they hold that depending on the sharpness or dullness of one's karma, those with powerful evil karma enter directly into hell.

Those whose wholesome karma is powerful are born directly as devas or humans, and there is no intermediate state (*antarābhava*) for them. Regarding the calculation of those who have attained the outflow-free state (*anāsrava*):

there is retrogression for those in the first fruit (*srotāpanna*), while for those in the second fruit (*sakṛdāgāmin*) who enter the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) and abandon afflictions through conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), there is the possibility of retrogression.

For an Arhat, it is logically certain that there is no retrogression from the outflow-free state; however, the retrogression of the two preceding fruits involves being led away [from their attainment].
Regarding the Arhat’s retrogression, the analogy of the sand well is cited: there are bricks above and below with sand in between; when the middle sand collapses, it falls downward.
This discusses how what people reckon as the non-outflow (anāsrava) state is non-retrogressive, yet one may retrogress from meditative concentration (dhyāna).
One who has attained the "lightning-flash" concentration of the desire realm finds this concentration difficult to grasp and sometimes loses it; this is termed "retrogression from the non-outflow."
The Sarvāstivādins maintain that the Buddha-body is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); the Mahāsāṃghikas maintain that the Buddha-body is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*);

The response body (*nirmāṇakāya*) is conditioned and the true body (*dharmakāya*) is unconditioned; this is the causal basis for the tenets maintained by the Sarvāstivāda school.
According to the Sarvāstivāda, that which is conditioned is impermanent; however, what is taught by the Mahāsāṃghika is that it is unconditioned.

The Sarvāstivāda maintains that because the mind lacks continuity, it is impermanent; whereas the Mahāsāṃghika maintains that because the mind possesses continuity, its meaning is established as permanent.

Furthermore, the *Abhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* (Treatise on the Heart of Abhidharma) adopts the Sarvāstivāda position, asserting that because the mind possesses continuity, it is permanent. Thus, the Sarvāstivāda explains: [the mind is impermanent].

Regarding the five desires as obstacles to the Path, the *Saṃghīka* school maintains that they do not obstruct [the attainment of the Path], while the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (Cheng lun) calculates that there are both obstructions and non-obstructions.
The *Sarvāstivāda* school states that the four fundamental dhyānas of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) can give rise to the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*).

The *Mahīśāsaka* school states that both the realms of form and desire (*kāmadhātu*) can universally give rise to the five kinds of preparatory stages (*prayoga*), and no treatise clarifies that this is not the case.

Regarding those who give rise to the five preparatory stages (*prayoga*) within the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), only the Vātsīputrīya school asserts that they arise in all three realms while one is still an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).

Through conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), one abandons the afflictions; upon reaching the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), one further cultivates untainted knowledge (*anāsravajñāna*) at a later time to abandon the remaining afflictions.
Since the preparatory stages for abandoning [afflictions] in the formless realm are actually those previously generated, it is therefore possible to say that they arise in all three realms.

The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* (Cheng lun) states that [the nature of giving] resides solely in the mental ground (*manobhūmi*), taking the volition (*cetanā*) associated with the relinquishing of wealth as its primary substance, while it is also manifested through body and speech.
The *Abhidharma-piṭaka* (Pi tan), following the Sarvāstivāda school, maintains that the two types of karma—material and non-material—are exclusively wholesome in the mental ground;

In the *Abhidharma* (Vibhāṣā), it is maintained that there definitely exists "constructed form" (*nirmāṇa-rūpa*). What is described as constructed form in the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*, however, does not exist [as such].

Furthermore, Yuan further explains this in terms of both the general and the specific. Generally speaking, the forty stages of mind collectively constitute the four reliances (*catvāraḥ pratisaraṇāni*).

Because they act as a refuge for the world, they generally belong to the stage of disciples; because they extensively proclaim the Buddha-dharma,
specifically, the first reliance is the stage of disciples, the fourth reliance is the stage of teachers, and the two intermediate reliances are both teacher and disciple.

The combination of the four elements constitutes a person; after death, the spirit departs while the body does not. This is called "thus-gone" (*tathāgata*), "not thus-gone," "neither thus-gone nor not thus-gone.

If one calculates it as impermanent, it is because they perform actions for the sake of fame and profit in this present life. As for those who calculate it as both permanent and impermanent, some say that the spirit is of two kinds: the first...

If one calculates it as neither impermanent nor eternal—if it were eternal, there would be no demerit or merit;
if it were impermanent, there would likewise be no demerit or merit. Why? Because if it were eternal, suffering and pleasure would not differ, just like space.
Empty space is not moistened by rain nor can it be dried by wind or sun; yet if there were no impermanence, suffering and pleasure would not undergo transformation.
For example, when wind and rain enter a cowhide, it rots and decays. Because of my own mind, I have said that there must be a self (*ātman*), but it is neither eternal nor impermanent.

The seven propositions of the view of annihilation (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*): 1. If śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas maintain such a doctrine as:

It states: "The three provisional designations (*prajñapti*): the provisional designation of phenomena (*dharma-prajñapti*) is established through causes; the provisional designation of sensation (*vedanā-prajñapti*) is established through continuity;

the provisional designation of names (*nāma-prajñapti*) is established through mutual dependence. Regarding the statement that "the five aggregates are in combination" (*saṃghāta*), this is the provisional designation of phenomena; since it speaks of "combination," it is identical to being established through causes.

It is the same as the case of a tree, which exists because of its roots, trunk, branches, and leaves; thus, there is a name "tree. This is a conventional designation (*prajñapti*). "Feeling" (*vedanā*) refers to the act of experiencing (*anubhava*).

Because of the roots and trunk, the tree can be experienced; because one experiences the tree, the tree exists. From beginning to end, this is a conventional designation of continuity (*saṃtati-prajñapti*).

By means of these names, one grasps the characteristics of two phenomena and speaks of these two types; this is called the conventional designation of usage (*upacāra-prajñapti*), as in the case of the tree.

The name and the branches and leaves are called "grasping" (*upādāna*). These two names refer to the two types of phenomena that constitute the tree. The lower branches and leaves of the name are the branches and leaves of the phenomena;

the four great elements below the name are the phenomena. Thus, these two names and two phenomena—when they depend upon one another to give rise to the name "tree"—constitute dependent designation (*upādāya-prajñapti*).
In the first dhyāna, the kalpas and lifespans are equal; from the second dhyāna onwards, the kalpas are shorter while the lifespans are longer, and so forth.

Regarding "vitality" (*jīvita*) as a factor dissociated from mental concomitants (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*), the *Commentary on the Hundred Dharmas* (*Bai fa shu*) states: "The term 'conditioned formations' (*saṃskāra*) refers here to the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). There are two types of formations:

first, associated formations (*saṃprayukta-saṃskāra*), which are the mental factors (*caitta-dharma*); second, dissociated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*), also called 'factors dissociated from mind,' because they do not associate with the mind."

Because it is not a mental factor (*citta-dharma*), it is distinguished from associated formations (*saṃprayukta-saṃskāra*). The phrase "also not matter" excludes non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*);

according to the *Śata-dharmaka-śāstra*, there are twenty-four non-associated formations: (1) acquisition (*prāpti*), (2) life-force (*jīvita*), (3) generic similarity (*nikāya-sabhāga*), (4) the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*), (5) the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), (6) the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), (7) the retribution of non-conception (*āsaṃjñika*), (8) names (*nāman*), and (9) phrases (*pada*).
1. Substance (dravya), 2. Birth (jāti), 3. Aging (jarā), 4. Abiding (sthiti), 5. Impermanence (anityatā), 6.

Regarding the nature of these factors, if one follows the *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā*, it says: "The formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayukta-saṃskāra*) include acquisition (*prāpti*), non-acquisition (*aprāpti*), homogeneity (*sabhāgatā*), the two attainments of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti* and *nirodha-samāpatti*), life-force (*jīvitendriya*), characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), the group of names (*nāmakāya*), and so forth. for the six [hells] beginning with Saṃjīva (Reviving), one day and night is respectively equal to the lifespan of the gods of the desire realm; their actual lifespans are likewise the same.

Regarding the ten precepts: first, not deficient; second, not broken; third, not pierced; fourth, not mixed; fifth, following the Path; sixth, non-attachment;
seventh, praised by the wise; eighth, mastery; ninth, conforming to meditative concentration; tenth, complete fulfillment. "Not deficient" means: [as previously stated].
Precepts that are "fundamentally grave" refer to the four *pārājika* offenses. Precepts that are "unbroken" refer to the thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses.
Precepts that are "unpierced" refer to the *pāyattika* and other such offenses. Precepts that are "unmixed" refer to the precepts associated with meditative concentration (*samādhi-samvara*).

Precepts that "accord with the Path" refer to following correct principle and perceiving the truth. Precepts that are "unattached" refer to being undefiled by the delusions of thought. These are praised as the sovereignty of wisdom.

Distinguishing [the precepts] according to the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) by way of their fulfillment in accordance with meditative concentration, and elucidating the ten precepts of the Great Sūtra from the perspective of the Middle Way, they are:
first, the prohibitory precept; second, the pure precept; third, the virtuous precept; fourth, the unimpaired precept; fifth, the indivisible precept; sixth, the Mahāyāna precept;
seventh, the non-retrogressive precept; eighth, the conforming precept; ninth, the ultimate precept; and tenth, the precept that fully possesses all pāramitās.
In the *Madhyamaka-śīla-śāstra*, the first four precepts correspond to the sequence of the first four [precepts] in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*.

However, where they differ at the fourth [precept], the treatise refers to the "precept of non-confusion" (*asaṃkīrṇa-śīla*), whereas the Great Sūtra refers to the "precept of non-deficiency" (*avikala-śīla*). Although the names "non-confusion" and "non-deficiency" are identical in the treatise, their meanings differ:
the treatise takes "deficiency" (*vikala*) to mean being impaired and thus unfit for use, while the Sūtra takes it to mean having even the slightest deficiency.
Because it is free from impairment, it corresponds to the "unmixed" [precepts] discussed in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*; because it follows the path, it corresponds to the "unattached" precepts;
because it is praised by wisdom, it corresponds to the "Great Vehicle" precepts; because it is sovereign, it corresponds to the "non-retrogressive" precepts;
because it accords with meditative concentration, it corresponds to the "ultimate" precepts; and because it is complete, it corresponds to the "fully endowed" precepts.
The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* fully possesses the precepts of the various pāramitās; one should simply rely on this correspondence and need not alter it.

The *Zi-zhu-shu* (Commentary by Zi) states: "The tip of an autumn hair. A hair-tip is minute. The *Wen-xuan* states: "The trees of Confucius were uneven;
from a hair-tip they grew to the size of a fathom. The commentary notes: "After Confucius passed away, his disciples each planted a tree from their own country within the cemetery.

What was originally as small as a hair-tip eventually reached the size of a fathom. A "fathom" (*gǒng*) refers to the span of both hands joined together. [This concludes the section on] the Virtue of Laozi.
The Sūtra says: "A tree that embraces the arms grows from a tiny sprout; a nine-story tower begins with a mound of earth;
a journey of a thousand li starts from beneath one's feet.
The Records say: "In the River of Nirvāṇa, there are seven kinds of sentient beings."

In one section of the Great Sūtra, six rivers are generally taught: the river of birth-and-death, the river of nirvāṇa, the river of afflictions, the river of Buddha-nature, the river of wholesome dharmas, and the river of unwholesome dharmas. These are paired two by two: regarding the river of birth-and-death, it discusses those who attain escape and those who do not;
regarding the river of nirvāṇa, it discusses those who attain entry and those who do not; regarding the river of afflictions, it discusses those who are able to sever them and those who are not.

The *Discourse on the Severing of the River of Buddha-nature*, the *Discourse on Being Able or Unable to See the River of Wholesome Dharmas*, the *Discourse on Reaching the Ultimate or Not Reaching the Ultimate of the River of Unwholesome Dharmas*, and the *Discourse on Being Able or Unable to Depart from [the River]*—in the thirtieth fascicle, the "Lion’s Roar" chapter states:
"Suppose there are seven kinds of people by the side of the Ganges River; this is a metaphor for the river of birth and death. The river of birth and death encompasses all.
Regarding the thirty-two fascicles of the *Kāśyapaparivarta*, it states: "There are seven sentient beings within the Ganges River.

This is a metaphor for the river of *nirvāṇa*. Since the river of *nirvāṇa* pertains specifically to the *pariccheda-vipariṇāma* (segmented transformation) in order to distinguish the particular from the universal, it speaks of "seven persons" who do not cultivate the three types of wisdom; this refers to the river of *nirvāṇa* according to the *pāryāya-śāsana* (Shared Teaching).
Since the Ganges has already been used as a metaphor for *nirvāṇa*, it is said that [the person] is "in the middle of the river of *nirvāṇa*.

Regarding the passage in the subsequent section explaining the "Chapter on Faith and Understanding" (*śraddhādhimukti-parivarta*), one must understand that the text currently cited is a quotation; therefore, the text of the subsequent section should state:
"On the bank of the river there are seven kinds of people. As for these seven types of beings: the first is "constantly submerged," like a large fish whose body is heavy and sinks deep.
The first is a deep analogy for the icchantika. The second is like a large fish whose body is heavy and which sinks back as soon as it briefly emerges;

this is an analogy for ordinary beings who possess a small amount of wholesome roots. The third is like emerging and then remaining still, such as the timi fish whose body stays in shallow water while delighting in seeing light;
this is an analogy for the four foundations of mindfulness and the stage of "warmth" (ūṣmagata). The fourth is like having emerged and then pervading...
1. Observing the four directions like a fish is a metaphor for those at the stage of the "summit" (*mūrdhan*) and those who have attained the first fruit (*srotāpanna*). 2. Five:
Like a fish that, having observed the four directions, moves for the sake of food is a metaphor for those who have attained the second fruit (*sakṛdāgāmin*).

3. Six: Like a fish that, having moved, stops again is a metaphor for those who have attained the third fruit (*anāgāmin*). 4. Seven: Reaching the other shore is a metaphor for the Arhat, the Pratyekabuddha, and the Buddha.
*Timi* (等也坘彌) is correctly transcribed as *di* (都奚切) with the lower tone for the second syllable, followed by *mi* (迷);
in full it is *timigila*, which is translated here as "the large-bodied fish. Regarding the *śi* (䱜) fish, it is pronounced *cang* (倉各切).
The *Boluozhi* (博物誌) states that the *xi* (鱕) or *xi* (䱜) fish has a bone called a *teng* (鐇) located in front of its nose; its shape is like that of a hatchet. Thus, in Jiangdong...
People call a hatchet "jīn" (斤) or "fù" (斧). Both characters "jīn" (鱭) and "fù" (鐇) are pronounced with the *fanguan* (甫煩) rhyme.
I do not have time to explain them here; as noted in the fifth record of the *Zhiguan* (止觀), the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, fascicle 32, states:
"There may be Buddha-nature in icchantikas, but there is no [Buddha-nature] in those who possess roots of goodness. This was not so in ancient times.
The Master [Huiyuan] said that this refers to the nature of the "evil realm" (*āpatti-bhūmi*): there is Buddha-nature in those with roots of goodness, but none in those who are *icchantikas*.
The Ancient Master [Tanyan] said this refers to the "conditioning cause" (*pratyaya-hetu*) nature: both types of persons possess it.

Furthermore, regarding Buddha-nature where both types of persons lack it, the Ancient Master said this refers to the "direct cause" (*hetu-hetu*) nature. Furthermore, regarding Buddha-nature where both types of persons lack it, the Ancient Master said this refers to the "fulfillment" [nature].
If one interprets the nature of the cause (*hetu-bhāva*) in this manner, it reflects the provisional meaning (*neyārtha*) of the Separate Teaching (*pratyeka-yāna*).

If it were the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), it should be stated that both icchantikas and virtuous persons possess the nature of inherent merit (*prakṛti-guṇa*). Specifically, icchantikas possess the potential for cultivated evil, whereas virtuous persons lack it;

and while icchantikas lack the potential for cultivated good roots, virtuous persons possess them. Thus, these two types of people differ, and there is no such thing as a "non-retrogressive nature" (*avaivartika-dhātu*) common to both.

This is because none have yet entered the stage resembling [the true nature]. However, the *Fuxing* (Subcommentary) states that both lack it; the claim by ancient masters that this refers to the "nature as the revealing cause" (*liaoyin xing*) is an error.
The ancient masters merely stated they lacked the "nature of the fruit of fruits" (*guoguo xing*), and further stated they lacked the "fruit-nature" (*guoxing*).

The *Fuxing* also mentions those with "wholesome roots" (*shangen ren*); while some ancient masters claimed these were the "conditions-nature" (*yuanxing*), the present text states that those with wholesome roots are... [the nature].

Regarding the nature of the "revealing cause" (*jñāna-hetu*), the former masters stated that for those who possess roots of goodness, the ten thousand virtues constitute the revealing cause, which is also termed the "conditioning cause" (*pratyaya-hetu*).

Therefore, the present text and the *Fuxing ji* each cite one side [of this teaching]. Furthermore, regarding the statement in the present text that "in the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) the cause is evil, while in the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) the cause is good," both instances of the word "cause" (*hetu*) must be read as subordinate [to the truths they qualify]; that is, [the cause of] evil [is the conventional truth, and the cause of] good [is the ultimate truth].
This refers to both the cause and the virtuous cause. A sutra states that *meigui* (玫瑰) refers to a fire-jewel (*huazhu*);

furthermore, it is said that among stones, those that are beautiful are called *mei* (玫), while those that are perfectly round are called *gui* (瑰). Guo Pu remarked: [the former is like the color of rose buds, and the latter is like the color of the *meihua* flower].
The stone-bead is also known as langgan; it originates from Mount Kailash (Kunlun) and Mount Kaoming.

Regarding these seven treasures, their enumeration varies across the sūtras and śāstras: sometimes crystal is omitted while amber is included, or sometimes coral is excluded while red pearls are taken instead.
Regarding *candana* and *agaru-candana*:
*candana* has been explained as above; as for *agaru*, the *Yiwuzhi* (Record of Strange Things) states that it comes from the kingdom of Jiaozhi (Junnanshoku).

When one wishes to harvest it, the tree must first be cut down and laid on the ground. After a long period, the outer layers rot away, while the heartwood remains firm; when placed in water, it sinks.

It is said that *schenkang* (agallochum) is next; when it is between the "heart" and "white" grades and is neither particularly fine nor hard, such that when placed in water it neither sinks nor floats but remains level with the surface, it is called *jianxiang*.
The *Muguanye wuzhizhi* (Record of Strange Things from the Muguanye Region) states that this is called the "fragrant tree. It grows for a thousand years, its root becoming exceedingly large.

One must first fell it and let it lie prostrate for four or five years; only then may one go to examine it. After such a long period, the rotten parts of the roots decay away, leaving only the central nodes.
Firm, resilient, and fragrant, its aroma stands alone. The *Guangzhi* states that it originates from Jiaozhou and the western regions;
the *Bencao jing* says that the wood fragrance (*moxiang*) is also called "honey-flavored" (*mimi*), and its taste is pungent and warm.

The term *tóngzǐ* (boy) is a general designation for those aged seven or eight years and above who have not yet married. The *Shìmíng* (Explanation of Names) states: "At fifteen, one is called a *tóng*.
Thus, in the ritual texts, there is the term *yángtóng* (yang-boy); furthermore, hornless oxen and sheep are called *tóng*, and a mountain without peaks is called a *tóngshān* (boy-mountain).
A place devoid of grass and trees is called "bare" (*tóng*); this is because it resembles those who have not yet undergone the capping ceremony.
Regarding the *Rénwáng niànsòng fǎ* translated by Jiāo Lìqū, as for the painted images therein, one must not use animal-hide glue; instead, use various [vegetable-based adhesives].
If there is no fragrant resin (*gandhāguru*), use boiled glutinous rice water to mix with the pigments; the rest is as explained in the text.
The Record states: "As when the Buddha ascended to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven," etc., as in the first record of the *Zhi guan* (Mo-ho chih-kuan).
The Āgamas state that when the Buddha ascended to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, he employed his supernormal powers to restrain his disciples so they would not know his location.
The two kings, longing for the Buddha, fell into great distress. A minister said to the king, "Construct an image to offer in worship.
King Udayana fashioned one from *candana* sandalwood, while King Bimbisāra fashioned one from purple-gold; both were five feet in height. These were the first to be summoned.
When artisans were offered precious rewards for their craftsmanship yet remained unable to create it, Viśvakarman manifested as a human being and came to build it for the king;
the sound of his axe falling reached up to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, and those who heard it attained liberation.
If one follows the *Mingxiang ji* (Records of Miraculous Omens), there are a total of eighteen locations in this land where images and other objects were created.
The *Mingxiang ji* in ten volumes was compiled by Wang Yan of Dayuan during the Southern Qi dynasty;

the *Dongxia Sanbao Gantong Lu* (Record of the Responsive Communications of the Triple Gem in the Land of the Rising Sun) in three volumes was compiled by the Śramaṇa Yanzong of Hongfu Monastery during the Great Tang. Within its middle volume, it lists sacred images that have manifested...

The causes for these descents consist of fifty articles; the first also cites the *Mingxiang ji* (Records of Miraculous Auspiciousness), stating that in a dream during the Han dynasty, a divine person appeared, and so forth.

The third lists the account of the stone image in Wu, stating that in the first year of the Jianxing era of Emperor Min of the Western Jin, a fisherman named Hua Yan from the mouth of the Hudu Estuary in Songjiang, Wuxian County, Wujun, saw from afar within the sea...
The two men appeared floating upon the water; the fishermen, suspecting them to be sea deities, summoned shamans and priests and prepared sacrificial animals to welcome them.
However, the wind and waves grew even more violent. A lay follower of the Buddha named Zhu Ying, hearing of this, sighed and said, "Could this not be a descent of the Great Awakened One?
He then purified himself through fasting, prostrated himself, and went to welcome them; thereupon the winds and waves became calm as they drifted down the river.
The two men followed the tide into the estuary; as they drew closer, it gradually became clear that they were stone statues.

Upon examining the inscriptions on the backs of the statues, one was named Vipaśyin and the other Kāśyapa. It was impossible to determine their imperial era, yet the calligraphy remained distinct. The statues stood seven feet high.
The śramaṇa Fákāi, having come from the Western Regions, declared that according to the sūtras, there are two stone statues in the East.
There were those who, by making offerings, paying homage, and visiting [the image], were cleansed of the sins accumulated over many kalpas.

Furthermore, there was an image manifested through the devotion of Wu Pei, the Governor of Wuxing. This was the eighth [image]. It was listed among the works of Zhou Yi, of the Eastern Jin dynasty. Pei’s rank reached that of Governor of Wuxing;
his family had served the Buddha for generations, and his daughter was especially diligent in her practice. One day, while a household servant was fishing, he suddenly saw...

A golden light overflowed the river, reflecting upward along the current; immediately casting down his net, he obtained a golden image about three feet high, its features solemn and radiant, floating upon the water and remaining still despite being pulled or pushed. He hurried to inform the King, who sent the Princess by boat to welcome it.
Seeing it from afar, she felt joy in her heart, prostrated herself, and reached out to pull it toward her, whereupon she obtained it.

When she was on board the ship at home, she made offerings to the image of the Buddha. One evening, she dreamed that the Buddha’s left knee was in pain; upon waking, she examined the statue and found that the knee indeed had a hole.
She immediately repaired it with a golden hairpin. What is now called "the daughter of Wu Pei" is merely a corruption and abbreviation of the original text.
*Jātī* (招提) means "the four directions" in this [language].
*Puṇḍarīka* (分陀利).
This is called the White Lotus Sutra.

Regarding the *Baihutong* (Comprehensive Explanation of the White Tiger), it was at the White Tiger Hall that Emperor Xiaozhang of the Later Han dynasty convened a group of Confucian scholars to discuss the similarities and differences among the Five Classics.
The work consists of ten volumes in total, compiled and finalized by Ban Gu upon imperial decree, which he then presented for the Emperor’s perusal.
The *Jing* (Classic) states that music was created;
the *Shiben* (Book of Origins) states that during the era of the Yellow Emperor, Ling Lun created music.
The *Shuowen jiezi* states that "gu" means to strike a drum. The *Shiben* states that the Yi people invented the drum;
when it is struck with a mallet, it is called a "gu," and when it is shaken with the hand, it is called a "bei."

*Chui* (吹) is pronounced with the *chi* (尺) and *wei* (偽) finals; it refers to wind instruments. The *Monthly Ordinances* (*Yueling*) states: "Order the Master of Music to practice the *chui* [wind instruments]. This refers to the *jiao* (角) [horn].

The *Tongdian* states that it is not recorded in the historical annals and may have originated among the Qiang or Hu peoples to alarm the Middle Kingdom; Ma Rong, however, says it originated in Wu and Yue.
It is shaped like a clam shell (*bai*).
The *dali* (large lǐ) can hold several shēng; it is blown simultaneously to keep time with the music and also originated from the Southern Barbarians.
Regarding the *xiāo*, the *Shìběn* states that it was created by Shùn; its shape is uneven, resembling the wings of a phoenix, consisting of ten tubes and measuring two chi in length.
Regarding the name *lai*: in previous generations there was the *dongxiao*, which is no longer extant today. Cai Yong stated that the *xiao* is made by binding bamboo together with a base;
the large version has twenty-three tubes and the small version has sixteen. If long, the sound is deep (*zhuo*); if short, it is clear (*qing*).
By filling the base with honey or wax and adjusting its thickness, the sound becomes harmonious.
The *Fengsu Tong* (Comprehensive Account of Customs) states that the flute was created by Qiu Zhong; it is fourteen inches long and has seven holes. As for the *qin*:

The *Shiben* states that the qin was created by Shen Nong; the *Qinzhuo* states that Fu Xi made the qin for the purpose of cultivating the person, regulating the nature, and returning to one's true essence.
The *Baihutong* states that "qin" means "prohibition," as it prohibits evil and rectifies the human heart.
The *Guangya* states that its length is three chi and six cun and six fen, corresponding to the three hundred and sixty-six days of the year.
The five strings represent the Five Elements: the great string is the ruler, broad and harmonious yet warm; the small strings are the ministers, pure and upright without disorder.
King Wen and King Wu added two more strings to symbolize the bond between ruler and minister.
The *Erya* states that a large *qin* is called a *li* with twenty-seven strings, though the instrument no longer exists today.
The *konghou* was created by the musician Hou Tiao during the reign of Emperor Wu of the Han dynasty; some say it was created by Hou Hui.
Its sound was "kan-kan," responding to the rhythm, and was thus called *kanhou*. The pronunciation later shifted to *konghou*. As for the character "Hou," it was derived from the music.
The artisan’s surname was Er.
Because the Han Emperor sent the Princess of Wusun to marry the Kunmi (the King of Wusun) and feared she might feel longing and nostalgia during her journey, he dispatched this artisan.

The *zheng* and *zhu* lutes were modified for use as music on horseback; they were played with the hands like a *pipa*, with the forward movement of the hand called "striking" (*pi*) and the backward movement called "grasping" (*ba*). The *niao* cymbals...
The *Tongdian* states: "The *náo* resembles a set of chimes (*biānzhōng*) but lacks tongues; it has a handle and is shaken to signal the cessation of the drums.
Among the Han military musical pieces (*gǔchuīqū*), there are the *Nàogē*. The *Shìmíng* says: "The sound of the *náo* is 'nào-nào'."
The entry on *tongbo* (cymbals) states: "People of Chang'an call a dew-dish (*lupan*) a *tongbo*. A record says that this term does not exist in Chang'an, or perhaps it is a phonetic shift.
Now, according to the *Tongdian*, it says: "The *tongbo* is also called a copper dish (*tongpan*); it originates from the West."

Among the Rong tribes and the Southern Man, these [metal vessels] are several inches in diameter and bulge like floating bubbles; they are strung together with leather thongs and struck against one another for musical entertainment.
In the larger states of the Southern Man, they are several feet in diameter; thus we know that the term "copper basin" (*tóngpán*) has been transformed into "dew basin" (*lùpán*).
The commentary states:
The *Book of Han* says that Chang’an was originally named Xianyang. When the Han Founder first stabilized the empire, he intended to make Luoyi the capital;
however, due to the remonstrance of Lou Jing, the Emperor sighed and said, “I shall establish my capital here at Chang’an, and my descendants shall do likewise.”
Regarding the name, it was changed from Chang'an to Chang'an (Constant Peace) during the Yao Qin period;

since Master Shi translated the scriptures while in Qin, they are now collectively referred to as Chang'an. The reason it is not mentioned here is that we adopt the designation used by the Han dynasty, following its original usage.
The *Śīla-sūtra* does not permit the creation of half-body images, stating that doing so incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta*;

likewise, sūtras such as the *Śubhalakṣaṇa-samudgata* and the *Pātayantika* merely state that one must not create half-body images, without mentioning the specific term "offense of *duṣkṛta*" and so forth.

Nevertheless, within those sūtras, when first clarifying the failure to uphold the five precepts or the commission of the six grave offenses (*ṣaḍ-guruka-dharmāḥ*), each instance explicitly states that one incurs both [the loss of merit] and the offense.

Since the offense of the mind does not arise [in this case], there would be no falling away; however, the present text does not permit the creation of half-body images, and I have merely borrowed this passage for that purpose, adding the two characters "virtuous marks" (shànxiàng). Let the readers take note of this.

The record states: "The *Xuanyan ji* (Records of Manifested Verification) was compiled by the Prince of Linchuan of the Song dynasty, Yi; it includes both the *Xuanyan ji* and the *Youming lu* (Records of the Hidden and Visible Worlds).
[Compiled by] the Prince of Chen-si."
The *Wei Zhi* states that Cao Zhi, styled Zijian, was the third son of Emperor Wu of Wei.
He was initially enfeoffed as the Prince of Dong'e, later changed to the Prince of Yongli, and posthumously received the title of Prince of Chen-si.
On the Private System for Translating the Seven Cases:

Now, it is understood that there are eight cases (*vibhakti*): first, the agent; second, the object; third, the instrument; fourth, the purpose; fifth, the point of departure; sixth, the possession; seventh, the locus; and eighth, the vocative.
Because the seven cases are used frequently while the vocative case is rarely employed, they are simply referred to as "the seven. [This concludes the section on] the Western Regions.
If one wishes to study and read the inner and outer scriptures of the Dharma, it is essential to understand the eight grammatical cases (*vibhakti*) of phonology (*śabda-vidyā*);
only then will one know the precise distinctions between words and their meanings. 1. *Prathamā* (the first case) is the direct nominative case;

for example, when a person fells a tree, the name of that person is directly stated, which causes the essence of the sound to be understood. 2. *Dvitīyā* (the second case) is the objective accusative case; for example, the tree that is being felled.
Therefore, it is called "karma" (action). Third, *puruṣaṇā* is the term for the instrument (*karaṇa*), as in "by means of an axe one cuts"; therefore, it is called the "instrument.
Fourth, *puruṣārtha* is the term for the purpose (*sampradāna*), as in "for the sake of a person one cuts"; therefore, it is called the "purpose.
Fifth, *puruṣāt* is the term for the source (*apādāna*), as in "because of a person one builds a house and so forth"; therefore, it is called the "source."
Furthermore, "from" (*prati*) signifies the cause; "belonging to" (*pratiṣaṭsa*) signifies the sense of subordination, as when a servant belongs to a master, hence it is called "subordinate";
"at" (*pratiṣa*) signifies the sense of location, as when a guest relies upon a host, hence it is called "located at.
"At" carries the meaning of "relying upon. In the *Yogācārabhūmi*, these seven types are designated as the "seven loci," and for this reason—
Because this is a general rule for generating understanding, there are only the eight grammatical cases (*vibhakti*) of the Sanskrit language;
to these are further added the vocative (*sambodhana*), which is called "calling" because it is the sound used for summoning. Now, each of these eight sounds has three types:
first, masculine; second, feminine; and third, neither masculine nor feminine. For now, this explanation is given based on the masculine gender.
The term *puruṣa* (梵名) is transcribed as *lúshā* (盧沙)—the character *shā* being pronounced with the initial of *zǎi* (崽) and the final of *suǒ* (所).

Furthermore, the *Fódào lùnhéng* states that Prince Cè of the Wèi Dynasty possessed the qualities of a jade vessel from childhood; by the age of ten, he was already capable of composing literary works.

Whenever he read the scriptural texts, he would linger over them in deep admiration and praise, regarding them as the ultimate pinnacle of the Supreme Way (*zhìdào*). Consequently, he composed the *Zhuǎndú* (Recitation of Transitions), employing the seven musical tones with their various ascents, descents, and melodic modulations.
The echoes of these [chants] have been such that the world’s recitations all take them as their model.

Once, while traveling at Mount Yushan, he suddenly heard the resonance of Brahma-heavenly sounds in the air—clear, soaring, mournful, and elegant; their tones moved his heart. He listened alone for a long time, yet those in attendance heard nothing.

Daosheng was profoundly moved by this divine principle and gained a deeper realization of the correspondence of the Dharma. Thus, he admired those sounds and adorned them by transcribing them into *fanbai* (Brahma-chants).

He composed this treatise and established its script as a model for future generations; it was from this point that the radiant glory of the Sanskrit sound began. Furthermore, the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Gaoseng zhuan*) states:

"The golden words have been translated, yet the resonance of the Sanskrit has not been transmitted. During the Wei dynasty, Chen Siwang (Cao Zhi) deeply loved prosody and devoted his mind to subtle sounds.
Having mastered the auspicious resonance of the *pañca-vārṣika* assembly, he was further moved by the divine inspiration at Mount Yushan. Thus [the hymns] were composed.
This is used to treat the fundamental origins and auspicious responses as the core for students.

If one collects the *Lunheng* and the sevenfold inflections (*saptavibhakti*) and finds them identical to the records, they may not necessarily be exactly like the sevenfold inflections of the *Śabdavidyā-śāstra*; let students reflect upon this.
The *Yushan Xingzheng Ji* (Record of the Expedition to Mount Yu) states that Mount Yu is located on the banks of the river in Jizhou.
It concerns the account of the monk Lingsheng (*Ghaṇṭāśabda*) from the *Xianyu Jing* (Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish).
When King Prasenajit was about to set out on a military expedition, there was a bhikṣu in the Jeta Grove whose physical form was extremely short and ugly, yet whose voice was exceptionally wonderful;
as he raised his voice in loud chanting, the sound was so harmonious and flowing that the entire army leaned in to listen, never tiring of it.
The king then asked the Buddha, "For what reason is this bhikṣu’s physical form so exceedingly ugly?"
The Buddha said to the Great King: "In the past, there was a Buddha named Kāśyapa who, having finished delivering sentient beings, entered parinirvāṇa.
The King collected his relics and erected a stūpa to make offerings to them, then commanded the supervisors to each take charge of one side of the construction.
Among them was one supervisor who was indolent and failed to complete his portion alone; the King consequently rebuked that man."
Filled with fear, he addressed the king, saying, "This stupa is too large; when will it be completed? After the king had departed, the stupa was entirely finished and stood clearly visible.
That man immediately repented his previous transgression and, taking a single golden bell, placed it at the top of the stupa's spire.
He then made a vow, saying, "May the sound of my voice be extremely exquisite in all future births."
The Buddha’s name is Śākyamuni; he has enabled me to see him so that I may cross over the suffering of birth and death. By virtue of these causes and conditions, such is my karmic retribution:
because I once resented the great size of the stupa, my body is extremely short; yet, because I offered bells as a gift, I have now attained liberation.
The Brahmajāla Sūtra strictly prohibits this; what need is there for further insistence?
One must not listen to the sounds of conchs, drums, horns, lutes, harps, zithers, flutes, oboes, singing, shouting, or the music of courtesans.
If one intentionally makes such sounds, one commits a minor offense (light defilement).

Regarding those who arrive here and offer flowers, incense, and so forth, the *Bodhicittotpādana-sūtra* translated by Ci'en states: "If one offers even a single flower as a gift, one obtains the flowers of the seven factors of enlightenment;
by offering incense, one obtains the fragrance of the fivefold Dharma-body; and by offering a banner, one obtains dhāraṇīs."
Because it turns away all evils, giving a canopy results in obtaining the four immeasurables (*catur-apramāṇa*) that cover sentient beings.
As the *Karmavibhaṅga-sūtra* states, each obtains ten virtues, such as when a sentient being prostrates before a Buddha-stūpa and obtains ten merits:
first, a beautiful appearance and voice; second, others believe their words; third, fearlessness when among a multitude; fourth, being cherished and protected by devas and humans.
1. Possessing the power of the five perfections; 2. Being closely attached to by sentient beings; 3. Constantly drawing near to all Buddhas; 4. Possessing great merit and retribution;
5. Reborn in the heavens at the end of life; 6. Realizing nirvana.
The Sūtra states:
"Namo" (the *mo* is pronounced with the *hu* and *qie* tones), which is also called "Vandana" or "Panna. The text of this passage cites the *Pañcaśīla-sūtra*.

From this, we know that it is sentient beings who utter the words of taking refuge; "taking refuge" (*guiming*) is precisely *namo*.

In terror, they joined their palms in refuge.

The record states that in the country of India to the west of China, "Nagasena" is the name for an elephant; this bhikṣu was born at a time when a large elephant in his household was born simultaneously with him.
His parents therefore named him Nāgasena. Nāgasena said:
"The statement by the various śramaṇas that the fire of the world is not as hot as the fire of hell is likely erroneous;
it should be corrected to 'Nāgasena said: It was made by the King. Thus, that sūtra says: "The King again..."
The question "Nagasena, you sramanas say that they are equal," etc., should be stated as:
"The King said, 'Take a small stone and place it upon a worldly fire,' etc.

When it is said that evil people die and fall into the *niraya* hells, one should say: "All śramaṇas likewise say that when people commit evil, they die and fall into the *niraya* hells.

One should correct "one person dies and is born in niraya" to "is born in the Brahma-heaven. The above text contains an error, or perhaps it stems from a different version of the scripture;
please investigate this further. [The Assembly at Huālín Garden]
This refers to the three assemblies under the Dragon Flower tree. When Maitreya descends to be born, within the Jambudvīpa continent there will be no mountains, hills, valleys, or ravines;
the ground will be as level as a whetstone. The trees will grow tall, and the population will be small. The three poisons will be diminished.
The city will be named Ketumatī, and there will be a brahmin named Śubhavyūha who will serve as Maitreya’s father and mother; his name will be Mahāvyuha.
The Inscription on Maitreya: His son’s body was sixteen *zhang* tall; at birth, his vision reached ten thousand *li*;

the light from the sun upon his head illuminated four thousand *li*. He shall sit beneath the Dragon Flower (*Nāgapuṣpa*) tree within the Huālín Garden—the tree being forty *li* high and its breadth likewise—and there attain Buddhahood. The *Dàchéngfójīng* (Mahāyāna Sūtra on Becoming a Buddha) says: "Flower..."

It is called the Dragon-Flower Tree (*nāgapuṣpa*) because its trunk resembles the head of a dragon; it is also called so because its branches are like precious dragons spitting forth flowers made of a hundred jewels;

furthermore, it is called so because its seeds emerge from the Dragon Palace. Moreover, the *Ekottarika Āgama* states that the Dragon-Flower Tree is one yojana in height and five hundred paces in breadth.
He said: "By the power of the practitioner's roots of goodness, the aspects of words and meanings arise upon the consciousness of the Tathāgata," as explained previously in the section on hearing.

The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states that there is an interpretation according to which, through the power of the primary condition consisting of the listener’s roots of goodness and their original vows, the aspects of word and meaning arise within the Tathāgata’s consciousness.

These arising aspects of word and meaning are produced by the Buddha’s roots of goodness for the benefit of others and are termed "the Buddha’s teaching. As for what is called "word" (*vyañjana*), it refers to the *yukti*... [text continues].
The *Śatasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā* states: "In brief, the essence of all sūtras is twofold: first, the letter (*vyañjana*), and second, the meaning (*artha*).
