In the new edition from Yuezhou, the character "lǎo" (old) was erroneously written as "chōng" (to fill).
The character "zī" (beard) refers to the hair on the upper lip above the mouth.
The thirty-six items consist of twelve each for the internal, external, and intermediate categories, totaling thirty-six; alternatively, there are twenty-six internal and ten external items:
hair, body hair, nails, teeth, thin skin, thick skin, muscle, sinew, bone, marrow, spleen, kidneys, liver, and gallbladder.
The lungs, large intestine, small intestine, heart, stomach, excrement, urine, filth, tears, nasal mucus,
saliva, pus, blood, veins, yellow phlegm, white phlegm, rheum, fat, marrow, brain, and meninges— these are called the thirty-six substances.
The character for "moon" (月) is correctly written as the character for "belly" (肚). This is a notification to the customs house.
"Baoying" (retribution) is pronounced *jiāngǔ* (with *jiān* being the correct character). It means "intervals and barriers," as well as "coming and going.
It also describes the appearance of rugged hardship and the manner of establishing or arranging things.
The Sūtra states:
"The *chī* (owl) [is pronounced with the initial *chī* and the final *chǐ*; it is a bird with large eyes that loves to eat mice] and is also called a 'strange bird.
The *xiāo* [is pronounced with the initial *gǔ* and the final *yáo*; it is the bird of unfiliality]."

The *diao* (vulture) and the *jiu* (bearded vulture). The *diao* is also called the "red-beaked" [bird], capable of eating deer and elk. Regarding the *jiu*, the *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it is black in color and has many offspring.
It is further said that those from the south have yellow heads and red throats, possessing all five colors; those from the Western Regions are described as being bluish-yellow and red.
This refers to the "eyes.
The commentary states that the three characters "five hundred people" (五百人) in the third line of the verse above are an error; they should instead be four characters.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra on the Eight Types of Pride* states: first, pride; second, excessive pride (*mānātimāna*); third, inferiority pride (*ūnamāna*); fourth, overweening pride (*adhimāna*);

fifth, self-pride (*asmimāna*); sixth, false pride (*mithyāmāna*); and seventh, arrogance (*mada*). Zhiyan (Zhang’an) stated that the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* includes great pride (*mahāmāna*) as the eighth.

Pride (*māna*). "Māna" refers to one whose wisdom and understanding surpass all others such that none can equal them. "Great Pride" (*atimāna*) refers to regarding those who are equal as superior, or regarding those who are superior as equal.
"Pride beyond pride" (*mānātimāna*) refers to regarding those who are mostly inferior as being merely slightly inferior, when in fact there is a vast difference.
"Self-pride" (*asmimāna*) consists of viewing the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) as a self and becoming attached to what belongs to the self (*ātmīya*), arising from wrong views.
Pride (*māna*) is when one truly lacks merit yet considers oneself to possess it. The *Mahāvibhāṣā* also enumerates seven types of pride:

(1) pride (*māna*), (2) excessive pride (*atimāna*), (3) pride beyond pride (*mānātimāna*), (4) the pride of "I am" (*asmimāna*), (5) overweening pride (*adhimāna*), (6) inferiority pride (*ūnamāna*), and (7) false pride (*mithyāmāna*).
The seven prides in the *Abhidharmakośa* are identical to those in this text. The *Abhidharma* (*Vibhāṣā*) also lists seven prides: (1) pride (*māna*) and (2) excessive pride (*atimāna*).

The three types of *māna* (conceit), four types of *adhimāna* (overweening conceit), five types of *asmimāna* (the conceit "I am"), six types of *ūnamāna* (inferiority conceit), and seven types of *mithyāmāna* (false conceit).
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* also enumerates seven types of conceit: first, *māna*; second, *atimāna*; third, *mānātimāna*; fourth, *asmimāna*; fifth, *adhimāna*;
sixth, *ūnamāna*, which refers to claiming to possess virtues when one actually lacks them; and seventh, *mithyāmāna*. These can be understood through their respective explanations.

This refers to what is stated in the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*: "The various teachings also explain pride (*māna*) by means of the seven types of pride. Therefore, it was cited here merely to demonstrate that point.
[Next is] the nature of arrogance (*mada*).
The character for *xing* (nature/lineage) should be written as *xìng* (surname). The new edition of Yuezhou uses the character *xìng*.
The *Jì* (Record) states that "few surnames" (*guǎxìng*) refers to those who say it is a surname of the lowly and humble.
It is said that the Cui and Lu clans are noble surnames of high status. The Bodhisattva Precepts state: "Those of small surnames are lowly, base, humble, poor, and destitute;

those of great surnames have high-ranking households, abundant wealth, and are learned and prosperous. How could these [members of the Cui and Lu clans] possibly be considered people of meager lineage?
The *Book of Jin* states that Shi Chong’s courtesy name was Jilun. His wealth was vast and accumulated; his residences were grand and magnificent.

His gold, jade, silks, and musical instruments were all the finest of the age, and his culinary delicacies exhausted the rarest treasures of both land and water. He [rivaled] the high-ranking relatives Wang Kai and Yang...
Among the followers of [Zhu] Xi, extravagance and luxury were held in high esteem.
The *Book of Jin* (Jin shu) states that Pan An—whose courtesy name was Anren—was handsome in appearance; in his youth, he would often carry a crossbow while walking through Luoyang.
Whenever women encountered him on the road, they would all join hands and circle around him, throwing fruit at him until his cart was full before returning home.
At that time, Zhang Zai was extremely ugly; whenever he walked out, children would pelt him with tiles and stones, and he would return home exhausted.
The Sūtra says:
"Scorpions are more numerous than the earth; they resemble spiders hanging upside down, their tails being venomous. When they sting a person, the pain cannot be stopped for a day.
People of the time call them 'tàlàzǐ' (撻剌子), about the size of a thumb."
Regarding the *yòuyán*, the large variety found in Jiangnan is the centipede (*wǔgōng*). Some also say that those with green bodies and yellow legs are *yòuyán*,
while those with reddish-brown bodies and red legs are centipedes.
The *Ji* (Commentary) states: "The *huǐ* is three inches long and as thick as a finger.
According to the *Erya*, it says: "The *fú-huǐ* measures three inches across, and its head is as large as a thumb (*bò*). Guo Pu explains:
"Its body is three inches wide and its head is as large as a person's thumb. This refers to a specific species of snake named *fú-huǐ*; it is not the name of a fish.
The character "cháng" (長) here is an error; it should be "bó" (博). "Bò" (擘) is pronounced as "bǎi" (百).
"Jíqū" (蝍蛆)—"jí" (蝍) is pronounced as "jí" (即), and "qū" (蛆) is pronounced as "zǐyúqiè" (子餘切)—is the name of an insect. The *Erya* states that it resembles a locust but has a large belly and is long.
The horn can eat the brains of snakes.
Some say it can subdue snakes; those who claim this are mostly barefooted, but such talk is harmful, for one must not disregard the law of karmic retribution.
Cien said: "The *cizhen* (red-footed snake) is very effective for subduing snakes; those that are large and over a foot long, with red feet, are excellent. Those that are yellow are not fit for use.
Many people roast them until they turn red, but this is not the true variety. The commentary to the *Bencao* states:
"Those with red feet mostly come from Jingkou, Changshan, Gaoli Mountain, and Maoshan; those with yellow feet are also very numerous."

There is one creature, the centipede (*jijuzu*), which is incapable of being used [for other purposes] yet possesses the nature to subdue snakes; upon suddenly seeing a large snake, it climbs it and devours its brain.
The *shougong* (lizard) and *yan-yan* (gecko):
when they are in a house, they are called *shougong*; when they are in a marsh, they are called *yan-yan*.

The *Erya*, in its "Explanation of Fishes" (*Shiyu*), states: "The *yōngyuán* (蠑螈), *zhé* (蜥), *yì* (蜴), *wányán* (蝘蜒), and *shǒugōng* (守宮). - *Yōng* is pronounced *róng*; *yuán* is pronounced *yuán*.

- *Zhé* is pronounced *xī*; *yì* is pronounced *yì*. According to Master Ying’s phonetic commentary and the *Cien* (Zhiyan) *Śāstra*, it is called *chùshù* (虫束) in Shandong and *bìgōng* (壁宮) in Shaanxi.
The *Bowuzhi* (Treatise on the Wondrous Record) states that if one raises it in a vessel and feeds it vermilion, [it will lose its regenerative power].
The substance of the *shā* (lizard) is entirely red and weighs seven *jīn*. When ground with ten thousand pestles and applied to a woman’s body, it does not fade for the rest of her life;
however, if she engages in sexual intercourse, the mark fades away. Thus it is called "the palace-guard" (*shǒugōng*). Emperor Wu of the Han dynasty tested this and found it to be true.
It is also named *yuánshàn*, further titled *yíngyuán*, and also called *xīzhì*. When on stone it is named *xīzhì*; when in marshes it is a *yuánshàn*. In...

The *shè* (house-lizard) is the same creature as the *shǒugōng* (palace-guardian), which is called the *yíngyuán*; furthermore, people in the region south of the Yangtze River call the *shǒugōng* the *wànyán*.
It is also said that when it dwells on a wall it is a *wànyán*, and when it dwells in the grass it is a *xīchì*.
The *Sūtra* states: "The hundred-legged [insects]"; the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "Those without legs are the thousand-headed *lao* insects; those with many legs are the centipedes (*wugong*);
those with a hundred legs are the dung beetles (*qieqiāng*); those with two legs are like peacocks; those with four legs are like oxen and horses. (From the *Bencao*).
The commentary states: "The centipede has a great many legs.
*Yòu* (pronounced yù jiù) is the name for an animal resembling a *zhāo* mouse; it is reddish-yellow with a large tail and eats mice; in Jiangdong, it is called..."

*Shèng* (鼪) is pronounced with the *qìng* rhyme of *jìng*; *shòu* (鼦) is pronounced with the *dīng* rhyme of *gōng*. *Yòu* (狖) and *yuò* (貁) have the same pronunciation as above. The *Jì* (Record/Classic) states:

"If one writes the character *yuò*, the *Yùpiān* says it resembles a *lí* (wildcat)," which is likely an error; it should instead state that it belongs to the genus of monkeys (*yuán*). The character is also written as *yòu*, referring to the black monkey.
The *Jì* further states: "If it rains, [the monkey] hangs upside down from a tree," etc.; this should also state that the character is likewise [written as *yòu*].
It is called the *yuì* (pronounced *yòu*). The *Erya* states: "The *yuì* has a nose like a seal and a long tail. Guo Pu says: "The *yuì* resembles a macaque but is larger;
it is yellowish-black in color and its tail is several feet long. Its tail-end has a fork, and its nose is exposed and turned upward.
When it rains, it hangs itself from a tree to plug its nose with its tail, or sometimes with two fingers. People of Jiangdong do this as well.
"Taking and raising them": *yòu* and *róu* are both names for animals resembling monkeys. *Yòuchóng* (snakeworm) is the name of an insect resembling a rat;
*yòu* is also a type of rat. *Lí* (wildcat).
It is also written with the characters 狸 (lí, pronounced with the *li* and *li* finals) and 貍 (lí, pronounced with the *miao* and *li* finals), and 豸 (zhì, pronounced with the *zhi* and *er* finals).
Regarding 鼷 (xī, pronounced with the *hu* and *ji* finals), the record states that "to sting" (*chē*, pronounced with the *shi* and *zhi* finals) refers to insects that discharge poison.
The character "chou" (臭) is pronounced with the departing tone (qùshēng). It refers to the dung beetle (*śalabha*).
It is the name of an insect; it is also called a *kīṭa* (dung beetle). The *Erya* states: "The *kīṭa* is the *qiāngkāng*. Guo Pu explains:
"A black-armored insect that feeds on excrement and soil. [It is also associated with] foxes, wolves, and jackals (*śṛgāla*).
The wild dog (*yěyīn*) can climb trees at night; its color is greenish-yellow, and it moves in packs like dogs, howling at night with a voice like that of a wolf or a fox.
A wolf is a *lángchāi*; the *láng* resembles a dog, while the fox is a demonic beast. Also known as the *yěgān*, it is ridden by ghosts and possesses three virtues:
its color is moderate, its forequarters are small while its hindquarters are full, and when it dies, it turns its head toward its home hill (*shǒuqiū*).

The character *cuǎn* (咀) is pronounced with the initial *lǚ* (呂). A glossary states that *cuǎn* simply means "to chew. *Jiáo* (嚼) is pronounced with the initial *yuē* (約); it refers to chewing and gnawing (*jiào*).
It denotes the act of biting with the teeth.

The first character (齧) is pronounced as *nì* (also written as 嚌); the second character is pronounced as *jié* (*wǔ jié*). It refers to biting with the teeth until they sink in, or tasting until reaching the teeth.
The character *yǎo* (齩) is pronounced as *wǎo* (*wǔ jiǎo*). *Luó* (羸).
The phonetic transcription is *lì wēi* (力危).
The *Jīngyīn* (經音) states that it means to grasp or seize with the hand; the *Shìmíng* (釋名) states it means "sudden" (*zú*), referring to seizing something momentarily.
This means "to say. *Zhā* (樝) is pronounced with the side-radical *cè* (側) and the phonetic *jiā* (加).
Chè (pronounced chì or chīliè). Jāi.
*Wǎi* (five-tone, level): the barking of dogs fighting; it also refers to dogs snapping at one another in defiance.
*Chī* (earth-tone, level): opening the mouth to show the teeth.
*Hūn* (upper radical: *hú*, level tone; lower radical: *lí*, entering tone) and *fèi* (upper radical: *fú*, departing tone; lower radical: *fèi*, departing tone).
To howl, bark, and give birth to offspring.
"Producer" (*shēngchǎn*) means to advance, to nourish, and to create. To bring about transformations based on things is called "producing.

It is also "birth. The *Yùpiān* also states that hatching from an egg is called *fú*. *Fú* is correctly written as *fū*. Among the nine types of creatures, those without milk are said to be "egg-born.
Regarding "milk," the *Shuōwén* says: "The birth of humans and bird chicks is called 'milk' (*rù*). (The pronunciation of *rù* is *zhù*.)

The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states: "The similar cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) obtains a fruit of uniform outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*). The *Ji* (Commentary) says: "The similar cause is that which is similar [to its effect], belonging to its own category (*nikāya*) and level (*bhūmi*), and is prior in time;
it refers to the five categories (*pañca-nikāya*) and nine levels (*nava-bhūmi*), but this is discussed solely with respect to the past taking the present as its cause."

The *Abhidharmakośakārikā* states: "The efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*), the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), the similar-type cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*), the universal cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*), and the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*)—these six types of causes are accepted.

The similar-type cause consists of similar factors within their own category (*nikāya*) and level (*bhūmi*). Paths produced previously act as causes for subsequent paths; across the nine levels, they produce only equal or superior results.

The same applies to those produced through preparatory effort (*prayoga*). This includes those consisting of hearing (*śruta-mayī*), reflection (*cintā-mayī*), and so forth. Now, [the author] cites these various [passages].
The commentary explains the passages used here; the remainder is found in that *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*. It says:

"As for the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), it refers to similar dharmas acting as a homogeneous cause for similar dharmas. That is to say, wholesome five aggregates act as a homogeneous cause for wholesome five aggregates;
defiled [dharmas] for defiled [dharmas]; and neutral [dharmas] for neutral [dharmas], each acting as a cause for the others in mutual relation."
Regarding the *sabhāga-hetu* (homogeneous cause), the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states: "Because the fruit resembles its cause, it is called 'equal' (*sama*);
because it arises from a cause, it is further called a 'stream' (*niṣyanda*). Thus, the fruit of the stream is termed the 'fruit of equal outflow' (*niṣyanda-phala*).

Since the homogeneous cause obtains this fruit of equal outflow, it is said that the homogeneous cause is 'similar. Furthermore, within one's own category (*nikāya*) and level (*bhūmi*), [it acts] for its own category..."
Within one's own stage (*svabhūmi*), there are five categories (*nikāya*) that serve as homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*).

These consist of the afflictions (*kleśa*) belonging to the four truths of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), which constitute four categories, and the afflictions abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), which constitute one; thus, they total five. The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* asks:

"What meaning does the term 'category' (*nikāya*) intend to reveal here? It answers: "It reveals the sense of a 'group' (*saṃgha*). For example, the term 'monk category' (*bhikṣu-nikāya*) refers to the community of monks (*bhikṣu-saṃgha*). The same applies to the term "Brahmin category" (*brāhmaṇa-nikāya*).

The term "gate" (*dvāra*) refers to the assembly of Brahmins; the term "group" (*gaṇa*) refers to a multitude of followers whose meanings differ though they are identical [in function], just like the fourfold assemblies mentioned in the sūtras.

"Grounds" (*bhūmi*) refers to the nine grounds—namely, one ground of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and eight grounds of the form and formless realms (*rūpa-ārūpyadhātu*)—making nine grounds in total.

Among these, that which is abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) serves as a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) for that which is abandoned through the vision of suffering.

The same applies to what is abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*). If one belongs to the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), it serves as a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) for that which belongs to the realm of desire;

the same applies by analogy to the realms of form (*rūpadhātu*) and formlessness (*ārūpyadhātu*). If [dharmas] from different stages (*bhūmi*) are compared with one another, they possess no causal relationship;
therefore, it is said "of its own category and stage" (*sva-nikāya-bhūmi*). Regarding "arising previously," the treatise says: "Furthermore, this is not the case for all [dharmas]. Why?"
This means that those factors born previously are the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) for similar factors—both those already born and those yet to be born—that arise subsequently.

Thus, past factors [are causes] for the other two time periods (past and present), and past and present factors [are causes] for the future, and so forth; all such cases should be explained in detail.
Furthermore, the universal homogeneous cause (*sarvatraga-sabhāga-hetu*) exists only in the past and present, as it does not exist in the future. This concludes the section on causes.
One should know that the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*) produces the ripening fruit (*vipāka-phala*), while the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) produces the dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*).

The homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) and the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*) produce the concordant fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*), whereas the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) and the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*) produce the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*).

The term "fruit of human effort" refers to the functional activity inherent in all phenomena; because it is like the exertion of a person (*puruṣakāra*), it receives the name "fruit of human effort. Furthermore, the dominant fruit is so called because it is preeminent.
The fruit of the superior [cause] is called the *adhipati-phala* (dominant fruit); that which ripens as a different category is called the *vipāka-phala* (ripening fruit).
These are fully explained in various treatises and in the *Zhi guan bu zhu* (Supplementary Notes on Calming and Contemplation).
The Sūtra says: "a mound of earth."
The *Yinyi* (Explanations of Sounds and Meanings) states that it means "to pile up earth," and also says it refers to "a small mound of earth at a corner.
Regarding "pò" (撲),
the *Tongsu Wén* (Popular Texts) states that to overturn by force is called "pò."

The Record states: "Since the disciples of the Buddha also practice the six modes of cultivation and so forth—such as taking the first dhyāna as the superior and sublime object to be sought above, and regarding the lower realm as suffering, coarse, and obstructive to be renounced—if one discusses the causes and effects together, there are twelve [factors].
However, non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) focus exclusively on seeking dhyāna, whereas the disciples of the Buddha employ it [with] right [view]."
This refers precisely to the characteristic of mutual entry (*xiāng rù zhèng xiàng*).
The Sūtra says "nǔ xíng" (naked);
according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means "to bared one's shoulder" (*tàn*) and also "to have a bare body."
The *Jì* (Record) states: "Regarding the sixty-two views, there is a chapter by Zhǐshàn explaining them.
Zhǐshàn says: "There are two meanings to the sixty-two views. First, regarding the view of self (*ātman-dṛṣṭi*), there are fifty-six [positions]:

that is, for each of the five aggregates (*skandha*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), one calculates four propositions, totaling twenty; the same applies to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*). In the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), however, [the form aggregate] is excluded."

Since there are only sixteen [factors] regarding form (*rūpa*), one knows that the three realms together comprise fifty-six. Regarding the six types of extreme views (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), they constitute sixty-two;
this is because each of the three realms calculates either annihilationism or eternalism. Thus, it is known that this is discussed in terms of the three realms.

Second, regarding the three times and the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), each calculates annihilationism or eternalism, taking the two views of existence and non-existence as their root. That is to say:
The four propositions regarding form being "gone" (*gata*) and so forth apply likewise to the other four aggregates, totaling twenty propositions; this calculates the past.
Furthermore, the four propositions regarding form being "eternal" (*nitya*) and so forth apply likewise to the other four aggregates, totaling twenty propositions; this calculates the present.
Furthermore, the four propositions regarding form being "finite" (*antavān*) and so forth apply likewise to the other four aggregates, totaling twenty propositions; this calculates...

The future [time] as well; thus, the three times multiplied by twenty make sixty, and with the addition of both existence and non-existence, they total sixty-two. This is based on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
The twenty [types of views], such as the view of a self-body (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*), and so forth.

That is to say: "The aggregates are the self," "the self is apart from the aggregates," "the self is within the aggregates," and "the aggregates are within the self"—all five aggregates being thus treated results in twenty propositions of the view of a personal body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).

For example, if one reckons one of the five aggregates (*skandha*) as the self and considers the remaining four as its servants and so forth—this corresponds to the sixty-fifth view in the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*. That is, within each of the five aggregates, one reckons the other four as the self;

for instance, "form is the self, while feeling is the servant, and perception, volition, and consciousness are the ornaments, the cave-dwelling, and the three [other] aggregates. This applies similarly to the other aggregates when combined with the self.
Including "I" and "what belongs to me," there are thirteen phrases for each of the five aggregates, thus forming sixty-five phrases in total.
Consequently, for each aggregate, one instance is "I" and three instances are "what belongs to me.
This is fully explained in the fifth fascicle of the *Zhi guan* (Calming and Contemplation), which cites the *Āgama* regarding the primary eon (*kalpa*) and so forth.
The *Dīrgha Āgama* states that these fundamental and derivative views do not exceed sixty-two.

There are eighteen fundamental views regarding kalpas (*pūrvakalpa*) and forty-four derivative views regarding kalpas (*aparāntakalpa*), totaling sixty-two. Regarding the number eighteen: there are four sets of four propositions along with two fundamental views.
As for the first set of four propositions: (1) the view that the world is formed and destroyed over twenty kalpas; (2) the view... [text continues]
Forty eons for the three views and eighty eons for the fourth; with swift wisdom, he explains that each and every phrase refers to the self and the world.
Regarding the second set of four phrases: first, the view that the self and the world are partly eternal and partly non-eternal;
second, the calculation based on play and laughter; third, the calculation arising from loss of mindfulness; and fourth, with swift wisdom, he explains the third set of four.

Regarding the propositions: first, that the self and the world are finite; second, that they are infinite; third, that they are finite in the upward and downward directions but infinite in the four cardinal directions;
fourth, that they are infinite in all directions. Furthermore, regarding the fourfold set of swift-witted inquiries:
first, "Do I not know and not see whether there is retribution for good and evil, or no retribution? Second, "Do I not know and not see whether there is another world, or no other world?"
3. "World-Honored One, I do not know and do not see what is good and what is evil. 4. "Foolish and dull-witted, answering questions according to others.
Regarding the two fundamental phrases: first, through concentrated mindfulness, one knows that sentient beings exist in the future without causes or conditions;
second, through swift wisdom, one speaks of the final kalpa and final views. Regarding the forty-four phrases, the first is as follows:
In the first of the four sets of four propositions, there are four regarding the existence of perception (*saṃjñā*): (1) after my death, I shall be born with form and perception;
(2) I shall be born without form and with perception; (3) I shall be born without form and with perception [variant: with form and perception];
(4) I shall be neither with form nor without form, yet with perception. The second set of four propositions is formulated by contrasting finitude and infinity with the existence of perception.
Regarding the third set of four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*): by pairing "having pleasure" and "being without pleasure" with "having perception," one forms the four propositions.
Regarding the fourth set of four propositions: first, having perception; second, having various perceptions; third, having limited perceptions; and fourth, having immeasurable perceptions.

Regarding the second [section], there are two sets of four propositions. As for the first set of four propositions: by pairing "having form" and "being without form" with "being without perception," one forms the four propositions.
The first set of four propositions is identical to the initial four, differing only in that "non-perception" (*asaṃjñin*) replaces "perception" (*saṃjñin*).
The second set of four propositions consists of applying the categories of "finite" (*antavān*) and "infinite" (*anantavān*) to "non-perception," forming four propositions as in the preceding text.

The third set of four propositions is explained by simply changing "non-perception" to replace "perception. Regarding the two sets of four propositions in the third section, the first four concern those who possess form (*rūpin*).

Regarding the fourfold propositions concerning the formless realm (*ārūpya*) in contrast to "neither-perception-nor-non-perception" (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), and the subsequent fourfold propositions concerning "finite" and "infinite" in contrast to "neither-perception-nor-non-perception":
these two sets of fourfold propositions, together with the preceding four sets of four, constitute thirty-two propositions.
Furthermore, there are seven propositions regarding the view of annihilation (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*). First, if a śramaṇa were to argue as follows: "I..."
1. The body is born from father and mother and ultimately returns to destruction; 2. the various devas born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are subject to annihilation;

3. the various devas born in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) are subject to annihilation; 4. from the sphere of infinite space up to the seventh, the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).

Next, there are five types of eternalism (*śāśvatavāda*): 1. reckoning that one attains *nirvāṇa* by indulging in the five desires of the present; 2. [the view that it is attained] in the first dhyāna.
Three [factors] for the second dhyāna, four for the third dhyāna, and five for the fourth dhyāna; these seven "constants" comprise five groups totaling twelve phrases.

The three knowledges (*tisro vidyāḥ*) and the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍ abhijñāḥ*) consist of the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), recollection of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti*), and the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*); these are the three knowledges.

The six supernormal powers consist of the divine eye, the divine ear (*divyaśrotra*), knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), recollection of past lives, mastery over the body (*ṛddhividhi*), and the exhaustion of outflows. In the *Vibhāṣā*, it is asked: for what reason are the other three not established as "knowledges" (*vidyā*)?
The divine body (*rddhi-viṣaya*) is merely a matter of craftsmanship; the divine ear (*divya-śrotra*) is merely hearing sounds;

and knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*) merely takes another's mind as its object. Therefore, these three are not established as "clear knowledges" (*vidyā*). As for the other three that are so established:

the divine eye (*divya-cakṣus*) gives rise to weary detachment by knowing future suffering, and knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti*) gives rise to weary detachment by knowing past suffering.

Because they are free [from defilements], the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) enables one to practice correct contemplation and sever the afflictions; therefore, these three are established as "clairvoyance" (*vidyā*).

"Spiritual power" (*ṛddhi*) is named after the mind of heaven, while "penetration" (*abhijñā*) is named after the nature of wisdom. This innate nature of wisdom, which penetrates and illuminates without obstruction, is precisely what constitutes supernormal power (*abhijñā*).

In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, it is asked: "What is the distinction between penetration (*abhijñā*) and clairvoyance (*vidyā*)? The answer is: "Directly knowing the past is called penetration; knowing the past [with clarity] is called clairvoyance."
To understand the causes and conditions of past actions is called "clarity"; to see directly that one dies here and is born there is called "knowledge";

to know the convergence of causes, conditions, and opportunities is called "clarity"; to speak of the exhaustion of outflows is called "knowledge"; and to know that with the exhaustion of outflows there is no further birth is called "clarity."

The text states: "Regarding the nature of the objective realm (*viṣaya*), as for discussing 'nature,' there are five kinds. What are these five? First, the nature of the direct cause (*hetu-hetu*); second, the nature of the revealing cause (*parijñāna-hetu*); third, the nature of the conditional cause (*pratyaya-hetu*).

To these three, two additional kinds are added, which together constitute the five kinds. [End of passage] Regarding what is added: 1. The nature of the consummating cause (*pariniṣpatti-hetu*). 2. The nature of the sustaining cause (*anugraha-hetu*). These two are added to the aforementioned three to form the fivefold classification.

Regarding these two categories, there are various differing explanations: some say that the nature of the objective realm (*ālambana-svabhāva*) and the nature of the fruit (*phala-svabhāva*) are added;

others say that the nature of the fruit (*phala-svabhāva*) and the nature of the fruit-of-the-fruit (*phala-phala-svabhāva*) are added; and still others say that the nature of the cause (*hetu-svabhāva*) and the nature of the cause-of-the-cause (*hetu-hetu-svabhāva*) are added. As for the interpretation of their meaning:

the Prajñā of empty wisdom is called the "revealing cause-nature" (*paridīpana-hetu-svabhāva*), while immeasurable merit is called the "conditioning cause-nature" (*pratyaya-hetu-svabhāva*); this applies to all dharmas.

Within [all things], there is entirely present the nature of peace and bliss, which is called the "nature of the true cause" (*hetu-bhāva*). The distinction between good and evil phenomena is called the "nature of the objective sphere" (*viṣaya-bhāva*).

When discussed solely in terms of the merit of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*) and bodhi, it is called the "nature of the fruit" (*phala-bhāva*). When discussed concurrently with the merit of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*) and nirvāṇa, it is called the "nature of the fruit-of-fruits" (*phalaphala-bhāva*).

When discussed solely in terms of the twelve links of dependent origination as objective phenomena, they are called the "nature of the cause" (*hetu-bhāva*); when discussed concurrently with the wisdom that contemplates dependent origination, they are called... [the nature of the fruit].
Although there are various differing explanations regarding the nature of causes, their number must necessarily reach five.

If one treats the "nature of the object" (*viṣaya-bhāva*) as a distinct category, then the "nature of the fruit of the fruit" (*phala-phala-bhāva*) is subsumed under the "nature of the fruit" (*phala-bhāva*). Conversely, if one opens up the "nature of the fruit of the fruit," then the "nature of the object" is subsumed under the "causal condition" (*pratyaya-hetu*).
If one were to eliminate both the "nature of the cause" (*hetu-bhāva*) and the "nature of the cause of the cause" (*hetu-hetu-bhāva*), then the nature of the cause would...
Since the nature of being a cause that is subsumed under the "causal cause" (hetu-hetu) can be understood as being subsumed under the "evidentiary cause" (jñāpaka-hetu),

it may be inferred that the nature of the result (phala-bhāva) is implied here. Although this passage mentions only four natures and does not explicitly state the nature of the result, it is either because the term "Buddha" encompasses it,
or simply because the text is abbreviated.

The *Shuji* (Commentary) states: "The sixteen aspects correspond to the three gates of emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Specifically, as recorded in the *Zhiguan ji* (Record of Stopping and Contemplation), the two aspects of emptiness (*śūnya*) and non-self (*anātman*) under the Truth of Suffering correspond to the gate of emptiness; the four aspects of cessation (*nirodha*), tranquility (*śānta*), excellence (*praṇīta*), and renunciation (*niḥsaraṇa*) under the Truth of Cessation correspond to the gate of signlessness (*animitta*);

and the eight aspects under the Truths of Origination and the Path, along with the aspects of suffering (*duḥkha*) and impermanence (*anitya*) under the Truth of Suffering [correspond to the gate of wishlessness]."
Second, the sixteen modes of practice corresponding to the gate of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*): the names and meanings of these sixteen modes are as found in the *Dharmadhātunirdeśa-krama*;

here they are briefly recorded. Because the five aggregates arise and perish, they are impermanent; because they are oppressed by impermanence, they are suffering; because they lack the characteristics of unity or difference, they are empty;
because they lack self and what belongs to a self, they are non-self; and because afflictions summon results, they are the origin (*samudaya*). By means of...

Because it produces the fruit, it is called a "cause" (*hetu*); because it assists through conditions, it is called a "condition" (*pratyaya*); because it can bring about future existence, it is called "arising" (*samudaya*);

because there is no suffering in *nirvāṇa*, it is called "cessation" (*nirodha*); because afflictions have perished, it is called "extinction" (*kṣaya*); as this is the foremost, it is called "sublime" (*praṇīta*);

because it transcends birth and death, it is called "detachment" (*niḥsaraṇa*); because it leads to *nirvāṇa*, it is called the "path" (*mārga*); and because it is without error, it is called "right" (*samyak*).
Because it is the site of the Sage, it is called the "trace" (pada); because it carries one to the goal, it is called the "vehicle" (yāna).

The three gates of liberation are also called the three samādhis and the three gates of emptiness. Because all phenomena are without self or what belongs to a self, it is called the gate of liberation of emptiness (śūnyatā-vimokṣamukha).

Because characteristics such as identity or difference cannot be apprehended, it is called the gate of liberation of signlessness (animitta-vimokṣamukha). Because there is no volitional activity, it is called [the gate of liberation of wishlessness].
Since the gate of liberation through non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*) involves no volitional construction, one has no aspirations or requests regarding the triple world;
therefore, it is called "wishless" (*apraṇihita*). Non-action is also termed "wishless.

The marks of the environment and the body of the fundamental Vairocana refer to the environment and the body of the provisional means and the true retribution [realms] outside the dharma-realm.

It continues until the verse states: "Upon the thousand petals surrounding [the central lotus], there further appear a thousand Śākyamunis.
On each of the ten billion lands within a single petal, there is a Śākyamuni; each sits beneath a Bodhi tree and simultaneously attains the Way of Buddhahood. Thus it is said.

As for the statement: "At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha first sat beneath the Bodhi tree and attained unexcelled, perfect enlightenment"—this refers to the Trace Buddha (jìfó), a manifested response-body (yìnghuà shēn) residing within this realm on the same earth as ordinary beings.
Therefore, the ten billion lands of the Sahā world are merely upon a single leaf; thus, the *Wénjù jì* (Record of the Textual Phrases) explains: "When I first sat... and so forth.
The "site of enlightenment" (bodhimaṇḍa) refers to the site of enlightenment of the transformation Buddha within the traces; this is the intended meaning here.
Since the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* is formed by the binding [of vows] and the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* is likewise able to bind, how could that which is bound be different?

One should know that the presiding master of the *Avataṃsaka* assembly is named Śākyamuni, and this is spoken in reference to the fundamental Buddha. As for the manifestation from the traces, this is the response-body (nirmāṇakāya) of Śākyamuni.
Therefore, the *Miaoxuan* states: "The reason Śākyamuni preached the Sudden [teaching] is precisely because of this.

Furthermore, among the characteristics of the beginning and end of the Dharma taught during the five periods, there are none that are not the manifested transformation-body (nirmāṇakāya) of Śākyamuni in this land. The *Wenjuji* states:

"In the stage of reality, the one who is to succeed as a Buddha (upapadya-bodhisattva) supplements the transformation Buddha by manifesting the passage through the five flavors; this is exactly what is meant here. Second, following from the traces...

As for the manifestation of the one named Vairocana, as clarified in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-ṭīkā*, it explains that when the Tathāgata manifested the *vyañjana-kāya* (exalted special body) to preach the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, those of inferior capacity were unable to endure it; thus, he removed his jeweled necklace and put on soiled garments.

Furthermore, it clarifies that in the two *Sūtras* (*Prajñāpāramitā*) and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, he manifested the exalted special, supreme response-body (*vaipākika-kāya*) four times, with infinite and immeasurable radiant forms and appearances.

The "limit" (the *bāhya*) refers precisely to the manifestation, from above this realm of shared dwelling (*sahā-loka*), of the Buddha of the inferior response-body (*nirmāṇa-kāya*)—the sixteen-foot transformation Buddha—as the Buddha of the superior response-body (*vairocana-kāya*), the honored and distinguished *śānta* (tranquil) fundamental Buddha beyond the world.

Therefore, manifesting the fundamental Buddha of the honored and distinguished *śānta* from the provisional trace is not unique to the two *parivarta*s of the *Avataṃsaka*; the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* likewise manifests it in its entirety as a symbolic representation.

Because it elucidates the Dharma of the true reality (*dharmatā*), the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-ṭīkā* states that the fourfold manifestation of signs is "manifesting the fundamental from the traces" and also "manifesting the superior from the inferior.

If the *Brahmajāla-sūtra* says, "I, now as Vairocana, sit upon the lotus pedestal; around the thousand petals, there further appear a thousand Śākyamunis," this is manifesting the fundamental from the traces.

If it says, "I am now Vairocana, sitting upon the lotus pedestal; from the thousand petals surrounding me, I further manifest a thousand Śākyamunis," this is manifesting the superior from the inferior.

Yet, manifesting as inferior is also a manifestation of the trace from the origin; these two layers of origin and trace are fully detailed in the *Fanwang pusa jie shu* (Commentary on the Brahma Net Bodhisattva Precepts).

However, since the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* already clarifies that Śākyamuni’s manifested transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) is sixteen feet tall and thus inferior, the current *Wenju* (Textual Commentary) and *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary) explain only the majestic, sublime form (*vairocana-kāya*) of Vairocana as presented in the *Avataṃsaka*.

Regarding the statement that at the Deer Park, Śākyamuni’s six-foot stature was inferior and he wore soiled robes, this is merely a provisional distinction made between the Great and Small Vehicles concerning the superior and inferior characteristics of the robes and ornaments of Sāmbhogakāya (Sahaja) and Nirmāṇakāya (Śākya). In reality, within the *Avataṃsaka* itself, there exists the aspect of the Nirmāṇakāya body of Śākyamuni, which is divided and inferior.
If it were not so, then the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* would not clarify that in this land [of Jambudvīpa], [the Buddha] manifests such forms.
Regarding such passages as, "Śākyamuni left home at seven and attained enlightenment at thirty," and "When I first sat upon the site of enlightenment"—
how should these descriptions of the *nirmāṇakāya* (trace-body) Buddha be interpreted? Therefore, one must not conflate the Dharmatā-Āśraya (Dharma-nature treasury),

the *sāmbhogikakāya* with its marks and signs, or the *vairocanakāya* with the *vaimātrika-kāya*, with the beginning and end of the thousands of millions of *nirmāṇakāya* Śākyamunis who manifest within the realm of segmented birth and death (*paricchinna-bhava*).
This is the body of arising and ceasing.

Therefore, the seven categories and six perfections are fully subsumed [within these]:

among the seven factors of enlightenment, the factor of equanimity (*upekṣā-saṃbodhyaṅga*) is excluded and is subsumed under generosity (*dāna*); among the eightfold path, right speech, right action, and right livelihood are subsumed under ethical discipline (*śīla*);

and among the five faculties and five powers, the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*) and the power of mindfulness (*smṛtibala*) are subsumed under the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
The mindfulness factor of enlightenment among the eightfold noble path is subsumed under patience;

the right effort among the four right endeavors, the faculty of energy among the five faculties, the power of energy among the five powers, and the right effort among the seven factors of enlightenment are subsumed under diligence;

and the concentration factor of enlightenment among the four bases of psychic power, the faculty of concentration among the five faculties, and the power of concentration among the five powers are subsumed under meditative concentration.

In the intermediate concentration (*dhyānāntara*), the eight factors of the Noble Eightfold Path— with the factor of right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*) being subsumed under meditative absorption (*dhyāna*)—

the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*) among the five faculties, the power of wisdom (*prajñābala*) among the five powers, the investigation-of-dharmas enlightenment factor (*dharmapravicayasaṃbodhyaṅga*) among the seven enlightenment factors, and the enlightenment factors of joy (*prītisaṃbodhyaṅga*) and right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) and right thought (*samyaksaṃkalpa*) among the eight factors of the Noble Eightfold Path, are all subsumed under wisdom (*prajñā*).

The *Wenju* (Textual Commentary) states: "The Bodhisattva Precepts Commentary on the *Śīlasaṃgraha*, etc., says: 'The three aggregates—restraining oneself (*saṃvara*), gathering wholesome dharmas (*kuśaladharma-saṃgrāhaka*), and benefiting sentient beings (*sattvārtha-kriyā*)—these names originate from the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* and the *Bodhisattvagaṇḍavyūha*, and do not apply to the Tripiṭaka.
The Great Being’s restraint (*mahāsattva-śīla*) encompasses both the cessation and the engagement of the three karmas; here, we follow [the former]."

The manifestation of body and speech is called the *saṃvara-śīla* (precept of restraint). To give rise to the bodhicitta upon this restraint and diligently cultivate all virtues is called the *kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla* (precept of gathering virtuous dharmas).
To benefit sentient beings is called the *sattva-artha-kriyā-śīla* (precept of benefiting sentient beings). The *Ratna-avadāna-sūtra* states: "The ten *pāramitās* are called the *saṃvara-śīla*;
the eighty-four thousand dharma-gates are called the *kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*; and compassion is [the *sattva-artha-kriyā-śīla*]."
The precept of joyful relinquishment is called the "precept of gathering sentient beings" and is also called the "precept of benefiting sentient beings.
The Record states: "That [precept] is named 'extracting from suffering' and should be understood as that which ought to be practiced."

This "Chapter on Accumulation" specifically clarifies that within the state where neither the real nor the existent prevails, contemplation and observation flow together;
purity and defilement are both manifested without obstruction; they are harmonized without fixed direction as one enters the gate of non-duality;

both extremes are simultaneously negated as one correctly enters the Middle Way. This chapter illuminates both truths simultaneously, fusing purity and defilement, and extensively elaborates upon the principle of "neither real nor unreal."

Regarding the meaning of the "dual flow" of the literary expression of the provisional and the realization of the Path, the commentary on the passage concerning that Buddha’s admonition regarding bodily fragrance and so forth states:
"In that land, fragrances constitute the Buddha-work; there are no followers of the Two Vehicles, and it consists purely of Bodhisattvas. This appears to be a Land of True Reward (sambhoga-kṣetra).
However, even within the Land of Common Residence (sahā-kṣetra), there are both pure and impure realms, and there is also the transformation through the One Vehicle. There is no contradiction here.

Regarding the third distinction: it was not yet known to which land [the fragrance] definitely belonged, so he questioned the Buddha. The Buddha commanded a Bodhisattva to gather the fragrance of his body;

why did he not gather the fragrance of the rice? The answer is that the rice was also gathered, because the rice from that land circulated throughout the ten directions and came here to this Sahā world, where it stopped and perfumed the three thousandfold world-system. This is to accommodate those of the Three Vehicles by means of the rice of the One Vehicle, which has been reduced and diminished.
"Vehicle" (*yāna*) also carries the meaning of "gathering" (*saṃgraha*); however, because the Bodhisattvas travel to other lands, the Buddha cautioned them.
As for the rice, it was sent by the Buddha for them to portion out themselves; there is no room for the Buddha to command them himself.

Regarding the fragrant rice, the statement that he "ordered the Bodhisattvas to gather the fragrance" does not mean to collect and eliminate it until it is completely exhausted. Here, "gathering" (*saṃgraha*) has the sense of restraint, moderation, and careful deliberation. This is the meaning of the *Sūtra*.
Since the faculties [of beings] should not be allowed to exceed their capacity, this is called "attending with the ears.
Now, because that land is like the Land of True Reward (*vipākaphala-bhūmi*), it is instructed that Bodhisattvas should restrain their bodily fragrances and so forth;

likewise, through the *samantabhadra* method, the magnificent and superior *vairocana*-like manifestations are condensed, causing those that are inferior and small to enter this Sahā world by means of the *samantabhadra* and other magnificent dharmas.

The physical form and appearance of the *svabhāva-kāya* (nature-body) are boundless because they are fundamentally explained in terms of the actual retribution (*vipāka*) outside the realms (*dhātu*).

Dhyāna consists of ascending toward superior and wondrous states and becoming weary of the lower realms as suffering, coarseness, and hindrances; when cause and effect are discussed together, there are twelve stages.
However, while non-Buddhists pursue dhyāna exclusively for its own sake, disciples of the Buddha employ the characteristics of the mundane to enter the characteristics of the supramundane.
