Expedient wisdom is likened to the chariot, which is peerless.

I have examined the meaning of the text and added further assistance to it. Why is this? The text states that "expedient wisdom refers to the cart," because it is a provisional designation established through teachings that lack fixed names;
therefore, it must also be stated that "expedient wisdom refers to the cart" as being a conditioned product created by a son.

This is the intended meaning of the responsive application of expedient wisdom. The text states that "true wisdom refers to the cart" as being the transcendence of existence and non-existence, free from words and letters.
Therefore, it must further be stated that true wisdom (real-jñāna) regards the chariot as non-existent because it is not identical [to the parts];
this is true wisdom, being neither identical nor separate. The text says that expedient wisdom (upāya-jñāna) illuminates the city as existent in order to guide sentient beings;

therefore, it must further be stated that expedient wisdom illuminates the city as non-existent, for it is a provisional designation within the teaching. The text says that true wisdom illuminates the city...
Because this non-biased truth is not ultimate, it must further be stated that "real wisdom illuminates the city as being both existent and non-existent," for it is free from words;
thus, the provisional and the real are discussed in terms of existence and non-existence respectively regarding the chariot and the city.

The text says, "Provisional wisdom illuminates the chariot as three because of the three conditions"; therefore, it must further be stated that "provisional wisdom illuminates the chariot as one" in contrast [to the former].
From the perspective of principle, the text says that "real wisdom illuminates the chariot as one," because it unifies [all] into the One Vehicle;

yet it must also further state that "real wisdom illuminates the chariot as three," because all are secret and wondrous. The text says that "expedient wisdom illuminates the city as one," because it is the pervasive truth;
yet it must also further state that "expedient wisdom illuminates the city as three," because it corresponds to the three types of people. The text says "real... [and so forth].
Since the city illuminated by wisdom is the treasury of the three Tathāgatas, it must further be stated that the city illuminated by true wisdom is the one Great Nirvāṇa.

Since the text states that the city illuminated by expedient wisdom is "quiescent" because it is a cessation like ash, it must further be stated that the city illuminated by expedient wisdom is "active" because it must be constructed and established.
Since the text states that the city illuminated by true wisdom is "active," it implies its extinction.
Because this is a transformation, it must further state that "true wisdom (sajñā) illuminates the city as quiescent, because it is free from the clamor of the two extremes.
The text says, "expedient wisdom (upāyajñāna) illuminates the chariot as a vehicle for entering the remainderless [nirvāṇa]";

it must also further state that "expedient wisdom illuminates the chariot as quiescent, because it brings to rest the running back and forth. The text says, "true wisdom illuminates the chariot as quiescent, because it emerges without movement."
It must also be further stated that true wisdom (bhūta-jñāna) illuminates both the movement of the vehicle and the two extremes;
thus, for both the provisional and the real vehicles and cities, there are three aspects each: first, movement and stillness.

*Hai* (also written as *gai*) is explained in the *Fengsu tong*: ten thousand is a myriad; one hundred thousand is a *yi*;
one billion is a *zhao*; ten billion is a *jing*. From *jing* arises *zi*; from *zi* arises *hai*; from *hai* arises *rang*; from *rang* arises *gou*;
from *gou* arises *jian*; from *jian* arises *zheng*; from *zheng* arises *zai*. That which even the earth cannot bear is called *zai*. Thus, ten billion is...
A hundred billion is a *jing* (京), a thousand billion is a *zi* (秭), and ten thousand billion is a *gai* (垓).
Thus, the *nayuta* mentioned in the prose section corresponds to the tenth numerical position in the fifty-two numbers of the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*. That text states:
"The beginning of numbering is one; ten ones make ten; ten tens make a hundred; ten hundreds make a thousand; ten thousands make..."
Ten *lakṣas* make one *vilakṣa*; ten *vilakṣas* make one *atula-koti*; ten *atula-kotis* make one *koti*;
ten *kotis* make one *madhya*; ten *madhyas* make one *ayuta*. *Ayuta* is synonymous with *nayuta*;
the difference lies merely in the terminology used by the new and old translations.
The commentary states that among the words in the "Repetition of the Request" (Chung-ch'ing),
there are seven characters where there should be four; this is because, within the long prose section, there are seven categories, and since three are now omitted,

"Camp and retinue" (*yingcong*) refers to the guards and attendants; "attendants" (*shiwai bucong*) refers to the department of those who serve and follow. "Tranquil seclusion" (*yanji*).
"Peaceful" (*yan*) means tranquility (*xi*). This refers to what was stated in the preceding text: "tranquil and silent. Regarding "poisonous beasts, water, and grass":
the poisonous beasts are a metaphor for delusions and entanglements; the water symbolizes meditative concentration (*samādhi*); and the grass is used as a simile for wisdom (*prajñā*).
The *Jì* (Commentary) states: "Furthermore, the failure to include the third [point], 'unable to proceed further,' in the verse is an error.
The *Sūtra* says: "At this point, wishing to turn back," which refers precisely to the third section of the prose (*chángxíng*), where it says:
"The path ahead is still long, and now one wishes to turn back. Thus, the current text simply does not include that [third point] in its versification.

The passage concerning "the middle path" is illustrated by the ear in the preceding text; in the subsequent verse, this illustration is combined with the middle path, which then versifies the failure to proceed along that middle path.
As for the two passages that do not versify the "white guide," these are merely alternative textual presentations.

Furthermore, the remark in the lower section stating that "it also does not versify the failure to proceed" is likewise an error. The Sūtra states that "being unable to cross over birth and death" constitutes the third "inability."

Ninth, the eight stages, the eight liberations, and so forth."

From the first dhyāna up to the cessation of perception and feeling, entering one dhyāna after another without interruption, is precisely the nine successive attainments (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*).

From "internally possessing form while perceiving external forms" up to the cessation of perception and feeling, turning away from the five desires and abandoning the mind of attachment, is precisely the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*).
The *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*, in the "Buddha-way Chapter," refers to this as "the garden of dhāraṇīs."

The forest of untainted dharmas, the bathing pool of the eight liberations filled with the tranquil waters of meditative concentration, compassion as the woman, the sincere good heart as the man, and ultimate emptiness and stillness as the house—this current passage explains its meaning by employing the intent of that sutra.
Therefore, that commentary states: "The *dhāraṇī* of holding the garden’s flowers and fruits prevents others from stealing them."
Likewise, upholding the causes and conditions of wholesome dharmas serves to obstruct all unwholesome dharmas. Forest trees provide shade and coolness;

likewise, the various untainted wholesome dharmas are free from all feverish afflictions. Entering the nine meditative absorptions (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*) and realizing the truth is called the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*) or eight renunciations (*aṣṭavaiśāradya*).
Their cultivation and perfection reside within the nine absorptions; because the absorption is full like water filling [a vessel], the eight liberations are like a pond.

She shall immediately conceive and be freed from thoughts of lustful desire. Furthermore, the *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra* states:

All of this is due to the power of the original vows of the Tathāgata Akṣobhya. Furthermore, it is said that within that Buddha-field, none of the hosts of Pāpīyān Māras can obstruct the bodhisattvas or śrāvakas;

This was accomplished by the Tathāgata Akṣobhya while he was practicing the bodhisattva path.
Because it is sustained by the power of practice, in the land of Amitābha, women, those with deficient faculties, and those of the two vehicles do not arise;
even the very name of the evil realms does not exist, let alone their actual presence.

By violating these three grades, one falls successively into the three evil realms. As for those who follow the vehicle of emptiness (*śūnyatā-yāna*), there are likewise three grades: the inferior grade consists of the śrāvakas.

The middle-grade *pratyekabuddha* and the superior-grade bodhisattva of the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*)—that is, those who provisionally employ the vehicle—are also of three grades: the inferior grade is the *śrāvaka* of the Tripitaka Teaching;

the middle grade is the bodhisattva of the Shared Teaching who has emerged into the provisional (*niryūha*); and the superior grade is the bodhisattva of the Distinct Teaching (*pratyeka-yāna*), that is, the middle vehicle.
The inferior grade is the bodhisattva of the Distinct Teaching; the middle grade is the bodhisattva of the Perfect Teaching (*pūrṇa-yāna*); and the superior grade is [the Perfect Teaching].
If the Buddha’s precepts are lax while the vehicle is both urgent and lax, this is a defiled land;

because śrāvakas and bodhisattvas together constitute the Saṃgha, and because the precepts are lax, the five turbidities defile the land. Because the vehicle is also lax, it is taught as the three vehicles;
yet because the vehicle is also urgent, it reveals the One Vehicle—this refers to the Sahā world. When the precepts are urgent while the vehicle is both lax and urgent, [it is likewise so].

That which is "strict regarding the precepts" refers to the Pure Land; because the precepts are strict, the land is free from the five turbidities. That which is "relaxed regarding the vehicles" refers to the opening of the three vehicles;

because the vehicles are relaxed, it reveals the two vehicles. An-yang (Sukhāvatī) is precisely this. "Relaxed regarding the vehicles but strict regarding the precepts" is the Pure Land, where the Saṃgha consists exclusively of Śrāvakas.
"Relaxed regarding the precepts but strict regarding the vehicles" is the defiled land, where the Saṃgha consists exclusively of Bodhisattvas.
"Interwoven" refers to the mutual entanglement of phrases such as "hasty in practice but lax in precepts" to distinguish between purity and defilement.

Regarding those of the lower grade who are born in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang), they constantly hear the Dharma being preached by Amitābha and Avalokiteśvara while within the lotus flower.

Those born in that land in the lower grades all dwell beneath lotus flowers;

Regarding the ten vehicles and ten objects (*daśayāna-daśaviṣaya*), as well as the refutation of the pervasive horizontal and vertical [aspects] of the ten vehicles—both in their horizontal and vertical dimensions—there are both common and specific [teachings]. As for what is called "specific," it is like the inconceivable object (*acintyālambana*) which exhausts reality.
The fundamental nature is called vertical; encompassing the ten dharma realms is called horizontal. Seeking upward from the mind is called vertical; transforming downward is called horizontal.
Settling the mind so it penetrates principle is called vertical; the sixty-four stages are called horizontal. Destroying pervasive delusions to the ultimate is called vertical;
the mutual observation of various gates is called horizontal. Reaching the precious destination is called vertical; examining and eliminating obstructions is called the horizontal path.

The progression from one category to the next is called "vertical" (豎); the mutual comparison of categories is called "horizontal" (橫). The progression from the primary to the auxiliary is called "vertical";

the mutual comparison of dharmas is called "horizontal. The progression from one stage to the ultimate is called "vertical"; the universal inclusion of each stage is called "horizontal. The progression from patience to diligence is called "vertical";

the mutual comparison of the adverse and the favorable is called "horizontal. The entry and abiding in non-attachment is called "vertical"; the departure from the three similar dharmas is called "horizontal."
"Horizontal" (heng) refers to the mutual relationship among the ten [stages] within each individual stage when discussed in general terms;

"vertical" (shu) refers to the gradual deepening from one stage to its ultimate limit. This is explained according to the Perfect Vehicle (Yuan-sheng). If contrasted with the Partial Vehicles (Pien-sheng), the designations "horizontal" and "vertical" are likewise applied.
Furthermore, as "neither horizontal nor vertical" manifests the inconceivable, it is also neither horizontal nor vertical. Moreover, this may also be so.

It is said that the previous seven vehicles are called "horizontal" (transverse) knowledge of stages, while those that proceed beyond them are called "vertical. This refers to the ten vehicles having both horizontal and vertical aspects.

Regarding the realm of the aggregates (*skandha*), if one does not discuss their arousal, there is neither horizontal nor vertical. Within the realm of afflictions (*kleśa*), when the sharp and dull proclivities (*anuśaya*) are complete, it is called "horizontal";

within the sharp, when one reaches the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) and further reaches the ineffable; and within the dull, when one reaches the three poisons (*viṣa*) in a single moment (*kṣaṇa*) with extreme gravity—these are called [the distinctions].
The four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and spirits and demons within the vertical illness are called "horizontal arising and mutual overcoming" (*yingsheng xiangke*).

Within the vertical karma, the opposition between obscuration (*āvaraṇa*) and the perfections (*pāramitā*) is called "vertical obscuration and perfections. Their mutual relationship with one another is called "horizontal. Within the horizontal demons, there are three types:
first, evil followed by goodness; second, falling into the Two Vehicles; and third, external views within the internal [Buddha-dharma].

Regarding the "vertical" fourfold propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*), the four gates are viewed in relation to one another as "horizontal. Within the [pride of] *śrāvakas*, attaining the various *dhyānas* is called "horizontal," while attaining the first fruit up to the fourth fruit is called "vertical.
Within the *dvaya-yāna* (the two vehicles), viewing the Four Truths in relation to one another is "horizontal," while viewing the causes and conditions in relation to one another is "vertical.
Within the Bodhisattvas, the self-practice of their respective stages is "horizontal," while viewing the three teachings in relation to one another is "vertical."

This is the vertical and horizontal arrangement of the ten objects (*daśaviṣaya*). Within the "Pervasive Destruction of Dharmas" (*dharmavyāptibhañjana*), practicing the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*) vertically according to the single gate of non-arising (*anutpāda*) is called "vertical";
considering the infinite other gates in relation to the gate of non-arising, those other gates are called "horizontal.
This is the vertical and horizontal arrangement within the pervasive destruction.

the twelfth is "The Solid Relics of All Buddhas. This refers to the fact that the Tathatā-Dharmakāya of all Buddhas is indestructible within this sūtra.
The remaining sixteen names are as explained in the supplementary notes to the "Introductory Chapter" (*Nidāna-parivarta*).

Regarding "skillful deliverance," as recorded in the sixth fascicle of the *Zhiguan* and the seventh fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, it provides two analogies for skillful and unskillful physicians:

using needles and medicinal herbs is called "unskillful deliverance," while employing incantations and esoteric arts is called "skillful deliverance. It is also like two ways of crossing a river: using a raft made of grass is called "unskillful."
The "raft for crossing" refers to both the "skillful raft-crosser" and the "two rafts.
This is because it clarifies the proximity to the fruit; it is named thus to prevent misunderstanding.

If, within the context of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, one further distinguishes the essence and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the four teachings (*catur-yāna*), the text states: "Dry soil is a metaphor for the first contemplation; moist soil is a metaphor for the second contemplation;

mud is a metaphor for the third contemplation; and water is a metaphor for the Perfect and Sudden (*yuan-dun*) contemplation. Furthermore, it serves as a metaphor for the teachings, wherein the Tripitaka does not expound the Middle Way.

Just as dry soil represents the general and moist soil the particular, the Separate Teaching (Biaojiao) is like mud and the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) is like water. The *Fuxing* (Supplementary Commentary) states:
"The *Shu* (Commentary) explains the Sūtra; the contemplation is categorized according to the Four Teachings, and the teachings are categorized according to the Five Periods.

One should know that both teaching and contemplation are established through the categorization of teachings, and it is only through this that the profundity of that section [the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*] is revealed as 'uniquely wondrous. That [section] employs the Four Teachings to explain contemplation; the first three..."
In the teachings of the Tripitaka, sentient beings are likened to high ground; the practice of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) to digging and excavating; and the realization of principle to clear water.
In the Separate Teachings (*Pratyekabuddha-yāna*), dry wisdom is likened to dry soil, the stage of nature (*dharmatā-bhūmi*) to moist soil, and the vision of truth to clear water.

In the Distinct Teachings (*Vaipulya*), the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*) is likened to dry soil, the contemplation of the provisional (*prajñapti-vipaśyanā*) to moist soil, and the vision of the Middle Way to clear water. In the Perfect Teaching (*Ekayāna*), [the analogies continue as follows:]...
The five stages (*pañca-vastu*) constitute dry earth; the six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*) constitute moist earth; and the first stage of abiding (*prathamā-bhūmi*) constitutes clear water.

This is according to the "Teachings" section [of the *Tiantai sijiao yi*], specifically within the gradual teaching of the four periods. The Tripitaka teachings constitute dry earth; the Vaipulya and Prajñāpāramitā teachings constitute moist earth;

the Lotus Sutra constitutes mud; and the view of the Middle Way constitutes water. These two interpretations both take the first stage of abiding as water, but here we rely on the perspective of cultivation.
The contemplation of "only" (but) refers to the practice of sudden contemplation; the initial mind of the Perfect Teaching is both termed "pure water.

This differs from that commentary, which definitively takes the first stage (*prathamā-bhūmi*) as "pure water. Although their designations of stages differ—being either initial or final—their essence is non-dual.

Therefore, what is presented here is precisely the arising of contemplation based upon the sutra. Furthermore, the subsequent text states, "taking [the time] is not exhaustive and is not sequential," and so forth; this is because...
The current explanation of the five periods belongs to our own school; however, if one examines the *Wenju*, it appears to be another’s theory of the five periods.

This other’s system of five periods merely opens up the gradual teaching (*jiànjiào*) to form five stages, such as the teaching with marks (*yǎngxiàng jiào*) prior to the twelve years [of the Lotus Sūtra], as explained in the tenth fascicle of the *Xuánwén*.
This is because these commentaries were already composed by Jiaxiang himself before he returned to Tiantai; although he later did indeed join the school of the Great Master of Tiantai,
the commentaries had already been circulating since the Tang dynasty among the various virtuous masters.
It is not known why everyone says that the *Lotus Sūtra* merely opens [the path] for the two vehicles;
this is simply because it was a text composed by Master Jiaxiang before he had yet understood the *Wonderful Dharma*. Furthermore, such a view has existed since antiquity.
As the preceding text states, "to cause the meaning of 'opening' to be well-established," one must now employ the character "今" (jin), or perhaps use the character "垂" (chuí) instead of "今."
Now, the character "wei" (謂) is added beneath the character "zi" (字).
Regarding "counting sand," as explained in the *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary on the *Zhiguan fuxing zhuanhong jue*),
when Sudhana traveled south to the country of Yaśovatī, he studied the art of counting sand under the spiritual friend Īśvara, the ship’s captain.

The Lord of Mastery in Dharma-gates said: "I previously studied and trained under Mañjuśrī in the dharma-gates of writing, calculation, and seals, entering the divine knowledge of craftsmanship and understanding all dharma-gates.
Constantly accompanied by ten thousand youths on the banks of a river, I surrounded myself with them and played at piling up sand; through this dharma-gate, I came to know the writings of the world."

Regarding the dharmas such as calculation, realms, and bases: from the bodhisattva’s method of calculation—where one hundred *lakṣa* make a *koṭi*, up to thirty successive levels of calculation including the "unspeakably unspeakable" (*anabhilāpyānabhilāpya*)—by means of this method of calculation, one comes to know the vast heaps of sand spanning immeasurable *yojanas*, as well as the heaps of sand in the ten directions, and so forth. Thus it was observed by Master Fashi.

Upaśīra is translated here as "Sovereign" (Īśvara). This means that because he has already thoroughly mastered the ocean of the Buddha-dharma and is able to skillfully ferry others across the ocean of birth and death, and because his deep faith in all dharmas is indestructible, he is called "Sovereign.
In the current text, the character *wén* (文) should be *shī* (施); thus, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "He saw the shipmaster outside the city gate."
Surrounded by hundreds of thousands of merchants and other immeasurable multitudes dwelling on the seashore,

he dwells there expounding the Dharma of the great ocean and skillfully revealing the ocean of the Buddha’s merits; this is explained in full according to the sutra, as indicated here in conjunction with the old translation of the *Avataṃsaka*.
Appendix: The Three Turnings of the Five Periods.

Regarding the three turnings: first, taking the conditioned as conventional and emptiness as ultimate; second, taking both emptiness and the conditioned as conventional and that which is neither empty nor existent as ultimate;
third, taking both emptiness and the conditioned, as well as that which is neither empty nor existent, as non-duality. Both duality and non-duality are...

"Being conventional is neither dual nor non-dual; this is the truth. Now, examining these words, they are merely supplementary to the meaning of the five periods [of the Buddha’s teaching], for they involve transformation, application, and sequence.
As for "supplementary to the five periods," these are mostly established by Jiaxiang (Jizang) in the past;
I shall not cite them in full here. As for the remaining two [periods] being merely listed, I suspect their listing is intended as an illustration. Regarding the citation from the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*:

Regarding the "one" among the three vehicles (triyāna) clarified in that sutra—which stands apart from the three as a single vehicle for a specific capacity—this differs from the "one" within the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, which is both provisional and real.
The *Wenju* states: "If one were to open [the teaching] into three, the three characters 'original,' 'transcendence,' and 'falling away' would be omitted. It further states:
"As for 'without attachment' (*avikṣepa*), 'attachment' (*yi*) may be glossed as 'relying' (*yi*); it can also be written as 'leaning' (*yi*)."
The scripture states:
"It is thus; it is as before. Here, "it is thus" refers to what follows. [This is a] punctuation mark.
"Chou" (逗) means to stop or to dwell; "chou" may also be written as "du" (讀), and "du" is pronounced like "chou.
The *Wenju* (文句) states: "Twelve *nàshù*;

*nàshù* is the same as *nàyóuhé* (那由他). This has been the case in all translations of the scriptures since ancient times. From the character "zheng" (徵) in the preceding text, one knows that [it refers to] "he" (荷).
The character "qiè" (切) is pronounced according to the rhyme of "qīn" (親) and "shū" (疏). It is specifically read as "zhǐlǐ qiè" (陟里切).
A record states: "I have previously examined one fascicle each of the *Mahāyāna-śikhara-rāja-sūtra* and the *Vaipulya-śikhara-rāja-sūtra*, but I did not find [the passage] therein."

This passage is erroneous. Within the text it says: "Furthermore, the question regarding the twelve nayutas of kalpas of Tathāgata Śikhin and so forth is entirely from the *Sūtra of the Necklace* (*Ratnavyūha-sūtra*); why then must one consult the *Śikhin-sūtra*? Thus, we know it is an error.
The text states: *Sākyam-pundarīka* is translated into Chinese as "Equal" (*děng*), also as "Sātām," and further as "Saddharma," which means "Sublime Dharma. *Puṇḍarīka* means "White Lotus.
According to Sengyou’s catalog, this scripture was lost to translation and appended to the Western Jin period; since it is indeed from the Jin, [it is included therein].
Regarding those who refer to the language as "Han" (Hanyǔ), some say that because the arrival of the Buddha-dharma began in the Eastern Han, later translators were made to not forget its origin.
Others say that because the Han dynasty was long-lasting, subsequent translators all took its beginning as their standard.
This is also like how, because the Tang dynasty was long-lasting, people today often speak of it as "Tang-language" (Tángyán). Various [explanations exist].
The text frequently uses Chinese terminology; please understand it according to this underlying meaning.
The Master said: "The Dharma-body has neither coming nor departing; the Reward-body is majestic and sublime; the Response-body universally responds to all things."

The Record states: "Although it says 'three bodies,' the intent is to use the Dharma-body and Reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*) to refute the Master of the Earth (Dilun school), who held that there is no one coming from outside;

[the phrase] 'no one comes from the east' is incorrect, and 'none emerge' is incorrect for those who surge forth. As for 'majestic and lofty,' this should not refer to being inside a stupa. As for the 'response body' (*nirmāṇakāya*), it should not be limited to this alone.

In this Record, since it already states that the Reward-body is majestic and lofty, it should not be inside the stupa; although it mentions "three," [it refers specifically to the Dharma and Reward bodies].

Since the body and mind take the *dharmakāya* and *saṃbhogakāya* to refute the masters of the earth, we know that Śākyamuni’s entry into the stūpa was certainly not as the *saṃbhogakāya* with its majestic, towering, and magnificent marks;
rather, it was merely his *nirmāṇakāya*, a body of transformation born through successive stages.
Therefore, while the *Śāstra* speaks of Prabhūtaratna’s *nirmāṇakāya*, this sutra refers to it as "that Buddha’s power of supernatural penetrations and vows."

When the jeweled stūpas emerge throughout the worlds of the ten directions at the places where the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is being preached, how much more so in the case of Prabhūtaratna, who possesses his entire physical body with its relics, and Śākyamuni, whose physical body has been reduced to fragments?

Is it not the case that both Prabhūtaratna and Śākyamuni sitting together within the stūpa are merely transformational bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) belonging to the category of segmented birth-bodies (*bhavāgra-śarīra*)? If this were not so, why would this be?
Therefore, it is said that although the "three bodies" (trikāya) are mentioned, the underlying intent is to exclude the Earth-Master’s [position] by referring to the Dharma-body and Reward-body;
does he not also speak of the Response-body? Thus we know that when the Record states, "it is not even the Response-body," how much less could it possess all three bodies?

This is a refutation of his ignorance regarding the fact that what can manifest is actually the Response-Transformation body, the segmented birth-body. This is why it is said, "although it is called..."
The intention behind the Three Bodies (trikāya) doctrine is precisely this: to use the Dharma-body and Reward-body to refute the masters of the Earth [who hold only to the physical form].
Siming established that the Master of the Lotus Sūtra is the "excellent" *vairocana-kāya* (尊特身), as opposed to the "inferior" sixteen-foot body;

he stated that worldly people do not understand the subtle excellence of the Lotus Sūtra’s opening of provisional means (*upāya*) to reveal the ultimate, and thus they cling only to the greatness of the physical body and its many marks.
Because [the Buddha] is of the *vairocana* (exalted) category, when he is seen [in that form], it is dismissed by saying, "He is so majestic as to be unsuitable for within a stūpa.
This is a common worldly interpretation used to refute that [view]; however, one must not rely on this to claim that the *Lotus Sūtra*’s manifestations are not of the *vairocana* type.
For instance, as the *Shuji* (Commentary) states: "Since it is not even the *nirmāṇakāya*, how could it possess the three bodies? Yet this is not the ultimate principle of our own school.

Regarding the passage beginning with "It is said that they are equal," etc., it says: "Alas! Siming did not understand the *Ji* (Commentary), which states: 'They are not even the *Sambhogakāya*, so how could they possess the three bodies?
This is a rebuke for failing to understand what is being indicated and instead rashly making arbitrary judgments, claiming this is not the teaching of our own school that exhausts the principle.
Both the *Wenju* and the *Ji* clarify that for the Master and Disciple of the *Lotus Sūtra*, both their bodies were inferior and both were hidden in patient endurance."
To endure such clumsiness is indeed to conceal superiority while manifesting inferiority. Zhiyi of the Four Clarifications established the Lotus Sutra as the primary teaching;

he took what was inferior and made it superior. How could this be a transmission of the Tiantai teachings? If you claim that the *vairocana-kāya* (honored and distinct body) is not a body with many great marks, why does the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary on the *Mohe zhiguan*) state: "Since this is true of the body, it is likewise for all other marks"? [It continues: "He sits upon a lotus pedestal."

And since [the Buddha] up to Akaniṣṭha is all of this same nature, why did the preceding text cite the small body and the large body to prove the sixteen-foot [body] and the *viśeṣa* (extraordinary) body?
Is it not the case that our patriarch merely clung to the largeness of the body and its many marks as being the *viśeṣa* body?
Furthermore, he said that worldly people do not know the subtle excellence of the *Lotus Sūtra*’s opening of the provisional to reveal the ultimate; they simply cling to the body [as the truth].

Since the Great Aspect (mahā-lakṣaṇa) is frequently the *viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa* (extraordinary mark), it is dismissed based on its visual appearance by stating that it is "majestic and towering" (*ai-ai*) and should not be within a stūpa;

is this not a most extreme contradiction of the scriptural text? Furthermore, while the text states that the *saṃbhoga-kāya* is "majestic and towering," the commentary (*ji*) instead says that being "majestic and towering" should not be within a stūpa.
If one were to follow what Siming established, one would be taking the inferior as superior.
If identity means there is no distinction, would this not be precisely what is prohibited in the *Ji* (Record)? It is certainly not appropriate for [the Buddha] to be within the stupa;
this is because identity implies the inferior becomes the superior, and that which is superior must be majestic and towering.

The *Wenju* on the *Guanwuliangshoujing* states that the *Zhunte* (Exalted) body of the Buddha is "majestic and dignified," and Siming also says that the inferior form of the sixteen-foot body with its thirty-two marks is precisely this [exalted state].
If the supreme majesty of the Honored One is so towering and magnificent, then the inferior is itself the superior;

for it is precisely within the stupa that this towering magnificence resides. Since the *Wenju ji* (Record of the Textual Phrases) states that such towering majesty cannot exist within the stupa, one knows that Siming’s claim that the inferior is immediately the superior is erroneous.

The Record states: "The eighth [point], 'Not as it is,' is found in the sixth record of the *Zhiguan* (Calming and Contemplation). The first chapter, the Homage Preface, of the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* says:

'Neither arising nor ceasing, neither permanent nor annihilated, neither identical nor different, neither coming nor departing; one who can thus explain dependent origination skillfully extinguishes all conceptual proliferation.'"

I prostrate my head in homage to the Buddha, the foremost among all dharmas; therefore, one should know that these eight non-illuminations are the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) taught by the Buddha, explained in accordance with that.
Therefore, the *Anle-xing pin* (Chapter on Peaceful Practices) does not concern the "leaping forth" [of the bodhisattvas]; this text is clearly a refutation of the Ci'en school. Thus, Ci'en stated:

"This *Anle-xing pin* clarifies the practices to be performed, while the subsequent *Yongchu pin* (Chapter on Leaping Forth) clarifies the person who performs them. If there were no practices to be studied..."
By what means do people establish virtue? If there were no one capable of practicing it, that Dharma would have no cause for widespread dissemination;
therefore, there are the "Practice of Peaceful Bliss" and the "Emergence. One or two passages below in the record should be understood according to this principle.
How is it that your memorials and petitions never touch upon this?

You linger here while debating other schools; though you are firmly closed off from the profound and subtle contemplation of principle, you merely explain the meaning through phenomenal characteristics.
Yixiu Jue said: "Since my early years, I have accumulated learning and have also investigated commentaries and sought out sutras and treatises to make distinctions."
Statements such as "failing to know when to cease with names and marks" likely refer to the commentaries and treatises of other schools.
If one seeks the commentaries of Tiantai, then contemplation accords with the sutras; what cause for concern would there be in being sternly rebuked by the Tathāgata?

It is because people do not understand this that they rashly claim that studying the teachings and listening to the sutras are merely expedient matters of phenomena for those of inferior or middling capacity.
To engage in Chan meditation with such a disposition is truly a profound and supreme capacity—alas, how lamentable! How can one be so foolish?
I dare say that traveling across rivers and seas, traversing mountains and valleys, seeking teachers and visiting friends, is for the purpose of propagating the Dharma.

Once you have recognized the meaning of Tiantai, why must you laboriously seek elsewhere through further Chan practice? Master Guanding of Qingliang also said: [The text continues with the Master's verse.]
It is said that those of old did not associate with virtuous friends but merely venerated the pursuit of texts;
as their years grew advanced, they sought to abandon the teachings to pursue Chan meditation. This not only suppressed the Buddha-mind, but also led subsequent learners astray.

I have therefore carefully extracted the profound essence of the Three Contemplations of Tiantai and Huisi, so that the teachings may accord with the intent of the ineffable and the mind may become one with the minds of all Buddhas—there is no need for further elaboration.
Looking at his countenance, it seemed as though he possessed a separate gateway for transcending the machinations of the mind.

When this wise man was nearing death, he spoke the *Treatise on Contemplating the Mind* (*Xinxin lun*), lamenting how his disciples had followed him for many years, contemplating the mind for some time, yet remained ignorant of how to investigate its true nature.
They did not inquire into why the mind is unstained; instead, they clung to internal dharmas and external words, merely memorizing notes to rush off and transcribe the various sutras and treatises.

Yet, those who wander aimlessly cannot cut off speech and set aside writing; though one might open a great thousand-fold world-system sutra from within a single mote of dust, it is for this reason that the *Śikṣāsamuccaya* (Treatise on Contemplating the Mind) must be taught.

Among those who come seeking the Dharma, many hear and grasp the words but do not know to inquire about contemplating the mind, and thus fail to attain true and real bliss. As for those seekers of the Dharma who practice samādhi, they attain it... [text fragmentary].
It is certainly not that they do not know how to inquire about the contemplation of the mind; it is because blind Zen practitioners have no vision.

Thus, one knows that the explanations of this school regarding the Buddha’s sutras harmonize the contemplation with the scripture, unlike worldly Dharma masters who merely push their own achievements toward higher ranks.
The subtle, profound, and far-reaching pointing-out of mental contemplation is not like the "darkly realized" Zen masters of the world, who are like those who wrecked a donkey cart. [End of] Excerpt.

As explained in the *Supplementary Notes on Śamatha and Vipaśyanā*, regarding the *Book of Changes* (*Zhouyi*), it says: "Pán-huán (盤桓): advantage in abiding in constancy. The *Correct Meaning* (*Zhengyi*) states:
"Pán-huán is the appearance of not advancing; here it refers to the state of coming to rest."
Below this, it should state "twenty-six fascicles.

The statement that there are "eleven fascicles" is entirely erroneous; it should instead say "seventeen fascicles," as one fascicle, the *Dharmodgata*, remained behind in the inner palace of Chang'an.
Thus, the version of the *Lotus Sūtra* transmitted to Jiangdong contains only twenty fascicles.
From the first chapter, the "Introduction," up to the "Maitreya's Questions" and ending with the "Dharma Master" chapter, there are ten chapters in total;

this confirms that from this point onward there are seventeen chapters. The Guangzhai [Commentary] intends to explain the Great Dharma by providing a brief exposition on the revelation of the traces and the manifestation of the remote [truth], whereas the Shi [Commentary] intends to expound the meaning of the Great Dharma by providing an extensive exposition on the revelation of the near and the manifestation of the remote.
This is now explained by breaking it down according to the school’s tradition. The scripture states that "k'an-shih" (龕室) refers to the niche-chamber of a stūpa;

it is also called a "dragon-appearance" (龍貌), and further described as the chamber beneath the stūpa. The north-south axis is called "lengthwise" (縱), while the east-west axis is... [the text here is incomplete].

It is said that *viśāla* means a wide fishing net or a railing; *vedikā* refers to a balustrade or handrail. *Tamālapatra* is translated here as "naturally stainless" (*prakṛty-avimala*), while *candana* is translated in the sense of "virtuous sandalwood.
The meaning of "bestowing joy" (*sukha-dāyin*) is as explained in the supplementary notes to the first fascicle of the sutra.

The Record states: "As fully explained in the 'Inclusion of Dharmas' section of the *Śikṣāsamuccaya* (or *Treatise on Stopping and Contemplation*), that text extensively clarifies the six categories—principle, affliction, wisdom, practice, stage, and teaching—as subsumed within stopping and contemplation. To record them all would be exhaustive;
however, selection, joy, removal, equanimity, concentration, mindfulness, and vigor are called the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*), as described in the 'Great Householder' chapter."
This likely refers to the many fields and residences that can serve as a swift refuge for the body; it takes the actual realm as the basis upon which wisdom relies.

Briefly stated, this refers to the eighteen emptinesses (*aṣṭādaśa-śūnyatā*); extensively stated, it refers to the immeasurable emptinesses. Furthermore, it refers to the hanging flower garlands, which are a metaphor for the four means of attraction (*catvāri saṃgrahavastūni*) and the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
It specifically refers to the hanging flower banners and the sprinkling of fragrant water on the ground. "Flowers" represents the four means of attraction, while "banners" represents...

The "conditions" (*pratyaya*) for the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) refer to walking, standing, sitting, lying down, and speaking; the "objects" (*viṣaya*) refer to forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena (*dharmas*).
[The character] *jiè* (籍) should be written as *jiè* (藉).
After attaining Buddhahood, one then first makes vows, and so forth.

If one follows the scriptural text, this refers merely to the great vow made by Prabhūtaratna while practicing the bodhisattva path, rather than a vow first made after he had already attained Buddhahood;
therefore, we know that this is a vow from within the causal stage and a supernormal power (ṛddhi) upon the fruition stage.
Thus it is said: "That Buddha, by means of his supernormal powers and the force of his vows," and so forth.
In the sūtra, during the first of the three transformations of the Sahā world, it is not stated that there are no hells, hungry ghosts, animals, or asuras; rather,
it says that only the assembly for this gathering remains, because in the *Dharmodgata-parivarta*, Mañjuśrī emerges from the Dragon Palace and proceeds to the [Vulture] Peak.
The Vulture Peak and the daughter of the Dragon King suddenly appeared before the Buddha; this is the first transformation.

If there were no beings in the hells, among ghosts, animals, or asuras, they would not remain at this assembly. How could there be this [meeting] where Mañjuśrī emerges from the Dragon Palace and proceeds to the Vulture Peak?
Because of such inconveniences, it is said that in the first transformation there are no beings in the hells, ghosts, or animals, yet they still remain here.
Hui-liang [argues] that this is because the Dragon Palace is categorized within the realm of animals;

it is only during the second and third transformations that there are no longer hells, hungry ghosts, or animals. Yet, in the text of the first transformation, the hells, hungry ghosts, animals, and asuras are not excluded—how profound is the underlying intent!
One should first point this out and understand its significance when reaching the "Sudatta" chapter.

Forests, thickets, and wildernesses are called "lin" (forests); furthermore, a cluster of trees is also called a "lin. A marshy area without water is called a "sou" (thicket); it refers to a marshy thicket.

"Jewel curtains" (*bǎomàn*)—the character *màn* is pronounced with the *mò* and *bàn* finals—those on the sides are called *wéi* (curtains) and those above are called *màn* (canopies). "Netted lattice" (*wǎngluó*) refers to a lattice formed by interlacing nets.

Regarding the "eight paths," the *Erya* states: "That which has four-way access is called a *qú* (crossroads)," with the commentary noting that it is an intersection where roads branch out in four directions.
"Eightfold intersection" (*aṣṭāpada*) is called *chóngqī* (崇期); the commentary states this refers to four roads crossing each other, or alternatively, the paths of the eight directions.
It uses gold for cords to demarcate the eight roads. "Village" (*grāma*) means to encamp and dwell; it means to assemble the multitude. "Settlement" (*sanniveśa*) means to establish a residence.
A place where the multitude dwells together is called a village-settlement (*grāmanivāsa*).

*Mucilinda* is translated here as "Stone Mountain" (*śaila-parvata*). *Mahā* is translated as "Great. As for the "Mountain King," this refers to the ten mountain kings such as Snowy Fragrance (*Himavat*) mentioned in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

"Jeweled interlaced canopy" (ratnajāla-avataṃsaka): it is a canopy adorned with interlaced jewels that receives the dew; furthermore, the canopy is either covered or exposed; furthermore, it is a manifestly exposed canopy;
furthermore, it is a canopy upon which various jewels are interlaced and spread over both the covered and exposed portions.

The text states, "transforming the lands three times," and also refers to them as "soil and fields" (*kṣetra*). In Sanskrit, this is called a *buddhakṣetra*. That which is the place where things are produced is termed "soil and fields";
that is, the birthplace of the Buddha, and also the place where all dharmas are produced. These three transformations may refer to the *sahā* (co-resident) pure land.

For instance, in the case of *śamatha-vipaśyanā* (calm abiding and insight) and so forth, within each of the two paramitas of *dhyāna* (meditative concentration) and *prajñā* (wisdom), two types are opened up, such that six become ten. Why is this?

Just as the perfection of concentration (dhyāna-pāramitā) opens up the perfection of aspiration through the power of knowledge, the perfection of vigor (vīrya-pāramitā) opens up the perfection of supernatural powers (ṛddhi-pāramitā),
the perfection of wisdom (prajñā-pāramitā) opens up the perfection of skillful means (upāya-pāramitā) through the knowledge of the paths (mārgajñatā),
and the perfection of all-aspect knowledge (sarvākārajñatā) opens up the perfection of truth (satya-pāramitā), so too should it be understood.
When opened, there are ten [sections], but there are only six; as for the mention of "various kinds," I have not yet seen it cited in the text of Mañjuśrī.
The Sūtra says, "purple-gold colored," and so forth.
First, the ten powers (*daśabala*) consist of the power of knowing what is possible and impossible, up to the power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).
Second, the four fearlessnesses (*caturvaiśāradya*) consist of the fearlessness regarding all-knowledge, up to the fearlessness in proclaiming the path leading to the end of suffering.

The four means of attraction (*catuḥsaṃgrahavastu*) consist of generosity, kind speech, beneficial conduct, and cooperation. [The eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha] consist of the absence of physical failure, up to wisdom.
Knowing the present world without obstruction is called the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*).

The *Wenju* (Textual Commentary) states that it refers to the "bottom of a casket" (*liandi*), while the *Yinyun* (Phonetic Commentary) says it is the name for a vessel for holding mirrors—meaning one with a square bottom—or a vessel for holding incense. It is correctly written as [the character for "casket"].
*Luán* (pronounced with the *lì* and *yán* initials): Regarding the "tortoise-back" (*guībèi*), the *Shuōyuàn* states that the numinous tortoise has five colors, resembling jade and gold;

its upper part is high, symbolizing Heaven, while its lower part is level, following the pattern of Earth. Here, "prominent" (*lóng*) refers to being high, and "pedicle" (*fū*) refers to the top of the foot.
*Màn* (pronounced with the *fǔ* and *wú* initials): The *Jīngyīn* states that "flesh-membrane" (*ròumàn*) refers to the webbing between the fingers. Golden light.

"Clear" (*ming*) means like a webbed membrane; "membrane" (*man*) is pronounced *mo-bàn* (cut at the second tone). It refers to silk fabric without patterns. "Heel" (*gen*) is pronounced *gēn*; it refers to the back of the foot.

"Ankle" (*huǎ*) is pronounced *hú-wǎ*; it refers to the bone of the foot. As for "the deer's calf-muscle" (*lù shuǎn cháng*), "calf-muscle" (*shuǎn*) is correctly written as *zhǎn* and pronounced *shì-yuǎn*.
This refers to the calf-muscle of the King of Deer, Eneya. "Eneya" translates here as "Golden"; thus, it is the Eneya [deer].
The Prince Cakra has golden calves like those of the king of deer; the Buddha is likewise, and this is why he is compared to him.

The *Zuochan Sanmei Jing* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of Seated Meditation) explains it in the same way. Some say that while the fur of the deer-king is mostly black, his calves are slender and long, with proportions perfectly suited;
"gàn" (pronounced as in *gǔ* and *àn*) refers to a dark red color, and "jié" (pronounced *jiē*) refers to the eyelashes being upright.
*Jie* (睫) and *jia* (夾) refer to the eyelashes; the lashes are inserted into the orbital rim. *Jia* (頰), pronounced with the ancient rhyme *xie*, refers to the cheek.
*Bi* (髀) should be written as *bi*; it is also written as *bi*, pronounced with the rhyme *li*. *Wan* (腕), pronounced *wu guan*, refers to the wrist.
*Ka* (髂), pronounced *ku jia*, refers to the pelvic bone. *Qi zhong* (奇中): *qi* is pronounced *ju yi*. *Kuan* (髖), pronounced *ku kun*, refers to the upper part of the buttocks.
*Ti* (體) is the body. *Hun* (臀) is correctly written as *kuān* (髖); the upper radical is pronounced *kǎo*. It is glossed as *kuān*;

it is correctly written as *kāo* (尻), though if written as [the character with the "radical" #], it is pronounced *tú kún*, and its current form is *kāo* (尻), which is incorrect. *Qí* (齊) should be written as *qí* (臍). *Yè* (齶) is pronounced *wǔ gè*; it refers to the gums (*yǐn*).
*Yǐn* (齗) is pronounced *yú jīn*; it is the flesh at the roots of the teeth. *Bì* (鬢) is pronounced *bì rèn*; it is the hair above the cheeks. *É* (額) is also... [text truncated].

The character "é" (額) [in the phrase] "zuò é wǔ bǎi qiè" is an error for the character "zōu" (肞). The *Jīngyīn* states that it should be written as [the character for] "chǔ" (楚), with the phonetic value "jiē qiè," meaning the jaw or the area beside the chin.
The phonetic value of "gé" (閤) is for "gé" (頜); the phonetic value of "hàn" (頷) is "hú gǎn qiè. The *Jì* (Record) states:

"That many modern versions [of the text] claim this feature appears both in the *Dàlùn* (Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra) and in various sūtras is an erroneous attribution. I maintain that these auspicious marks are entirely based upon the excellence of the Bodhisattva.
This is because it is a *śīla-sūtra*. Thus, that sūtra states that the eighty secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*) consist of twenty for the fingers, which constitute twenty marks;
eight places on the front and back of the hands and feet are level and full; six places—the two ankles, knees, and thighs—are exquisitely beautiful;

six places—the shoulders, elbows, and wrists—and three places—the crotch, the middle of the spine, and the hips—are beautiful; and two places—the buttocks and the two haunches—are beautiful; and the male organ is concealed within a sheath like that of a horse.

The three folds at the waist, the navel, the two sides, the two armpits, and the two breasts constitute eight [marks]. The abdomen, chest, spine, and neck constitute sixty secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*).

The upper and lower teeth, the upper and lower lips, the chin, the two cheeks, the two temples, the two eyes, the two eyebrows, the nose with its two nostrils, the forehead, the two kneecaps, and the two ears being round and full—these constitute eighty secondary marks. [This concludes the section on] the phonetic power of the *Ānanda-gāthā*.
"Jue" (月) means "skin. The *Bodhisattvabhūmi-saṃgraha-sūtra* (菩薩地持經) speaks of the two horns (*śṛṅga*), not the two kneecaps (*jānu*).
The *Bodhisattvabhūmi-saṃgraha-sūtra* and the *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra* (菩薩善戒經) are largely identical in their original texts; they differ only in the translators.

One should know that because the wording and phrasing have varying degrees of detail compared to what is listed in the sūtras, these specific points are cited for illustration. Regarding the two marks of the "hanging dewlap" (*ūrṇā*):
This is because the current text contains thirty-four marks (*lakṣaṇa*). I have previously compared the *Fajie cidi* (Gradual Order of the Dharma Realm) with these current marks;
however, the *Fajie cidi* further mentions "the area between the two armpits is full" and "the upper body is like that of a lion," while the *Wenju* (Textual Commentary) mentions "a lion-like chest.

Please examine these matters in detail. As for the eighty secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjana*), how do they correspond to the current text? To what extent... [text ends]... please provide a detailed comparison.

The *Tathāgata-garbha-sūtra* (often referred to as the *Bodhisattva-utkṣepa-garbha-sūtra*) differs from many other sūtras; this is because the very end of that sūtra refers to itself as the *Garbha-sūtra*.

Regarding the passage in the *Amitāyurdhyāna-sūtra* which says, "those who dwell long upon the lotus pedestal," this refers to being born from the womb (*garbha-jāti*), yet in reality, it is not [birth from] a womb.

This is explained as follows; thus, the *Sūtra on the Visualization of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life* states that those born in the lowest of the lower grades dwell within a lotus flower for twelve great kalpas before the flower finally opens—this being the longest duration spent upon the lotus pedestal.
Since it is said that this is truly not "womb-birth," it differs from the *Great Original Sūtra of Immeasurable Life*, which [speaks of those with] a mind of doubt.
One who cultivates various merits may be reborn in that borderland and undergo womb-birth (*garbhaja*), which must not be confused with [the pure land].

This is because the third visualization on the mind in the *Sixteen Visualization Sutra* contains no doubt regarding this, and the eleventh visualization on Mahāsthāmaprāpta states that one does not undergo womb-birth.
However, if one follows the *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra*, it says that people in the Land of Ultimate Bliss dwell in the womb.

Just as the Yāma gods dwell within palaces, and so on, up to the point where it is said that they cannot emerge from within the lotuses—those sentient beings dwelling within the lotus-wombs perceive them as being like gardens or palaces;

furthermore, these lotus-wombs are identical to the "womb-birth" (*jarāyu-ja*) described in the *Mahāvaipulya* [sūtras]. Therefore, the differences and similarities between the sūtras and śāstras cannot be treated as uniform.
Furthermore, the *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra* states: "If one sits cross-legged within a flower, one will be spontaneously born through transformation.
This is no different in meaning from the "spontaneously born" (upapāduka) beings mentioned in the *Mahāvaipulya* [Sūtra].

One must understand that the "transformative birth" and "womb-birth" described in the *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra* are identical to the "transformative birth" and "womb-birth" in the *Mahāvaipulya*; however, what the *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra* calls "womb-birth" refers specifically to a "flower-womb."

I have heard that those who dwell for a long time upon the lotus pedestal in the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* (the Sixteen Contemplations Sutra) are considered "womb-born" (*garbhaja*). How can this be distinguished?

Moreover, the preface to the commentary on the *Sixteen Contemplations Sutra* states that they "sit upon golden lotuses and are born through transformation" (*upapāduka*). I hope you will examine this matter in greater detail.
The Sūtra states: "A thousand-petaled lotus flower," and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says:
"There are three kinds of flowers: first, human flowers, which have more than ten petals; second, celestial flowers, which have one hundred petals;
and third, Bodhisattva flowers, which have one thousand petals. Alternatively, it is said that there is a pond upon the summit of Mount Hua.
There is a thousand-petaled lotus flower that grows among humans; if one consumes it, they will attain the transformation by flight (ascend on wings).
*Sāgara* is translated here as "the Brine Sea" (*xianhai*). *Jihe* means "how much" or "to what extent. *Poyou*—Cien says this is a particle of speech;
today it is said to mean "still" or "indeed. *Chizi* (the infant): the *Jingyin* (Phonetics of the Scriptures) states this refers to the period between birth and being held in one's arms.
Furthermore, benevolence (*ren*) and yielding (*rang*): loving others and benefiting all things is called benevolence; putting others before oneself is called yielding. In the *Ji*, it is asked:
"Beyond the three thousandfold world-system, there is no further great ocean; why then does Mañjuśrī still say the ocean has come?
The answer explains this by means of three principles.
Now, it is said that although there was no great ocean during the first transformation, there were dragon palaces and the assembly on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa was retained;
since the dragon palace is categorized within the realm of animals, the text concerning the first transformation does not state that there were no hells, hungry ghosts, or animals.
This is precisely the scriptural evidence for Mañjuśrī emerging from a dragon palace and proceeding to Vulture Peak. If the first transformation had no hells...
Regarding the hells, ghosts, and animals, how could there be such events as the sudden emergence of dragon maidens?

From this, we know that the sutra mentions the great ocean merely to clarify that beneath its floor lies a dragon palace; in reality, the surface of the great ocean has already undergone transformation.

Therefore, one must not cling to the literal words "from the great ocean" while discarding the statement regarding the "emergence from the dragon palace. This is recorded in the third [section] of the *Ji* (Record).

The meaning [of this] contradicts the sūtra; let scholars examine it in detail. Furthermore, this point must be understood within the subsequent "Entrustment" section, specifically in the discussion concerning the differences between the compassionate grace of the state of peace and the impure realm.

The *Wenju* (Commentary on the Words) states: "The first half-verse clarifies that by upholding the sūtra one attains liberation; the following two verses clarify the accomplishment of the two bodies."
Regarding the statement of "two bodies," these are the birth-body (*janma-kāya*) and the true-body (*dharma-tathatā-kāya*). The true-body is also called the *dharmakāya*;
is this not the subtle and pure *dharmakāya*? The birth-body is also called the *nirmāṇakāya*; is this not that which possesses the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor characteristics?
If it were not so, how could the two lines of scriptural text correspond to [the qualities of] accomplishment?
Regarding the two bodies (*dvikāya*), the *Miaoxuan* (Profound Meaning) in the section on the "Excellence of the Three Dharmas" states:

"Profoundly penetrating the characteristics of sin and merit, one universally illumines the ten directions"—this refers to the subtle and wondrous reward body (*vipākakāya*). "The pure Dharma-body is endowed with the thirty-two marks"—this refers to the response body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
Thus, we know that the present statement regarding the "accomplishment of the two bodies" must be understood in accordance with the *Miaoxuan*, as it corresponds to the two passages of the sutra.
Regarding the two bodies—the Dharmakāya and the Nirmāṇakāya—within the commentary on the two lines of the sūtra concerning their accomplishment, it states:
"Having deeply attained the principle of the Dharmakāya, one is immediately endowed with the marks and signs. Is this not because the Dharmakāya possesses the characteristics of the Nirmāṇakāya?

Is this not because the True Body (Svabhāvakāya) possesses the characteristics of the Birth Body (Janmakāya)? Zhiyi of Siming stated: "The Dragon Girl praised the Buddha’s Dharmakāya as being endowed [with these marks]."
The marks (lakṣaṇa) manifest this as being inferior because they are fully possessed by the Dharma-body; yet the marks are uniquely sublime (viśiṣṭa).
Therefore, Jingxi [Zhanran] classifies them as being identical to the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, wherein each and every mark and excellence (lakṣaṇānuvyañjana) is equal to empty space.

This wondrous body is not called "uniquely sublime"; what other body, then, could be designated as such? Furthermore, he refutes others by stating that the true Dharma-body possesses the marks of birth.

If one were to claim that the thirty-two marks result from slander, I now ask: regarding the two lines of scripture concerning the four clarities (*sijiao*), and the *Wenju* and *Miaoxuan* concerning the two bodies—the birth-body and the dharma-body, the true and the responsive—how can you recklessly accuse others of slander when the meaning of these texts is so clear?
If you were to charge that the dharma-body is fully present within the birth-body and the responsive body, then that would indeed constitute slander; yet such is the intent of the *Wenju*.
Furthermore, to claim that both the *Miaoxuan* (the *Fahua xuanyi*) and this [text] constitute slander is incorrect.

Moreover, since the true Dharmakāya possesses both superior and inferior functions, how could one hear it said that the Dharmakāya’s possession of marks refers exclusively to the *zunte* (lofty and special) form? How could it be that the inferior nirmāṇakāya does not possess the Dharmakāya, nor is its function called "great"?
Is it only by taking the *zunte* form alone to be the possession of the Dharmakāya that its function is named "great"? Wisdom! [This is a rhetorical exclamation.]
If it is capable of merging with the essence and giving rise to great function, and can serve as the body and so forth, why must one invariably point to the *zhuntè* (extraordinary) body?
Is it not that when the Dharmakāya possesses such [function], it is called "great function"? If you claim this body is not called *zhuntè*, then what other body could be pointed to as *zhuntè*?
The patriarchal teachings are as clear as the midday sun; for what reason do you obscure and block them?

As for the observation that the *zunte-shin* (Sambhogakāya) is indeed the *shana-ta* (Svābhāvika-kāya), since the *Miaoxuanji* already identifies "profound penetration" and "universal illumination" with the *boshen* (Nirmāṇakāya), does this not also encompass the *zunte-shin*?
This is because the *shana-boshen* (Svābhāvika-nirmāṇakāya) consists of both the self and the other;
the "self-retribution" (*zi-bao*) is universal illumination through wisdom, while the "other-retribution" (*ta-bao*) is radiance.

If the Universal Illuminator (Pien-chao) is so, how much more so his other retributions, which are also called the "Exalted Response" (sheng-ying)? This is because the response cannot be without wisdom, nor can wisdom be without the response.

Since the scriptural text states that Vairocana has profoundly penetrated [reality] and is the wondrous and profound mystery, and further correlates this with the retribution body (pao-shen), is the retribution body not indeed the Honored Unique Body (tsun-te-shen)? Now, let us turn the question back upon the Dharma of Siming.

The Master profoundly understands that since the Universal Radiance has already been identified with the Reward Body (*saṃbhogakāya*), if this body were not called the "Exalted and Special" (*viśeṣa*), what other body could then be designated as such?
If one points to the thirty-two marks of the Form Body (*rūpakāya*) as it is, how can this be distinguished from the Birth Body (*janmakāya*) or the Responsive Body (*nirmāṇakāya*)?
If one takes the inferior responsive body of Śākyamuni—sixteen feet in height and possessing the thirty-two marks—to be [the Exalted and Special], then it would simply be the Śākyan body.
The light, color, and form of that *saṃbhogakāya* are immeasurable and boundless. In the newly translated *Avataṃsaka*, what is wrong with rendering *Rocana* as *Vairocana*?
Why must it be refuted [by some] on the grounds that "the *dharmakāya* and *saṃbhogakāya* are not distinguished, nor can the three and two be discerned"?
Is it not because Zhizhe (Jingxi) was unaware of the secret principle of the mutual identity of the three and one within the Middle Way of response and stimulus (*ganying*)?
If the Zang [commentary] merely fragments the facts in this way, it loses both the progression and the retreat of the argument. Alas!

By identifying Śākyamuni with Vairocana and regarding the inferior response-body as the superior response-body, it is evident that retribution and response are no longer distinguished, nor can the three and two be discerned.
It is truly lamentable, truly lamentable, that people of the world do not understand this but instead transmit and practice based on mere reputation! It is indeed like the *Jingxi Leitong*.
The marks and embellishments of the Avataṃsaka are equal to empty space; this is precisely the meaning of relying on emptiness so that marks vanish.

It is not that marks lack form, but rather that they manifest as the Dharma-body within the Middle Way, which is like space. How can one delusively recognize this and claim it is merely a teaching of having specific marks?
To take principle for a phenomenon—is this not confusion?
The Sūtra speaks of the "Stainless World" (Vimalā-loka) in the south;

Master Li says that because the mind has attained *arhatship* (the state of being free from outflows), it is called "stainless. Because it correctly accords with original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*), it is named the "South.

Furthermore, the south represents illumination, emptiness, and detachment. Within the eight trigrams (*bagua*), the trigram *Li* corresponds to the heart-mind, for its center is empty. Thus, the heart-mind is the principle of *Li*.
"Because it is void and non-existent, clarity returns to rely upon the mundane world, and the Eight Trigrams are used to represent it.

I maintain that this interpretation is not elegant or appropriate. Why is this so? Is it because those who attain Buddhahood in other directions do not possess a true mind or are not free from defilement?
Furthermore, if there were no "voidness within the midst," by what means could it be represented? If one understands the Southern World of No Defilement (Amoghasiddhi’s realm)...

Because the conditions for his transformation were nearing maturity, he went there to achieve enlightenment in response to them; thus, within the eight trigrams (*bagua*), there is nothing to be grasped beyond the manifestation of *li* (the hexagram of fire).
How much more so, then, is the fact that Master Li [Falin]—in his veneration of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and his extensive disparagement of other scriptures—did not possess universal insight.
Alas! The people of this world have failed to obtain the Tathāgata’s exegesis as categorized by the present school’s analysis of teachings (*jiao*) and categories (*bu*).
That the teachings of an entire era were compiled and authored while allowing partial views to arise spontaneously—how lamentable, how lamentable! The *Wenju* (Textual Commentary) states:
"The *Tāijīng* (Womb Sūtra), Māra, Brahmā, and the daughters of Śakra."
The three—Māra, Brahmā, and Śakra—along with their daughters, these four types of persons, shall all attain Buddhahood in this very body, without casting off the present form nor receiving another.
As for those referred to as "daughters," in the world of past Buddhas, all the people at that time received female bodies;
seventy-two trillion women attained [Buddhahood] in a single day and at a single moment.
The Buddha-way does not involve abandoning the body nor receiving a body;

yet that sutra speaks of Brahmā Kings and Śakra appearing in bodily form to become Buddhas, and how the celestial maidens of Brahmā and Śakra all attained the fruit of Srotāpanna. One should further reflect carefully upon the fact that the Brahmā King possesses palace women.
The Record states: Others say there are ten stages, etc.

Ci'en cites the *Gayāśīrṣa-sūtra*, which speaks of four types of bodhicitta: first, the bodhicitta of realization, referring to entry into the first bhūmi; second, the bodhicitta of practice, which refers to the sixth bhūmi;
third, the bodhicitta of non-retrogression, which refers to the eighth and ninth bhūmis; and fourth, the bodhicitta of one-life-to-enlightenment...
The stage of generating the mind [of enlightenment] corresponds to the tenth bhūmi; this dragon girl, however, is one who manifested as a dragon girl upon the fourth generation of the mind.
She gave birth to eight daughters.
The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu* (Benxing jing) states: Not far from the city of Kapilavastu, there was a city named Devadaha.

There lived an elder named Suprabuddha who had eight daughters: the first was named Mati, the second Anantamati, the third Mahāmati, the fourth Anantamati, the fifth Keśinī, the sixth Gominī, and the seventh Tanu.
The eighth daughter was named Mahāprajāpatī, which means "Great Wisdom" (Mahāprajñā) or "Pure as Brahmā.
King Śuddhodana welcomed eight women in marriage; he took the first and the eighth as his own queens, while giving the remaining six to his three younger brothers.
Mahāprajāpatī is also called Mahāmāyā, and Yaśodharā is translated as "Fame" (Yaśas).
Regarding Māyā—here translated as "Queen of Heaven" (Tianhou), Gautamī, or Gopamī—this is rendered as "Most Victorious" (Zuisheng) or "Mistress of the Multitude" (Zhongzhu).
The *Nyāyabindu* states that she was born of the Gautama clan and was the most excellent among humans, with the exception of the gods, because she was born from the Sun;
thus she is called "Most Victorious. There are five distinct lineages [of the Śākya clan].
First, the Gautama clan; second, the Ikṣvāku clan; third, the Āditya clan; fourth, the Śyāmaka clan;
fifth, the Śākya clan—these are all distinguished in detail as fully set forth in various texts. [The term] "bong" (nasal obstruction) refers to a nasal ailment.
*Ōng*: pronounced with the *qie* (phonetic approximation) of *wū gòng*, meaning nasal congestion. *Líáo*:
pronounced with the *qie* of *luò xiāo*, meaning to have no reliance or support.
It is indeed as Piṇḍola knows: that [King Udayana] lost his kingdom seven years ago, and whether the Dhyāna Master Tanyou was advanced enough to become a king.

The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states: "Piṇḍola was originally a minister of King Udayana; because of his diligent application, the king permitted him to leave the household life, whereupon he attained arhatship.
At a later time, the king went out of the city to pay his respects at the monastery. The monastery was located outside the city..."
When they were twenty *li* away, the various sycophantic ministers saw Piṇḍola not rising to greet the king;
they immediately spoke with malicious intent to the king, and the king, accepting the words of these flatterers, was on the verge of killing him.

Later, when Piṇḍola saw the king entering the gate, he immediately descended from his seat and went seven paces to meet him. The king said, "Virtuous One, you have always been difficult to move, yet now—"
"Why did you rise from your seat to welcome him? Piṇḍola replied, "Because the King previously had a kind heart, I did not rise to welcome him;
now that he harbors evil intent, if I do not welcome him, he will surely have me killed. The King said, "Excellent!

My disciple has foolishly accepted the words of flatterers and failed to distinguish between the ordinary and the holy. The King requested to repent for his transgression; although he was thus spared from hell, Piṇḍola immediately—
The record concerning the King states that because he rose to welcome [the monk] for seven paces, he would inevitably lose his royal throne seven days later.
Subsequently, it happened exactly as recorded: the military forces of another state arrived, captured the king, and imprisoned him with his feet shackled for seven years.
At Mount Longshan, at Yunmen Monastery west of Ye in the Qi dynasty, there was the Zen Master Sengchou, who followed Zen Master Daofang.

Having practiced and mastered *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, and further relying on the Dharma of the Four Foundations of Mindfulness (*catur-smṛtyupasthāna*) from the Noble Conduct of the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, he later went to the Chan Master Dao Ming of Zhaozhou to receive the instruction on the Sixteen Stages of Special Excellence (*ṣoḍaśa-viśeṣa*).

At that time, Emperor Xiaoming of the Wei Dynasty, having long revered his virtuous character, issued three successive edicts summoning Master Tanyou, who declined them, saying: "Under heaven, there is no land that does not belong to the King; I beg only to remain..."

Sengchou’s practice of mountain asceticism was also consistent with the Great Way, and the Emperor subsequently granted him permission. Upon his arrival at the Qi court, Emperor Wenxuan also issued an edict, stating:
"I have long heard of your reputation for virtue and have always hoped to meet you in person. I now command the Governor of Dingzhou to escort the Master to Ye to transform the multitude.
Thereupon, Master Chou immediately shook out his robes and departed the mountains, while the Emperor personally prepared the imperial carriage to receive him.
He went out to the suburbs to welcome Master Chou, who then preached that the three realms are fundamentally empty and that the same is true for the physical land;
that worldly glory and transitory phenomena cannot be preserved forever. Upon hearing this teaching, the Emperor’s hair stood on end and his sweat flowed.
He constructed a vihāra eighty *li* southwest of Ye City, naming it Yunmen, and invited the Master to reside there, providing him with the state treasury for its support.
The funds were divided into three portions: one part for the state, one part for personal use, and one part for offerings to the Triple Gem and the assembly of sages.
An imperial decree sent money and silk to be stored in a treasury within the monastery.
