The delusions of the two vehicles are shattered and the flourishing stage of mindfulness becomes the nature of phenomena—that is, the middle (*madhyama*), which is not either of the two extremes. The principle of the Middle Way is thereby revealed.
The Buddha, having realized this principle, attained parinirvāṇa in the interim.

Regarding the eighteen kinds of emptiness and so forth mentioned in the text, I shall now briefly indicate those that are difficult to perceive. First is the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*), which is the foremost among all phenomena.
This Nirvana is also empty because even Nirvana does not exist; thus it is called "empty. Regarding "inner emptiness" and the absence of the six entrances (*ṣaḍāyatana*):

this refers to the non-existence of the entry of the six sense faculties (*indriya*). "Entrance" (*āyatana*) means "entering" or "penetrating," and since these six faculties are that which consciousness penetrates, they are called the six entrances.
They are also called "faculties" (*indriya*); a faculty is that which can produce [consciousness], and all six possess the function of generating consciousness. As for "self" (*ātman*)...
"Mine" (*mama*) refers to that which can be reckoned as "mine. Because one reckons the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) as "mine," the *Fuxing* (Subcommentary) states:
"The aggregates (*skandha*) are what I am; that which can be reckoned is 'mine. Taking up that which is reckoned is called the aggregates and sense bases;
to recklessly reckon the aggregates is called the 'self,' and that which belongs to the self is called 'mine' (*mamakāra*). 'Great Emptiness' (*mahāśūnyatā*) refers to the ten directions."
That which is square and all-pervading is called "great"; because this cannot be apprehended, it is termed "Great Emptiness" (*mahāśūnyatā*).

Regarding "emptiness of the unapprehendable" (*anupalambha-śūnyatā*): because all phenomena are empty, all dharmas are unapprehendable; since even this non-apprehension is itself unapprehendable, it is called "empty.

Regarding "emptiness of dispersion" (*vibhava-śūnyatā*): by means of emptiness, the notions of self and person (*pudgala*) and the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are dispersed and destroyed, leaving nothing remaining.
Because of these remaining [factors], it is called "emptiness.
The *Ji* (Commentary) states: "A detailed explanation of the separation and combination is found in the fifth fascicle of the *Zhi guan* (Stopping and Seeing), etc.

When one seeks the mind within the sense organs (*indriya*) and does not find it, this is 'internal emptiness' (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*). When one seeks the mind within the sense objects (*viṣaya*) and does not find it, this is called 'external emptiness' (*bahirdhā-śūnyatā*). When the sense organs and sense objects are combined..."

When examined and not found, the mind is empty internally and externally; when detached from examination and not found, it is the emptiness of emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*); when examined through the four natures and not found, it is the emptiness of nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*);
when examined through the four propositions and not found, it is the emptiness of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*). That which has no spatial divisions is called great emptiness (*mahā-śūnyatā*);

when the supreme is sought and not found, it is the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*); when the causes and conditions of the four propositions are not found, it is conditioned emptiness (*saṃskṛta-śūnyatā*).

The emptiness of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-śūnyatā*) cannot be apprehended; this is called the emptiness of the unconditioned. When sought through the four propositions, the arising of the mind cannot be found—this is the emptiness of beginninglessness.

When the cessation of the mind cannot be found—this is the emptiness of dispersion. When neither arising nor cessation of the mind can be found—this is the emptiness of ultimate reality (*atyanta-śūnyatā*).
When emptiness itself cannot be apprehended—this is the emptiness of all things (*sarvadharma-śūnyatā*). Since all forms of emptiness cannot be apprehended, there is nothing whatsoever.
The non-apprehension of the view that emptiness exists is the emptiness of existence; the non-apprehension of the view that existence does not exist is the emptiness of non-existence;
and the non-apprehension of both existence and non-existence is the emptiness of both existence and non-existence.

These, combined with the eleven emptinesses and twenty emptinesses from the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* and the seven emptinesses from the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, total eighteen when separated, all of which are fully contained within those scriptural texts.
Regarding "thunder" (*leiting*), the *Erya* states that a swift clap of thunder is called *ting*. To speak of the general and the specific, as well as the horizontal and the vertical:
the "specific" refers to the ten vehicles having both horizontal and vertical aspects. If one understands the meaning of the specific, the general can be inferred accordingly.

For example, the "Inconceivable Realm" (*bùsīyì jìng*) reaches the bottom of the true reality (*shíxiàng*) and is thus called "vertical"; it encompasses the ten dharma-realms and is thus called "horizontal," and so on until [the stage of] detachment.

The love for the Dharma (*dharmatṛṣṇā*) is "vertical" when it enters and abides [in the stages], and "horizontal" when it pertains to the three similar dharmas; this is fully explained in the eighth fascicle of the *Fuxing* (Subcommentary).

"yellow" (*huang*) refers to the center, meaning that the Sage dwells in the center of the world to govern the myriad lords. One who belongs to the gate of this "yellow house" is therefore called "yellow."

Regarding the six truths and the twenty-five truths: first, the truth of the Lord (īśvara); second, the truth of the basis (āśraya); third, the truth of activity (kriyā);
fourth, the truth of general characteristics (sāmānya-lakṣaṇa); fifth, the truth of specific characteristics (viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa); sixth, the truth of māyā—these are the six.

Regarding the twenty-five principles (*tattva*): first is the principle of primordial darkness (*mūla-tattva*). From this arises intellect (*buddhi*); from intellect arises the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*);

from the ego-sense arise the five objects of sense (*viṣaya*); from the five objects arise the five gross elements (*mahābhūta*); and from the five gross elements arise the eleven faculties (*indriya*).

These twenty-four are "that which belongs to me" (*mama*) and all depend upon the spiritual self (*puruṣa*), which is called the "principle of the master" (*īśvara-tattva*). Thus, subject and object are unified.

Regarding the "eight [types of] diligence" and so forth being like the second [category], the text in the seventh [section] of the *Dīrgha Āgama* states that within each of the four matters there are respectively those who arise in diligence and those who arise in indolence; these are called the eight. This refers to alms-seeking, maintaining [the precepts], and so forth.
When one has prepared for almsround and encounters illness like that of a beggar, if one is unable to proceed, one should think:
"I have failed to obtain alms; my body is exhausted and cannot endure traveling on the path; it is fitting that I rest for a while.
If, after obtaining alms, one again thinks: "My body is heavy and cannot endure traveling on the path," this is called the arising [of thoughts] before and after almsround.
Laziness: if one undertakes even a small amount of work, one immediately thinks, "I am now utterly exhausted and unable to practice the Path.
If one intends to undertake work, one thinks, "I shall do it tomorrow; there will surely be exhaustion.
If one has walked even a short distance, one thinks, "I have walked this morning and my body is utterly exhausted. If one intends to walk even a little, one thinks... [and so forth].
Thinking, "I shall certainly become exhausted when I travel tomorrow," or if one encounters even slight affliction, one thinks, "I now have a serious ailment and my body is exhausted.
Or, if the illness improves, one thinks, "The illness has not long been cured and my body is still exhausted.
For these reasons, these eight are called laziness; the eight forms of diligence are different from these.
If one does not obtain alms, one should reflect: "I have slept little and am capable of practicing the Path. If one has obtained alms, one should reflect:

"I am satiated and my physical strength is sufficient; I am capable of practicing the Path. If I am about to engage in manual labor and it would cause me to abandon the practice of the Path, I should now apply myself with diligence.

If I am to engage in manual labor tomorrow, I should reflect that it will obstruct the practice of the Path and must therefore apply myself with diligence in advance. If I am traveling, [one should likewise reflect].

At times one reflects on abandoning the practice of the Path; if it is clear that one must travel tomorrow, one reflects on abandoning the Path; if one contracts a serious illness, one reflects on the end of life;
if one suffers from a minor ailment, one reflects on the fear that it may increase. For this reason, these eight are called the "eight forms of diligence.
Within the phrases, "to go" (*xing*) refers to traveling; within the phrases, "to employ" (*li*) refers to performing labor.

Regarding the prohibitions against face-to-face insults, metaphors, and insults involving wholesome dharmas, the *Sifen chao* states there are three types of insulting speech: first, face-to-face insults, such as saying, "You are born into a family of sweepers";
second, metaphorical insults, such as saying, "You resemble the offspring of sweepers"; and third, insults by comparison with oneself, such as saying, "I..."
There are also three kinds of those who revile with wholesome dharmas such as the "refuse-remover" lineage and so forth:
first, those who revile face-to-face; second, those who revile by means of metaphors; and third, those who revile by means of analogies. One should reflect upon these according to what precedes them.

Regarding the prevention of face-to-face reviling and metaphorical reviling, this refers precisely to reviling face-to-face and reviling by means of metaphors. Therefore, in the *Dhāraṇī-parivarta*, it says that one is thus slighted, saying to you: "You..."
All such [beings] as these— those whom the Buddha, in the "Chapter on Never-Disparaging," disparaged and yet bestowed upon with the name "Never-Disparaging"—
are all subsumed within the category of those who revile through wholesome dharmas;
reflect upon this, Kruṣṇa.

The *Wenju* states: Regarding the *Abhidharmakośa*, it says that karma created in this life which ripens in this very life is called "karma to be experienced in the present life" (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya-karman*);

karma created in this life which ripens in the second life is called "karma to be experienced in the next life" (*upapadyavedanīya-karman*); and karma created in this life which ripens sequentially from the third life onward...
The term "ripening" (vipāka) refers to karma that bears fruit in a subsequent life; one should reflect upon this meaning according to the principle of the present life and those following it.

This "non-existence" refers to the fact that when one speaks of the essence and nature of the *sukhāvatī* (the realm of tranquil light), distinctions such as purity and defilement, or beauty and ugliness, cannot be found;

it is a state of cessation and total extinction. The ten realms, the three thousand worlds, and the three lands—both the environment and its inhabitants—are empty and non-existent, yet they are like a wish-fulfilling jewel or a great round mirror, transparent throughout from surface to core and pristine within and without. Nevertheless, all things exist in relation to this realm of tranquil light.
Purity and defilement clarify the essential virtues of the *sìguāng* (the serene light); whether pure or defiled, beautiful or ugly, they are all perfectly complete.

These arise solely from the essential virtues of the *sìguāng*, which inherently possess the wondrous provisional [nature] of the three lands, thereby giving rise to the phenomenal functions of the ten realms and the three thousand [realms].

Furthermore, Siming established the Dharma-body’s quiescent land and the ultimate principle of the true mark (*dharmatā*), in which the aspects of essence and appearance are perfectly distinct. Now, I ask Siming: [how can you claim otherwise?]
Regarding this formulation, one must deeply consider whether it is intended to establish the meaning of the three bodies and four lands as distinct entities,
or as a teaching on their mutual identity, or as a discourse that follows exclusively from the perspective of principle, or as an expression of the interrelation between phenomena and principle.
I earnestly hope that future scholars will examine the text’s explicit and implicit statements and clarify their respective characteristics by applying these same criteria.
When the principle of the markless (animitta) is thus established, the wondrous purport of our own school becomes vividly manifest before one’s eyes.
This is fully detailed in the third fascicle of the *Mohe Zhiguan* and its commentaries;
therein, various masters of the Mahāyāna teach that the Dharmakāya is the substance, while Prajñā and Vimukti are its two functions, which may indeed be separated by successive lifetimes.

"Spanning across worlds and extending through both the pure and the defiled"—this definition refers to the vertical (*tong*). Furthermore, it is said that while the substance and meaning are fully present without distinction, there is a difference between concealment and manifestation;
yet, if one says they are both non-different, this does not avoid being horizontal, and if one says they differ in concealment and manifestation, this does not avoid being vertical.

Please take this passage and contrast it with the current text’s theory of "one horizontal and two vertical. The *Miaoxuan* states: "The 'Aiding' (Zi) and 'Accomplishing' (Cheng) [stages] come first."
Contemplative observation comes first and the true nature follows; this is vertical differentiation. These three are all distinct, which constitutes horizontal differentiation.

The principle-vehicle is inherently possessed, while the following-vehicle and the attained-vehicle are acquired; that only after the Path does True Suchness exist and then transform sentient beings is the meaning of verticality.
The four phrases regarding mutual illumination are as explained in the *Mysterious Text* (*Xuánwén*).
In the *Mysterious Text*, it first refutes the falling into substantialist attachments regarding object and wisdom; next, it establishes them according to the *siddhānta*;

and finally, it clarifies their inconceivable mutual illumination. This is like mirrors reflecting one another, or as a single earth can produce a sprout, and that sprout can in turn produce [another].
Regarding the first stage (*bhūmi*): since wisdom is both the object of the mind and the mind itself, and as both are mind, they are both the *dharmadhātu*.

When mind and mind illuminate one another, what is there that is improper? As for the phrase "to gather and fold" (*shè xié*), it is treated as "to gather and cite" (*shè dié*) within the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* [commentary].

Now, examining this closely, "shè shè" (both pronounced with the *zhè* rhyme) and "xié" (pronounced with the *liè* rhyme) likely do not accord with the intended meaning of the text. It is correct [to read it otherwise].
One must form *chē* (pronounced *tú xié* in the *qièyùn* system), meaning a double-layered garment; *shè* is also written as *shè* (pronounced *shè* in the *qièyùn* system).
To bring the Dharma into a sentence is called *chē-chē*; to bring a sentence into the Dharma is called *chē-shǔ*.
Why do you harshly disparage the virtue long established [in this sutra] merely to resolve a doubt?
Cien (Ci'en) says: "The *Ayuṣpramāṇa-parivarta* and the *Guṇaparikīrtana-parivarta* arise sequentially to resolve the preceding doubts.

The previous section on the emergence [of the assembly] all spoke of the Buddha’s transformed hosts being vast and their ranks high; now, the presiding host of the assembly has a doubt, which is now resolved through the Dharma."

The body is fundamentally without arising or ceasing; the transformation Buddha has recently attained [enlightenment], while the reward body has long been realized. Why, then, should this great assembly have any doubt?
One should know that if one were merely to resolve these doubts, one could not manifest the fact that the original Buddha has long been established;
since this is absent in the various sutras, such an error would exist. The Master of the Record (Jizang) condemned this, let alone others who all judge it to be for the purpose of circulation.
Regarding the classification of the thirteen chapters as constituting the "Correct Equality," this is the interpretation held by Cien (Kuiji) and other schools;

it is for this reason that [the author] refutes them. As for "the unsurpassed seed": "The path you practice is the bodhisattva path" refers to those who have regressed from their initial resolve but have resolved to practice again; because the roots of goodness previously cultivated have not been extinguished, they are transformed.
The one who brings forth the Unsurpassed and teaches and transforms sentient beings is the Bodhisattva who leaped forth from his finger; other meanings may be inferred accordingly.
As for the character *xi* (奚), it is pronounced with both the level (*ping*) and departing (*qu*) tones, though it is likely intended to be read with the departing tone.

*Xi-xie* (奚屧): *xie* is pronounced *xian-yè* (先叶切); it refers to the inner lining of a sandal. *Xi-ji* (奚屐): *ji* is pronounced *qú-jí* (渠戟切); it refers to wooden clogs or sandals. The *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary on the Profound Meaning) states: [text follows].

A "path" (*xi*) refers to a main thoroughfare; that which is written as "tied" (*xi*) refers to the ties on the collar of a garment. Furthermore, regarding the passage below which says, "The past again has two:
first, the near reveals the distant," the character "past" (*guòqù*) is missing one "upper" (*shàng*) radical;
it should read "upper-past" (*shàng guòqù*), followed by "again two."
The text states that there are five admonitions and seven requests combined from beginning to end;
it should further state "eight requests," because the passage concerning Śāriputra receiving the mandate corresponds to one request.
Furthermore, there are three stoppings; thus, there are eight requests, five admonitions, and three stoppings. Moreover, this is also the case for Maitreya in the introduction.

The section on Maitreya’s inquiry and Mañjuśrī’s response regarding the emergence from the earth consists of Maitreya’s inquiry as to where [the bodhisattvas] have come from, how they have gathered, who their teacher is, and the request that the Great Assembly together invite the Tathāgata;
the Tathāgata’s admonition not to be confused, indolent, or regressive; the arising of doubt due to attachment, followed by further inquiry because of that doubt;
and finally, the arrival of Samantabhadra from the east with the request, "I pray you, speak of this," and so forth. This is further divided.
The Buddhas from the ten directions who came with their respective bodhisattvas as attendants all gave rise to doubts and each addressed their Buddha.
All the Buddhas said, "Maitreya has already asked; you yourselves shall hear it through him.
Since all the Buddhas thus deferred to Maitreya, was there not also an invitation from the Buddhas? This is the invitation within the Gate of Traces (*jimen*).
In explaining the Buddha’s wisdom through the Chapter on the Original Gate, one requests that the Buddha’s remote lifespan be revealed for the sake of ultimate purity and coolness.

While in the *Avataṃsaka*, bodhisattvas and others request the Dharma of the ten stages from the bodhisattvas, it would be profoundly inappropriate for the bodhisattvas of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* to request the Buddha to preach the Buddha-dharma;
how much more so for Śāriputra and others, who conceal their inner realization while manifesting outwardly?
Furthermore, the questions of Maitreya and the answers of Mañjuśrī all manifest the Buddha-dharma;
they cannot be compared to the questions and answers between Vimukticandra and Vajragarbha concerning the Dharma of the Ten Grounds Bodhisattvas.
If one were to claim that the Ten Grounds and the Buddha-dharma are the same, why then, within the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, does it take a mere small fragment—no larger than a fingernail—of...?
Does this not weigh the soil of the boundless great earths throughout the ten directions?

Furthermore, in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra, and Maitreya each spoke of their own [realms] until they arrived at the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*; there, they all requested the Buddha to preach this very sūtra.

Thus, whether in terms of the provisional or the fundamental gate, or regarding the requests, the admonitions, the Dharma, or the persons, these features are found in no other sūtras; there must indeed be a profound reason for this.
Furthermore, Master Qingliangguan’s *Huayan Chao* states: "Now, this [translation] clarifies that the *Dharmapada* is inferior to this [Lotus Sūtra];
these belong to one school, while those belong to three schools—this is their first difference.
Those belong only to the Śrāvakas, whereas these three schools consist of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas—this is their second difference. Those have only three requests, whereas these have five requests."
Third, they differ in that the former [the *Ratnarāśi-sūtra*] relies solely on the invitation by humans, whereas this [the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*] includes the invitation by the Buddha;

fourth, they differ in their scope, as explained at length in the relevant commentaries (*shu* and *chao*). Although I am but a student of the final generation, I venture to say that Qingliang [Zhiyi] established his views based on personal sentiment, thereby disparaging the wondrous sūtra.
I shall therefore challenge Qingliang’s errors by citing the aforementioned passages concerning the "invitation" (*qing*) and "exhortation" (*jie*) from the sūtra itself.
The arising of the Dharma-body and so forth is also as explained in the *Wenju* (Commentary on the Words) of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*.

It states that one should not engage in deliberation regarding the lifespan of the Tathāgata, because the Dharma-body Bodhisattva resides in the pure land of the Dharma-nature (*dharmatā*), and thus does not belong to the category of birth in a physical body (*janma-kāya*). As for the birth-body Bodhisattva, if they are a householder...

Those comprised by devas, nāgas, and so forth, if they have left the household life, are comprised within the fourfold assembly; if they manifest through the expedient application of the *dharmatā-kāya*, they are likewise comprised within the eightfold assembly.
Now, you ask: "Does this not mean that the *dharmakāya* manifests birth? Is this not precisely the case where that text speaks of the *dharmakāya* manifesting through expedient means?
Since that text states that these are *dharmakāya* bodhisattvas and the pure land of *dharmatā*, they are not within the scope of verbal expression.
Since this is not mentioned in the current text, how much less need be said now that it has already been stated that one receives the Dharma-nature body and the stage of the Dharma-body?

Thus, there is no need for further elaboration. The subsequent explanation of the "Chapter on Wondrous Sound" states: "The teacher has already employed provisional means, and the disciple likewise conceals his reality;
both conceal themselves in silent endurance and tolerate their own clumsiness. Is this not precisely what is meant by being concealed within the Dharma-nature?
Does the reality of the Honored One’s sublime form bestow the provisional means of the inferior, segmented body?

Furthermore, since the *Wenju* states that the eighty *zhang* [body] is the Buddha’s great function (*mahāprayoga*), is it not the case that the inferior *zhanglü* [body] of the *Lotus Sūtra* is likewise a great function?
Moreover, since the *Wenju* says, "The Tathāgata approaches the trichiliocosm with compassion," why would this not also apply here? Nevertheless, although there are four...

The manifestation of the Buddha in a majestic and exalted form is merely a temporary appearance intended for symbolic representation; in reality, the *zhànglù* (sixteen-foot) body is fundamentally the exercise of provisional means (*upāya*) that conceals the supreme and manifests the inferior.
Only by grasping this true meaning can one understand that while the four Buddhas are identical in essence (*tathatā*), their functions differ.
Therefore, how could the Teacher of the *Lotus Sūtra*, appearing in a sixteen-foot body clad in soiled robes, ever contradict the essence of the Dharma-nature and the True Mark (*dharmatā-lakṣaṇa*)?

If you hold that the *Xuánqiān* (Profound Commentary) clarifies the "opening" [of the provisional]—whereby the soiled garment reveals the inner body as a jeweled necklace—and yet do not hold that the *Wénjù* (Textual Passages) and the *Jì* (Commentary) clarify the "bestowing" [of the provisional]—whereby the hidden reality manifests as the provisional—is this not to say that the *Xuánqiān* clarifies the "opening" while the *Wénjù* and *Jì* clarify the "bestowing"?
Are these not distinct? Is it not the case that by failing to recognize this distinction between "opening" and "bestowing," you fall into the error of either addition or subtraction?
Is this not a slander against [Zhi] Shu?
The Record states that among the ten gates of the *Xuánwén*, the section on "Distinguishing Similarities and Differences" includes:

first, destroying the traces to reveal the fundamental; second, abolishing the traces to reveal the fundamental; third, opening up the traces to reveal the fundamental; and fourth, harmonizing the traces to reveal the fundamental.

The fifth dwelling reveals the fundamental through the fundamental; the sixth dwelling reveals the fundamental through the trace; the seventh dwelling reveals the fundamental through that which is neither trace nor fundamental;

the eighth dwelling covers the trace to reveal the fundamental; the ninth dwelling uses the fundamental through the trace; and the tenth dwelling uses the trace through the fundamental. Regarding their similarities and differences:

the ten applications within the traces have already appeared in various teachings, whereas the ten applications within the fundamentals are not found extensively in any single sutra among those texts.
The previous passage stating "as fully explained in the Xuánwén" merely refers to taking the *traces* (*jì*) as "other" and "coarse," and the *origin* (*běn*) as "self" and "sublime," and so forth.
This is the intended meaning of explaining "the other" as "the self" up to the point of equality.

Cien said: Others may have doubts, asking, "If he has long since attained enlightenment and has constantly been teaching and transforming beings here, who were those such as Dīpaṃkara Buddha who attained enlightenment, entered parinirvāṇa, and taught the Dharma during the intervening period? To resolve this doubt, it says:
"In this manner, during that intervening period, Dīpaṃkara Buddha and the others likewise all used skillful means to preach..."
Other Buddhas do not exist apart from my own body as something distinct. Furthermore, regarding the "one":

first, it does not negate that Śākyamuni has truly achieved enlightenment and been teaching for a long time, while manifesting a new achievement; second, how could it negate the "intention of equality" among the four intentions, which speaks of others as oneself?
The intention of equality has already been cited previously.

As explained in detail in the *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary on the Profound Meaning), it is asked: "If there are superior-super capacities within the inferior-inferior dharma-realm—just as there are capacities of the nine realms within the hell realm—this may well be so;
however, how can there be capacities of the nine realms within the Buddha-realm? Answer: The term "capacity" (*jī*) means that which can be stimulated to respond.

If there is a superior capacity below, it encompasses both cause and effect; that is to say, one may seek a superior effect through an inferior effect, and an inferior cause may give rise to a superior cause. If there is an inferior capacity above, it pertains only to the effect;

that is to say, one may seek a superior effect through an inferior effect, and an inferior effect may give rise to a superior cause—such as when the capacity of the Buddha-realm exists within the hells.

This means that although one has resolved to seek the fruit of Buddhahood, if one breaks the precepts and falls into hell, one may still generate the capacity (*bīja*) for attaining the stage of perfection within that state;
the remaining eight cases are to be understood accordingly. If this is so, what is the difference between this and the capacity for Buddhahood existing within the realm of hell? Answer:

If the mind directed toward the Buddha-realm is strong, it is already called the benefit of the Buddha-realm. When [the capacity] exists within the other nine realms, it is called "the Buddha-realm existing within the nine [realms]."

Regarding the capacities of the realms (*dhātu*): if one has already fallen into the nine realms, they are termed the "nine realms"; as for the capacity for the Buddha-realm (*buddhadhātu*), it is as described in that text.
Furthermore, the passage below concerning "various foods" contains an error; the character "food" (*shi*) should be "form/color" (*se*).
The Sūtra states:

"In the Xia dynasty, it was called *sui* (year), taking the time for the planet Jupiter (*suixing*) to complete one revolution; in the Shang, it was called *si* (sacrifice), taking the completion of one cycle of the four seasons;

in the Zhou, it was called *nian* (harvest), taking the time for grain to ripen once; in the Tang and Yu periods, it was called *zai* (vehicle/carrying), taking the end of one cycle of things and the beginning of another. (10)
Two months constitute a year, and twelve years constitute a *kṛti*.
The *Record* states that the Buddha-nature has five names;
the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*, fascicle twenty-five, says: "It is also called *Lengyan*, it is also called *Prajñā*, and it is also called *Vajra*. (3)
"Obscurity" (*mèi*) is also called "Lion’s Roar" and is also called "Buddha-nature.

Regarding the differences in magnitude within the fundamental [nature], their mutual comparison of superiority and inferiority, and the horizontal and vertical discussions concerning this and that, Xuán says these refer to years and lifespan; "magnitude" refers to length and brevity.
In that fundamental text, one first distinguishes the lifespans of the Buddhas within the four teachings of the provisional traces (*jì*), and only then does it provide the judgment.

"Great" refers to the Mahāyāna, which is eternal; "small" refers to the Hīnayāna, which is impermanent. Since this is the case regarding their traces (*lakṣaṇa*), it is likewise so regarding their essence (*mūla*).
This is why they are called "great" and "small," being superior and inferior respectively, and thus differing from one another in terms of horizontal and vertical dimensions.

"Horizontal" refers to the ten directions; "vertical" refers to the present and the past. You should use this principle to interpret and clarify the text of the *Ji* (Commentary). I have previously sought [this meaning].

In that *Xuánwén*, these were briefly omitted and not yet distinguished as "horizontal" (*héng*) or "vertical" (*shù*). Regarding the sixfold interpretation (*ṣaḍvyākhyāna*) of the ancient masters and the threefold interpretation of the present master:
the various Hīnayāna masters explain that although the *prajñā* and the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) are already perfected, the fetters of the fruit still remain;

liberation is not yet complete, the body still partakes of coarse food, and it still bears impermanence. This is one aspect of excellence and two aspects of inferiority, which they liken to a fire running across a horizontal river. Furthermore...

It is said that first there is the body endowed with the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*), followed by the attainment of the *prajñā* of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), and only after the subsequent cessation of both body and wisdom is liberation fully realized.

Since there is thus a sequence of superior and inferior, or prior and posterior—comparable to three dots of water arranged vertically—if one enters the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), there is the body but no wisdom;
an Arhat in the formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu*) possesses wisdom but no body; and if one enters the nirvana without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*), [there is neither].
There is the liberation of solitary detachment (*ekavīra-vimukti*); these meanings are each unrelated. Taken individually, they are horizontal; taken together, they are vertical.
The Mahāyāna masters say that the *dharmakāya* is the essence, and that *prajñā* and liberation are inherently present from the beginning.

These two should possess this meaning of "vertical" (*tiryak*). Furthermore, it is said that the three virtues (*triguṇa*) are without before or after, being a single entity (*ekakāya*) that is fully possessed.
It is sufficient to understand that while the substance follows the meaning and thus has three distinctions, this is merely because the substance is horizontal while the meaning is vertical.

Furthermore, it is said that while substance and meaning are both without difference, there is a distinction between the hidden and the manifest; "both being non-different" refers to the horizontal, while "the distinction between the hidden and the manifest" refers to the vertical.

Now, we clarify that the Three Virtues are all inconceivable; why then do you suddenly speak of the vertical and the horizontal? This is based on principle (*li*); as for the body (*shen*), it is as follows: [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly with "身". The translation reflects the available portion.]
The constant perfection of wisdom and the complete severance of afflictions are both Buddha-dharma, identical within the single Dharma-realm.

This refers to their function in practice: they are three while being one, and thus not horizontal; they are one while being three, and thus not vertical. They are three without being three, and thus not identical;
they are one without being one, and thus not different. This refers to the application of the characters [of the names].
The *Commentary on the Subcommentary to the Xuanshi* (Xuanshi shuchao) contains this statement: "By means of the sequential [order], it reveals the non-sequential.
The *Wenju* states, while the *Zhenghui deng ji* says: "Riding upon sandalwood," and so forth.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The intermediate state (*antarābhava*) knows the intermediate state; entering the womb, one knows it; even upon emerging from the womb, one knows it—this is precisely right wisdom (*samyag-prajñā*). Māyā is here translated as 'Queen of Heaven.

Having already severed suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*), and having already cultivated and realized cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*mārga*), this is the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*).
Furthermore, not needing to sever anything further nor cultivate and realize anything further, this is the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*). [This is] the Flower."
Yan says that "riding the sandalwood pavilion" signifies being born from a womb with the perfect clarity of the Buddha’s seed-wisdom (*bīja-jñāna*).

The *Ruiying* says that "transforming to ride a white elephant, the essence of the sun-piercing radiance, and being born from a womb to become a Buddha" signifies that both residual habituations and active afflictions are completely exhausted.
Although both the new and old versions of the text have been consulted with care, their wording is erroneous; it should read "while following the intentions of others.
The *Jì* (Record) states that the *Jìngmíng shū* (Vimalakīrti Commentary) provides a detailed explanation of these characteristics.
To think that there is *nirvāṇa* by completely severing branches and leaves is to give rise to delusion regarding the *dharmakāya*.

If one perceives the *paramārtha-satya* (Ultimate Truth) and regards *nirvāṇa* as a single dharma, this is called "seeing one place. Because this view arises from ignorance (*avidyā*), it is termed a "ground-dwelling" view and is also called the "view of self-existence" (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
This is a view that arises from the *dharmakāya*. If, regarding the five [aggregates] of the transformed support and supported...
Dust arises from sensual desire; this is the ground of abiding in the love of desire (*kāmarāga-vāsabhūmi*). The transformation of form and mind is false discrimination;

this is the ground of abiding in the love of form (*rūparāga-vāsabhūmi*). When one transcends form and contemplates the mind, yet still perceives the existence of a mind, this is the ground of abiding in the love of existence (*bhavarāga-vāsabhūmi*), which is inverted perception.
In the *Avataṃsaka*, it is said that there are clouds of inconceivable incense and flowers; these are the [manifestations of] Bodhi.
The five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) experienced as the retribution of the most excellent and sublime fruits are the afflictions of thought (*vitarka-kleśa*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

That all Bodhisattvas enter, emerge from, and abide in hundreds of thousands of samādhis and dhyānas, yet their minds remain free from sensory objects (*viṣaya*), refers to the afflictions of thought of the form and formless realms (*rūpa-ārūpyadhātu*).
Regarding the ten gates of the *Xuánwén*: first, explaining the names; second, discerning the characteristics; third, providing an exegesis, and so on through the tenth.

The ten *siddhāntas* pass through the sutras; next, regarding the explanation of the sixth phrase, "only the Buddha [knows]," from this point down to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, which states that within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) there is no conceptual differentiation—this is still the text explaining the fifth phrase.
For the meaning of the first five phrases of the sutra is that true wisdom (*bhūtajñāna*) accords with reality, whereas the sixth phrase is...
This is because his skillful means (*upāya*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) are commensurate with reality. The concluding sentence of the text states: "The two wisdoms clearly examine the two truths.
The commentary on the fifth phrase explains: "That the Buddha must be fully endowed with both the provisional and the ultimate wisdoms likely reflects the meaning of the conclusion;
please examine this further. In the *Cān jīng* (Dhyāna Sūtra), "following the cause" refers to the cause being joy.
It is because of desire. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that "from the perspective of the fruit," the world is the fruit of the aggregates (*skandha*) and sense-bases (*āyatana*).

Regarding the passage in the *Xuanwen* which says, "The practice of initiating past good deeds cures and breaks present evil," and so forth: the *Xuanwen* contains fifteen sections analyzing this meaning.
Therein, it asks: "To bring about good for people, how does one sever evil? It answers: "To bring about good for people..."
The "old" refers to the correct severance of evil, while the "auxiliary" refers to the new counteractive measures that destroy evil.

The "old" refers to the correct production of good, while the "new" refers to the auxiliary. Thus, the "new" is termed "present," and the "old" is merely "past. Furthermore, the subsequent passage states:
"These employ the words regarding the provisional application found in the Chapter on the Five Buddhas, all using various causes and conditions to explain the present text."
This is an error. It was intended to mean that, down to the use of various causes, conditions, and parables, it is precisely as stated in this sutra:
"In order to cause the production of all roots of goodness, one uses various causes, conditions, parables, and phrases.
How could this possibly refer to the "expedient means" (*upāya*) mentioned in the chapter on the Five Buddhas, which speaks of "various causes and conditions"? Therefore, it is known to be an error.
In the fifth section on Cāṇakya, Cāṇakya explained to the bhikṣus the meaning of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, non-self, and cessation. Jingming (Pure Name) rebuked him, saying:
"Do not use a mind of arising and ceasing to explain the Dharma of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). Cāṇakya [replied]: "Non-arising and non-ceasing is the *wu* (non-being)."

The meaning of "constant" is that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are empty and do not arise; this is the meaning of suffering (*duḥkha*). That there is nothing whatsoever is the meaning of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

That there is no self and no non-self, being non-dual, is the meaning of non-self (*anātman*). That phenomena were originally not ignited and now are not extinguished is the meaning of quiescent extinction (*śānta-nirvāṇa*).
Regarding the passage below, if one understands quiescent extinction, it should read "if not quiescently extinguished"; please examine this more closely in the subsequent text.
Furthermore, it says: "If one were to first cite the previous statement regarding 'extinction,' one should instead have cited the previous statement regarding 'non-extinction.

As for the passage, 'If [the argument] reaches [the object], then the ordinary person can refute it,' etc., this text is likely erroneous. The scripture states: 'If it does not reach [the object] and yet refutes it, then ordinary sentient beings would be able to refute it.'"
If one reaches the point where [the view] is destroyed, the first thought should be destroyed. Furthermore, it is said in the Sūtras that vipaśyanā can destroy the afflictions (*kleśa*);
however, this meaning is not so. Why? When wisdom exists, there are no afflictions; when afflictions exist, there is no wisdom.
Who possesses wisdom and who possesses afflictions, such that one could say that wisdom destroys the afflictions?
The one who roars the lion’s roar of affliction (nāya) is none other than the Bodhisattva Siṃhanāda; therefore, Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are called "Lion’s Roar.
"Lion’s Roar" means to speak with certainty—that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature which is immutable.
*Vipaśyanā* is translated here as "contemplation" (*guan*); *śamatha* is correctly transliterated as *śamatha*.

"Shi" (止) here means "stopping" (*śamatha*). "U-pi-xia" (憂畢叉) here means "contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*); "shizheng" (止等) refers to these two together. Regarding the characteristics [of offenses], whether they are light or heavy, they are fully as explained in the sutras; I further request that you examine in detail the meaning of the substance of the conditions (*pratyaya*).

Furthermore, the *Nanshan lüchao* states: "One who deeply clarifies the characteristics of the Vinaya, thoroughly understands what is permitted and what is prohibited, as well as the light and heavy [grades of offenses], and weighs the root and the branches, is called one who 'understands the Vinaya' (*vinaya-vid*)."

Regarding the meaning of the gradual and sudden establishment of prohibitions and their presence or absence, the *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra-ṭīkā* states: "The disciplinary methods of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna precepts differ. The Bodhisattva precepts were established all at once as fifty-eight matters, whereas the Śrāvaka precepts were formulated as they were transgressed.
This is because the *Śāstra on the Principles of the Occasion* (Jīlùn) addresses the suitability of the faculties [of practitioners], and that *Śāstra* has three parts."

The Mahāsattva Yi (Yi-i) possessed deep faith and could hear [the precepts] all at once without resistance; the Śrāvakas of shallow understanding, however, could not accept them when heard all at once.

Furthermore, because these two types of Mahāsattvas did not constantly attend by his side, there was no opportunity for them to report matters as they arose. Consequently, the rules were established all at once.

As for the Śrāvakas, they were able to attend him constantly and had minor desires to report to the Buddha; thus, he waited until an offense occurred before establishing the precepts. This is the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*.
The establishment of these precepts originated with Śāntarakṣita when he conferred ordination upon Prince Sāgaramegha;
at that time, the various Mahāsattvas proclaimed fifty-eight matters and thus instituted them all at once. This was not the case for the Śrāvakas.

Furthermore, in the Mahāyāna there is the principle of sacrificing one’s body, whereas in the Hīnayāna there is not. Moreover, according to the Hīnayāna treatises, the meaning of relinquishing the precepts is based on four [conditions].

The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* and the *Samyukta-abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* state that there are four causes [for the loss of the precepts]: first, death; second, performing the ritual of renunciation (*karmavācanā*);

third, severing the roots of goodness; and fourth, the arising of both sexual organs. Regarding the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, if one who has left the monastic life returns home, they must perform the ritual of renunciation;

if they do not perform the ritual of renunciation, the essence of the precepts remains. Even if one commits a grave offense (*pārājika*), the precepts are not lost. Thus, it is said in the Vinaya: "I..."
Becoming a *śrāmaṇera* is gradual renunciation; becoming a layperson (*avadātavasana*) is sudden renunciation.
The reason for this is that when one maintains the precepts yet commits transgressions, the resulting karma and suffering are difficult to extricate.

Therefore, the opening for renouncing the precepts allows for coming and going without obstruction, as in the case of Saṃghamitra, who returned seven times to subdue Māra before finally attaining arhatship. Thus, the regulation for renunciation is fixed at exactly seven [times]. As for its...
Renouncing the precepts merely means that the essential substance no longer continues; it is the cessation of the category of the body of precepts (*śīla-skandha*).

If there is a transformation of faculties—such as a *bhikṣu* becoming a *bhikṣuṇī* and thereby giving rise to the *bhikṣuṇī* precepts, or a *bhikṣuṇī* becoming a *bhikṣu* and giving rise to the *bhikṣu* precepts—the precepts are not lost.
This differs from the case of those with both sexual organs (*ubhayavyañjana*), who lose their precepts. (From the four-fascicle *Vibhāṣā*).

There are five occasions for the relinquishment [of the precepts]: at the time of death, when the Dharma disappears, when one becomes hermaphroditic, through the commission of an offense, and by formal renunciation—these constitute the five.
Regarding the Mahāyāna precepts, according to the *Ratnakūṭa-alaṃkāra-sūtra*, the Bodhisattva precepts have a method for receiving them but no method for relinquishing them;
even if there is an offense, they are not lost. The *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra* states that the Prātimokṣa precepts [are lost] at the time of death.

When one abandons the path and leaves the monastic order, one relinquishes the nature-precepts (*dharmatā-śīla*) accomplished by a bodhisattva-mahāsattva; yet, until reaching the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), these are never abandoned midway.
Judging by this, there is a minor abandonment of the precepts, but no abandonment of the precepts in the ultimate sense.

If one follows the explanation in the *Bodhisattva-śīla-viniścaya-sūtra-śāstra*, the essence of the precepts arises through the expedient means of seeking to receive them; if one abandons the bodhisattva vow or increases [the defilements], [the precepts are lost].

Regarding the transgressions of the higher afflictions, the ten grave offenses (daśa-guruka-āpatti) are forfeited when their essential nature is destroyed; however, in the absence of these two conditions, they are only forfeited upon reaching Buddhahood.
The *Yogācārabhūmi* also explains it in this same way. Judging by this, both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna possess the forfeiture of precepts;
one can see this by reflecting upon the mutual presence or absence of such rules within them. If one were to harmonize these views, the *Ratnakaranda-śrāvakācāra* and... [text continues]

Regarding the *Commentary on the Meaning of Precepts with and without Objects and Abandonment* based on the *Treatise on Entering the Mahāyāna*, the explanations concerning the existence or non-existence of the meaning of "abandonment" (tyāga) in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*—namely, that there are precepts without objects and without abandonment—are as follows; please examine them further in detail.
Regarding the order of seating for the *śīlavibhāga-prāyaścitta* (the method of repentance for the division of precepts):
those who uphold the Mahāyāna precepts are separated by heaven from those who uphold the Hīnayāna precepts; the former sit above and first, while the latter sit below and last.

This is a division based on the distinction between the Great and Small Vehicles (*mahāyāna* and *hīnayāna*). If one first observes the Small Vehicle precepts and subsequently the Great Vehicle precepts, then the years of seniority (*kṣapa*) of the Small Vehicle are added to constitute the seniority of the Great Vehicle. If...
The great precedes the small; when one is in the small, one relies on the small, and when one is in the great, one relies on the great.
If we discuss "great" and "small" in terms of the Three Vehicles of the Tripitaka and Shared Teachings, the Bodhisattva is "great" when in the great and "small" when in the small.

Thus we know that when a Bodhisattva is in the Small Vehicle, they follow the stages and positions of the Small Vehicle, and when in the Great Vehicle, they follow the stages and positions of the Great Vehicle.
Because they sat in the second [row], the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that Śākyamuni had no separate assembly of bodhisattvas;
thus, Maitreya and Mañjuśrī sat in sequence among the śrāvakas. However, according to the *Brahmajāla-sūtra*, one should know that there was indeed a separate assembly of bodhisattvas.
Therefore, the two assemblies—the lay and the ordained—determine their respective ranks based on the vinaya rules of the Hīnayāna.

In the Hinayana, once the four grave offenses have been confessed and the *śaikṣa* (probationary) status for *saṃghāvaśeṣa* and lesser offenses has been completed, one attains purity by bowing in submission.

In the Mahayana, all ten grave and forty-eight light offenses are universally purified through confession. If one commits a grave offense among the ten, one should recite the Bodhisattva Precepts, prostrate before the Buddhas of the three periods of time, and perform a sincere and arduous confession until signs of purification appear, whereby the offense is extinguished. For the forty-eight light offenses, one performs confession before another person (*pratyekapratideśanā*).
Their transgressions are thereby extinguished; because the repentance methods of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna differ, it is said that they are "separated by heaven.

This is explained in detail in the *Zhiguan* (Mohe Zhiguan) and the *Nanshan Chao*. Furthermore, regarding the repentance methods of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, there are distinctions as to whether the seven groups of followers participate together or separately.
The bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, and śrāmaṇerīs are thus called the "seven assemblies.
Regarding what is meant by "the same or not," this refers to their commonalities and differences. To discuss the precept against killing:

the seven assemblies of bodhisattvas commit it equally, while the five assemblies of śrāvakas are largely the same but slightly different. That which is the same is that they all equally undertake the vow not to kill.

There are three differences: first, the difference between what is permitted and what is prohibited: a Mahāsattva may kill when he perceives the appropriate opportunity, whereas a Śrāvaka, even if he perceives such an opportunity, may not kill;
second, the difference between form and mind: a Mahāsattva disciplines the mind, while a Śrāvaka disciplines the body; third, the difference between light and heavy offenses:

harming one’s teacher constitutes a *ānantarya* (immediate) offense for a Mahāsattva, whereas it does not constitute an *ānantarya* for a Śrāvaka; furthermore, the Mahāsattva’s offenses are more grave than those of the Śrāvaka. It is also thus.

This may be called the seven assemblies receiving the Mahāyāna precepts as a single body of dharma; whereas receiving the Hīnayāna precepts involves distinctions such as the five precepts, the ten precepts, and the full set of precepts.
That the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna are both shared and distinct is likewise a matter of identity and difference.

For instance, regarding the prohibition against selling alcohol, both vehicles enjoin it, yet there are similarities and differences: they are identical in not permitting its sale, while they differ in that [the Mahāyāna] prohibits it more extensively.

The scholar benefits all things and thus sells with a sense of solemnity; the śrāvaka, however, trades for profit and merely commits an offense under the third category, which is governed by the precept against buying and selling.
Yet such a person is as ignorant of life and death as a bird or a rat.

"Existence and non-existence" (*cunwang*) refers to survival and extinction; "large and small" refers to opening and closing, and since survival and extinction are not fixed, one must not be ignorant of this.
"Bird-mouse" (*niaoshu*) refers to the bat. The *Erya* states: "The bat is called *fuyi*. Xing Bing says:
"It is also known as *fuyi*. Guo Pu says: "People of Qi call it the 'Immortal Mouse' (*xianshu*). It can fly through the air and enter burrows; if someone catches it,"
When it flies through the air, it resembles a bird; when it seizes a bird, it enters its burrow like a mouse.
Yet, it is neither truly a bird nor a mouse. Thus, the *Buddhapiṭaka Sūtra* says: "For example, when a bat wishes to catch a bird, it enters its burrow and becomes a mouse;
when it wishes to catch a mouse, it flies through the air and becomes a bird. However, in reality, it lacks the function of a great bird, and its body is foul-smelling."
The defiled delight in darkness is likewise for a bhikṣu who has broken the precepts: he neither enters into the *poṣadha* nor the *pravāraṇa*, yet he is not employed as a servant by the king;
he is called neither a layperson (*avadātavasana*) nor one who has gone forth (*pravrajita*).
The Sūtra states that it is eight *tāla* trees high;
the *Xiyuji* (Records of the Western Regions) says its form is like this, resembling a palm tree of this region that reaches seventy or eighty feet at most in height.
When the fruit ripens, it is red in color and as large as a pomegranate; many people eat it. Some say that one *tāla* tree is [the height of]...
Seven *ren* (each *ren* being seven feet) constitutes the height of one *tāla* tree, which is forty-nine feet. Eight *tāla* trees thus reach a height of three hundred and ninety-two feet.
As for why the Sūtra mentions the number eight: since upholding this Sūtra must necessarily manifest the Dharma, "eight" refers to the Eightfold Noble Path;
the "Garden of Dhāraṇī" represents the total integration of these paths, and the "Bathing Pond of the Eight Liberations" symbolizes the manifestation of the ultimate truth.
The Dharma-gate of the Hundred Thousand Bhikṣus of Wisdom-Light: The Hall of Śakra represents the abode of the Buddha-fruit;
the thirty-two halls represent the stages of the causal position, within which the bhikṣus reside. Great Parinirvāṇa is the cave of meditative concentration;
the straight Great Path serves as the place for walking meditation (caṅkrama); gentleness and patience serve as clothing; and the joy of Dharma and dhyāna—
Delightful food and drink represent the four dhyānas; the bed and bedding represent true nature (*tathatā*); the practice of contemplation and refinement represents the dhyānas;
and the Prajñāpāramitā and other dharmas represent medicinal decoctions. Please examine this symbolic representation of the Dharma further.
*Sumana*, also called *somanas*, is translated as "flower that well-gathers the mind. Its flowers are yellowish-white and very fragrant;
the tree itself is not large, reaching only three or four feet in height, and it droops like a canopy. *Campaka* is also called *campaka*. This...
The so-called yellow flower is small and fragrant; it is extremely abundant in the Western Regions. Regarding *atimuktaka* oil:
*atimuktaka* was formerly translated as "well-thought-of" (*shansi*) flower, also called "sesame" (*juyingzi*), and further referred to as "this."
Since there is no [Sanskrit] equivalent, it is not translated. "Fumigating incense" refers to various flowers and fragrant herbs.
One mixes these with sesame seeds (*tila*) until they are thoroughly saturated, then presses them to extract the oil; this oil is then burned as an offering and is called "fumigating oil.
Sesame seeds are *hú-má* (胡麻). The character for "mixing" (*móu*) is pronounced *wū hé qiè*. The preceding text mentions "ox-head sandalwood" (*gośīrṣa-candana*), which is the True Dharma.

The *Nianjing* (Sutra on Recollection) states: "In the northern continent there is a mountain named High Mountain (*Gao-shan*), which abounds in the fragrance of ox-head sandalwood (*gośīrṣa-candana*).
Because the peaks of this mountain resemble the head of an ox, and because sandalwood trees grow upon these peaks, it is so named.
Alternatively, some say that 'Ox-Head Mountain' (*Gośīrṣa-parvata*) is its name, and since this fragrance originates from there, it is named after it."

The Record states: "Regarding the two gates of 'present' and 'past,' 'present' and 'past' should actually be called 'original' and 'traced. The answer is that there are two ways of understanding this: first, they generally refer to the original and the traced; second, when specifically corresponding to multiple objects, one should say "two.
Furthermore, regarding the specific correspondence to multiple objects, it may also be said: "The answer consists of two [parts], which generally refer to [the original and the traced]."

The distinction between the Original and the Traces corresponds to many objects; I fear this may be a transmission of subtle error. "Zhì" (秩) means "directly" or "in order," referring to the sequence or the preface.
"Hàojiān" (好堅) refers to Kalinga, as explained in the *Zhi-guan-ji* (Record of Stopping and Contemplation).
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* asks: "Among all the merits of the Buddhas, none can surpass them;
in all the heavens and earths, who may be considered supreme? It answers: "The Buddha is unsurpassed; there is none superior to the Buddha.

For example, there is a tree named 'Good and Firm' (*Sudṛḍha*) that has stood for a hundred years with its branches and leaves fully developed. One day it sprouts forth and rises to a height of a hundred *zhang*. This tree, having emerged..."
When he sought a great tree to provide shade for his body, the tree deity said: "In all the worlds, there is none greater than you;

all trees are within your shade. The Buddha was likewise thus: though he remained in the stage of a bodhisattva for immeasurable billions of years, upon attaining Buddhahood in a single day, none could surpass him.
Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that the kalaviṅka bird...
When the sound has not yet emerged from within the egg of this bird, it already surpasses all other birds; the Bodhisattva is likewise.
Before emerging from the "egg" of ignorance, his Dharma-sound already surpasses the "eggs" of the two vehicles. The term *kaṅkara* refers to a bird's egg;
*kalaviṅka* means the "bird of beautiful voice."
The text states: "To be 'xièrán' (reassuredly clear) and so forth.
The *Commentary on the Zhuangzi* says it is an expression of joy and pleasure. The Preface to the *Zuozhuan* of the Spring and Autumn Annals says:

"Like the soaking of rivers and seas, like the moistening of fat and dew; when one is as if ice were suddenly melted and as if reason were naturally harmonized, only then has one attained [the truth]. Therefore, this...
"Shi" (釋) takes the meaning of "dispersing and dissolving. The preceding text mentions "a hundred spans" (*bǎiwéi*);
the *Zhuangzi* commentary states that one span (*wéi*) is one foot in diameter, thus a hundred spans is ten *zhàng*.
The scripture asks: "How much merit will one obtain?"
In this sixth sutra, there are twenty-nine characters pronounced with the level tone (*ping sheng*). Among them, one character is glossed as "should be" (*dang wei*);

eighteen characters are glossed as "how much merit will be obtained" (*de ji suo fu*); two characters are glossed as "is this not much? (*ning wei duo bu*); two characters are glossed as "then it is as if" (*ze wei yi jian*);
and two characters are glossed as "the ocean is the foremost, being the most profound and vast; Mount Sumeru is the foremost... (*hai wei di yi, zui wei shen da; Xu mi shan wei di*).
"First" means it is the most supreme and the foremost; this itself has four aspects of being foremost:
it is foremost as illumination, foremost as venerable, the Pratyekabuddha is foremost, and the Bodhisattva is also foremost.
Just as the Buddha is the King of all Dharmas, so too is this sutra. It possesses three characters of training that prevent one from being further afflicted by greed and desire.
"Affliction" (惱) also does not apply here; it has two characters and three meanings, which cannot serve as a metaphor.
"To be seen with joy by others" (為人喜見) has three characters and three meanings.

"To create seven-jeweled terraces and piles of sandalwood as offerings" (作七寶臺栴檀為積以為供養) has one character and three meanings. "Named 'Never-Disparaging'" (名號之為常不輕) has one character and three meanings.
There are thirty-two characters pronounced with the departing tone (*qùshēng*). Among them, twenty-seven characters are explained as:

for parents, for kinsmen, for people, distinguishing [the teaching], rejoicing, explaining it to others—that is, explaining it through skillful means (*upāya*)—and if one explains it to others, this itself constitutes two [categories]: explaining it to others among the Trāyastriṃśa gods, and this itself...
There are two [reasons]: either he preaches the Dharma for people, or at times he manifests his body to preach the Dharma for sentient beings—for devas, humans, and asuras;
for those seeking the state of a śrāvaka; for those seeking the state of a pratyekabuddha; for all bodhisattvas;
to preach extensively for the sake of people who bear the name "Not-Disregarded" (Adīnapramāṇa); and furthermore, to preach for the sake of the fourfold assembly. Thus it is said.
For the sake of all people, for the sake of all bodhisattvas who seek the Buddha-way, you should now expound it;
for the sake of all sentient beings, you are their father. To speak it for others, there are five points of instruction:
namely, for the sake of this sutra, for the sake of hearing the Dharma, for the sake of entrustment, for the sake of gladdening sentient beings, and in order to cause them...
"Ren" (人) refers to lanes and alleys;
those running north-south are called *qian* and those running east-west are called *mo*. The rest may be inferred accordingly, just as with "front" and "back."
To distinguish this:
the phrase "bi" (比) here is read as *bǐ* (恐取毗必切).
The *Jì* (Commentary) states:
"Śikṣā is translated here as 'learning' (*xuéfǎ*). For women, this is fully explained in the *Lüyào* (Vinaya-śāstra).
The Sūtra says: "Sentient beings of the six destinies and four modes of birth—those born from eggs, those born from wombs, those born from moisture, and those born by transformation."
In the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* and the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, it is consistently stated that "gati" (destiny/realm) means "to arrive at" or "the place to which one goes.

Thus, the six [realms] can be understood; however, if the asuras are combined [with another category], there are only five, because the destiny of the asuras is not fixed, as they may belong either to the devas or to the pretas.
The specific references mentioned in the commentary—such as those in the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* (Zhiguan)—are of a nature already familiar and need not be cited here in detail. [End of note.]

The character *pú-mèn* (蒲悶) is correctly written as *tèn* (坌). The *Vajraśāstra* states: "Sentient beings" refers to those who receive the vital winds (*prāṇa*) and possess emotional consciousness (*saṃjñā*).
What, then, does this mean? It refers to those born from eggs, such as birds; those born from wombs, such as humans; those born from moisture, such as insects;
and those born by transformation, such as devas. The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states: Humans and animals possess all four modes of birth; so too do the hells and the various heavens.
Regarding those who are born solely by transformation (*upapāduka*), it is explained in the treatise that *preta*s may also be born through both the womb (*jarāyu-ja*) and transformation.
As for those with form or without form, those with perception (*saṃjñin*) or without perception (*asaṃjñin*), or those who are neither with nor without perception (*naiva-saṃjñin-nāsaṃjñin*):
where do these four modes of birth (*yoni*) abide, and what constitutes their essence? This [passage] demonstrates that those with form...

This refers to the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*) and the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*). That which is "formless" (*arūpin*) refers to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). This, moreover, has many varieties.

That which is "with perception" (*saṃjñin*) refers to the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) and the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), because they possess the perceptions of space and consciousness.

That which is "without perception" (*asaṃjñin*) refers to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*). That which is "neither with perception nor without perception" (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñin*) refers to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
There are many texts that analyze this *saṃjñā-vastu* (the sphere of perception); for now, I shall rely on the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
The explanation of its name and meaning follows the *Fajie Cidi* (The Sequential Order of the Dharma Realm).
Regarding those without feet, with two feet, four feet, or many feet, the *Erya* states:
"Those without feet are called *zhai*; those with feet are called *chong*. One can know this through the categories of two-footed and four-footed creatures;
as for those with many feet, such as centipedes and the like, they have already been distinguished in the aforementioned passages concerning the seven treasures and so forth.

The *Mahāśāstra on Instruction, Exhortation, Benefit, and Joy* states: "To instruct means to show people birth-and-death and nirvana; to benefit means to teach people the three vehicles and six perfections, leading them to abandon evil and practice good by preaching the Dharma for their benefit;
to gladden means to guide them toward transcendence and praise their conduct according to what they have practiced. This refers to the prediction [of enlightenment] mentioned below.
Master Ci'en (Yuanze) states that this means "rejoicing" (*anumodana*), as the Dharma Master provides clear assistance.

The *Ji* (Commentary) states that at times the Great Master (Zhiyi) relied on the *Bhadracaryā-praṇidhāna-sūtra* (Puxian guan) to judge the five grades of practice as being within the stage of "likeness" (*sādharmya*) regarding the six sense faculties.

The *Sushu* (Sub-commentary) to Zhanran’s *Guanshin lun* states: "The *Bhadracaryā-praṇidhāna-sūtra* clarifies that the five grades are equivalent to the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*)," though this remains to be further examined.
The *Zhiguan* states: "If one relies on the *Puxian guan*, then the five grades [of practice] constitute the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*) and the five minds;

the Buddha’s intent is difficult to fathom, and thus there are different explanations according to the capacities of beings. The *Miaoxuan* states: "Relying on the Mahayana repentance, one gives rise to the initial mind of 'following with joy' (*anumodanā*) and perfect faith, thereby attaining one *dhāraṇī*";
it further states: "The *Puxian guan* clarifies that prior to the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), there are ten [stages]."
The "stage" (kṣetra) refers to the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*). The *Śūxing qiji* states:

"Regarding the 'one-turning dharani' (*ekāvartā dhāraṇī*), although it is discussed vertically in terms of stages as being prior to the six faculties and the seventh stage of faith, when explained comprehensively, it pertains to the initial mind. It further states:
"By the power of samādhi, the six faculties gradually become pure, as fully described in the sutras; once the six faculties are purified, one is touched on the head by all Tathāgatas."

The bestowal of prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) is precisely the entry into the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*); thus we know that the Great Master’s rank resides within the five grades and is also situated within the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*).
The seventh stage of faith is named "Revolving Dharani" (*āvartana-dhāraṇī*), which signifies revolving from the conventional into emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
Therefore, he may be called a "Bodhisattva of Revolving Dharani. Thus, the text at the end of the "Chapter on Analysis" states: "To divide one..."
The five grades consist of two types of mind; these five grades are precisely the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*).

Therefore, Nanyue stated that the meditative concentration entered by the Great Master was the preliminary skillful means (*pūrvayoga*) of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*, and what he manifested and maintained was the *svādhiṣṭhāna-dhāraṇī*.

Thus, Emperor Yang of the Sui dynasty replied to his final instructions, saying: "The five grades and ten stages of faith are already as bright and clear as day; they are fully recorded in the *Bai lu* (Records of the Hundred)."
Regarding the ten preliminary stages prior to the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) within the *Samantabhadra-bodhisattva-sūtra*: from the passage beginning with "If a bhikṣu...

up to "one who recites the Mahāyāna" and "one who practices the Mahāyāna," [the stage] where "those flowers are golden in color, buds but not yet blossomed" likely corresponds to the first stage of faith (*śraddhā*).
Following this vision, the practitioner further engages in repentance; this likely corresponds to the second stage of faith. Thus it is seen by the practitioner.
Having already rejoiced and paid homage, one departs from fear; this is the third stage of faith and following. Having made this vow, one departs from fear day and night during the six periods;
this is the fourth stage of faith and following. At that time, the practitioner sees all the Bodhisattvas arrive; this is called the initial contemplation of the realm of Samantabhadra.
This is likely the fifth stage of faith, and it is also likely because this constitutes the five grades of contemplative practice; thus it is said "immediately."
Taking the five grades as the five minds of the ten faiths is not correct if one divides those five grades into ten.
