The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) states: Regarding the passage in the sutra where Mañjuśrī extensively explains the lower parts, it should rather say, "In the sutra, the Buddha extensively explains the lower parts for Mañjuśrī. The sutra says:
"Good son, I shall now explain for you the characteristics of the causes and conditions of the lower-part jewels. Good son, if there is a person whose spirit..."
With unimpeded mastery like that of Mañjuśrī, and likewise with me, whose eloquence is also unimpeded,
the two of us shall, throughout a single kalpa, constantly use our eloquence to preach the Dharma for immeasurable and boundless sentient beings,

causing them to abide in the stage of a Bodhisattva bound to one more birth (*ekajātipratibaddha*). Furthermore, we shall exhaust all supernatural powers to provide various garments, bedding, and requisites.
“Is the merit of those people who provide food and drink as offerings to these bodhisattvas great or not?

Ānanda said to the Buddha, “It is very great, World-Honored One. “Good son, if there were another person who, with flowers and incense, made offerings to even a single four-line verse from this sutra, and furthermore made offerings to those who read and recite it, the merit of this person would again [be greater].”
It surpasses what we two have accomplished; how much more so for one who practices and recites throughout their entire life!
The merit of such a person is beyond measure. As stated in the sutras regarding worlds that are inverted or worlds that are upright, these are merely comparisons of their relative excellence.

*Piṇḍapāta* (often transliterated as *fēnwèi*) is translated here as "alms-food" (*tuóduò*), because it refers to food falling into the alms bowl. It is also called *fēnwèi*, meaning "begging for food.
Alternatively, it is said that one begs for food and distributes it to the monks and nuns, protecting them so that they may cultivate their spiritual practice.
Therefore, it is said that *piṇḍapāta* (alms-gathering) is the Sanskrit term for this; these words are all applicable [to the mind].
In that specific passage, it merely posits four propositions as the cause:
"Is the mind caused by the mind? Is the mind not caused by the mind? Is the mind both caused and not caused by the mind?"

Therefore, the mind is neither a non-cause nor a non-non-cause of the mind. Furthermore, regarding the previous phrase, the character "zhāng" (chapter) in the statement "the initial opening of the chapter speaks of both manifesting and remaining silent" is an error; it should be the character "zhē" (to obstruct/preclude).
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 28, on the Lion’s Roar Dharma Gate:
Like a lion king born of a pure lineage, dwelling in deep mountains and vast valleys,
with square jaws, large bones, a body full of flesh, a large head, long eyes that are lustrous and clear, high and broad brows, and sharp, white fangs.
With a pure mouth and nose, large, thick, solid, and full jaws, teeth that are dense, even, sharp, and white, a tongue that is red and long,
ears that are high and well-placed, glossy and lustrous hair, a broad upper body with firm flesh, a long spine and slender waist,
a non-protruding belly, a long tail and sharp claws, and feet firmly planted upon the ground— he emerged from his dwelling place by the great power of his body.
Stretching its neck and yawning, it strikes the ground with its mouth, manifesting great majestic power;

not missing the proper time for its meal, it displays the signs of early morning, expressing the strength of the Lion King to intimidate the deer, bears, brown bears, tigers, leopards, wild boars, and their like;
awakening those who have long been asleep, it subdues those who are haughty, powerful, and influential, clearing a path for itself while letting out a great roar.
When he roars in this manner, those who hear it are either filled with joy or struck with fear: those dwelling in holes hide and shrink away; those living in water dive deep;
those hidden in the mountains remain concealed; the elephants in the stables shake their chains and flee wildly;
and the birds in the sky fly high and far away. The Lion’s Roar of the Buddha is likewise: from the ancient [practice] of the six *pāramitās*...
Born into the great lineage of the four noble lineages, dwelling in the deep and precipitous valley of meditative concentration within the great mountain of nirvāṇa,
possessing the head of all-knowledge, with the cheeks of accumulated roots of goodness, the eyes of untainted right view, the luster of cultivated insight,
the high and broad eyebrows of meditative concentration and wisdom, the white and sharp tusks of the four fearlessnesses, and the mouth fully endowed with the analytical knowledges and liberations.
His four right efforts are firm and full; his thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are like even teeth; he cultivates the meditation on impurity and extends his tongue to lick his ears;
his eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are lofty and supreme; his hair and body-hair are lustrous, bright, and white;
his upper body is firm and well-set; his three manifestations are clear; his spine is straight and upright; and his abdomen does not protrude.

With patience as his waist and slender [discipline], he possesses the long tail of secluded practice; established in the four bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*), he has the five faculties (*indriya*) of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*);
his claws are sharp, and he possesses the force of the ten powers (*bala*). He is fully endowed with immeasurable, untainted (*anāsrava*) qualities and the equipment of all Buddhas.
He dwells in the abode of the kings of all Buddha-samādhis, issues forth the four unhindered knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), and stretches out upon the ground of all dharmas, remaining unimpeded.
Liberating beings through the ten powers and great majestic strength,
he does not fail to manifest the marks of the Dharma King at dawn for all the worlds, including devas and humans;
he awakens those among the various non-Buddhist teachers and their followers of false views who are slumbering within the Four Noble Truths, and subdues their attachment to the self.
Regarding the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*): they weaken the power of indolence and pride, open the way for those of other teachings, and provide a discourse on the path of various false views.
Those who practice erroneously feel fear; those who believe in the Right Path rejoice; the dull-witted are made sharp; disciples are comforted; and non-Buddhists are defeated.
When long-lived devas who have long enjoyed celestial pleasures realize impermanence, such sentient beings hear the Four Noble Truths.
The lion’s roar causes all to give rise to a mind of revulsion; because they give rise to a mind of revulsion, they attain detachment;
because they attain detachment, they enter nirvāṇa—this is called the lion’s roar among the assembly.
This is the twenty-seventh Dharma-gate of the Pāri Tree from the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra.

In the Heaven of the Thirty-three there is a Pārijātaka tree; its roots penetrate the earth to a depth of five yojanas, it rises a hundred yojanas high, and its branches and leaves spread fifty yojanas in all directions. When the leaves ripen, they turn yellow;
seeing this, the devas feel joy in their hearts, thinking, "These leaves will surely fall before long. Once the leaves have fallen, they again feel joy.
He rejoices at this branch, thinking: "In no long time it will surely change color. When the branch has changed color, he again gives rise to joy, thinking:
"This color will in no long time surely produce a bud. Having seen it, he again rejoices, thinking: "This bud will in no long time surely produce a calyx.
Having seen it, he again rejoices, thinking: "This calyx will in no long time surely open. At the time of its blossoming, its fragrance pervades everywhere.
Its radiance shines afar for fifty *yojanas* and extends for eighty *yojanas*.
At that time, when the gods dwell below and enjoy pleasures during the two months of summer, my disciples are likewise so.

The yellowing of the leaves is a metaphor for my disciples who contemplate leaving the household life; the falling of the leaves is a metaphor for my disciples who have first shaved their hair and beards.
The changing of color is a metaphor for my disciples receiving full ordination through the white-four-fold formal act (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*);

the initial swelling of the bud is a metaphor for my disciples generating the bodhicitta; the opening of the bud is a metaphor for the Bodhisattvas of the ten stages attaining the vision of the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*);
the full blossoming is a metaphor for the Bodhisattvas attaining *samyak-saṃbodhi*; and the fragrance is a metaphor for [the Dharma] throughout the ten directions.
The light of sentient beings upholding the prohibitive precepts is a metaphor for the Tathāgata’s name, which is unimpeded and pervades the ten directions.

The three months of summer are a metaphor for the three samādhis. The thirty-three devas experiencing joy is a metaphor for the Buddhas attaining the bliss of permanence and so forth within Great Nirvāṇa. The meaning of the "Elephant Body" Dharma-gate is extremely detailed.
Regarding the word "all" (*sarva*): that sutra states that the elephant has six tusks and seven limbs that touch the ground.

As for these "seven limbs," the *Nirgrantha Sutra* says that the Great Elephant Treasure has seven limbs by which it stands well-supported; namely, the four feet, the head, the trunk, and the tail—these constitute the seven limbs.
The *Uposatha-sūtra* (in the *Bén xíng jí jīng*) states: "Upasena" [means] "Supreme General" in the Sui language. The *Qǐng guān yīn jīng* states:
"In the great city of Rājagṛha, there was a bhikṣu named Upasena. It further states that these are seven-character verses.
The verse on the Protectors of the Dharma states: "I command Dhṛtarāṣṭra and the others to protect with a compassionate heart those who receive and uphold this sutra.
There are twenty-six lines of verse. It further states: "In the sutra, the initial entrustment to Upasena was his own request;
that is, Upasena asked: 'How does the eye, in conjunction with form, maintain its grasp, and so forth?'"
That which is fully contained in the *Bǎilù* (The Hundred Records) has already been requested from the *Bǎilù*;

furthermore, one should use a tooth-stick (*yángzhī*) and take mindfulness as the basis for sitting meditation, adding the recitation of sutras as the tenth item. Regarding the *Zhèngxíng yí* (The Ritual of Correct Practice), it was composed by Vinaya Master Nanshan in two fascicles;
currently, this text is missing from all collections of the Vinaya school. As for the *Xiūyúànhuà* (Cultivating the Illusory Transformation), it is a sutra.
It is said that [all things] are like illusions, transformations, echoes in a valley, and so forth.

In the *Zhiguan*, the phrase "like a plantain tree, a bubble, a dewdrop, lightning, and so forth" contains an error in the character for "hard" (*jian*); it should be the character for "tree" (*shu*). The sutra states:

"Like an echo in an empty valley, like a plantain tree," and continues, "even unto being like an illusion, a transformation, a dewdrop, and lightning. Furthermore, it may also be read as "like" (*ru*) [in all cases].
Regarding the heart pulse, the Sūtra states: "From the tip of the heart, forty channels descend;

one takes the central channel among them, causing the vital energy (prāṇa) to proceed peacefully through it for fourteen finger-widths (aṅgula). From the great channel, it emerges and reaches the tongue and its associated channels.
As for whether the path of the asuras exists or not, this is subsumed under the category of contentious debate within the Great Sūtra.

The eight cold and eight hot hells are as described in the fourth fascicle of the *Śāstraviniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī* (Shiqian), specifically in the seventh section. Each of the eight hot hells has sixteen minor hells as its retinue:

first, Sañjīva (Reviving); second, Kālasūtra (Black String); third, Saṃghāta (Crushing); fourth, Raurava (Wailing); fifth, Mahāraurava (Great Wailing); sixth, Tapana (Heating); seventh, Pratāpana (Extreme Heating); [eighth, Avīci (Unrelenting)].
The eight hot hells constitute the eight hot hell-realms: first, Arbuda; second, Nirarbuda;
third, Aṭaṭa; fourth, Hahava; fifth, Huhuva; sixth, Utpala; seventh, Padma; and eighth, Mahāpadma. These are the eight cold hells.

Regarding the phrase "one is born with human affairs, yet death is as yet unknown," it should be stated that this is "as yet unknown. This text originates from the *Analects*, but here I have merely extracted its essential meaning for use.
The *Zhi guan* (Cessation and Contemplation) says: "[He] slays all the bandits of the fetters (*saṃyojana*)."
"Kill" (殺) should be written as "kill" (殺).

The *Fuxing* (輔行) states: In the *Saptabuddha-mantra-sūtra*, it first clarifies that each of the seven Buddhas possesses a *dhāraṇī* and explains their merits as a method of repentance (*pratideśanā*).
First, that which was spoken by Vipaśyin Buddha: there are eighteen thousand illnesses, all of which are cured by a single mantra named *Suluduohe* (蘇盧都訶);
in the Sanskrit language, this is called *Niyata* (決定). Second, that which was spoken by Śikhin Buddha: the *dhāraṇī* is named *Husuduo* (胡蘇多);
this means "removing all oppressive heat and afflictions. Third, that which was spoken by Viśvabhū Buddha...
The name of the divine mantra spoken [by the first Buddha] is Mīṣadhu, which in this language means "Golden Drum.
The fourth, the Dharani spoken by Krakucchanda Buddha, is named "Vajra Banner. The fifth, the Dharani spoken by Kanakamuni Buddha, is named "Sound Resounding Throughout the Ten Directions.
The sixth, the divine mantra spoken by Kāśyapa Buddha, is named "Utmost Salvation of the Multitudes."
The divine mantra spoken by the Seventh Tathāgata, Śākyamuni, named "Golden Light Radiance," is as described in the sutra.
[This concludes the section on] the Thirty-five Buddhas.

In the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya-śāstra* (Fu-fa-zang), it is stated that after the grave offenses were extinguished, people called him the "Pure Vinaya Master.
The tradition records that the Venerable Śāṇakavāsin possessed great merit and was prophesied by the World-Honored One as the final Vinaya Master.
Once, while he was among the assembly, there was a bhikṣu whose sister-in-law came to the monastery carrying food to offer him; however, the fire of lust blazed up within him.
Sheng immediately engaged in sexual intercourse with her, thereby committing a grave transgression. Having done so, he immediately repented and reproached himself:
"I am a great fool to have committed such an evil deed. I am certainly no longer a śramaṇa or a son of the Śākyas.
I shall place my robes and bowl upon a three-pronged branch and wander everywhere, crying out in a loud voice: 'I am a sinner! I ought not to wear again the dyed robes of the Buddha-dharma.'"
"Since the transgression is grave, you will certainly enter hell; where can you find protection?
Then Śāṇakavāsin said to the bhikṣu, "If you can now follow my instructions, I shall cause your sin to be naturally extinguished.
The bhikṣu joyfully replied, "I accept your teaching. At that time, Śāṇakavāsin immediately manifested a transformation through his supernatural powers.
He prepared a fire pit with fiercely blazing flames and commanded the bhikṣu to throw himself into it.
At that time, for the sake of extinguishing his transgressions, the bhikṣu cast his entire body into the great fire pit. Immediately, the fierce flames transformed into something cool and refreshing;
they reached no higher than his knees and caused him no harm whatsoever. Then, Śāṇakavāsin said to the bhikṣu: "By you..."

With a virtuous mind, he issued a formal admonition and repented of all his transgressions, whereby all his sins were utterly destroyed. He then preached the Dharma for him, and [the listener] attained arhatship.
For this reason, the world universally called him the Vinaya Master Qingjing (Pure). In the *Yinyi* (Explanations of Words and Meanings), it is stated that the character "qi" (奇) is an error;
it should correctly be "qi" (歧), meaning "to divide. This distinction between the secular and the monastic has its basis in authoritative sources.

In the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, it is stated that for laypeople, the five precepts and eight precepts—when broken in their most serious form—are termed "borderline offenses" (*pārājika*).

However, if one has left the household life, such a person cannot receive the precepts at all. Now, as for the upāsaka, since it is said that he has already received the name [of the precepts], this does not obstruct his reception of them;
this is based on the Mahāyāna *Ākāśagarbha-sūtra* and is not according to the Hīnayāna. Thus, we know that the "borderline offense" is not unique [to the monastic code].
This refers to a bhikṣu who, having abandoned the precepts with the intent to receive them again, is called an "outsider beyond the shores of the Buddha-ocean.
As stated later in the text: "Although the Xiangbu school differs from this regarding internal matters, it is like the Nanshan school which possesses teachings upon which one can rely;
please reflect on this carefully. This is also a detailed account of the grave offense that results in the loss of the precepts, as found in the *Wenju Buzhu*.
Citing the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, the debate therein distinguishes between the loss of precepts through committing a grave offense (*pārājika*) and the non-loss of precepts.
Those who claim not to have abandoned [the precepts] actually mean that abandonment itself constitutes the loss; those who claim not to have lost them mean the opposite.
Furthermore, the preceding passage stating "that place is defiled" is likely an error; it should read "people are interspersed among them," rather than meaning "defiled."
It is called "mixed" (*miśra*). The *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* speaks of being "intermingled and interspersed"; does this not also imply impurity?

these are then applied across each of the seven bases, such as the first being sexual misconduct and the second being the bodily orifices.
"Three times seven is twenty-one; as for the precepts for men, excluding the urinary tract, there are only fourteen.

By using one’s own seven poisons to afflict others, one incurs fifty-six precepts; regarding the objects of the precepts on non-sentient things, one likewise incurs seven precepts for each.

If one understands that while the conjunction of mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) can perceive the various distinct functions of individual phenomena, there is definitively no sense of "conjoined perception" within that process, then it follows that the eye-faculty alone is designated as "capable of seeing. Regarding the Dharma I have seen, I further observe it myself and speak of the method of observation;

Furthermore, though I could run as fast as elephants, horses, or chariots, such is the conduct of this śramaṇa.
"I cannot catch up to you as you run so swiftly; this must surely be the Tathāgata. At that moment, Aṅgulimāla spoke these verses:

By means of these words of sincere truth, he caused the mother’s womb to be free from harm.
When Aṅgulimāla spoke thus to the woman according to the teaching, the woman’s womb was immediately liberated. At that time, the bhikṣus addressed the World-Honored One, saying, "Aṅgulimāla..."
"What meritorious deeds did he perform today to become so intelligent and handsome? What evil deeds did he commit today that his killing of living beings is beyond measure?
By what causes and conditions has he encountered the Buddha and attained the Way? The Buddha told the bhikṣu:
"After the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, there was a king named Mahāphala who had no sons. He prayed for male and female offspring."
At that time, the King’s consort gave birth to a son. Later, the King took a consort for the Crown Prince;
however, from then on, the Prince committed acts of lawlessness and indulged in debauchery with various women. Consequently, the people of the kingdom seized and killed the Prince.
As he was dying, the Prince made this vow: "May those who have killed me come to repay this grudge in the future. Furthermore—
Furthermore, he caused me to encounter a true person and swiftly attain liberation. At that time, the Great Fruit King was none other than Aṅgulimāla;
at that time, the prince was none other than Aṅgulimāla; and at that time, the people of the country were none other than those now being executed.
Because of his vow at that time to encounter a true person, he has now encountered the Buddha and attained realization.
From the stage of Arhat upward, I have extracted the essential meaning of those scriptures and requested that this text be used to correspondingly explain and resolve them;
furthermore, it serves to correct errors found in the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) regarding what it cites, while also making clear those points which were overly concise and difficult to discern.
Regarding Vasumitra (also known as Vasumitra),

By reason of this manifestation, one does not commit any transgression against the bodhisattva precepts and generates great merit;
that is to say, when a bodhisattva sees a robber or thief who, out of greed for wealth, intends to kill many beings,

When this matter arose, he reflected: "If I were to take the life of that evil person, I would fall into hell;

It would be better for me to kill him and fall into the *naraka* hells than to let him undergo the suffering of the karma of immediate retribution. Having thought thus, he felt profound shame and remorse, out of compassion.
If one intentionally takes another's life, by reason of these causes and conditions, there is no violation of the bodhisattva precepts, and much merit is generated.

Daoism is subsumed within the Nine Schools (*jiu liu*).

The first, Virtue (De), flows from the humility and reverence of the *Zhou Yi*; the three Yin and Yang energies flow in accordance with the heavenly calendar and its phenomena, reverently bestowing the seasons upon the people.

The stupas are magnificent and their construction brings about immense merit; yet these are truly insentient things—how could they possess benevolence or wisdom?
Fools, believing in them, exhaust their precious wealth in vain, leading only to waste. Therefore, they must be cleared away; all such scriptures and images shall be destroyed.
That parents’ kindness is profound, yet śramaṇas show them no respect, is a most extreme form of rebellion that the laws of the state cannot tolerate.
"I am withdrawing the household goods to honor filial piety; this is my intention. What do the assembly of monks think?
At that time, Dharma Master Huiyuan stepped forward from the crowd and declared, "That the true Buddha has no image is indeed as Your Majesty’s decree suggests.

However, living beings who possess ears and eyes rely on the scriptures to hear of the Buddha and depend upon images to manifest the Truth. If these are now abolished, there will be no means by which reverence can be inspired."

The Emperor said, "If the True Buddha of empty space is known by all within themselves, why did living beings not know of this True Buddha of empty space before the time of Emperor Ming of the Han, when scriptures and images had not yet reached this land?
He was unable to answer. Daoyuan again asserted, "If one could know the Dharma within oneself without relying on the scriptural teachings, then the Three Sovereigns—"
"Before the advent of written characters, people should have naturally known the Five Constant Virtues and other such laws.
Why then did the people of that time merely recognize their mothers and fail to know their fathers, being no different from birds and beasts? The Emperor again gave no answer.
Huiyuan further argued, "If you claim that because images are insentient, serving them brings no merit and they must therefore be abolished, then what of the seven ancestral temples of the state?"
"How could such an image be a sentient being? Why do you falsely revere it? The Emperor did not answer this objection, but instead said:
"The Buddhist scriptures are the laws of foreign lands; since they are not required in this land, I have abolished them.

Regarding the Seven Ancestral Temples established by previous dynasties, I also do not consider them correct and intend to abolish them as well. Yuan said: "If you consider the laws of foreign lands to be improper..."

That which is employed in this land was spoken by Zhongni and originated from the state of Lu; since Qin and Jin were also lands [of the same tradition], they too should have been abolished and not put into practice.
Furthermore, to regard the Seven Temples as improper and intend to abolish them is to fail to honor one's ancestors.
If the ancestors are not honored, the order of the *zhao* and *mu* lineages will be lost. If the order of the *zhao* and *mu* lineages is lost, then the Five Classics will become useless.
"If Confucianism existed previously, where are its teachings now? If that were so, then the Three Teachings would all be abolished; how then could one govern the state?
The Emperor said, "The territories of the states of Lu, Qin, and Jin were indeed distinct, yet they were all under the single transformation of the Son of Heaven;

therefore, they are not comparable to the Buddhist scriptures. Regarding the difficulty concerning the Seven Temples, the Emperor was unable to answer. Yuan said, "If one considers Qin and Lu to be the same..."

Regarding those who follow the teachings of the One Transformation and practice them: although the borders of China and India differ, they are both equally situated within the four seas of Jambudvīpa.
How could the rule of a Wheel-Turning King not be the same? [If you] do not follow the Buddhist scriptures, why allow them alone to be abolished?
Furthermore, the Emperor gave no reply to Huiyuan, who said: "To withdraw monks from the monasteries and return them to their homes to exalt filial piety is the way of Confucius."
The Sūtra also says: "To establish oneself and practice the Way so as to bring honor to one's parents is itself the act of filial piety;

why must one return home? The Emperor said: "The kindness of parents is profound; they provide for one another and nourish each other with physical care. To abandon one's kin for those who are distant does not constitute ultimate filial piety.
Yuan said: "If it were as you say, then Your Majesty has both parents at your side; why do you not release them?"
"Suppose a man were conscripted for long-term service for five years and did not see his parents. The Emperor said, "I too follow the rotation of shifts to return home and serve them.
Yuan said, "The Buddha also permitted monks to cultivate the Way according to circumstances during winter and summer, and to return home to attend to their parents' needs during spring and autumn.
Thus, Maudgalyāyana begged for food to send to his mother, and the Tathāgata carried her coffin to the burial site. This principle is universally applicable; has it not?"
The deposed Emperor could not provide an answer, so Yuan [Zao] spoke out defiantly: "Your Majesty now relies on the power of the Prince to willfully destroy the Three Jewels;
you are a person of false views destined for the Avīci Hell, where neither noble nor base are spared. How can Your Majesty not be afraid?
The Emperor turned a look of great rage upon Yuan and stared directly at him, saying: "I only require that the common people obtain..."
"I find no pleasure in this," [Hui]zheng replied, "nor would I decline the sufferings of hell. You, Your Majesty, transform people through heterodox teachings;

you have currently planted the karma for suffering. When you must enter Avīci Hell together with me, what joy could there be? The Emperor’s arguments were exhausted, and he had nothing further to say in response;
he merely said, "Let the assembly of monks withdraw for now," and the officials recorded the names and surnames of the disputing monks.

The Emperor had already carried out atrocities in Guanzhong, where the Buddha-dharma was almost entirely eradicated. Upon conquering the territory of Qi, he returned and sought only to destroy it further.

A former monk named Rendao Lin submitted a memorial requesting that the Buddha-dharma be permitted, stating that the so-called "eastern tour" was actually a tour of Ye (the capital of Qi) for the purpose of conquering Qi and eliminating the precious Dharma.
Less than a year after the destruction and extinction of the Buddha-dharma, a pestilence broke out.
As his internal qi festered and his physical sores broke out externally, his evil signs became manifest; there was no repentance that could be pursued, and he subsequently passed away.
When Emperor Wendi ascended the throne, the former monk Wang Mingguang wrote a letter titled "A Response to Wei Yuansong’s 'On Refuting the Buddha-Dharma,'" which elucidated the Buddha-dharma;
it is fully contained in the *Nanshan Guanghongming Ji*. There is no need to trouble oneself by recording it here at this late stage of the Liang dynasty.
Regarding the Eastern Capital (Dōtōjō), the *Hongming ji* states that at the end of the Liang dynasty, [Emperor] Xue [Chà] became a monk.
He was the grandson of Emperor Wu and the son of Crown Prince Zhāomíng; he ascended the throne and used the reign title Dàdìng. [Emperor] Kuǐ was Chà’s son;
he succeeded to the throne and used the reign title Tiānbão, remaining on the throne for twenty-three years. The reign title of Northern Qi Wénxuān Emperor was also [Tiānbão].

The reign was titled Tenpō (Tenpō), lasting only ten years before the Emperor passed away. Upon the initial accession of Emperor Wu of the Northern Zhou, he established the era name *Hōtei* (Bǎodìng);

in the fifth year, it was changed to *Tennō* (Tiāntuó). In the eighth month of the third year of this era, he convened civil and military officials, as well as monks and Daoists, at the Daidō-den (Dàdé Diàn) to personally lecture on the *Líjì* (Book of Rites).
In the second month of the fourth year, he assembled the various officials, monks, and Daoists to discuss the teachings of Śākyamuni and Laozi.
In the first month of the first year of Jiande, the Emperor visited Lidu Monastery to lecture on the affairs of debate between officials and monastics, as well as laypeople and clergy.

In the twelfth month of the second year, he assembled the hundred officials, monks, and Daoists to deliberate on the sequence of the Three Teachings, establishing Confucianism as first, Daoism as second, and Buddhism as last.
In the fifth month of the third year, he abolished the two teachings of Buddhism and Daoism; however, in the sixth month, he subsequently established Tongdao Monastery.
In the fourth year of Daoguan, he launched a campaign against Qi; in the fifth and sixth years, he conquered Qi and changed the era name to Xuanzheng.

In the sixth month of the first year of Xuanzheng, the Emperor passed away at the age of thirty-six. The Crown Prince ascended the throne, changed the era name to Daxiang, and subsequently to Dacheng.
He soon transferred the throne to his son and styled himself the Heavenly Sovereign (Tianyuan Huangdi). In the tenth month, he restored the dual honors of both Buddhism and Daoism.
In the sixth month of the second year of the Xiangzhi Jingdi era, the two teachings of Buddhism and Daoism were restored.

Regarding the statement that "the Five Classics" refers to the five divisions of the Vinaya: among the fifteen matters listed above, according to the *Hongming ji*, there are seventeen matters, namely:

exhorting the practice of equality; exhorting those who are not equal to achieve equality; exhorting the practice of the Mahāyāna; exhorting mindfulness of the poor and destitute; and exhorting the relinquishing of stinginess and greed.

Exhorting others to confess their transgressions; exhorting the benefit of the people; exhorting officials to serve the people; exhorting harmony among men; exhorting that greed for love be the cause [of compassion];

exhorting the establishment of market profits; exhorting the practice of respectful support; exhorting the establishment of the Three Piṭakas free from greed; exhorting the establishment of the Three Piṭakas in small measure;
exhorting that there be no soldiers in monasteries; exhorting the Sangha to instruct the Sangha; exhorting respect for the Mahāyāna; truly the Secretariat of the Great Tang.
The Director Yu Shinan once composed the *Brief Discourse on Emperors and Kings*, in which he wrote: The Prince said:

"If one considers the martial talent and military skill of King Wu of Zhou, who led his troops with personal example—if Heaven had granted him more years so that he could fully exhaust his strategic calculations, would he not have been able to unify the realm and become a sagacious sovereign of an era? The Master replied: "King Wu was indeed valiant, courageous, and resolute."

He possesses the strategic talent that surpasses ordinary men; observing his humble demeanor and encouragement of the officers, as well as the strictness and clarity of his laws and decrees, even Goujian and Rangji could not have excelled him.
However, while his plans for conquest and seizure are renowned throughout the realm, his virtue of benevolence and wisdom is unheard of in the world.
This is the extraordinary talent of a fierce general, not the capacity of a sovereign ruler.
The young master said, "Is it right or wrong to destroy these two teachings? The Master replied, "It is not. The young master said, "I beg to hear the explanation.
The Master said, "The Dharma of the Śākya clan is a discourse beyond forms; it is empty and non-existent, free from stagnation, and forgets both self and others.
It transcends birth and death and returns to quiescent extinction. As for the meaning of Laozi—"

Thus, the teachings of "the valley-spirit does not die" and "the mysterious female organ endures forever," leading to longevity and long vision, with the soaring dragon and riding crane, belong to the doctrines of this world.

As for the cessation of evil, the exaltation of benevolence, the overcoming of cruelty, and the removal of killing—these are all beneficial to the transformation of the state and do not conflict with secular canons.

Now, if one were to claim that these constitute the teachings [of Buddhism] simply because the monastic community violates the Vinaya and the Daoist practitioners transgress the scriptures, [it would be a grave error].
One may discard such words and sever ties with them; how is this different from blaming the pestle for resisting and thus discarding Yao, or resenting the Miao tribes and deposing Yu?

To see the waters of the Hulu overflow and seek to block the source at the distant Yellow River, or to behold the Kunlun Mountains glowing in the sun and suddenly cast down a metal mirror—such a person fails to realize that the virtue of moisture flowing downward brings profound benefit, nor do they understand that the function of transforming raw flesh is of great merit.
To view the vast ocean from the perspective of a frog is to be restricted by what one sees; the delusions of the long night of saṃsāra lead one to self-inflicted suffering through drowning.
It is truly lamentable that scholars have been so misled. The third emperor of the Later Wei, whose name was Tàowù, ascended the throne and changed the era name to Shìguāng.
He issued an edict to pit all śramaṇas in the various provinces, destroy the Buddhist teachings, and dispatched generals to carry out these tasks.
After the official had burned and plundered the monasteries, there was a monk known as Baitu (White-Foot) who stood at the palace gate with his mendicant’s staff.

The Emperor was greatly enraged and ordered him to be executed; yet though he was repeatedly beheaded, the head would not separate from the body. The Emperor then invited him up to the hall, prostrated himself before him, and repented his transgressions—this being different from the case of Emperor Wu of the Zhou dynasty.
Nevertheless, the Emperor also suffered from a severe illness and passed away, until Emperor Wencheng restored the Buddhist faith once again.
Emperor Wuzong of the Great Tang, named Yan, was the fifth son of Emperor Muzong. At the age of twenty-seven, he ascended the throne and changed the era name to Huichang.

He reigned for six years and was posthumously titled Zhaosusheng. Initially, while still a prince in the provinces, Wuzong had taken a keen interest in Daoist arts and practices of spiritual cultivation;
in the ninth month of autumn in the year of his accession, he summoned the Daoist Zhao Guizhen.
Eighty-one persons, including these, entered the inner palace where the Emperor personally received the dharma registers (*dharmaloka*).

On the right, She Yiwang Zhe submitted a memorial stating that at the commencement of a royal enterprise, it is inappropriate to accord excessive devotion to such matters; the memorial was presented but not examined.

In the sixth month, Liu Xuanjing, a Daoist priest of Mount Heng, was appointed as Silver Light Commandery Duke and Left Assistant in the Palace Library, while Liu Yan was appointed as Left Assistant in the Palace Library.
Yang Yanmo submitted a memorial offering earnest admonition, but it was not accepted; consequently, Yanmo was demoted to the post of *Hùcáo* (Accountant) in the Henan Commandery.
In the third month of the fourth year, the Emperor appointed the Daoist Zhao Guizhen as the *Xiàodào Mén Jiàoshòu Xiānshēng* (Professor of the Left and Right Daoist Gates).

At that time, the Emperor was intent on studying at Mount Shen and served Guizhen as his teacher; taking advantage of his favor, Guizhen frequently spoke in opposition to the Buddhist teachings before the Emperor.
In the fifth year of the Pō-xìn era, during the first month of the spring, an imperial edict was issued to construct the Wàngxián Terrace at the Southern Suburban Altar.
At that time, Zhào Guīzhēn was receiving exceptional favor and courtesy from the Emperor; consequently, when an official of the Censorate submitted a memorial criticizing this, it was not accepted.
Zhào Guīzhēn then became closely allied with the Róufó Mountain Daoist Dèng Yuǎnqǐ and others to slander and destroy Buddhism, and his petition to demolish monasteries was carried out. (4)
In the seventh month, a census was conducted throughout the empire to inventory all monasteries and the number of monks and nuns;

subsequently, monasteries were consolidated, with only one monastery remaining in each prefecture, two monasteries remaining in each ward of the Upper and Lower Capitals, and thirty monks retained at each.
The salt and iron commissioners were entrusted with the disposal of the copper statues and other materials from the abolished monasteries throughout the empire.
Cast iron images and the like shall be melted down to produce agricultural implements; gold and silver images and the like shall be smelted and delivered to the Department of Revenue (Du-zhi).
All gold and silver images possessed by the families of officials and commoners must be surrendered to the Palace within one month after the issuance of this edict.
Those who fail to comply shall be dealt with according to the laws prohibiting the use of copper. Furthermore, the number of monasteries demolished throughout the empire totals four thousand.
Of the more than six hundred monasteries, those who returned to lay life among the monks and nuns numbered approximately twenty-six thousand and five hundred.

In the third month of the sixth year, the Emperor’s consumption of medicinal elixirs caused him to become agitated and his moods to deviate from the norm; as his illness grew critical, he was unable to speak within ten days.
When the chief ministers requested an audience, he did not grant it, and neither the court nor the common people knew whether he was well or ill. Public sentiment...
He died in fear and anxiety on the twenty-third day of that month at the age of thirty-three. The court historian says:
It was evident that Xiao Yan and Yao Xing were merely deluded by false learning; they failed to realize that the First Emperor of Qin and Emperor Wu of Han had not truly sought the Way.

Consequently, they became entangled in the words of heterodox paths and one-sidedly rejected the teachings of foreign lands. How much more so when the teaching that came from India in the west was about to...

For a thousand years, the people have been steeped in these practices until they became their established custom; they revere its teachings more than state law and delight in its followers no differently than those who have attained immortality.
How could one suddenly destroy and incinerate them? To do so would breed resentment among those who prostrate themselves and provoke the anger of the common folk.
The actions of a wise monarch do not startle the sentiments of the people; as such, these [practices] were preserved by previous dynasties.
In truth, this was indeed the Middle Way. Emperor Xuanzong, whose personal name was Chen, was the thirteenth son of Emperor Xianzong;
he ascended the throne in the third month of the sixth year of Huichang at the age of thirty-seven. He changed the era name to Dazhong.

In the fifth month, by imperial decree, eight additional Buddhist temples were established in each of the Left and Right Quarters (the capital’s monastic districts), and the Daoist Liu Xuan was subsequently executed.
This was because the twelve individuals, including Jing, had deluded Emperor Wuzong with heterodox and deviant teachings, leading him to abolish and destroy the Buddhist religion.
Consequently, an imperial edict was issued at the end of his reign to consolidate and reduce the number of monasteries.

Although it was claimed that the teachings of foreign lands do not detract from the source of governance, the people of the Middle Kingdom have long practiced these ways; therefore, this excessive reform was deemed an error that ought to be rectified.

As for those monasteries at sacred mountains and auspicious sites throughout the various provinces and prefectures that were abolished during the Yingshanchang era of the fifth year [of the reign], if there are veteran and renowned monks who are able to restore and rebuild them, they shall be permitted to reside and maintain them as their own; no prohibitions shall be imposed.
The Emperor has always held Confucian scholars in high esteem and devoted his attention to the imperial examinations; at times, he would travel incognito among the people to seek out talent.

He listened to public opinion to observe the success or failure of his selection of officials; whenever he faced his ministers and subordinates, he was solemn and respectful, seldom uttering casual words.
When a high official presented a memorial, he would burn incense and examine it with his own hands.
At that time, the administration of the Great Middle Way possessed the spirit of the Zhenguan era. For over ten years, there were voices of praise.
His imperial way and sovereign strategy were carried forward, remaining flawless from beginning to end; even the Wen and Jing emperors of the Han could not surpass him.
He was posthumously titled Emperor Shengwu Xianwen, and his temple name was Xuanzong. The court historian’s eulogy states: "Among the eminent rulers of the late period, none was truly like Xianwen.
He discarded the chaff and retained the grain, distinguishing the virtuous from the hidden; Hexi and Longyou returned to his domain, and the northern tribes submitted to the Han."
The miasma has been dispelled, and even today the elderly sing in praise of the enlightened ruler. Let us now examine this:
Emperor Wuzong claimed that Buddhism was a parasite that wasted the national resources, subverted the law, and harmed the people; he therefore proceeded to abolish and destroy it.

Yet within half a year, he fell gravely ill and died a sudden death—what benefit did this bring to the people, and what advantage did it provide to the state? Emperor Xuanzong then restored the Shengshou Monastery.
Having filled fifty years on the throne, the Emperor’s Way and Imperial Virtue remained flawless from beginning to end;
was this not because Buddhism brings benefit to the state and profit to the people?

Thus we know that the Buddha’s teaching and its most divine transformations, though meeting with destruction three times, thrived all the more each time—were it not for the spiritual penetration of a Great Sage, who could have achieved such a thing?
In the first month of the fourteenth year of the Yuanhe era of Emperor Xuanzong, at Famen Temple in Fengxiang, there was a "National Protection" True Body Stūpa.
Inside the stūpa was a single joint of a finger bone of Śākyamuni Buddha.

The Emperor ordered the Palace Messenger Du Yingqi to lead thirty palace women, bearing incense and flowers, to welcome it into the Great Inner Quarters; it remained within the Forbidden City for three days.
The Emperor then sent [the image] to various monasteries, where princes, dukes, officials, and commoners rushed to offer donations, fearing only that they might be left behind.
When Han Yu served as the Vice Minister of the Ministry of Justice, he submitted a memorial to remonstrate against this;

in that memorial, he stated that Buddhism is the law of the barbarians and further argued that in ancient times, when the Yellow Emperor occupied the throne for one hundred years, he lived to the age of one hundred and ten.
King Mu of Zhou reigned for one hundred years; during his time, the Buddha-dharma did not yet exist.
It was only from the era of Emperor Ming of the Later Han that the Buddha-dharma first appeared, yet Emperor Ming reigned for only eighteen years.

From the Song, Qi, Liang, and Chen dynasties, through the Northern Wei and subsequent periods, the practice of worshipping the Buddha gradually became more earnest, yet the duration of these reigns was even shorter. Only Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty reigned for forty-eight years.
One year later, he was forced by Hou Jing and died of starvation as his state was destroyed.

Furthermore, it was said that the Buddha does not wear the ritual robes of the former kings, nor does he speak the ritual words of the former kings; it was also said that the Buddha does not know the way of sovereign and subject, or father and son;
furthermore, it was said that the Buddha’s bones were withered and decayed, foul and impure, and that they should be consigned to water and fire to forever sever their root; it was also said—

"If the Buddha possesses spiritual power, may whatever calamities or blessings befall my person. Upon this memorial, Emperor Xianzong was greatly incensed and intended to inflict the ultimate punishment.
Pei Du and Cui [Yuan] submitted a memorial, saying: "Han Yu has offended Your Majesty’s ears; he truly deserves punishment.
We humbly beg that you grant him some leniency in order to encourage those who offer remonstrance. The Emperor replied: "Yu says that I worship the Buddha too much..."

Even those who have transgressed against me, I still grant them my forbearance; yet to claim that since the Eastern Han dynasty’s embrace of Buddhism, all emperors have met with premature deaths—how contradictory such a statement is!
As a subject, I, Yu, dare to be so audacious and reckless, and truly cannot be pardoned.
At that time, public sentiment was filled with alarm and regret, even such that the imperial kinsmen and various nobles considered my punishment too severe.
When the matter was discussed, he was demoted to the post of Prefect of Chaozhou. Upon arriving in Chaozhou, Han Yu submitted a memorial of thanks, stating:
"Your servant, through deceit and delusion, and lacking knowledge of ritual propriety, submitted a memorial regarding the Buddhist bone relic; my words were irreverent.

To rectify my name and punish me according to the law, ten thousand deaths would be but a light penalty. Yet Your Majesty, moved by compassion, considered that while my words may be blameworthy, my heart—"

Furthermore, there is no other reason why you have specially exercised your judicial authority to appoint me as the Prefect of Chaozhou; your imperial grace is so vast that even heaven and earth cannot measure it.
Even if one were to split open one’s brain and gouge out one’s heart, how could this suffice as a token of gratitude? I, Yu, am truly prostrate with fear and awe, bowing my head repeatedly.
I shall exhaust my thoughts and refine my efforts to atone for my transgressions, harboring my grief until the ends of heaven, even unto death.
With eyes closed in humble contemplation, I pray that Your Majesty, the Emperor, will take pity on me. Upon receiving this memorial, Emperor Xianzong said to his ministers:
"Yesterday I received the memorial from Han Yu; thinking back on his remonstrance regarding the Buddha’s relics, I realize he truly loves me.
How could I not know this? Nevertheless, as a subject, it was improper for Han Yu to speak thus of the Sovereign—that my service to the Buddha has shortened my years."
Because I detested this ease with which he sought to employ Han Yu again, I first spoke of it;

observing the responses of the ministers, Huangfu Bo replied that Han Yu was ultimately too wild and reckless, and suggested he be transferred to a prefectural post, whereupon he was appointed as the Prefect of Biaozhou.
Now, let us examine this: Han Yu claimed that emperors who venerated Buddhism...
Your life is short, yet Emperor Xianzong has already rebuked you; now he further interrogates you, saying: "Before the Three Dynasties, there was not only no Buddhism, but also no Laozi or Confucius.
After Emperor Ming of the Han, it was not only that the Buddhist Dharma came from the West, but also that the teachings of Confucianism and Laozi existed.
How can you claim that there was no Buddha before the Three Dynasties and that [the state] lacked [these teachings]?"
If the lifespan of those who lived after Emperor Ming of the Yonghan era was short despite the presence of the Buddha, then the karmic retribution for holding such a false view is not light.
Furthermore, Mūkarāśi said, "If the Buddha possesses spiritual power, his blessings and calamities should be visited upon my person. Yet, the Buddha has long since forgotten both love and hatred;

how could he inflict blessings or calamities upon beings? It is simply that people invite loss or benefit for themselves through their own acts of disparagement or praise. Since Mūkarāśi thus disparaged [the Buddha]...
When the Buddha was about to suffer the ultimate punishment and was demoted to the post of Prefect of Chaozhou, was this not a calamity that befell his own person?
Upon arriving in Chaozhou, he submitted a memorial to express his gratitude and repent for his transgressions, whereupon he was appointed as the Prefect of that very state;
was this not a blessing that befell his own person? The court historian remarked that although Han Yu disparaged Buddhism, his Way did not flourish widely—truly a well-founded statement. Han...

Furthermore, regarding Mochou’s claim that Buddhism is the law of the barbarians (*yidi*), this is exactly as refuted in the *Xuanqian Buzhu* (Supplementary Notes on the Profound Signpost) and in the supplementary notes below;
it is established that the Buddha was from Central India and that Buddhism is not the law of the barbarians.

Han Yu was arrogant and failed to distinguish between regions, mistakenly claiming it was a barbarian law—just as he is rebuked in treatises such as the *Poxie Bianzheng Lun* (Treatise on Refuting Heresy and Distinguishing Orthodoxy).
Yu further claimed that the Buddha does not wear the ritual robes of the former kings, does not speak the words of the former kings, and does not know the way of ruler and subject or father and son;

this too is an extreme form of delusion. It arises from never having read the Buddhist teachings and failing to comprehend the principles of birth and death—a disparagement of the Great Sage, the Dharma King, as exemplified by Xiao Yu, whom one might call a denizen of the Avīci Hell.
The prisons were established precisely for such people; how could this be mere empty talk?

Han Yu further claimed that the Buddha’s bones were withered and decayed, and requested they be consigned to fire and water to sever their root forever. Yet, how could these withered and decayed bones have remained until now without perishing?
The three sagely Emperors of the Sacred Song—Taizong, Zhenzong, and Renzong—composed verses, hymns, and praises concerning Śākyamuni.
How could water or fire ever sever the root of the Buddha’s tooth? This petty official Han Yu harbors such perverse views and reckless arrogance as to reach this extreme—how tragic, how tragic!
As for *chenghuang* (city walls and moats): where there is water, it is called a *chi* (moat);

where there is no water, it is called a *huang* (ditch). As for the *liuhe* (six directions): these are the four cardinal points together with heaven and earth. Zhuangzi spoke of that which lies beyond the six directions.
The Sage preserves [the Way] but does not discuss it; within the six directions of the universe, one discusses but does not debate. "Kǎn kě" (kǎn-kě) means many misfortunes and difficulties.
"Pín" (pín)—in the *Zhuāngzǐ* text, the pronunciation is given as "bǐn" (bǐn); the commentary states it means to knit the brows.

Nowadays, the character "pín" (pín) is more commonly used; "pín méi" (knitting the brows) means to frown. "Shēn" (shēn) means to sigh or chant. Xīshī was a beautiful woman of Yùe. She had already suffered from heart disease.
When she frowned in pain, her facial features were so upright and beautiful that even while frowning she became more lovely;

though others may imitate her, how could they equal the beauty of Xi Shi’s frown? *Maoqiang*—the character *qiang* being pronounced as *liáng*—was a beauty of antiquity, namely the favorite consort of the King of Yue.
*Lijī*—the character *lì* being pronounced as *zhì*—was the wife of Duke Xian of Jin. (Zhuangzi)
In the "Qi Wu" chapter, it says this: "The neighbor's daughter was an ugly woman.
Indeed, all the texts from the Three Sovereigns downward are the authentic text of Zhuangzi, not the words of a commentary. These characters appear in the "Tian Yun" chapter of the *Zhuangzi*.
*Zhā* (柤): pronounced *zéjiā* (側加切). *Jú* (橘): pronounced *jūyù* (居聿切). *Chōu* (柚): pronounced *chōuyóu* (抽余救切). The tastes of these four fruits—sweetness and bitterness—are as follows.
Yì (異): To chew; the phonetic components are *mò* (沒) and *xià* (下). Jiè (齧): To bite; the phonetic component is *jiǎo* (狡). The correct form is *yǎo* (齩). Wǎn (挽): To pull;
the phonetic component is *yuǎn* (遠). Yuán (猿): The sound is *yuán*. Jū (狙): The phonetic component is *shí* (十) and *yú* (余). Yī (衣): The phonetic component is *yú* (於) and *jì* (既).

This means that regarding evil, he has realized the truly wondrous Path; this is a great falsehood called "claiming superhuman qualities" (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*), for although he has not actually realized it, he says he has realized it himself.

Among the evils, one attains the wondrous Path through two *pārājikas*. Furthermore, if one speaks with the mouth that "sexual misconduct does not obstruct the Path," and after being exhorted by means of a formal motion followed by three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*), does not comply, one commits a *pāyattika*. This is called two *pārājikas* and one *pāyattika*.
If one only personally engages in sexual desire or instructs another to engage in it, but the other has not yet acted, then it is one [offense].

If one commits sexual misconduct oneself, it constitutes one *pārājika* and one *sthūlātyaya*. Now, since this refers to instructing another who has not yet committed the act, it is merely called a *duṣkṛta*.
There is a version of the text which claims that if one instructs another to commit the act, it constitutes one *pārājika* and one *pāyattika*, but this is an error;

The Vinaya states: If monks and nuns instruct one another to perform [an offense], the instructor commits a *sthūlātyaya*; if they do not perform it, they commit a *duṣkṛta*.

For the three lower groups of disciples, whether they instruct one another to perform or not to perform [the act], they all commit a *duṣkṛta*. If they actually perform it, they are subject to *parivāsa* (exclusion), with the exception of the *duṣkṛta* for those in the lower sections of the code, where they likewise commit a *duṣkṛta*.

The ancients did not establish "perfect purity" (yuanjing) as a distinct category, instead treating it as a provisional means (*upāya*) in relation to the *saṃbhogakāya*. Regarding various texts that critique this, the *Miaoxuan* states:

"The followers of the *Dilun* school say that there is only 'intrinsic purity' (*xingjing*) and 'provisional purity' (*fangbianjing*). That which is called the 'Nirvana of intrinsic reality' (*shixiang*) is named intrinsic purity Nirvana;
that which is accomplished through the cultivation of causes is named provisional purity Nirvana. Now, we take the principle of nature (*lixing*) as intrinsic purity."
That which is accomplished through the cultivation of causes is the "perfectly pure nirvāṇa" (pariśuddha-nirvāṇa); this is the logical sense (*artha*).
That which is like the extinction of fire when the fuel is exhausted is the "conventionally pure nirvāṇa" (upāya-śuddha-nirvāṇa); this is the literal phrasing (*vyañjana*).

"To the south of the Snow Mountains, extending three sides toward the sea in a circular perimeter of ninety thousand [yojanas], its name is Great Xia (Mahācīna); this is Vajra."
The "Wheel" (Cakra) is the center of the earth where ordinary beings, sages, and great kings dwell together. If one dwells in a remote borderland, the earth tilts toward it;
thus, while the Great Xia (Bactria) has its back to the mountains and faces the sea, the Divine Land (China) lies to the southeast of Mount Kunlun.

According to the interpretations of Wang Shao and others, this region is the land where the Yellow Emperor traveled spiritually to Huaxu—that is, the kingdom of Great Xia. If one points specifically to the Great [Xia]...
It may be acceptable to refer to China as "Shenzhou" (the Divine Land) during the Xia dynasty, for it was there that the Wheel-Turning Kings and Sage Emperors resided throughout the ages;
thus, its designation as Shenzhou cannot be equated with that of this region [India].
As Mencius said, "Shun was a man of the Eastern Barbarians, and King Wen was a man of the Western Barbarians"—how could one judge a person merely by their origin?

If [Confucius] originated from the Yi tribes yet did not employ their ways, how much more so for the Buddha, whose origin was fundamentally not that of a Yi state—how can you falsely claim that the Buddha was a Yi?
Li Zhongqing’s *Four Anomalies* states: "Laojun was the ancestral teacher of the flourishing Zhou dynasty during the time of King Wen;
Śākyamuni was the master of Jibin during the time of King Zhuang. This is the Dharma of Lin.
The Master offers four analogies, saying: "As in the records cited above, we shall now further challenge this point.
Laozi was born on the fifteenth day of the second month in the twelfth year of the Dingmao cycle during the reign of King Ding of the Zhou dynasty;

since it was not the time of King Wen, how can you recklessly point to him [as his successor]? Li Zhongqing’s *Five Anomalies* states: "The Lord Lao manifested his traces during the era of the Zhou kings and remained hidden three times."

Third, it clarifies that more than five hundred years ago, when Śākyamuni was due to be born in a Hu (barbarian) country, one [Buddha] would perish and another be born, with a lifespan of only eighty years.
Master Lin’s Five Similes states: "As cited in the records, we shall now further challenge this:
the Buddha was born in Central India, which is certainly not a Hu country; Hu is originally a region of mixed barbarians, whereas Vārāṇasī is the capital of the truly holy. How could this be?

It is erroneous to claim that [the Master] was born in the land of the Hu; upon examining various historical records, orthodox canons, and other texts, there is no mention of his appearing or disappearing through three periods of concealment and manifestation.

Only figures such as Zang Jing and various Confucian scholars and Daoists have used analogical reasoning to claim that what Confucius taught regarding the essence of benevolence (*ren*), righteousness (*yi*), propriety (*li*), and music (*yue*) constitutes a single unity. Furthermore, during the time of King Nan of Zhou, Yu Bao...
First, when he was afflicted by illness, the Lord of the Old Man (Laojun) bestowed upon him the One Hundred and Eighty Precepts and the *Taiping Jing* in one hundred and seventy chapters;
this constitutes the second instance. During the reign of Emperor An of the Han dynasty, he transmitted the Teaching of the Sole Orthodox Pledge of Might (*Zhengyi Mengwei*) to Zhang Daoling;

at that time, he claimed to be the Pillar Secretary of the Zhou dynasty, sent by the Most High (Taishang); this constitutes the third instance. Therefore, it is said: "Three concealments, three [manifestations]."
This is now clearly evident; let us for a moment challenge this claim. To manifest physical forms and establish teachings, one must necessarily rely on those with whom there is a karmic affinity;
to exhort and transform others to lead them across, one must necessarily depend upon a community of disciples. How could it be that during five hundred years there were no disciples at all?

To appear three times and then withdraw three times, yet never to be seen by disciples receiving instruction or personally inheriting the lineage—this is as remote and obscure as the Milky Way. Where does such a claim come from? It is but an empty rumor circulating among the common folk.

When Zhou was driving his inferior small carriage with disheveled hair and drooping whiskers, he came to Han, where flutes and drums gathered like clouds as two attendants followed him floating through the air at Baosou;
yet no account of this has been heard in the *Shenxian zhuan*, nor is this marvel recorded in the *Qixie ji*.
To touch my breast and deliberate on the matter, such preposterousness is even more extreme. Furthermore, the five anomalies and five metaphors are fully contained within the *Bianzheng lun*.
Those who require them should seek them out, as they cannot be recorded here in full.

They are available in such works as the *Zhengzhen lun* (Treatise on Distinguishing the Authentic), the *Bianzheng lun* (Treatise on Discerning the Correct), the *Xiaodao lun* (Treatise on Laughing at the Dao), the *Xinjing* (Mirror of the Mind), the *Poxie lun* (Treatise on Refuting Heterodoxy), and the *Muzi* (Discourse of Mouzi).
Furthermore, the Śramaṇa Xuanyi of Foshouji Monastery in the Tang dynasty composed the three-fascicle *Zhengzhen lun*, which extensively refutes the Daoist school.

The deities of heaven are fallacious and the scriptures are empty. During the Wude era of the Great Tang High Ancestor, the Grand Astrologer, Chao-san Dafu, Zhuan Yi, submitted a memorial in eleven articles to destroy the Buddha-dharma.
Although Xiao Yu, the Director of the Secretariat, rebuked him, he was ultimately unable to suppress these heterodox arguments. At that time, there were the monks Falin and [Fatai] of Jiefasi...

The Master submitted a memorial to present his *Poxie lun* (Treatise on Destroying Heresies) and *Bianzheng lun* (Treatise on Distinguishing the Correct), entrusting the task of exposing the fallacies of Dou Yi to [the official] Chuan Yi;

the full text of these arguments is not cited here, but scholars should examine them carefully. In the fifth year of the Tiānhé era of Emperor Wǔ of the Northern Zhou, Zhēn Luán, whose surname is pronounced "Zhēn-chāng-lín-qìe," served as the Sīlì Dàfū (Grand Master of the Office of the Metropolitan Police).

At that time, Ān Fǎ... (Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment of a historical record concerning the Buddhist scholar Jizang and the anti-Buddhist polemics of the Northern Zhou period. The final sentence is incomplete.)
The Master composed the *Erjiao lun* (Treatise on the Two Teachings), asserting that because the Daoist teaching lacked a founder, there were only two teachings: Confucianism and Buddhism.
During the Han dynasty, there was Mouzi, who wrote a treatise titled *Mouzi lihuo* (Mouzi Resolving Doubts), which thoroughly refuted the delusions of the Daoists.
Even now, there are still those of inferior character who claim, "We are both members of the monastic order; what distinction is there between us that we should judge one another as right or wrong?
As the *Lunheng* cites, on the twelfth day of the sixth month in the third year of the Xianqing era of the Tang dynasty, the Emperor [visited] Ximing Monastery...
When his merit and virtue were perfected, he summoned monks and Daoists into the inner palace to debate.
At that time, the śramaṇa Huili of Daci'en Monastery challenged the Daoist Li Rong on the meaning of the "Six Caverns" (*Liudong*). Li Rong was unable to respond and said:
"Master, please do not treat me with such contempt. While I was in Shu, I had already heard of your reputation; I did not expect to meet you today in the celestial court."
Huiheng said, "Since we have met in person for discussion and both are renunciants under the same teacher, do not trouble yourself with contentious matters or challenge my wisdom.
Hui Li replied, "One might as well go outside to exchange pleasantries; this present assembly must ultimately determine what is heterodox and what is orthodox.
Huiheng said, "Li and I are both renunciants; yet when examining our outward forms and investigating our affairs, how can we be the same? Sir, your hair has turned white."

"Not clipping the hem of one's meditation robe, yet not removing [the hair], holding peach-wood talismans in hand and hanging red pouches at the waist, wandering from door to door to exorcise ghosts and from alley to alley to stroke children—this is fundamentally no different from licentious sacrifices and heterodox sorcerers. How could it be the same as our pure and empty Buddhist disciples?
Rong was greatly incensed and said, "If you consider clipping the hair to be virtuous, why do you not shave your eyebrows? He asked this standing right there. What was the point?
Li Rong replied, "Since eyebrows are of the same substance as hair, it is established that they are one and the same kind of hair. If you pluck your beard, you are likewise plucking your eyebrows;
since you too have one kind of hair, why do you shave your head but not your beard? Li Rong then fell silent and had no reply.
Li stood up and rebuked him, saying, "In the past, Pingjin died at the ten difficulties; Li Rong dies in a single word. To discuss virtue is like this."

He stood up to express his gratitude, arguing that his merits were no less than those of the sages of old; thereupon, he withdrew from his seat, and the Sovereign laughed heartily, saying, "He has washed away [all impurities]," and so forth. *Tàotài*.

*Tāo* (洮) should be corrected to *táo* (濤); *tài* (汰) should be read with the phonetic *tú dài* (徒帶). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it means "to rinse and wash. The *Dazhidu Lun* (Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra) commentary states that it means "to clarify and cleanse."

Regarding the term "sages and worthies," this refers to the skillful means (*upāya*) of the sages within the family of worthies; how could these worthies further proceed from the state of being a worthy?
This passage is likely erroneous. Please evaluate it by comparing the stages and positions of the three teachings of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* with those of the Perfect Teaching (*yāna*).

Thus, the skillful means of the three teachings constitute the contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*) of the Perfect Family at the stage of the five ranks; the sages and worthies of the three teachings correspond to the ten stages of the six sense faculties of the Perfect Family.
Because faith and the increased path reduce birth, one knows that the stage of Expedient Means (upāya) belongs only to the outer ordinary beings (bāhyapṛthagjana),

whereas the stage of Worthiness (arhat) belongs to the inner ordinary beings (adhyātmapṛthagjana). Thus, when the three schools are compared against the Perfect (pariniṣpanna) and Indeterminate (aniyata) categories,
there is a distinction between the inner and outer within both Expedient Means and Worthiness regarding their entry into the Indeterminate.

Question: Regarding the various meanings in the *Xuánwén*, it is stated that "first there is opening, and subsequently there is abolition," and so on, even up to the reply which says, "The *Xuánwén* relies on metaphors," etc.

Now, I say: if we rely on the initial passage in the *Zhǐguān* explaining the names, which cites the three metaphors of the lotus from the *Fǎhuá jīng* to illustrate the provisional and the real—where first there is bestowing, then opening, and finally abolishing—the text itself is self-evident; thus, its reality is identical to that of the *Miàoxuán*.
Regarding the clarification within the "Discrimination of the Ultimate" (*zhìliǎojiǎn*) that first there is bestowal (*shī*), then abolition (*fèi*), and finally opening (*kāi*):
this is merely a matter of literary structure, which naturally implies a sequence; in reality, the underlying meaning does not contradict one another. Why?

Because since the initial bestowal involves both the provisional (*quán*) and the real (*shí*) arising together, it is immediately after this arising that abolition is discussed; furthermore, between this arising and abolition, there is the stage of opening.
It is said that we shall now further examine the four types of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, all of which are real and not false.

Thus we know that the underlying intent is indeed consistent with the principles of bestowing, opening, and abolishing. I earnestly hope you will contemplate this. As for the questions and answers in the *Commentary* (*Ji*), they may perhaps be intended for a specific occasion;

I respectfully request that you examine them in detail. Question: The distinctions made in the *Commentary* regarding the present text on "abolition" differ slightly from those in the *Miaoxuan*; what is the reason for this?

How should one answer this? Here, the teaching is categorized according to its flavor; since the three provisional [teachings] are abolished within the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, how could the provisional aspects of the four periods and various schools not likewise be abolished?
Thus, we know that this current abolition of the provisional is no different from what is stated in the *Miaoxuan*.
There are dharmas that are grasped but no dharmas that are relinquished;

this is merely said to be "no relinquishing" because they lack an object-condition (*ālambana*). However, if there is an object-condition, there is also relinquishing, as will be explained in the following text.
The *Cetiyasūtra* states that "cetiya" is also called "zhiti" (支提) or "zhidi" (支帝); in this land, it is translated as "a place worthy of offerings."

If one follows the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* and the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* regarding their interpretation of the Three Jewels, the meaning differs slightly, as is briefly explained in the *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary on the *Zhiguan*) and the treatises themselves.
If one follows the *Adbhuta-dharma-sūtra*, which compares the merit of the three refuges, it states that [the merit of] teaching the four continents and the six heavens of the desire realm...
The merit of attaining the four fruits of the śrāmaṇya is not equal to that of the three refuges;

furthermore, among these, there was a son of the Trāyastriṃśa gods who manifested the five signs of decay and was destined to be reborn as a pig. Hearing his voice of sorrowful lamentation, Śakra, Lord of Devas, summoned him and addressed him, saying:
"You should take the three refuges. Immediately, following these instructions, he was liberated from that state and born [in a higher realm].
Thereupon, the Tathāgata spoke these verses: "All who take refuge in the Buddha shall not fall into the three evil realms;

having exhausted their outflows among humans and devas, they shall then attain Nirvāṇa. At that time, the son of heaven, having taken the triple refuge, was born into the family of a *śreṣṭhin* and subsequently attained renunciation, becoming one who has reached the stage of *aśaikṣa*. The *Mahāvibhāṣā* states: "Many take refuge and turn toward [the Triple Gem]."
Taking refuge in mountains, rivers, forests, trees, gardens, groves, stupas, or temples is taking refuge out of fear of others;
such a refuge is not secure, such a refuge is not supreme, and the destination one reaches cannot free one from suffering.

However, those who take refuge in the Buddha’s Bodhi, who take refuge in the Dharma of Nirvana where craving has been exhausted, and who take refuge in the Sangha of both learners (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond learning (*aśaikṣa*), are able [to realize] the Four Noble Truths.

Through wisdom, one perceives that this destination is peaceful, this destination is supreme, and this destination can bring liberation from all suffering. To take refuge in the Buddha does not mean taking refuge in the physical body;

rather, it refers to the two jewels of Dharma and Saṃgha, as can be seen in the text. The *Sarvāstivāda* school states: "Unlearned great wisdom and all meritorious virtues constitute the Buddha-jewel;
the unconditioned cessation of suffering (*nirodha-satya*) is called the Dharma-jewel; and [the noble] sound is the Saṃgha."
Hearing that the Sangha of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) and those still in training (*śaikṣa*) is called the Jewel of the Sangha, one takes the Three Jewels as one's refuge;
"refuge" has the meaning of providing protection. It is like a person who, having committed an offense against a king, flees to another country seeking protection.
The king says: "If you now wish to seek fearlessness, do not leave my domain, nor do you violate [its laws]."

My teaching necessarily provides mutual protection for sentient beings; it is likewise so. Those who have committed offenses within the cycle of birth and death and turn toward the Triple Gem to seek protection, with sincere hearts directed solely toward the Triple Gem and no other destination, do not violate the Buddha’s teachings; against such persons, even demons and evil forces can do nothing.
This is explained at length in that text. Furthermore, it cites the *Abhidharmakośa*, which states: "Among the prohibitions, one must specifically abstain from alcohol."
The *Śāstra* states: "Because those who drink alcohol are mostly heedless and cannot guard the other vows (*saṃvara*), one abstains from drinking alcohol in order to protect those others.

How, then, is it known that drinking alcohol is included among the prohibitory offenses (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*)? It is because it lacks the characteristics of an intrinsic offense (*prakṛti-sāvadya*).
Since all intrinsic offenses consist only of actions performed with a defiled mind, even when one drinks [alcohol] while treating an illness, [it is not an intrinsic offense]."
Regarding various alcoholic beverages, those who do not become intoxicated or deranged and whose minds remain unstained may drink them; this is what those who uphold the Vinaya say.

The masters of the Abhidharma, however, say it is not an intrinsic offense (*prakṛti-sāvadya*). Nevertheless, for the sake of those who are ill, the prohibitions and permissions regarding the precepts are generally relaxed;
yet, at another time, the drinking of alcohol is prohibited again to prevent one from committing an intrinsic offense on that account.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* records four types of ordination, while the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* records five types of ordination and also five types of the fourfold [ordination].
According to the *Nanshan jiyao benshu* (Essentials of the Nanshan Vinaya), it states that the *Mahāsāṃghika* recognizes eight types of ordination:

namely, the natural [ordination], the "come hither" (*ehi bhikṣu*), the five [groups], the eight [precepts], the twenty [precepts], the dispatching of a messenger, and the one who has previously returned [to the faith]. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* records twelve types of ordination: first, the natural; second, the single utterance; [and so forth].

Three [cases] of two words, forty-one assemblies, five [types of] breaking [the precepts], six [cases of] destroying false views, seven [cases of] receiving full ordination through the first [method], eight "Come hither" (Svāgata), nine three-word [ordinations], ten eight-respect [ordinations], eleven *karmavācanā*, twelve twenty-member [sanghas], thirteen dispatching messengers;
in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, monks and nuns each have five [categories], totaling eleven: one "Come hither," two breaking of fetters, three three-word [ordinations], four...

In border regions, five persons [constitute a *saṃgha*], whereas in the central lands, ten persons do; these five cases pertain to monks (*bhikṣu*). First, the Eightfold Respectful Ordination (*gurudharma*);

second, the ordination before a group of twenty; third, ordination by messenger; fourth, for those who were minors but have since returned to the community; fifth, for those in border regions where ten constitute a *saṃgha*. These five cases pertain to nuns (*bhikṣuṇī*).
If one considers both monks and nuns together, the categories of "Come hither" (*ehi-bhikṣu*) and "Formal Ritual" (*karmavācanā*) subsume the groups of five and ten persons respectively.

Thus, the ten types for both monks and nuns actually constitute only five types. Furthermore, according to the *Śāriputra-abhidharma-śāstra* (or *Daśādhyāya-vinaya*), there are ten ways of receiving the precepts:

first, the natural precept without a teacher, which is the Buddha himself; second, the self-vow, such as that described in the *Dharmatrāta-dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (or *Dharmapada-piṭaka*), wherein at the moment of the vow, the discipline of body and speech is fully and naturally established;
third, attaining the Way, as in the case of the five bhikṣus; fourth, through debate on doctrine; and fifth... [text fragment].
1. Welcome; 2. The three refuges; 3. The fivefold assembly; 4. Sending a messenger; 5. The eight heavy [offenses]; 6. The *karmavācanā*.
Furthermore, there are many treatises such as the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, the *Mātṛkā*, and others that clarify differences in the reception [of precepts].
"Ma" refers to the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* (the *Sarvāstivāda-śāstra*); "Ga" refers to the *Mātṛkā*; and "Jian" refers to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*.
*Vibhāṣā-ācārya-mātṛkā* refers to the *Vinayamātṛkā-sūtra*. Because it extinguishes all unwholesome dharmas, it is called *vinaya*;
because it can definitively resolve the correct meaning without contradicting what is taught in the sūtras, it is called a *mātṛkā-sūtra*, and is also known as the *Vinayamātṛkā-śāstra*.
