*Mātṛkā* here means "mother of wisdom. Entering this samādhi, one composes treatises to expound upon the sūtras; thus [it is so named].

Therefore, it is said that the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* (Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra) speaks of seven ways of receiving the precepts: first, receiving the precepts through the realization of the Truths (*dṛṣṭasatyaka*);
second, receiving the precepts by "Come hither" (*ehi-bhikṣu*); third, receiving the precepts by the three utterances; fourth, receiving the precepts by the three refuges;

fifth, receiving the precepts by self-vow (*svapratijñā*); sixth, receiving the precepts by the eight rules (*aṣṭa-dharma*); and seventh, receiving the precepts by the formal motion and three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*). Regarding these...
Among the seven types [of ordination], those who obtain the precepts through the realization of the Truth (dṛṣṭiprāpta) are obtained by only five people; no others obtain them.

Those who obtain the precepts through the "Come hither" (ehi-bhikṣu) formula were obtained while the Buddha was in the world; after his parinirvāṇa, they cannot be obtained. Those who obtain the precepts through self-vow (svayaṃ-pratijñā) are obtained by only Mahākāśyapa alone.
Those who obtain the precepts through the eight dharmas (aṣṭadharmaprāpta) are obtained by Mahāprajāpatī alone, through the formal motion and three proclamations (jñapti-caturtha-karman).

After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, all of these *karmavācanā* procedures were obtained. The *Mātṛkā* states that there are ten ways of receiving the precepts: first, without a teacher; second, by one’s own declaration;
third, through the realization of the truths (*satyadarśana*); fourth, by means of questioning and answering; fifth, by the three refuges; sixth, before a group of five monks;

seventh, before a group of ten monks; eighth, before a community of both bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs; ninth, for those who have committed the eight grave offenses; and tenth, by sending a messenger. This is from the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā-śīla*.

It is said that one obtains the precepts through the "Welcome" (Svāgata), obtains the precepts through the Three Refuges, obtains the precepts through receiving instruction, obtains the precepts through answering questions, obtains the precepts through receiving the weighty Dharma, obtains the precepts through being sent by another, obtains the precepts through the eightfold formula, and obtains the precepts through the formal act of *jñapti-caturtha-karman* requiring ten monks.
The "Welcome" refers to Cunda and others; "receiving instruction" refers to Kāśyapa; "answering questions" refers to Śubhūti.
Kāśyapa-śrāmaṇerī received the heavy precepts; that is, Bhadrākapilā received the eight heavy precepts and thereby attained the precepts.

Regarding the "eight utterances," this refers to having performed the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations) before the bhikṣuṇīs, and then performing the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* again before the bhikṣu-saṃgha.

Thus, the precepts are obtained through the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*; this is the method currently in constant use. The *Vinayamātṛkā-sūtra* states that there are five ways of receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*).

Regarding those called bhikṣus, there are five ways by which they receive full ordination (*upasampadā*): first, the "Come, O Bhikṣu" (*ehi bhikṣu*) ordination, whereby one immediately receives full ordination;

second, the "Threefold Declaration" (*tri-vācikā*) ordination, whereby one immediately receives full ordination; third, the "Fourfold Motion and Threefold Karmavācanā" (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*) ordination, which is known as receiving full ordination;

fourth, the ordination received by the Buddha’s command and permission, whereby one immediately receives full ordination; and fifth, the "Higher Ordination" (*ūrdhva-upasampadā*). Why is this? Because [the Buddha] did not grant ordination while he was in the world.
Regarding the precepts, those who receive them directly from the Buddha and attain arhatship are called those who have received the "superior" ordination (*agra-upasampadā*).

These are the five types of receiving the precepts for bhikṣus. As for bhikṣuṇīs, there are likewise five ways of receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*): first, practicing according to the teacher’s instruction is called receiving full ordination;

second, obtaining full ordination through the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations); third, [obtaining it] by following the teacher’s instruction... [text fragment].

Fourth, receiving full ordination by dispatching a messenger; fifth, receiving full ordination through the "Come hither" (ehibhikṣu) formula; sixth, receiving full ordination from above (the *ūrdhvabhikṣu*).
Furthermore, it is said that being able to accomplish—or failing to accomplish—the non-commitment of all evils is called receiving full ordination.
Moreover, within the Vinaya Piṭaka, one who can discern right from wrong and is able to practice with faith is therefore called one who has received full ordination. Furthermore...

To be able to accomplish the method for severing the five hindrances is called receiving full ordination; to be able to eliminate applied and sustained thought is also called receiving full ordination;

to be able to relinquish attachment to the meditative mind is also called receiving full ordination; to be able to relinquish suffering, pleasure, grief, and joy is also called receiving full ordination;

to be able to transcend the four formless attainments is also called receiving full ordination; furthermore, to receive the three refuges and the five precepts is also called receiving full ordination.
Receiving the eight precepts of the fast is also called "receiving the full ordination" (*upasampadā*); receiving the ten precepts of a *śrāmaṇera* is also called "receiving the full ordination.
Furthermore, partial reception of the precepts is also called "receiving the full ordination," and being able to contemplate wholesome karma is also called "receiving the full ordination.

Moreover, being able to achieve the stage of the lineage (*gotrabhūmi*) is also called "receiving the full ordination. As for the stage of the lineage, it refers to a person who listens to the Dharma in the presence of a Buddha.
With body and mind free from laxity, one achieves accomplishment in every thought-moment; by virtue of this mind, one attains sudden self-awakening and realizes the stage of *srotāpanna*.

A *srotāpanna* is precisely the seed-nature (*gotra*) of wholesome dharmas. [One thus traverses] the four fruits and four stages of approach, the eighth stage, the stage of seeing the truths (*darśana-bhūmi*), the stage of attenuation (*tanu-bhūmi*), the stage of freedom from desire (*vītarāga-bhūmi*), and the stage of having completed what was to be done (*kṛtāvī-bhūmi*), up to the solitary awakening of one who has no teacher.

These are all termed "receiving full ordination" (*upasampadā*). It is also termed "receiving full ordination through the six perfections," and it is also termed "receiving full ordination through the good speech [of the Three Refuges]," which is called the "three utterances.
The student should know that the texts concerning the reception of full ordination for the three vehicles are found herein.
There are ten types of impure mental states: first, arising spontaneously; second, receiving the teacher’s instruction, which is the self-vow; third, transcendent advancement.

1. These are the five bhikṣus. 2. The fourth [ordination] by asking about happiness refers to Śudāya. 3. The third is the three refuges. 4. The sixth is "Come, O Bhikṣu. 5. The seventh is for groups of five persons. 6.
The eighth is the formal dharma, which refers to the eight weighty rules (gurudharma). 7. The ninth is ordination by sending a messenger. 8. The tenth is for groups of ten persons.

In the *Abhidharmakośa*, there are ten types: 1. self-enlightenment; 2. entering the assembly of those fixed in rightness (*samyaktvaniyāma*); 3. accepting the words of the Great Teacher with faith; 4. asking [about the precepts].

The answer is that there are fifty types of ordination assemblies (*saṃgha*) in the Middle Kingdom: five [for monks], three for those who take refuge, six for those who come in person (*svāgata*), seven for those who accept with faith, eight for those who honor the Dharma, eight for those sent by messenger, and nine for those who uphold the Vinaya. According to the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī*, there are seven types of monastic assemblies:

four for monks and three for nuns—namely, (1) coming in person, (2) taking refuge, (3) abbreviated *karmavācanā*, (4) extensive *karmavācanā*, (5) coming in person, and (6) sending a messenger. (Note: The seventh is included in the preceding categories.)
The seven types of *karmavācanā* (formal ritual procedures), when further augmented by the Pratyekabuddha and the finite Buddha, become nine kinds.

In the older editions of the *Fuxing* (Subcommentary), the character "ga" (伽) is followed by an additional character "xin" (心); this refers to the ten types [of ordination] in the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra*.
Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* also clarifies the differences in receiving the precepts, but these are not recorded here.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations) initially states that [ordination] is "spontaneous" (*svayambhū*), whereas here it says "the Buddha calls out, 'Come, Bhikṣu.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* further states: "The Buddha had no teacher; he spontaneously attained full ordination. The *Dhyāna-pāramitā-sūtra* also says: "One spontaneously attains the precepts;
this refers to the Buddha, who was self-awakened without a teacher. Therefore, one should know that these passages are identical to those in the *Daśabhāṇavāra*.
Regarding the recitation, the present *Zhiguan* states: "The Buddha himself said, 'Welcome, Bhikṣu,' whereby one naturally attains the precepts.
One must know that this passage is identical to the *Ru Dacheng Lun* (Treatise on Entering the Mahāyāna).

Thus, the *Ru Dacheng Lun*, citing the *Vinaya-vibhāṣā*, explains that there are ten ways of receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*). What are these ten? First, when the Buddha himself says, "Welcome... [and so forth].
The passage concerning how a bhikṣu naturally attains full ordination (*upasaṃpadā*) up to the tenth point is contained within the *Śāstra*;

I shall not trouble you by recording it here. Viewed through this, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* explains "natural" [attainment] in reference to receiving the precepts from the Buddha, whereas the *Śraddhābalādhānāvatāramudrā-sūtra-śāstra* (Zhíguān) bases its explanation on disciples receiving the precepts. If scholars do not know to cite [these sources], they will fail to understand.
The text on *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* in the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra* is truly difficult to reconcile; let later scholars further examine how this relates to other passages.
The *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* states that it is the fifth [category] of the borderlands (*pratyanta-deśa*).
Some people say that those who uphold the Vinaya today all claim this passage is erroneous and should read "five persons.
However, if one examines the text of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* regarding the "tenfold reception," one will realize that the excellence of śamatha and vipaśyanā is derived from copying that meaning;
how could it possibly be an error? It is simply one among the five. One must be a fifth-grade Vinaya master to receive [the precepts] from such a person.

Regarding the remaining precepts, they are merely enumerations. As for the "Fifth Vinaya Master," he recited the *Prātimokṣa* once, up to thirty-two times, up to ninety-three times, the *Bhikṣu-prātimokṣa* four times, the *Dvavarga-prātimokṣa* four times, and the extensive recitation of the *Dvavarga-vinaya* five times.
I maintain that the entirety of *Śamatha* and *Vipaśyanā* is introduced into the Mahāyāna treatises, and that these ten [precepts] are received.
The fifth section on the "borderlands" (pratyantaka) in the *Vinaya-vibhāṣā* corresponds to the ninth instance of receiving the precepts (*upasaṃpadā*) in the treatise;

the tenth corresponds to the instance of receiving the precepts by ten monks in the Middle Kingdom. How can it be said that one must see the text of the "ten instances of receiving" in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* before one understands the meaning of the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*?
Furthermore, the *Fuxingzhuan* (Sub-commentary on the *Sijiaoyi*) also states: "The current text’s 'ten instances of receiving' correctly derives from the [Daśabhāṇavāra]."
Because the recitation also incorporates the doctrines of the Vaibhāṣika masters, there are one or two points of discrepancy;

furthermore, it is said that "one should know that the initial passage refers to spontaneity (*svabhāva*)," and "one should know that the present passage does not exclusively belong to a single school.
This is merely an error resulting from Jingxi’s failure to verify the passage concerning the "Ten Acceptances" in the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra*.
According to the intent of the *Nanshan Jieshu* (The Vinaya Commentary of Nanshan), ten persons in the Central Kingdom and five persons in the border regions must all maintain the Vinaya;

thus it is said that the performance of an act depends upon conditions, and if the conditions are lacking, the act fails. Since the successful completion [of the rite] cannot be achieved without relying on the maintenance of the Vinaya, the Nanshan school does not designate the fifth *karmavācanā* master as the "one who maintains the Vinaya" (*dharmavinaya*). This is according to Nanshan.
This is because the *Yeshu* (Commentary on Karma) also does not introduce the passage from the Mahāyāna treatise concerning the ten types of feeling;
therefore, it differs from the *Zhiguan*, which relies exclusively upon that passage on the ten types of feeling from the *Ru Dacheng Shi*.
The *Fuxing* (Subcommentary) says: "If one follows the *Sifenlü* (Dharmaguptaka-vinaya), it refers simply to the 'White-wood-tiao' (*Baimutiao*) of the frontier regions;
the character *tiao* is pronounced with a level tone (*pingsheng*). The *Sifenlü* states: 'In the east there is a country named White-wood-tiao. Nanshan says:
'I have carefully examined the *Liang Shi Gongzhi Tu* (Map of Tribute Offices of the Liang Dynasty), which states that the kingdom of Baimutiao from Western Tibet came here to present tribute.'"
Thus, while this [region] lies to the east of that [central land], the boundary monks there mostly employ the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* to adjudicate offenses;

since no other monastic community can be found to serve as a standard for comparison, there is no fault in doing so. Furthermore, the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states: "In the south there is a stupa named the Jingshan Stupa;
outside of it, they permit [the practice]. In the west there is a country with a mountain named Eṣālī, the Mountain of the Rishi’s Seed."
"Beyond the quarters" (fangwai) means that one hears there is a country in the north named Zhu; "beyond the quarters" refers to such things as hearing about [countries] beyond the quarters.
According to the *Shou lü wǔ rén dé shòu jù jiè* (The Five Persons Receiving Full Ordination Who Hold the Vinaya), these are the four directions, all of which have boundaries.

As for the term "Four-Part" (*Sifen*), the first part expounds the precepts for bhikṣus, the second part expounds the precepts for bhikṣuṇīs, along with the *Upasampadā-khaṇḍa* (the section on receiving ordination).
The *Aniyata* section is explained in the third part, and the *Kṣudraka-vastu* (Miscellaneous Matters) is explained in the fourth part; thus, this single body of Vinaya text consists of four parts.
As for what is called the "five-part" [Vinaya], it refers to another single body of Vinaya text that has five divisions:

the first part explains the Bhikṣu precepts, the second part explains the Bhikṣuṇī precepts, the third part explains the ordination (*upasaṃpadā*), and the fourth part explains the settling of disputes (*adhikaraṇa-śamatha*).
The *Saṃghabhedakavastu* is explained in five sections, and the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* is likewise;
these are fully enumerated in the Vinaya from the first *bhāṇavāra* through the tenth. As many people do not understand this, it is shown here.
*Sugata* is also called *Anuttara* and *Sugatu*; in this land [of China], it is translated as "Well-Gone" (*Shanshi*).
This refers to one who has received a hundred insults yet remains composed, accepting repentance and requests with a peaceful and relaxed mind.

First, a bhikṣuṇī who is a hundred years old, upon seeing a bhikṣu who has newly received the precepts, must rise to meet him, pay homage, inquire after his well-being, and invite him to sit comfortably. Second, a bhikṣuṇī must not revile or slander a bhikṣu.
Third, a bhikṣuṇī must not expose the faults or transgressions of a bhikṣu; however, a bhikṣu may expose and speak of the faults of a bhikṣuṇī.
Fourth, a śikṣamāṇā who has already trained in the precepts must seek to receive the full ordination (upasampadā) from the Saṃgha;
fifth, a bhikṣuṇī who has committed a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense must undergo the mānatva penance for half a month within both divisions of the Saṃgha;
sixth, within every half-month, a bhikṣuṇī must request a person to provide instruction from within the Saṃgha. Seventh...
Seventh, a bhikṣuṇī should not observe the summer retreat (varṣā) in a place where there are no bhikṣus.

Eighth, at the end of the summer retreat, a bhikṣuṇī must go before the saṃgha and request a person to perform the invitation for self-examination (pravāraṇā). This is based on the citations provided in the Nanshan Lüchao (The Vinaya Commentary of the Southern Mountain).

Regarding this nun’s beauty and so forth, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: A woman from the kingdom of Kāśī was exceptionally beautiful and fair; her value was equal to half the kingdom, yet even high ministers and great officials could not obtain her.
This woman subsequently resolved to leave the household life. Thereupon, all those of evil character gathered to deliberate.
She said, "If I receive the precepts, I must seize them from me on the road. When the nuns heard this, they did not know what to do and went to inform the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "From now on, I permit these Mūkaśī nuns to receive full ordination by dispatching a messenger.
The words for dispatching the messenger are fully contained in the Vinaya texts; there is no need to record them here at length.
It is also called "twelve utterances" because it consists of three *jñapti-caturtha* (one motion and three proclamations).

First, the *jñapti-caturtha* is performed among the nuns; next, one goes before the bhikṣus and performs the *jñapti-caturtha*; finally, returning to the nuns, one again performs the *jñapti-caturtha*.
Thus, it is by virtue of these *jñapti-caturtha* motions that it is termed "utterances. This was the case in all earlier translations. If one follows the Nanshan [Vinaya]:
The *Karmavācanā-vyākhyā* (Yeshu) merely mentions "eight utterances. Thus, it is said that the dispatching of a messenger involves eight utterances;

this refers to the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations) performed by both the twenty-member assembly of monks and nuns. Therefore, when the nun returns, she merely transmits the command of the monks, and the precept is thereby obtained;
there is no need for a third *jñapti-caturtha-karman*. This is because the *Sammohavinodanī-vaibhāṣya* on the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states only that the precept is obtained through eight utterances.
According to the *Cen boluomi* (Dhyānapāramitā), if one later returns to a nunnery to receive the precepts for her, this constitutes twelve utterances (*dvādaśa-vākya*).

Furthermore, the *Yeshu* (Karmasiddhi-prakaraṇa-ṭīkā) states that regarding "discourse on the meaning" (*lun yi*), as in the *Ekottarika Āgama*, the Buddha commanded Sudeva to explain the meaning of "permanent form" and so forth;
his preaching was without impediment and without timidity. The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states [the minimum age] is seven years.
This concerns the acceptance [of the precepts] through question and answer.
The six harmonies and ten benefits are:
first, commonality of precepts; second, commonality of views; third, commonality of conduct; fourth, kindness of body; fifth, kindness of speech; sixth, kindness of mind. These...

The six are all called the "Six Harmonies" (*ṣaḍ-sāmagrī*) because they externally accord with the virtues of others. The Vinaya states: first, to unify the Saṃgha; second, to cause the Saṃgha to rejoice;
third, to cause the Saṃgha to dwell in peace and happiness; fourth, to inspire faith in those who have not yet believed; fifth, to increase the faith of those who already believe;
sixth, to bring those difficult to discipline into subjection; seventh, to grant peace and happiness to those possessed of shame and remorse; eighth, to sever present [afflictions].
The nine types of outflow-tainted [dharmas] are abandoned, and the ten future outflow-tainted [dharmas] cause the True Dharma to abide for a long time;
because these ten are not without benefit to the assembly, they are called the "ten benefits. One should perform the *pratideśanīya* (confession) repentance.
The ninety *pāyattika* offenses are termed *suddha-pāyattika* (pure *pāyattikas*), as they differ from the thirty *naiḥsargika-pāyattikas*.

If one considers their essential nature (*āpatti-vastu*), they belong to the same category in terms of confession; however, because the thirty offenses arise from material things and involve a violation through greed and arrogance, leading to the forfeiture of the object and its entry into the Saṃgha, they are distinguished by the name *naiḥsargika*. Regarding the term *naiḥsargika*: [it means] that which is subject to forfeiture.
"Śeṣa" (捨) means "to relinquish. *Pāyattika* (波逸提) means "falling"; it is so called because one falls into the hells of burning, boiling, and concealment.
Therefore, it is said that this object should be relinquished before the Saṃgha, and the *pāyattika* offense should be confessed.
If it is a simple *pātayantika*, there is only the confession of the offense.

The statement that "natural offenses (prakṛti-sāvadya) are not extinguished" is made with reference to repentance through ritual action (vidhi-karma); it is only in this sense that one says natural offenses are not extinguished.

If, however, one refers to repentance by grasping the characteristics (nimitta-grāha), then natural offenses do not persist; thus, both the *Dhyāna-pāramitā* and the *Guangming wenju* explain [this] as ritual action.
If the ritual repentance (*vidhi-pratikramaṇa*) is accomplished, the transgression of non-action (*avijñapti-āpatti*) is extinguished, yet the debt of life remains to be repaid.

If the repentance based on grasping signs (*nimitta-pratikramaṇa*) is accomplished, not only is the transgression of non-action extinguished, but the transgression of nature (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) is also removed. If the repentance of non-arising (*anutpāda-pratikramaṇa*) can extinguish the root of ignorance (*avidyā*), how could its remaining branches and twigs persist?
Killing a human being constitutes five offenses; stealing constitutes three; sexual misconduct constitutes three.

If one attempts to kill a human being but the victim does not die, it is an offense of *thullaccaya* (grave offense). If one kills a non-human or an animal that possesses intelligence, understands human speech, and can assume a human form, and one employs the means to kill them, it is likewise an offense of *thullaccaya*.
If they do not die, it is an offense of *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing). If one kills [an animal] that lacks such capacity... [text ends].

If one commits an offense against an animal that has transformed into human form, it is a *thullaccaya*; if one perceives a human as such, it is a *pārājika*; if one perceives a non-human as such, or if there is doubt, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
If the act is committed by mistake or without harmful intent, there is no offense. Regarding theft: if one steals five *kārsāpaṇas* or more, it is a *pārājika*;

if one employs the means for theft but the amount is less than five *kārsāpaṇas*, it is a *dukkaṭa*. If the object cannot be obtained, it is a *dukkaṭa*. If one instructs another to steal, both commit an offense once the object is acquired.

If the one who receives the instruction takes a different object, or takes an object from a different location, the taker commits a *pārājika* offense and the instructor commits a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If one instructs another to take an object without the intent to steal, the instructor commits a *pārājika* offense while the one who receives the instruction is not guilty.
If one instructs a person to take an object by commanding them to steal it, the one who receives the instruction commits a grave offense (*guru-apatti*), while the instructor is not guilty.

If one perceives an object with an owner as having an owner, one commits a grave offense (*pārājika*); if one suspects it has an owner, one commits a *sthūlātyaya*. Regarding an object without an owner, if one perceives it as having an owner or suspects it does, one commits a *sthūlātyaya*.

Those who do not commit an offense include those who take what they perceive as their own, those who take it thinking it is discarded refuse (*pāṃśukūla*), those who take it temporarily, and those who take it thinking it belongs to a close friend.
Furthermore, theft is divided into four categories: first, the Three Jewels; second, humans; third, non-humans; and fourth, animals.
Fourth, regarding the four types of offenses: the distinctions among these four categories of transgressions are all contained within the *Lüchāo* (Commentary on the Vinaya).

As for committing sexual misconduct with the three realms of existence, this refers to engaging in sexual intercourse with three types of objects: first, humans; second, non-humans; and third, animals.

"Non-humans" refers to celestial beings (*devas*), ghosts, spirits, and so forth. Furthermore, there are five types of persons: women, young girls, those with both sexual organs (*ubhayavyañjana*), eunuchs (*ṣaṇḍha*), and men.
According to reports, there are two sexual organs for both males and females. As for their locations, women have three orifices: the anus, the urinary tract, and the mouth; men have only two.
If one commits a grave offense (*pārājika*) by inserting even a hair’s breadth into either of these two or three orifices, it constitutes a transgression.

If one employs the preparatory means (*prayoga*) with the intent to act but does not complete the act, it constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* offense. If one instructs another to perform the act, the instructor incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense, whereas the agent does not.
If a monk or nun instructs another person to perform an act that is either forbidden or permitted, both commit a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing).
If the corpse is half-decayed or completely decayed; or if one engages in sexual intercourse within the gaps between bones, in a hole in the ground, or in a hole in the mud;

or if one acts upon a path while perceiving it as a path, or with doubt, or while not perceiving it as a path—all these constitute a *sthūlātyaya*. If one perceives what is not a path as a path, or has doubt regarding whether it is a path, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.

For a bhikṣuṇī, a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, the offenses of *pārājika*, *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, *sthūlātyaya*, *pāyattika*, *pratideśanīya*, and *duṣkṛta* are not committed [in the following cases]:

if one does not wake up while sleeping; if one does not experience pleasure; or if there is no lustful mind. As for worldly persons, engaging with those who are not one's own wife, or through improper orifices (*amārga*), constitutes sexual misconduct.
To falsely claim to possess superhuman qualities (*uttarimanussadhamma*) in the presence of others, when the person understands the meaning, constitutes a lie.

If one who has committed a grave offense (duṣkṛta) does not recognize it as such, they commit a *thullaccaya*. If one says, "Spirits, devas, and nāgas have come to make offerings to me," or "I wish to speak to this person" when speaking to that person, and so forth, these are all grave offenses (*thullaccaya*). To claim for oneself, "I am a Buddha, a Teacher of Gods and Men," and so forth, is a *thullaccaya*.
If one speaks of superhuman qualities (*uttarimanussadhamma*) to an animal that cannot transform its shape, it is a *dukkaṭa*. There is no offense in cases of increased [virtue].

These include cases such as speaking out of pride, or speaking due to the ripening of karma, or laughing while speaking, speaking rapidly, speaking in private, speaking with desire, speaking erroneously about this while referring to that, and so forth.

Furthermore, if one has truly attained the Path yet speaks to laypeople of superhuman qualities (*uttaramanuṣyadharma*), saying "I have seen this" or "I know this," these constitute a *thullaccaya* offense.
Since even speaking of what one has truly attained incurs a fault when one harbors a contrary perception, it constitutes a grave offense.
The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra* (Duo lun) also clarifies that among the five, eight, and ten precepts, there are grave obstacles to the full possession of the complete precepts (*upasaṃpad*).

Master Nanshan cites the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra*, stating: "If a recipient receives the five precepts as a layperson, the eight precepts as a layperson, or the ten precepts upon leaving the home life, should they violate even one grave rule of the five precepts, they shall not receive the eight precepts, and so on, up to the point where they cannot receive the complete precepts."

Receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*) while acting as one's own preceptor (*upādhyāya*) is subsumed under the first of the thirteen obstacles (*antarāyika-dharma*). Furthermore, regarding the "obstacle of a grave offense" (*pārājika-antarakṛta*):
this refers to one who previously received full ordination but violated a heavy prohibition (*garuka-śīla*), then relinquished the precepts and returned with the desire to receive them again.
Because this person’s transgression is so grave, they are called one who stands outside the ocean of the Buddha; they are unfit to re-enter the pure precepts.
Master Hai states that, according to the treatises, among the five precepts for laypeople, the eight precepts, and the ten precepts for śrāmaṇeras,

those which are gravely violated are all termed "borderline offenses" (pārājika). Furthermore, it is said that if a layperson who has received the five or eight precepts violates even one of these grave rules,
they will not obtain the precepts if they later go forth into the monastic life.
Although the Xiangbu (Xiangzhou) school differs from this [Nanshan] internally, how can it compare when the Nanshan school possesses a teaching that can be relied upon?
The Xiangbu refers to Master Li of Xiangzhou, who produced the *Commentary on the Four-Part Vinaya* in ten fascicles and the *Commentary on the Karma* in three fascicles.
Nanshan once studied under his gate; as for the "lower" school, it refers to the region of the prefecture, which also takes its name from the administrative jurisdiction of that district.
Regarding the meaning of "office" (*shù*), I have searched the texts for an internal explanation but have not yet found one;

I suspect that the five groups and eight groups of lay followers are considered "external," while the *śrāmaṇeras* and other monastic communities are termed "internal. Jingxi followed Master Tan Yi of Kaiyuan Temple in Kuaiji in studying the *Vinaya*;
Tan Yi, in turn, relied upon Master Li’s *Vinaya Commentary* (*Lüshū*) and Master Xuan’s *Vinaya Abstract* (*Lüchào*).

The details and omissions, as well as the differences and similarities, are recorded in his own ten-fascicle *Fazhengyi ji* (Record on Elucidating the Correct Meaning), which clarifies the discrepancies between the two schools and unlocks the essential keys of the five capitals;
this is why Jingxi engaged in such instances of granting and withholding [approval]. Furthermore, that the subsequent text also censures Nanshan can be understood by analogy with this.
The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states: "If a person enters an unwholesome mind, an indeterminate mind, or even a state of non-consciousness, it is still called 'maintaining the precepts'.
Regarding the analysis of non-informative action (*avijñapti*), it asks: "What dharma is named non-informative action? It answers:

"When a mind arises that produces sin or merit, even during times such as sleep or fainting, that which constantly arises is named non-informative action. As it is said in the Sūtra: "If one plants trees or constructs..."
Question: It is said that wells and such are meritorious deeds performed by humans, which increase constantly day and night.

Someone asks: "If manifest actions such as prostration, giving, killing, and so forth can be seen, they must exist; however, since non-manifest action (*avijñapti*) is invisible, it should not exist. Answer:

If one says there is no non-manifest action, then there would be no such phenomena as the abstention from killing and so forth. Question: Is "abstention" (*virati*) not merely a name? Answer: [It is more than a mere name].
Regarding whether one acts or does not act, there is no way to answer [the objection] that one attains birth in the heavens by abstaining from killing and so forth.
If it is asked, "Is it not because of abstaining from killing that one is born in heaven? the answer is: "No, it is because of a virtuous mind. As it is said in the Sūtra:

"A person of diligence gains much merit according to the length of their life; because they gain much merit, they enjoy celestial bliss for a long time. If it were merely due to a virtuous mind, how could this be so?
Because those who possess great merit cannot always maintain a virtuous mind, it is further taught that the merit from planting trees and the like increases constantly;

furthermore, it is taught that the observance of precepts is firm. If non-informative action (*avijñapti*) did not exist, how could one speak of the constant increase of merit or the firm maintenance of precepts?
Moreover, mere action is not itself the act of killing; rather, the sequence of actions constitutes the dharma of killing.

Only after [the act] has been performed does one incur the sin of killing, as in the case of murder; since the killer incurs the offense at the very moment of killing, we know that there exists "non-manifest" (avijñapti) karma.

Furthermore, the mind lacks the restraint of the precepts. Why is this? Because even when a person is in a state of unwholesome or neutral mind, or is without mind, they are still said to be "upholding the precepts.
Thus, we know that at such times, non-manifest karma exists. As for what is called "non-... [the text continues].
Regarding those with wholesome, indeterminate, or mindless minds, the Sarvāstivādins clarify that one obtains the precepts through these four types of mind:

once the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal ritual of the fourth motion) has been completed, the "precept-form" (*śīla-rūpa*) is accomplished through the continuity of a wholesome mind; this is called obtaining the precepts within a wholesome mind.

If, prior to the sequential ritual, one constantly gives rise to a wholesome mind while performing the various preparatory acts, then at the time of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*, [the precepts are obtained].
If, while thoughts such as greed or anger arise within this mind, one accomplishes the form of the precepts (*śīla-rūpa*), this is called "attaining the precepts within an unwholesome mind.
This is because the precept is obtained through the power of the original wholesome mind and the wholesome instruction, and not through the power of the unwholesome mind.
Previously, when the formal ritual act (*karmavācanā*) of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* was initiated with a wholesome mind, [the candidate] might have been asleep or...
If one obtains the matter of the precepts (*śīla-rūpa*) while asleep or in a sleeping mind, this is called obtaining the precepts within an indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) state of mind.

Furthermore, when one first gives rise to the ritual action (*karmavācanā*) through a wholesome mind during the formal procedure of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*, and at that very moment enters the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), one accomplishes the matter of the precepts;
this is called obtaining the precepts within a mindless state. There are five such states of being without mind.
First, entering the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*); second, being born in the heaven of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-deva*), where mental activity does not function;
third, entering the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*); fourth, fainting; and fifth, deep sleep without dreaming. Furthermore, it is stated in the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*:

"Non-manifest action (*avijñapti*) arises once and is never abandoned; until its causal conditions are exhausted, it continues throughout one's entire life-form (*ātmabhāva*). The four minds and the three natures are always present from beginning to end."

The commentary explains: "The first 'arising' refers to the moment when the *kṛta-śīla* (active precept) ceases and the *avijñapti* (non-active precept) continues to arise. In contrast to this, it is called the 'beginning';

up to the fourth [moment], it is called the 'end. Because its substance is not lost, it is said that there are always four minds—namely, feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*).
In the present text, it says 'adding the mindless,' and the three natures are neither good nor evil."

This is a record [of the teaching]. Once it has been initiated, it persists constantly within the four types of mind and the three natures, without depending on causes and conditions for its formation or discernment;

therefore, it is said that "it does not rely on conditions for discernment. Thus, as soon as the *vijñapti* (informative action) ceases, the *avijñapti* (non-informative action) arises continuously, taking that which is neither matter nor mind as its essence, persisting until the end of one's life.
The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* and the *Samyuktābhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* both explain these four [aspects].

At that time, there are four ways to relinquish the precepts: first, by death; second, by performing the ritual act (*dharmakarma*); third, by severing the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*); and fourth, by the arising of both sexual organs (*ubhayavyañjana*).

In the *Abhidharma-nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, the addition of "relinquishing at the time of the disappearance of the Dharma" makes five. There is no relinquishment through the arising of two sexual organs because it involves the transgression of the precepts.

According to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, when one abandons the path and returns home, the ritual act must be performed for relinquishment; if the ritual act is not performed, the essence of the precept (*śīlaskandha*) remains.
If one commits a grave offense (*pārājika*), one does not lose the precepts, because the remaining factors and the remaining objects of the discipline continue to function as before.
Regarding the transformation of the faculties (*indriya-parivṛtti*): if the male faculty transforms into the female faculty, the bhikṣuṇī precepts are then suspended;

if the female faculty transforms into the male faculty, the bhikṣu precepts are then suspended. Therefore, the transformation of the faculties does not depend on having both sexual organs (*ubhayavyañjana*). — *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*.

It should be known that when a bhikṣu undergoes a change of gender (*vyañjana-parivṛtti*), he does not lose his restraint (*saṃvara*). One should understand that it is not by changing gender that one abandons it.
As for those who claim that changing gender constitutes abandonment, this is not the case; for in the Mahāyāna precepts, they are abandoned due to two conditions.

Thus, the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: "If one abandons the vow for enlightenment and commits the ten grave offenses through predominant afflictions, their substance is then nullified."

If these two did not exist, [the Buddha] would have ceased [teaching]; this is likewise stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, as has already been analyzed in the supplementary notes on the textual passages.
The sūtras and śāstras of the Hīnayāna collectively establish three aggregates (*tri-skandha*); even the essence of the Hīnayāna precepts is the third aggregate, and this is based upon [that system].

Regarding the Sautrāntika school’s position within the Sarvāstivāda—that the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) precept takes matter (*rūpa*) as its essence—Zhang’an, in his commentary on the "Recollection of the Precepts" chapter of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, states that although it lacks form and color, it can still be guarded and maintained.

He provides three interpretations of this: first, the Mahāsāṃghika school maintains that because there is no such thing as unmanifest matter, they themselves have neither unmanifest [matter] nor non-unmanifest [matter].
Furthermore, because there is no form and only the mind exists, it is said that [the precepts] can be guarded and maintained.

Second, the Sarvāstivādins maintain that non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*) is indeed form; this is what the Sāṃmitīyas also employ. Thus, there is non-informative matter itself, and yet there is also form.

Since form does not consist of physical obstruction, there is "unmanifested" (or "non-informative") conventional form; therefore, it must be guarded and maintained. Third, the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* of the Mahīśāsaka school.
Regarding the statement that "that which is employed is non-active (anabhisamskāra), neither form (rūpa) nor mind (citta)," such assertions are all points of contention.
Some teachers say that form consists of eleven types of form, while non-form refers to the mind and mental factors (caitta);

that which is neither form nor non-form refers to the fourteen dissociated formations (viprayukta-saṃskāra). Other scholars say that form consists of fourteen types of form, while non-form is merely...

The mind is neither form (*rūpa*) nor non-form; thus, it is "unmanifest" (*avijñapti*). Nanshan says: "Now, according to our own school, the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra*, the unmanifest precept takes that which is neither form nor mind as its essence.
'Neither form' means it is not composed of the great elements (*mahābhūta*) or their derivatives; 'not mind' means it is not the mind of cognitive apprehension (*ālambana-citta*).

That which constitutes the essence of the manifest precept is the volition (*cetanā*) of bodily and vocal karma. Regarding the essence of the unmanifest precept, the treatise states that it takes the volition of bodily and vocal karma as its essence.
The body and speech are merely the instruments for creating good and evil. Why is this? Because if a person kills without intent, they do not incur the sin of killing;
thus we know that the mind constitutes the essence. A text states: "The three types of karma are nothing but the mind.

Apart from the mind, there is no volition, nor are there the karmas of body or speech. If it were claimed that form (rūpa) constitutes the essence, this would be incorrect, for [form] consists of fourteen types.

All forms (*rūpa*) are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and do not possess the nature of either demerit (*apuṇya*) or merit (*puṇya*). The fourteen types of form consist of the five sense organs (*indriya*), the five objects (*viṣaya*), and the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).

The eleven types of form consist of the five sense organs, the five objects, and unmanifest form (*avijñapti*). The *Abhidharma-ṣaṭpādā-śāstra* (Six-Legged Abhidharma) states that there are two kinds of form:
first, form as an accumulation of atoms (*paramāṇu-saṃcita-rūpa*), such as the eye, ear, and so forth; second, the twelve [types] that are not composed of atoms.
The accumulation of matter is called non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*), which is subsumed under the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*). The *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* states:

"One should know that non-substantial matter is provisional matter (*prajñapti-rūpa*); it is not like the ten [real] matters, such as the eye and ear, which are substantial matter formed by the accumulation of atoms.
One should reflect accordingly on how, in the Mahāyāna, non-substantial provisional matter serves as the essence of the precepts (*śīla-svabhāva*).
The remainder is as distinguished in the *Supplementary Notes to the Mysterious Sub-commentary* (*Xuanshan Buzhu*).

However, although within the Mahāyāna the nature of mind (*cittatā*) is taken as the substance of the precepts (*śīla-tattva*), the *Fanwang Jieshu* (Commentary on the Brahma Net Sūtra Precepts) takes form (*rūpa*) as its substance; whereas this present text takes the mind as its substance. Whether it be form or mind, both are [the substance].

This is because it is the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of the Mahāyāna precepts. Thus, the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: "It is simply that [the transgression] does not arise; once it arises, its nature is non-arising.
Furthermore, the *Dharmabherī-sūtra* clarifies that there are only matter (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*), with no third aggregate.

The commentary on the *Vajrasamādhi-śāstra* maintains that the ten grave and forty-eight light offenses of the *Brahmajāla-sūtra* primarily guard against the mental ground (*manobhūmi*); therefore, the mind is taken as the essence of the precepts.
*Śikṣāpada* is translated as "that which should be learned.

In the *Sifen lü jieben* (The Code of Precepts of the Four-Part Vinaya), it is explained that because these offenses are subtle and extremely difficult to maintain, they are named after the act of learning them accordingly. They are also called *duṣkṛta*.

This refers to "bad action" (*kaukṛtya*) for the body and "bad speech" (*durukta*) for the mouth; because the fifth category is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing), it is said to be "separately located in the fifth.

If the first four categories also have preparatory stages (*prayoga*) that constitute *duṣkṛta*, they are said to be "commonly applicable across all categories," as will be clearly explained in detail below regarding the *duṣkṛta*.

This means that the *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense) serves as the preliminary retinue (*pūrva-parivāra*) for this [offense]; because it is the causal *sthūlātyaya* that functions as the preliminary preparation (*prayoga*) for a heavy offense, the thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses are listed after the heavy offenses.

Regarding those equal to the *sthūlātyaya*, the *Sudarsana-vinaya* translates it as "great obstacle to the good path" (*mahāntarāya-sudeśa*); subsequently, one falls into the evil destinies (*durgati*). Its essential nature (*svabhāva*) is as follows:

Because it is base and defiled, it is also translated as "great sin" (*mahā-āpatti*) or "coarse evil. Regarding the offenses resulting from this [category], such as the grave precept against sexual misconduct, there are four types:
first, the remote preparatory act (*dūre-prayoga*), which refers to when one first gives rise to the intention before moving body or speech;

the offense is merely censured in the mind, and upon repentance, the transgression is extinguished. Second, the intermediate preparatory act (*antike-prayoga*), which refers to moving the body and speech toward [the act].
It is said that when one intends to commit these [acts], the offense is extinguished only after confessing them before another person; both of these offenses are *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).

Regarding the three preparatory stages (*upakrama*): if one goes to the presence of that person or desires to touch their body but does not yet make physical contact, this constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense).
This is because one has resolved to engage in sexual intercourse, and since the touching was not for the sake of mere play or amusement, it constitutes a *sthūlātyaya*.
The *laiśa* (thief-like offense) does not constitute a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (offense requiring suspension); this offense is extinguished only through confession before another person.

The "fourfold physical contact" is the fundamental offense (*mūlāpatti*), for the first three [stages] serve to bring about the fourth grave offense. What is now called the "consequential *laiśa*" refers to the third of those three;
it is also termed the "arising *laiśa*" (*utpanna-laiśa*). If it were a "resultant *laiśa*" (*phala-laiśa*), it would be [the offense] alone.

*Tulan* (頭蘭) is also called *zheng* (正). *Zheng* refers to the fruit-branch (*guolan*), which is also termed "independent" (*doutou*). *Cong* (從) refers to the causal branch (*yinlan*), which is also termed "consequential preparatory effort" (*congsheng fangbian*);
this refers to the preparatory efforts for the offenses of the first two categories (*pian*) that follow [the root offense].

According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, if a grave offense arises from the first category, it constitutes a "proximate preparatory effort" (*jin fangbian*), and one must confess it before the entire Saṃgha.

If a light offense arises from the first category (pārājika) and a heavy offense arises from the second category (saṃghāvaśeṣa), one should confess it before an assembly of four bhikṣus outside the boundary (sīmā).

If a light offense arises from a saṃghāvaśeṣa, one should confess it before a single bhikṣu. Furthermore, the *pratideśanīya* (offenses requiring individual confession) that are independent by nature are also divided into three grades:
stealing food belonging to the Saṃgha, stealing property currently present before the ten directions (the community), stealing four *kārsāpaṇas*, and stealing valuable items belonging to non-humans.

These constitute the highest grade. To disrupt the *karmavācanā* of the Saṃgha, to steal property belonging to the Saṃgha or an individual in an amount of three *kārsāpaṇas* or less, and so forth, constitute the middle grade.

To store or use human hair, to shave the hair from the three areas [the head, face, and pubic region], to pour [liquids] into the lower part [of the body], to walk about naked, to wear the robes of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), to possess stone bowls, to eat raw meat or blood, and out of a mind of hatred to tear apart the three robes or the bowl—[these constitute the lower grade].

The destruction of stupas and the like constitutes the lowest grade (*mṛdu*). A *sthūlātyaya* offense is a category of transgression that encompasses both primary and derivative acts, and its nature includes both light and heavy degrees.
Since the seven categories (*sapta-nikāya*) and six categories (*ṣaṭ-nikāya*) of offenses all contain *sthūlātyaya*, their placement among the higher or lower grades has its specific justification.

In the Vinaya, those offenses listed after the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (Saṅghādisesa) are so positioned because they are subsumed under the division of precepts (*śīla-skandha*) and their formal names are grave, as in the first two cases.

The distant preliminary stages (*pūrvaprayoga*) of the second category, as well as independent primary offenses (*mūlāpatti*), are of the same class as those involving schism (*saṃghabheda*) and theft (*steya*).
Alternatively, those categorized under the *prātideśanīya* (offenses requiring confession) are subsumed under matters of decorum (*airyāpathika*) and are thus minor offenses;

examples include being naked or using one's hair [as currency], which constitute the light independent primary offenses of the second category. This is the section on the *sthūlātyaya* (grave offenses).

Regarding those subsumed under the three grades of *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses, because their characteristics are coarse and manifest—such as the *sthūlātyaya* and *duṣkṛta*—the names of the offenses are heavy;
these refer to the upper and middle grades of *sthūlātyaya*. As for the two types of *pratyantika* (proximate) offenses in the first two categories:

the *pratyantika* of the first category is the upper grade of *sthūlātyaya*, while the *pratyantika* of the second and third categories is the middle grade of *sthūlātyaya*. Those that arise independently and are not derived from the [other] two categories are...
Since this *pāyattika* (sthūlātyaya) is grave, it follows the two *pārājikas*. "Demeanor" (*viniya*) refers to minor and subtle aspects of the precepts;
since this *sthūlātyaya*—such as being naked—is distant from the two *pārājikas*, it is relegated to the fifth position.
Regarding the term "arising" (*jātaka*), it means arising from below the two *pārājikas*; that is, it is a superior-grade *sthūlātyaya*. It arises.
That which is light is the "subsequent preparatory act" (anantara-mūla); that which is grave is the "proximate preparatory act" (sāmantaka-mūla).
Among these, the middle-grade *duṣkṛta* must be confessed outside the boundary (*sīmā*); if it is of the lower grade, it is confessed within the boundary before a single bhikṣu.
Regarding "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*), it does not arise from the secondary categories (*dvitīya-varga*). "Independent" (*mukhya*) means it is not a preparatory act.
Furthermore, it is also called *guilicheng* (吉祥成), which is also named *guolán* (果蘭). As for the term *sēngcán* (僧殘), it is fully termed *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
*Saṃgha* means "community" (*saṃgha*), and *avaśeṣa* means "remainder" (*avaśeṣa*). If one commits this offense, defilement entangles the practitioner;
they are not entirely pure in their application, as there remains a residual offense that must be eliminated through the community (*saṃgha*). For this reason, it is called *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (僧殘).

Regarding what is called "the remainder" (*śeṣa*), as explained in the subsequent commentary, this refers to the rules established in the *Śīla-vinaya* (the section on offenses involving forfeiture) and below, as well as those prescribed in various other sūtras;
all such rules are termed "remaining precepts. If one follows the text of the sūtra itself, after the five branches of the precepts it further states that there are two kinds of precepts:
first, precepts of intrinsic gravity (*prakṛti-sāvadya*); second, precepts for avoiding worldly censure (*lokāpavāda*). These are precisely the "non-doings."
This refers to selling goods, wrong livelihood, and so forth.
This is fully explained in the *Shiqian* (Explanatory Notes), which reconciles various points of agreement and difference.

Regarding the precept of non-deficiency: the "prohibitory precepts" (*jinjie*) of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* constitute the fundamental karmic factors; this is discussed under the heading of "not breaking the precepts."
The "precept of penetration" refers to the Great Sūtra’s "pure precepts" and "wholesome precepts," which discuss the preceding and following auxiliary branches without confusion.
The "precept of non-intermixture" refers to the Great Sūtra’s "unimpaired precepts," which discuss the branch of purity regarding thoughts that are not various evil perceptions.
The "precept of following the path" and the "precept of non-attachment" refer to the Great Sūtra’s "unbroken precepts," which discuss the branch of maintaining right mindfulness with mastery.

The morality praised by wisdom, the morality that accords with meditative concentration, the morality of complete fulfillment, the morality of the Great Sūtra, the Mahāyāna morality, the non-retrogressive morality,
the conforming morality, the ultimate morality, and the morality that fulfills all the pāramitās— these constitute the factors for dedicating oneself to the unsurpassed path.
If one were to discuss only the ten pairs from the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*, then discussing "non-deficient morality" is precisely the [morality] of the Great Sūtra.

The *Vinaya-viniścaya-upāli-paripṛcchā* (Discourse on the Prohibitions) explains that not breaking the precepts corresponds to the "pure precepts" (*viśuddha-śīla*) in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*; not piercing the precepts corresponds to the "wholesome precepts" (*kuśala-śīla*) in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*;

and not mixing the precepts corresponds to the "unimpaired precepts" (*akhaṇḍa-śīla*) in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*. Regarding the term "unimpaired," while the name is the same in both the treatise and the sūtra, their meanings differ:

the treatise takes as its basis those cases where the precepts are so damaged and ruined that they are no longer functional, whereas the root sūtra takes as its basis even the slightest deficiency or impairment.

The discourse on the unadulterated precepts corresponds to the "Precepts of Non-attachment" in the Great Sūtra; the discourse on the precepts praised by wisdom corresponds to the "Mahāyāna Precepts" in the Great Sūtra;
the discourse on the precepts of mastery corresponds to the "Non-retrogressive Precepts" in the Great Sūtra;

the discourse on the precepts of conformity corresponds to the "Ultimate Precepts" in the Great Sūtra; and the discourse on the precepts of fulfillment corresponds to the "Complete [Precepts]" in the Great Sūtra.
Regarding the precepts that fulfill the various *pāramitās*, one should simply rely on this text; even if it contradicts one's own view, there is no need to alter the wording.

As for the statement in the *Miśraka-śīla* (The Unmixed Precepts) that "an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) can maintain them when entering meditative concentration," this is merely based on the Sarvāstivāda school; according to other sects, they can also be maintained by other states of mind.

The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states: Question: Some say that when one enters meditative absorption (*samādhi*), there is the restraint of dhyāna (*dhyāna-saṃvara*), but upon emerging from it, this is no longer present.

How is this to be answered? Answer: It exists constantly both during entry and emergence. This person has attained reality and does not perform unwholesome dharmas; being contrary to the breaking of precepts, they constantly refrain from evil.
Because the wholesome mind becomes increasingly superior, [the restraint] should be constant. Question: If [this applies to] dhyāna, what about the formless [attainments] (*ārūpya*)?
Question: Since there is no factor of breaking the precepts within [the state of restraint], by what contradiction is it called "virtuous discipline" (*śīla-saṃvara*)? Answer:
The nature of phenomena is such that all sages and noble ones attain virtuous discipline.

If discipline were to exist only through its opposition to the act of breaking the precepts, then one would only obtain virtuous discipline from those sentient beings who can be harmed; this would entail such a fault. Therefore...
Not so. The *Jingming shu* (Commentary on the Vimalakīrti Sūtra) cites the case of two bhikṣus who committed sexual misconduct, murder, and other offenses;

even as they were like Yongshi after committing grave transgressions, they subsequently awakened to the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), which became the causal condition for their attainment of Buddhahood in the present.

Therefore, the *Yinyezhang jing* (Sutra on the Obstructions of Lustful Karma) states: "In the past, immeasurable kalpas ago, after the Buddha Vimalaprabha had entered nirvana, there was a bhikṣu named Vyādhaprayukta.
For the sake of alms, he engaged in sexual misconduct with a woman; out of delusion, he further gave her poison so that she would kill her husband."

Because he had committed the grave sins of sexual misconduct and killing, Yongshi then felt remorse in his heart and went to the place of the Bodhisattva Nigrodha to confess his transgressions and seek absolution.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Nigrodha immediately manifested supreme supernormal powers;
having displayed these powers, he then preached the Dharma for him, fully elucidating the fundamental nature of all phenomena.

"Nature is empty and quiescent, free from all deluded thoughts. At that time, because he had heard this Dharma, the Bodhisattva Vīradatta immediately realized the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī: "The Bodhisattva Ghoṣila of the past is none other than the present Bodhisattva Maitreya;
the bhikṣu who realized the non-arising of dharmas at that time was the Tathāgata Ratnacandra."

Now, having briefly summarized the general meaning of that sutra regarding those who have attained Equal and Perfect Enlightenment beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the Western Quarter, one must therefore understand the discourse on the retributions for upholding or violating the precepts. The *Mahāyāna-jātaka-citta-bhūmi-sūtra* states:
"By firmly maintaining the highest grade of pure precepts, one transcends to dwell in sovereignty as a Dharma King; by [maintaining] the middle grade..."

Those who uphold the Bodhisattva precepts with superior-grade mastery of merit become Wheel-Turning Kings; those who uphold them with middle-grade mastery become Great Ghost Kings, under whose command all non-humans submit;
and those who uphold them with inferior-grade mastery become kings of birds and beasts, to whom all flying and crawling creatures submit.

Even if there are lapses in the pure precepts, because the power of the precepts is supreme, one still attains the status of a king. Those who uphold them with the lowest-of-the-low grade [attain the same].

King Yama dwells within the hells yet always possesses sovereign power; although he was born into the evil realms due to violating the prohibitions and precepts, because his observance of the precepts was superior, he attained the status of King.
For this reason, all sentient beings should receive the pure bodhisattva precepts.
Even if one who has received the bodhisattva precepts commits a transgression, they may still become a king—according to this text. However, as for the sages...
My original intention was simply to urge sentient beings to be equally diligent in both their practice of the precepts (*śīla*) and their cultivation of the Path (*yāna*).
Master Nanshan cites from among the eighteen categories of the *Vinaya*: "The two names *vinaya* and *lü* (律) do not appear together.
In his *Lüchao*, he states: "*Vinaya* is translated here as *lü*; it is the *vinaya* found within the eighteen categories of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*."
Regarding the two names, "Dharma" and "Vinaya," which do not function concurrently: the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states that there are eighteen categories:

what is Dharma and what is not Vinaya; what is Vinaya and what is not Dharma; offenses and non-offenses; light and heavy; those with remainder and those without remainder; the coarse-evil and the non-coarse-evil; what is commonly practiced and what is not commonly practiced;
what is prescribed and what is not prescribed; and what is taught and what is not taught. It further states: "What is Vinaya and what is not Vinaya"—this is [the definition].

When the term *vinaya* (律) is mentioned, *piṇī* (毗尼) is not; when the term *piṇī* is mentioned, *vinaya* is not. This is simply because the Chinese and Sanskrit terms are used interchangeably, which is why it is said that the two names are not used together.
Now, I shall briefly cite a commentary from the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-saṃgraha* to explain the characteristics of the eighteen dharmas of the heterodox and the orthodox:
the *Sarvāstivāda* school states that Devadatta enticed various youths with five practices, preaching what is not the Dharma as being the Dharma.
Regarding these five things that are not Dharma, to say they are Dharma; regarding those things that are Dharma, to say they are not Dharma;

regarding the Eightfold Noble Path, which is Dharma, to say it is not Dharma; regarding what is not the Vinaya, to say it is the Vinaya; regarding the five things that are not the Vinaya, to say they are the Vinaya;
regarding the Eightfold Noble Path, which is the Vinaya, to say it is not the Vinaya; and regarding what is not an offense, to say it is an offense—these are what the Buddha did not [permit].

To establish the precepts of the mind and yet claim that the arising of the three poisons within the mind constitutes a violation of those precepts is itself a transgression. To say there is no violation is incorrect;
for if one does not restrain oneself, then shaving the hair and clipping the nails would be a violation. The Buddha taught that regarding violations of the precepts, hair and nails possess life;
thus, to shave them is not a violation. To speak lightly of what is grave is like the case of the Utpala Dragon, who refused to repent because he had plucked a leaf from a tree.
This [position] then asserts that killing all grasses and trees constitutes a grave offense;

yet when speaking of what is light, it is because [the texts] refer to cases such as Sūdena and Dhanika, who—due to their prior conduct—could not incur a grave offense. Consequently, it is claimed that sexual misconduct and theft are light offenses.

As for those who say there is no *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (offense with remainder), they mean that while the four lower categories of offenses do indeed involve *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, they are referred to as "without remainder" because [in those specific instances] there is no remainder.
Regarding the statement that there is a remainder for those with a remainder: if one commits the four grave offenses, there is no remainder, yet it is said that there is a remainder.
Regarding the teaching of what is the constant Dharma and what is not the constant Dharma: the Eightfold Noble Path is the constant Dharma, yet it is taught as not being the constant Dharma;
what is not the constant Dharma is taught as the constant Dharma, namely, the five dharmas.

To teach what is not the Dharma as being the Dharma—such as saying that the four prohibitions (caturmahāśrāmaṇya) are minor while other sections are major—is called "non-teaching" yet asserted as "teaching.
To teach what is the true teaching as non-teaching—such as saying that the four prohibitions are major while other sections are minor—is called "true teaching" yet asserted as "non-teaching.
Regarding the five dharmas, the *Pañcavargika* states: first, not eating salt; second, not...
1. Eating milk; 2. Not eating fish or meat; 3. Begging for food; 4. Begging for food; 5. Begging for food; 6. Sitting in the open air during the eight months of spring and summer.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: 1. Wearing the *nāṃgaka* (hempen robe); 2. Begging for food; 3. Eating only one meal a day; 4. Sitting in the open air; 5. Abstaining from fish and meat.
The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states: 1. Begging for food; 2. Wearing rag-robes (*pāṃsukūla*); 3. Sitting in the open air; 4. Not eating ghee or salt.
Fifth, not eating fish or meat—these five [precepts] are all to be observed for as long as one lives.
The *Nanshan* (Nan-shan) states that *vinaya* is translated as "extinction" (*mie*). This is a name derived from its function and is by no means the primary translation;
therefore, translating it as "discipline" (*lü*) is the correct meaning. *Śīla* is translated here as "precept" (*jie*), and *prātimokṣa* is translated as "place by place" (*chu chu*).
The *Shijie jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts of Liberation) states: "Śīla is translated as 'jie' (precept). What is the meaning of 'jie'? The meaning of 'jie' is defined as 'caution' (*jing*).
It means to caution and discipline the three types of action (*trikarma*) so as to remain far removed from non-virtuous conditions; this clarifies its cause.

As transmitted in ancient traditions, one prevents what is wrong and forbids evil, thereby explaining the precept (*śīla*). However, while 'precept' applies to both good and evil, most sūtras and śāstras follow the usage of 'good precepts' (*kuśala-śīla*)."

Because it is by virtue of its meaning that it receives its name, the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* states that *śīla* is translated as "intrinsic goodness" (*xing-shan*); this is explained from the perspective of its essence (*tǐ*).

As the *Cittaviveka-śāstra* states, "Prātimokṣa, discipline (*diao-fu*), etc."; this is explained from the perspective of the mind (*xin*). Furthermore, in various treatises, there are references to "informative" (*zuo*) and "non-informative" (*wuzuo*) precepts;
these are explained from the perspective of karma (*ye*). Alternatively, it is said that they are "cooling" or "ascending to the heights"; these are explained through metaphor (*yu*).

Some say that because one observes oneself through the precepts, this is called the *Śīla-sūtra*; this is explained from the perspective of the teachings, yet it applies only to virtuous conduct and does not extend to evil dispositions.
One should follow what is clarified in the *Shansheng-jing* (Upāsaka-śīla-sūtra) and the *Abhidharma-samaya-prakaraṇa-śāstra*:

since the two types of precepts—good and evil—are mutually received and mutually forgotten, their functional efficacy is equal, and there is no distinction in their names or meanings. This allows for a comprehensive understanding that "precept" (*śīla*) means "prohibition. How is this known?

If one understands that good precepts and wholesome dharmas prohibit evil and maintain vigilance so that it does not arise, and understands that evil precepts and unwholesome dharmas prohibit good and guard against them so that they do not occur—seeking the meaning through this principle, there will be no doubt regarding "saṃjñā" (perception).

*Prātimokṣa* is translated here as "liberation" (*vimukti*). As cited in the treatise, the path-precept is called liberation, while the ritual-precept is called individual liberation (*prātimokṣa*). Following [the commentary]:

The fruits [of the path] are distinguished and illustrated by means of their provisional designations; because the nature of the Way is empty and pervasive, all phenomena are subsumed and eliminated through their general categories.

It does not follow conditions to become distinct, but is simply termed "liberation. The precepts of phenomenal events (*dharma-śīla*) are not like this: they arise according to specific conditions and, while those conditions pervade the ten thousand objects, the practice likewise follows them everywhere.
If one transgresses these observances, one is said to have attained liberation; otherwise, if one has not yet practiced, it is not termed "liberation" in the Vinaya.

This is the Dharma; it derives its name from the teachings. It involves the determination of gravity and lightness, the opening or closing of precepts, and the maintenance or violation of rules—matters that are not fixed by worldly standards.
To translate this correctly, one must consider that among the nine schools of secular thought, the "Dharma School" (the school of law) is but one.

Thus, while worldly laws are generally based on penal statutes and differ from the Path in their terminology, when it comes to reaching a verdict, one must necessarily rely on the constant Dharma; therefore, [it is so].

The character for "law" (律) combines the radical 亻 with 聿; it signifies taking up the brush. To adjudicate, decide, and rectify is not possible without the brush, which is thus the symbol of the Legalist school.
It is precisely because of this that "law" (律) is used as the translation for *vinaya*.

Xiao He maintained that the *Shiji* records Emperor Gaozu of Han saying: "I have made a pact with the various lords that whoever first enters the Pass shall be made king; I shall be the king of Guanzhong.
Furthermore, he established a covenant with the elders regarding three articles of law: those who kill shall die; those who wound others or commit theft [shall be punished].
"Reaching the crime" (*dìzuì*) means reaching the limit; it refers to abolishing the cruel administration of Qin, which merely extended punishment to the limits of the offense.

Under Qin law, if one person committed a crime, the entire family as well as their neighbors and associates were held liable. The three articles were: first, killing a person; second, wounding a person; and third, theft.
The "Annals on Punishments and Laws" in the *Hanshu* states: "When the High Ancestor first entered the Passes, he established a compact of three articles to eliminate and prune [the laws]."
The common people were greatly relieved by the end of their burdensome oppression. Subsequently, however, the four barbarian tribes had not yet submitted and warfare had not ceased;

thus, the Three-Article Law was insufficient to restrain wickedness. Thereupon, Xiao He, the Chancellor, selected from the Qin laws those items appropriate for the times and established the Nine-Article Code (*jiuzhang lü*).
"Compiled" (*zhu*)—the first character pronounced as *yun* (in the *shangsheng* tone) and the second as *shi* (in the *qusheng* tone)—means to gather together.

Xiao He codified the laws, abolishing the crimes of "participation in slaughter" (*can-yi*) and "collective liability" (*lian-zuo*), while adding the articles on "the commander of a division" (*bu-zhu*) and "one who has prior knowledge" (*jian-zhi*).

He further expanded the *Shi-lü* (Law on Affairs), the *Tan-xing* (Law on Punishment), and the *Yin-hu* (Law on Households) into three sections, totaling nine articles. Shusun Tong added eighteen sections of the *Bang-zhang* (Supplementary Chapters) to cover matters not reached by the existing laws.
Zhang Tang added twenty-seven sections of the *Yue-gong-lü* (Palace Law), and Zhao Yu added the *Chao-lü* (Court Law).
Six sections totaling sixty sections; furthermore, the statement below that "the Great Sūtra has thirty-three [sections]" is an error, for the text is actually in the thirty-fourth fascicle.
*Supplementary Notes on the Three Great Works*, Fascicle 12;
*Supplementary Notes on the Three Great Works of Tiantai*, Fascicle 13. *Zhi Guan* (Cessation and Contemplation); *Fuxing* (Aids to Practice).
Compiled by the Yongjia śramaṇa Shi Congyi. *Fuxing* (Commentary on the *Śīlaparivarta*) says:

This differs from the Vinaya texts (*vinaya-piṭaka*), in which the categories of offenses (*āpatti*) each have their own root, preliminary, and subsequent stages, as well as distinctions based on the mind, the object, whether the offense pertains to the transgression itself or the underlying matter, and whether they are combined or singular.
"Chapters" refers to the five categories of offenses, which constitute seven groups: first, *pārājika*; second, *saṃghāvaśeṣa*;
third, *pāyattika* (pāyattika); fourth, *pratideśanīya*; fifth, *duṣkṛta*—these are the five categories. [The other two are: first, *pārājika*;
second, *saṃghāvaśeṣa*; third, *sthūlātyaya* (sthūlātyaya); fourth, *pāyattika*; fifth, *pratideśanīya*; sixth, *duṣkṛta*; seventh, *durbhāṣita*.

Regarding these seven groups (*sapta-varga*): Nanshan asked, "What is the meaning of the five categories and seven groups? Why are they expanded or condensed? Furthermore, why are there six groups? He replied:

"The establishment of the five categories is what is clarified in our own school within the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, which simply speaks of 'five kinds of offenses,' 'five kinds of regulations,' and 'five groups of offenses.
As for the six groups and seven groups, these are found in the subsequent sections of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*."
Furthermore, the division into seven and five categories possesses three meanings, through which they enter into the fivefold classification: first, equality of name; second, equality of substance;
and third, ultimate equality. Lacking these three, one cannot be subsumed within the [fivefold] group. As for the distinctions between the six and the seven:
the six includes the *duṣkṛta* (minor offense) because it shares the same substance [as the others], whereas the seven excludes the "evil speech" (*pāruṣya*).
Because it is excessive, the body is termed "evil action" (*duṣkṛta*) and the speech is termed "evil speech" (*durukta*);

therefore, this category is divided into two. To provide a comprehensive explanation of these designations: regarding the *pārājika*, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* explains that its meaning is "extreme evil.
This has three senses: first, falling away or sinking, because by violating this precept one has no share in the fruits of the Path. Second...
Such a person is one who does not dwell in communion; they have not only lost the fruits of the Path, but moreover do not enter into the two types of Saṃgha.
Third, they fall away: once this body has been cast off, they fall into the Avīci Great Hell.
As stated in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, they fall into an unfavorable state; as stated in the *Caturvarga-vinaya*, it is like a person whose head has been severed, who cannot rise again.
If one violates this precept, one does not constitute a bhikṣu; this is designated according to the nature of the offense rather than as a formal name.
Furthermore, *pārājika* is translated here as "without remainder" (*wúyú*), a designation derived from the fact that, according to the communal rules, the individual is severed from the community.

Regarding *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, the *Śariputrābhidharma-vinaya-śāstra* (Shanjian lü) states: *saṃgha* means "the Sangha," and *avaśeṣa* means "initial"; it refers to the initial *karmavācanā* for concealment performed before the Sangha.
*Śeṣa* means "remainder," referring to the final *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) for the removal of the offense.
Because this rule is named after its object—the remaining portion of the purification process performed by the Saṃgha—it is called *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. The *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
"Saṃgha" means the community (*saṃgha*), and "avaśeṣa" means remainder. If one commits this offense, the defilement entangles the practitioner so that they are not entirely pure.
The offense of *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (requiring suspension) is expiated by the Saṃgha. In the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, it is explained that *saṃghāvaśeṣa* is as previously stated;
furthermore, it says "there is a remainder" (*avaśeṣa*), which is named because the practice of the Dharma is not yet severed. The *Vinayamātṛkā* states:

"As for *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, it is like a person who has been struck by another and is left with only the throat remaining; therefore, it is called 'residual' (*avaśeṣa*). It is necessary to deal with this matter promptly."
For the sake of rescue, the Vinaya states that if one commits this offense, one should be compelled to undergo *parivāsa* (probation) and so forth, because it is proximate to a grave offense.
The term *sthūlātyaya* has already been explained as before. As for *pāyattika*, its meaning is translated as "falling.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that it means "falling into the hells of burning, boiling, and concealment. The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* clarifies this in ten ways.
