There are one hundred and twenty types [of offenses] categorized into thirty; because these arise from matters of wealth and property, they involve the commission of greed and arrogance, and thus require forced relinquishment to the Sangha, which is why they are called *niḥsargika*.
*Niḥsargika* was formerly translated as "relinquishment and falling" (*she-duo*).

As for the remaining ninety [offenses], which are to be confessed individually to another person, although their essential nature (*āpatti-tattva*) belongs to the same category, the confession is identical. These are the *pratideśanīya* [offenses].
*Śaṇi* (舍尼) is translated as "confessing toward that [person]"; it is named after its remedial object.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "This offense should be confessed. This refers to the words for repentance found throughout this Vinaya.
Regarding *duṣkṛta* (突吉羅), the *Sudarsana-vinaya* says: "*Duṣ*" means evil; "*kṛta*" means to do. (4)
The *Vibhaṅga-vinaya-mūla* states that the meaning of *śikṣā-karaṇīya* is translated as "that which should be learned. A Hu monk explained it as "guarding the precepts.
Because these offenses are subtle and extremely difficult to maintain, they are named according to the practice of learning and guarding them as one goes along.
This one category is divided into two groups: those of the body are called "misdeeds" (*duṣkṛta*), and those of speech are called "misstatements" (*durbhāṣita*). These two... [are not...]

The precepts of concentration (dhyāna-śīla) are spoken of in terms of their objective basis as encompassing all six classes of offenses; however, if one discusses the actual substance of the offense, the doubt and lack of faith constitute a *duṣkṛta*.
The mention in the text of "three offenses" or "two offenses" is merely an abbreviated enumeration of instances involving doubt.

Among the seven methods for settling disputes (*saptadharmā vinayādhikaraṇa-samatha*), such offenses are also present, but they are included here because the parties are contending over the four types of disputes (*caturvidham adhikaraṇam*) while remaining mutually ignorant of the facts.

The seven medicinal prescriptions for restraint are employed to eliminate [transgressions]; since their textual meanings are extensive and their underlying principles and characteristics are profound, even laborious exposition would ultimately fail to exhaustively fathom them;
therefore, they are omitted here and not described. What has been explained above concerns the names and meanings of the *pien-zu* (aggregates of offenses).
Regarding the statement that each offense possesses its "root," "expedient means," and "subsequent action," first, the *pārājika* offense of sexual misconduct itself has its own...

There are four stages: first, the remote preparatory effort; second, the intermediate preparatory effort; third, the proximate preparatory effort; and fourth, the physical union, which is termed the fundamental act of sexual misconduct.
Since this is the case, one may infer the other cases—such as killing, stealing, and great falsehood—by analogy. This meaning is explained in detail in the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra*.
Regarding the first of the ten unwholesome paths of action, the karma of killing, it is like a butcher who, when about to slaughter a sheep:
First, having conceived the intent to kill, one rises from one's bed, takes the payment, and proceeds to the sheep market;

having paid the price, one seizes the sheep and brings it back to feed and water it, then delivers it to the slaughterhouse while holding a blade or staff, whether striking or stabbing it before its life has ended—this is called the preliminary application (*prayoga*) of killing.
According to the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra*, this is termed "conformity" (*anuvartana*).
At the very moment when this [victim] dies, the manifest and unmanifest karma (*vijñapti-avijñapti-karman*) of that [agent] constitutes the fundamental path of action (*mūla-karmapatha*) of killing.
Because the unmanifest karma of killing continues to follow and persist after that moment, it is called the "subsequent arising" (*pṛṣṭha*) of killing.
This applies even if, at a later time, one skins, cuts, trims, washes, weighs, sells, or cooks [the victim].
Or, when eating, praising its excellence constitutes a moment of informative karma (*vijñapti-karma*); such acts are likewise termed "subsequent to killing" (*pṛṣṭha-karma*).

Since this applies to killing, it should be understood accordingly for stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, and so forth. Furthermore, one should know that within the ten wholesome courses of action (*daśa-kuśala-karmapatha*), at the time of receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*), upon entering the ordination platform (*sīmā-maṇḍala*) and prostrating before the assembly of bhikṣus, one makes a sincere utterance to request a preceptor (*upādhyāya*).
From the teacher’s preliminary announcement (*jñapti*) up to the second *karmavācanā* and so forth—all these are called the preparatory application (*prayoga*) of wholesome karma.
At the single moment when the third *karmavācanā* is completed, the manifest (*vijñapti*) and unmanifest (*avijñapti*) karma is what is termed the fundamental path of action (*maula-karmapatha*).
From that point onward, until the four reliances (*catur-śaraṇa*) are proclaimed and other subsequent stages, the manifest and unmanifest karma continues to evolve in succession.
All such karma is termed "subsequent" (*pṛṣṭha*). Of the second category, there are three preliminary applications (*prayoga*); of the third and fourth, there is one preliminary application each;
and of the fifth category, there is only that which arises from mind, body, and speech, being solely the fundamental act (*maula*) itself, as there is no preliminary application.

However, because the volition (*cetanā*) that moves the body and speech also possesses distant and near preliminary applications, it is said: "If one gives rise to the thought desiring to cause the body..."
Wearing the three robes (*tricīvara*) and so forth in a disordered manner constitutes the preliminary preparation; this is detailed in the *Vinaya-śāstra*, so it need not be recorded here at length.
"Regarding the mind" refers to the mind capable of committing the offense. "Regarding the object" refers to the object upon which the act is based.
"If it is a sin" refers to offenses such as *pārājika* or *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. "If it is a matter" refers to sexual misconduct, theft, and so forth.
Regarding "matters such as these": because there are matters such as the transgression of the precepts, there are likewise offenses such as the transgression of the precepts.

The Abhidharma speaks of "the accusation of an offense" (*āpatti-udbhāvana*) and "the accusation of a matter" (*vastu-udbhāvana*); indeed, these are what are termed "offenses" (*āpatti*) and "matters" (*vastu*).

The *Maudgalyāyana-paripṛcchā-sūtra* states: "One who violates the *śaikṣa-dharmas* (minor rules of training) shall fall into hell for a lifespan equal to five hundred years of the Cāturmahārājika devas."
For ninety thousand years among humans, one falls into hell for violating a *pāṭidesanīya* offense;
for three hundred and sixty million years among humans, one falls into hell for violating a *pāyattika* offense;

for two hundred and forty million years among humans, one falls into hell for violating a *sthūlātyaya* offense; and for fifty... among humans... [one falls into hell for violating a *duṣkṛta* offense].
For sixty thousand *koṭis* of years, one falls into hell for committing a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense;
for two hundred and thirty-four thousand *koṭis* of years, one falls into hell for committing a *pārājika* offense;
and for nine hundred twenty-one billion and sixty thousand *koṭis* of years, one falls into hell for violating the Mahāyāna Brahma Net Precepts.
It is said that one who commits a *pārājika* offense remains in hell for two or three *kalpas*. "If double" means that one ceases [the practice] by committing two offenses;
"if single" means that one ceases by committing one offense. Therefore, the subsequent text speaks of "double observance and double violation," and so forth.
As for the "four reliances" (*catur-niśraya*), they are: reliance on rag-robes (*pāṃsukūla*), reliance on alms-food (*piṇḍapāta*), and reliance on dwelling at the foot of a tree (*vṛkṣamūla*).
Sitting on a seat made of decayed wood and relying on medicine made of decayed wood—by means of these four dharmas, one becomes a bhikṣu; the details are contained in the Vinaya texts.

Regarding the begging of a "life-buoy" (phun-nang), it is also said that according to tradition, those who cross the sea in the Western Regions mostly make bags from bird feathers or carry large [skins].
The bladders of oxen or sea-going ships, when lost at sea, are used to blow air into them so that one may float; it is often by means of these that people reach the shore.
Furthermore, it is said that there are many kinds of flotation bags (*pūlaka*), though they have not yet been fully detailed here. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
"From now on, I permit the bhikṣus to possess flotation bags made of either sheepskin or oxhide. This refers to what constitutes a flotation bag.
This is the authentic teaching, not mere hearsay. *Líng* (翎) is pronounced with the *rùndīng* (魯丁) rhyme; it refers to the feathers of an arrow.
*Pāo* (脬) is pronounced with the *pǔjiāo* (普交) rhyme.

That scripture, the *Lìwǔyísānlánerdītījī* (彼列五夷三蘭二提一吉), in its "Chapter on World-transcending Precepts" (*Lòushìjiānjièpǐn*), says: "If one discriminates between male and female, or non-male and non-female, by means of the mind..."

If a bodhisattva commits a pārājika offense by mentally discriminating between animals, hungry ghosts, men, women, or those who are neither male nor female, or between various devas, men, women, or those who are neither male nor female; or if they commit a pārājika offense through physical or verbal actions that render them incapable of attaining the Three Vehicles;
or if they receive the supramundane bodhisattva precepts yet fail to give rise to loving-kindness—[in these cases, they have committed a pārājika].
Compassion is the basis for a bodhisattva’s transgression of a pārājika offense if, through action of body or speech, they are incapable of attaining the three vehicles;
or if, regarding another's property— whether small or large, long or short, with color or shape, stationary or moving,
concealed or moved, sealed or stored— they give rise to the thought of theft.
If one intends to commit a *pārājika* offense, or if through bodily or verbal action one becomes incapable of attaining the Three Vehicles;
or if one gives rise to a mind of false speech and commits a *pārājika*, or through bodily or verbal action becomes incapable of attaining the Three Vehicles;
or if, regarding tree leaves, bark, or sap, one desires to take them with the mind—one commits a *bodhisattva-saṃghāvaśeṣa*. Or if by means of the body...

If one engages in verbal conduct that is incompatible with attaining the Three Vehicles, or gives rise to thoughts of singing, dancing, music, flowers, incense, and necklaces, this constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense for a bodhisattva.

If one engages in physical or verbal conduct that is incompatible with attaining the Three Vehicles, or gives rise to thoughts of high, wide, and large beds, this constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense for a bodhisattva. If, by means of body or speech...

If one performs actions with body or speech that are incompatible with attaining the Three Vehicles, yet conceives the thought that it is permissible to eat after midday, this constitutes a *pārājika* offense for a bodhisattva.

If one performs actions with body or speech that are incompatible with attaining the Three Vehicles, yet conceives the thought that it is permissible to handle gold, silver, or precious treasures, this constitutes a *pārājika* offense for a bodhisattva.
If one performs actions with body or speech that are incompatible with attaining the Three Vehicles... [text truncated]
If one conceives the thought that riding [a vehicle] is like shaving the body hair or clipping the nails into the shape of a crescent moon, this Bodhisattva commits a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If one’s physical or verbal conduct is incapable of attaining the Three Vehicles, yet one conceives the thought of cutting or chopping grass and trees, this constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If one’s physical or verbal conduct is incapable of attaining the Three Vehicles, yet one conceives...
If one slanders another’s reputation—whether regarding their physical appearance, lineage, wealth, technical skills, vehicles, physical strength, or the like—it constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If, through actions of body or speech, one causes another to become incapable of attaining the Three Vehicles, or if one [misappropriates] property belonging to the Buddha, Dharma, or Sangha;
or flowers, incense, or unguents; or clothing or precious jewels; or if a Bodhisattva...
If one steps upon or treads over a Buddha-stūpa, a place where the Buddha walked, a Bodhi tree,
or the site where he turned the Wheel of Dharma, it is an offense of *pāyattika*. If one is faithless and incapable of attaining the Three Vehicles,
or if one sticks out the tongue, moves the eyes, or violates the various dignified demeanors while harboring such thoughts, it is an offense of *dukkaṭa*.

If one performs actions of body or speech that are incapable of attaining the Three Vehicles—such as seeing the property, medicine, or various articles of another and falsely manifesting a desire for profit, or speaking of another's faults—if such a thought arises, one commits a *pāyattika* (offense requiring confession).

This refers to the aforementioned scriptural passage concerning those who perform actions of body or speech that are incapable of attaining the Three Vehicles; the same applies to the records (*jì*) therein.
The phrasing must be revised as follows: "Five *pārājikas*, five *saṃghāvaśeṣas*, three *sthūlātyayas*, two *pāyattikas*, one *pratideśanīya*, and one *duṣkṛta*.
Furthermore, that sutra states: The Buddha told Mañjuśrī, "There are two kinds of precepts, namely those of body and speech, not those of mind, consciousness, or intellect.
If precepts were of mind, consciousness, or intellect, there would be no person who maintains the precepts. Why is this? Because the mind..."

Because they are difficult to restrain when they take objects as their conditions (*ālambana*) and because they have no fixed abode, Mañjuśrī, there is no morality (*śīla*) in mind, intellect, or consciousness;

morality exists only in body and speech. This is because mind, intellect, and consciousness are not the locus of the offense of killing. Furthermore, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-vinaya-saṃgraha* states that there are four *pārājika* offenses:
first, for the sake of greed for gain, one praises oneself and disparages others; second, being personally stingy...

Regarding the three things that one who practices stinginess with the Dharma does not speak of: first, anger, harsh speech, and the infliction of harm with sticks or stones; second, refusing to accept repentance;
and third, slandering the Bodhisattva-piṭaka by teaching counterfeit teachings. Furthermore, it is said that a bodhisattva prohibits what is prohibited and permits what is permitted.
Moreover, the *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra* states that even a person of the Śrāvaka vehicle should not give rise to even a single [unwholesome thought].
To think of receiving a future body again is called the observance of precepts by a śrāvaka; for a bodhisattva, this is called a great violation of the precepts.
For a bodhisattva to be able to endure and accept the body throughout immeasurable kalpas without giving rise to weariness or aversion is called the observance of precepts by a bodhisattva;
for a śrāvaka, this is called a great violation of the precepts. For this reason, the rules of what is permitted and what is prohibited are taught for the sake of bodhisattvas.
Regarding the prohibitive precepts (*pratikṣepa-śīla*) taught for the sake of *śrāvakas*, what are called the "opening and prohibiting precepts" (*apavāda-anujñā-śīla*) of a bodhisattva?

If a bodhisattva, while engaged in the practice of the Mahāyāna, should commit a transgression against the precepts during the first part of the day, yet does not depart from the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-citta*) during the middle part of the day, the body of this bodhisattva’s precepts remains undestroyed. And so forth... [until]... how is it so?

For this reason, when a person of the Bodhisattva Vehicle observes the precepts of permission and prohibition, even if they should commit an offense, they ought not to lose mindfulness or give rise to groundless anxiety and regret that distresses their own mind. As for those who commit offenses against the Śrāvaka Vehicle, it constitutes a violation of the Śrāvaka’s pure precepts.
Why is this? Because the Śrāvaka upholds the precepts to sever and eliminate afflictions, seeking only [their own liberation].
Because of this meaning, the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* states that the Śrāvaka-yāna maintains only prohibitive precepts (*pratiṣedha-śīla*).

Setting aside the fruit while retaining the cause, the text further states: "If one distinguishes between cause and fruit to correspond with the name 'offense,' there are causal *sthūlātyaya* and resultant *sthūlātyaya*, as annotated previously; if it serves as the preliminary means for a grave offense, it is called causal *sthūlātyaya*."
The primary offense committed alone is termed *phalaṇa* (fruit).

Among the monks, the formal announcement (*jñapti*) is termed "lowering the mind" (*adhyāśaya-namana*); the separate residence (*parivāsa*) is termed "banishment" (*pravāsanīya*); and even the forfeiture of the thirty-five matters along with the "original day" (*mūla-ahar*) and so forth are termed "punitive banishment" (*tarjanīya-pravāsanīya*).

Regarding the procedure for making a formal announcement (*karmavācanā*) among the Sangha, the *Nanshan Chao* states: "The announcement of the pure monk requires that one fully observe the proper deportment.
The announcement is as follows: 'Venerable Sangha, please listen. I, the bhikṣu [Name], have committed a deliberate emission, which constitutes one *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
I do not recall the number of times it occurred, but I concealed it for one night, up to a hundred nights. I have now requested from the Sangha the period of concealment for a hundred nights.'"
The Saṃgha having already granted me the *parivāsa* (probation) for concealment for one hundred nights, I, the bhikṣu [Name], have already practiced it for several days;
there remain several days yet to be practiced. I inform the Venerable Ones that I am practicing the *parivāsa*.
If five or ten persons are assembled together, they should announce collectively: "Venerable Sirs, please listen."
The remaining phrasing is the same as in the previous case; if they do not all assemble, it likewise does not constitute a separate assembly. This is the method for a single person to confess.
If a virtuous or eminent person comes to the monastery, one must necessarily invite them into the residence and inform them;

it should not be done at the gate, as that would be considered frivolous and disrespectful. Regarding what is called "lowering the mind," the *Sudarsana-vinaya* states: "One performs the *mānatta*..."
*Nāntamānatta* (那埵摩那埵) is translated here as "subduing arrogance" (*zhéfú gònggāo*) and is also termed "humbling the mind" (*xià yì*).
"Humbling the mind" refers to serving the Saṃgha; the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* also calls it "analyzing and subduing" (*xīfú xià yì*).

Regarding the name "separate dwelling" (*biézù*, *parivāsa*), the *Nanshan chao* states that there are four types of remedies for the offense of *saṃghāvaśeṣa*: first, the remedy for the fault of the emotional concealment [of the offense].
This refers to *pārivāsika-pārivāsika*, which is translated as "concealment" (*chabang*) or "separate residence" (*biezhu*). The *Vinayamātṛkā-śāstra* asks:
"What is meant by 'separate residence'? It means residing in a separate room and not being permitted to share the same space as the Saṃgha.
Even if one enters among the monks, one may neither engage in conversation nor provide answers. Second is the treatment for concealment.
"Offenses" refers to *duṣkṛta* (transgressions), as will be explained later regarding the formal methods of confession; these precede and follow the *parivāsa* (probation) for concealment.
"The three disciplinary measures for *saṃghāvaśeṣa*" refer to the mental transgressions, namely *mānāpya*. *Mānāpya* means "pleasing the mind":
although one has previously rejoiced in one's own mind, by now giving rise to shame and remorse, one also causes the community of monks to rejoice because of what preceded it.
Because of joy, one shares it for a short time; because of that short time, one first attains the name of "joy. The community of monks exclaims:
"This person, through this [act], has repented and will no longer give rise to afflictions; they have become a pure person. Therefore, they are 'Joyful' (Pramoda).
The four methods for treating the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses are as follows: *ābhāṣaṇa*. *Ābhāṣaṇa* is translated here as "calling into the assembly" (*karma*).
*Mó* (the *Vinayamātṛkā*) further states that it means "uprooting the roots of transgression. The *Vinayamātṛkā* says: "Pure precepts arise, resulting in pure liberation;
because one skillfully maintains them, they emerge and proceed. The *Nanshan Jieshu* (Nanshan’s Commentary on the Precepts) states:

"The reason for including [the removal of offenses] among the twenty types of *saṃgha* is that the offenses of the two categories (the *pārājika* and *saṃghāvaśeṣa*) are as grave and profound as the karmic obstacles of death; therefore, many people and a powerful environment are required [to effect their removal]."

This is because those who have committed an offense must suppress their superior resolve and sever the continuity [of the transgression]. Furthermore, the *Yejieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states:
"In the border regions, where monks are few, five persons are employed; in the central lands, where monks are numerous, this number is doubled to ten.

For offenses involving the two grave categories (*pārājika*) or those bordering them, because the offender’s remorse is superficial, the number is doubled again to twenty persons. The present text follows this abbreviated approach. Therefore:

Regarding the phrase "up to and including," the methods for dealing with these matters, the terminology, and the various sections of the Vinaya texts—as well as those detailed in the *Sifen-lü shanbu suiji jiemo* (The Commentary on the Four-Part Vinaya)—are fully explained therein; I shall not trouble to record them here.

As for the "thirty-five matters of deprivation," the *Shanbu* states that there are seven different types of deprivation which together constitute the thirty-five. Of these, the first five matters involve depriving [the offender] of their followers.

Furthermore, there are five things one should not do: first, one should not confer the full precepts upon others; second, one should not accept dependence from others; third, one should not keep śrāmaṇeras;
fourth, one should not accept an appointment by the Saṃgha to instruct bhikṣuṇīs; fifth, even if appointed by the Saṃgha, one should not go [to perform the instruction].
The second set of five matters concerns the deprivation of one's wisdom and capability: first, one should not recite the Prātimokṣa; second, if...
1. One should not answer questions regarding the Vinaya within the Sangha; 2. If the Sangha appoints one to perform a *karmavācanā*, one should not do so; 3.
If the Sangha selects and gathers those of wisdom to deliberate on communal affairs, one must not be included in that instance; 4.
If the Sangha appoints one to carry out a mission of trust, one should not do so. These three and five matters involve the forfeiture of one’s compliance.
Furthermore, there are five things one must not do: first, one must not enter a village too early; second, one must not return at dusk; third, one should associate with bhikṣus;
fourth, one should not associate with laypeople or non-Buddhists; fifth, one should comply with the instructions of the bhikṣus and must not speak contrary words.
Regarding these four and five matters, if one violates them, it constitutes a subsequent offense that severs the continuity [of the precepts]; the first of these must not be committed.

One should not commit other offenses similar to this, namely the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (formal meeting) and the *pratikarman* (reproach). "Other" refers to those belonging to the lower categories [the *pāyattika* and *pratideśanīya*].
"Similar" means either similar in kind or similar by way of arising from this. Similarity in kind refers to offenses within the same category;

similarity by way of arising refers to cases such as being reproached for touching [a woman] and yet sitting in private with a woman. Thirdly, if it is more serious than this, it refers to committing a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense).
After having been disciplined, if one commits again any of the four offenses such as *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, one should not object to the *karmavācanā* (formal act);

five things should not be censured regarding the person performing the *karmavācanā*. Regarding these five matters, their provisions are confiscated: first, if a virtuous bhikṣu spreads out a seat for him as an offering, he should not accept it;
second, he should not accept another’s washing of his feet; third, he should not accept another’s [assistance in] settling [him].
Regarding the four items for washing the feet, one should not accept having one's leather sandals wiped by another. Fifth, one should not accept having one's body rubbed or massaged by another.

These six items deprive one of respect; that is, one should not accept the prostrations, inquiries after one’s welfare, joining of palms, welcoming, or the offering of robes and bowls from virtuous bhikṣus. Seventh, these five items deprive one of the realization of the truth.
Regarding other matters, one should not: (1) bring up the good bhikṣu for the purpose of making him reflect; (2) make a formal confession on his behalf;
(3) testify to other matters; (4) obstruct the *poṣadha*; (5) obstruct the *pravāraṇā*; (6) dispute with a good bhikṣu. These are the thirty-five matters.
As for "treatment by returning to the original day" (*mūlāpakarṣa*), the character "treat" (*zhi*) is to be inserted [before "day"].
The *Pingqu* (Commentary on the Equalization) states: "Regarding these two preceding cases, if one conceals [the offense], it is treated according to the former rule;

if one does not conceal it, it is treated according to the latter rule—in both instances, the offense is expiated. However, if within those two rules there is a repeated offense, both rules are violated;

in such cases, the *pārivāsika* (probation) must be granted again from the beginning (*mūlāpakarṣa*). For example, if one was undergoing a hundred-night *parivāsa* and has already completed fifty nights."
If one commits the same category of offense again, the previous fifty nights are all lost and one must undergo another hundred nights;
therefore, it is called "punishment for returning to the original day. Since this is the case for a hundred nights, it is likewise so for offenses committed during the six-night period;
because one has violated the Sangha's command, the previous disciplinary status is forfeited. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "Kāḷodāyin committed an intentional emission..."
While he was undergoing the six-night *mānatta* penance for a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense of intentional emission of semen that had not been concealed,
after [certain] days had passed and [other] days had not yet passed, he again intentionally emitted semen and committed another *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense,
which he did not conceal. Kālodāyin spoke to the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus reported it [to the Buddha].
The Buddha said: "One shall undergo *pārivāsika* (probation) for the original offense. The ritual procedures and textual passages for this *pārivāsika* are fully detailed in the Vinaya.
Question: For what reason is *pārivāsika* prescribed? Answer: It is for the purpose of analyzing and subduing the mind. Question:
Why is *pārivāsika* prescribed for the purpose of subduing the mind? Answer: If one returns to practicing according to the original [offense], it causes the mind to analyze and subdue itself.
A bhikṣu thinks to himself: "This person’s fetters and latent tendencies are heavy and thick;

I shall subject him to *mūlāpakarṣa* (treatment from the beginning) so that he may feel shame and not commit them again. At that time, the bhikṣus resolve to grant him *mānāpya*; for this reason, it is called *mūlāpakarṣa*.

The arising of [wrong] views immediately destroys right view; this should be corroborated by the twelve passages from the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* (or *Mahāyāna Sūtra*), which are omitted here for brevity.
Regarding the objects of the various views below, it is said that right view is destroyed. Citing the six heretical teachers, it says: "If one possesses shame and remorse, one falls into hell;
if one lacks shame and remorse, one does not fall into hell. This is from the tenth fascicle of the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*.
In fascicle seven, it is because the six teachers preached the Dharma for King Ajātaśatru.

Furthermore, in fascicle thirty-two, it clarifies that those who sever their roots of goodness distance themselves from virtuous friends, do not listen to the true Dharma, engage in unwholesome reflection, and do not abide in accordance with the Dharma;
specifically, they hold that there is no giver and no receiver, no cause and no fruit, no good and no evil, and no father and no [mother].
The statement that "there is no mother, no noble ones, no noble dharmas, and no nirvāṇa" likely contains an error regarding the "twelve [links]," as it contradicts other teachings.
Furthermore, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, fascicle 35, clarifies the sixty-two views; one should know that the arising of these sixty-two views is precisely the destruction of right view.
Moreover, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that Subhūti [spoke thus] for the sake of those seeking the three vehicles in future generations who hear...
The Buddha taught that emptiness is the nature of non-existence; however, because their offenses are grave and their wisdom dull, they grasp at the sign of emptiness and immediately ask:
"Who is defiled and who is pure? Why is an evil worldling called 'defiled,' while a virtuous renunciant is called 'pure'?
Such people do not understand the profound meaning of the Buddha’s words. Because they speak of this emptiness based on worldly matters, they ask: "What is it? regarding what was said.

Using the observance of precepts and so forth as the causal condition for the arising of false views—thereby destroying right view—and because of this destruction of right view, one destroys the precepts and deportment due to minor causes and conditions, lacking any sense of fear or restraint;
relying upon laypeople for sustenance, one then speaks falsely to seek profit, clothing, food, and the like, thereby sowing the seeds of the destruction of right livelihood. This is a transgression.
Therefore, one falls into the three evil realms. Now, in this record, it is stated that violating the first three groups [of precepts] is called "breaking the precepts" (*śīla-bheda*);
violating the lower four groups is called "breaking the dignified demeanor" (*ācāra-bheda*); and the four perversions and five perversions are called "breaking right livelihood" (*ājīva-bheda*).

This is entirely the intention of the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, for that treatise explains in detail the breaking of the precepts, the breaking of dignified demeanor, and the breaking of right livelihood.
Furthermore, regarding the passage below that states, "Since [one] takes emptiness as evil, it is analogous to the preceding [discussion of] greed and clinging," this is likely an error;
it should read, "it is analogous to the preceding [discussion of] the loving mind that destroys the *prātimokṣa* precepts. Moreover, regarding the passage that states, "Firmly adhering to views...

is analogous to the preceding [discussion of] greed for the five desires," etc., this is also likely an error; it should read, "it is analogous to the preceding [discussion of] being deeply attached to birth and death as having existence (*bhava*)."
The "karmas" and so forth refute the principle of the precepts.
Both belong to the *Brahma*-sound, for this land invokes that [Brahma] sound; thus, this region translates those words as a "land of culture and refinement" (*wenwu guo*).
It is said that "frontier lands" represent one form of praise and another of censure, resulting in these two distinct views,
as analyzed in detail in the *Xuanshan Bunzhu*.
Nanshan also established three types of repentance.

The text is found within the *Sifenlü xingshichao* (A Manual on the Practice of the Dharmaguptaka Vinaya). Now, Jingxi criticizes it in two ways: first, he criticizes the Lesser Vehicle for not permitting the repentance of grave offenses;

second, he criticizes its assessment of the practitioner's stage as being too high. However, the three types of repentance established by Nanshan are actually "repentance according to principle" (*lishan*), not "repentance through ritual action" (*shishan*).
If one follows the *Miaoxuan*, it states that the *śīlaskandha* (the collection of precepts) of the Lesser Vehicle does not permit the re-establishment of the precepts through repentance.
The *Tara-piṭaka* instructs that even one who has committed a grave offense should contemplate the Buddha-body; "Buddha-body" means contemplating emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
If this is so, although the Vinaya-piṭaka of the Hīnayāna lacks the principle of repentance for grave offenses, the Sūtra-piṭaka does indeed contain the principle of repentance for grave offenses.
Thus, when Jingxi states that there is no repentance for grave offenses in the Hīnayāna, he speaks merely from the perspective of the Vinaya-piṭaka, which does not establish such a practice.

The *Lǐchàn* (Ritual of Repentance) merely refutes [the Lesser Vehicle] from this perspective; however, if one were to refute it by relying on the *Lǐchàn* found within the Sūtra Piṭaka, that would likely not be the case.
Otherwise, how could one reconcile this with the text of the *Miaoxuan*? Question: If the Lesser Vehicle is thus [limited], how does it differ from the Mahāyāna? Answer:
The Mahāyāna Vinaya-piṭaka, such as that found in the *Brahmajāla-sūtra*, permits the repentance of the four pārājika offenses. It allows for their restoration.

Furthermore, because it increases one's reception [of the precepts], the "confession" (pratikarmāya) found in the Śrāvaka Vinaya-piṭaka—termed "learning through repentance" (xuehui)—cannot be compared to this.
Moreover, the Mahāyāna Sūtra-piṭaka, such as the Vaipulya sūtras and others, clarifies that through ritual confession (vastu-pratikarma), even the grave offenses of pārājika are eliminated;

one returns to original purity and once again becomes a Great Bhikṣu. In contrast, although the Śrāvaka Sūtra-piṭaka clarifies that one may repent heavy offenses by contemplating the principle (li), [it does not provide for such restoration].

However, there is no formal ritual for the repentance and eradication of *pārājika* offenses; this is why the third record in the preceding text states that the gates of the Hīnayāna teachings do not even permit such repentance.
All of this refers simply to the fact that within the *Vinaya-piṭaka* and the *Sūtra-piṭaka*, no formal ritual for the repentance and eradication of transgressions is established.
Nevertheless, both the *Wenju* on the *Guanwuliangshoujing* and the *Cān-bōluómì* clarify three types [of repentance].

Repentance (*pratikramaṇa*) is common to both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna; however, in Hīnayāna sūtras such as the Āgamas, it is taught that one who has committed a sexual transgression should cultivate the "snake-mouth visualization" (*sarpa-mukha-saṃjñā*).

If this visualization is perfected, the offense of lust is immediately extinguished. This is because repentance based on grasping signs (*nimitta*) is also termed "repentance of phenomena" (*vastu-pratikramaṇa*);

only "repentance of non-arising" (*anutpāda-pratikramaṇa*) is properly called "repentance of principle" (*tattva-pratikramaṇa*). Furthermore, the *Dhyānapāramitā-śāstra* states that within the Vinaya...
It has not yet been clarified how one confesses the four pārājika offenses; however, the *Āgama* scriptures clarify the repentance for these four pārājikas. That scripture states:
"One should invite thirty pure bhikṣus into the great assembly, and the bhikṣu who has committed the offense should personally disclose it.
The Saṃgha shall then perform the *karmavācanā* for him. Furthermore, before the Triple Gem, he should perform various ritual practices and recite the Prātimokṣa one thousand times."

One should know that through this, one immediately attains purification. Although the Vinaya-piṭaka of the Hīnayāna does not explicitly clarify the ritual procedures for repentance and the eradication of *pārājika* offenses, they nonetheless exist within the Sūtra-piṭaka.

If that is so, then although the Vinaya-piṭaka of the Hīnayāna has not clarified both the procedural (*kriyā*) and the principled (*tattva*) methods of repentance for eradicating the four *pārājika* offenses, all such methods are indeed present within the Sūtra-piṭaka. This is consistent with the standards of the Nanshan Vinaya school.
The *Chao* (Commentary) selects the sūtras of the Initial Teaching (*ādikarmika-yāna*) as being spurious, whereas Tiantai does not say they are spurious. Now, within the *Zhiguan*, it says:
"If one commits a minor transgression among the matters of violation, the Vinaya texts all contain methods for repentance;

if the method of repentance is successfully accomplished, it is entirely called 'pure,' whereby the precepts are purified and hindrances are transformed, making it easy to clarify through *śamatha-vipaśyanā*. This clarifies that one repents minor [transgressions] in reliance upon the Vinaya."

It causes the purification of precepts, the transformation of obstacles, and the accomplishment of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, thereby transforming the ordinary person into a sage. As for not citing the Vinaya texts regarding the ritual confession of grave offenses:

although disclosure (*āviṣkaraṇa*) and training (*śikṣā*) may indeed lead to purity and do not obstruct participation in monastic affairs, they cannot, in this very life, bring about transcendence from birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) or the attainment of the fruits of sainthood (*āryaphala*). Therefore, these are not cited here to clarify the accomplishment of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
Furthermore, the *Guangming wenju* (Text on Radiant Phrases) clearly explains the ritual procedures for repentance (*karmavācanā*) within the Vinaya;
it states that one who has purified all five categories of offenses according to the Vinaya texts is called "pure" (*viśuddha*).

This refers to the fact that repenting grave and heinous offenses (*pārājika*) does not obstruct one’s monastic affairs, and is not a matter of attaining meditative concentration or wisdom to transform the mundane into the sacred. The *Zhi guan* (Cessation and Contemplation) further states: "If one commits a grave offense..."

Regarding the statement that "in the Buddha-dharma, those who have died [as laypeople] have no repentance-method in the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna)": this clarifies that while the Small Vehicle has no method for repentance, if one relies on the Mahāyāna, its repentance is permitted;
this explains that by relying on the Mahāyāna, one repents the pārājika offenses so that śamatha and vipaśyanā become clear and lucid.

As for "the Small Vehicle having no method for repentance," this means that within the Vinaya-piṭaka of the Small Vehicle, there is no repentance for grave offenses based on ultimate principle (li); it does not mean that the Small Vehicle Vinaya-piṭaka lacks [repentance] altogether.

This refers to the ritual repentance for *pārājika* offenses; yet, although the Vinaya-piṭaka of the Hīnayāna lacks [a formal method] for repenting grave offenses based on principle, the Sūtra-piṭaka allows those who have committed a grave offense to contemplate emptiness and recollect the Buddha’s Dharma-body, which is precisely repentance according to the principle of non-arising.
This is fully explained in the *Miaoxuan* and the *Wenju* of the *Guanwuliangshoujing*; I hope that future scholars will carefully consider this.

"Jiān guān" (間關) refers to the manner of entering and exiting with difficulty; it also describes the appearance of traversing rugged terrain and enduring hardship to reach one's destination. "Dǐ zhài" (抵債) means to pay off a debt.
The Master Kai of the Western Capital said: "Because the power of the outflow-free [wisdom] is so strong, it is not a debt owed to the three miserable realms; thus it is called 'paying off a debt.

This is like the separate two-fold repentances for the Sangha in the Hīnayāna, or even such things as the provisional texts of the Lesser Vehicle regarding the expiation of the offense of *pārājika*."
"Sangha" (僧) means "a multitude," referring to four or more persons; "individual" (別) refers to three or fewer.

A communal confession (*sāṃghika-prāyaścitta*) is like the *mānatva* penance and formal acts (*karmavācanā*) performed among twenty monks; an individual confession (*pratyekaprāyaścitta*) is like the confessions for *pāyattika* and *duṣkṛta* offenses.
Because there are these two modes—communal and individual—it is called the "dual confession of Sangha and individual. As it is said:

Regarding the expiation of *pārājika* offenses: in the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*), one who confesses and seeks the eradication of a *pārājika* offense is merely termed a "learner through repentance" (*śikṣādattaka*).
They rank below the fully ordained monks (*bhikṣu*) and above the novices (*śrāmaṇera*). The *Sutra on Treating the Illnesses of Meditation* states:

"A bhikṣu who has committed a grave offense and performs repentance should remove his *saṃghāṭī* robe and wear an *antarvāsaka*; he should give rise to a mind of shame and remorse, and perform menial labor for the Saṃgha."
Regarding practices such as sweeping latrines or carrying away excrement, those who require the ritual for repentance should be instructed according to that Vinaya.
The formula for requesting it is as follows: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen! I, the bhikṣu [Name], have committed a pārājika offense of sexual misconduct without concealment.
Now I request the pārājika precepts from the Saṃgha. May the Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant me the pārājika precepts. This is requested three times.
The Saṃgha having requested the consent and asked for agreement, he replied: "Regarding the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for the *pārājika* precept, it should be said:
'Venerable Saṃgha, listen! This bhikṣu so-and-so has committed the *pārājika* offense of sexual misconduct without concealment; he now requests from the Saṃgha the *pārājika* precept.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, and the Saṃgha is willing to grant its consent, let the Saṃgha now grant the [pārājika] precept to this bhikṣu so-and-so.'"
The formal motion for the *pārājika* discipline is as follows: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu [Name] has committed a *pārājika* offense of sexual misconduct without concealment, and now requests the *pārājika* discipline from the Saṃgha.
The Saṃgha now grants the *pārājika* discipline to this bhikṣu [Name]. Which elders consent to the Saṃgha granting the *pārājika* discipline to this bhikṣu [Name]?"
"Whoever approves [of this], remain silent; whoever does not approve, speak. This is the first *karmavācanā*; the second and third are likewise spoken.
Since the Saṃgha has approved and granted the *pārājika* discipline to the bhikṣu so-and-so, and since the Saṃgha remains silent in approval, this matter is thus upheld.
The *Vinayamātṛkā* states: "Once the procedure for repentance (*pratideśanā*) via the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* has been performed, one is called 'pure' and maintains [the precepts]."
With this precept alone, although one cannot transcend birth and death, it prevents entry into hell.

committing a grave offense is termed "severing the head," which does not allow for repentance as a bhikṣu in this life, meaning one cannot transform from the mundane to the holy. In this life, one cannot transcend the mundane world to enter the state of sainthood; thus, the grave offense remains unextinguished. Nevertheless, because of the confession, one does not fall into hell.
These transgressions do not persist; as they are not of definitive meaning, it is difficult to infer their ultimate nature according to the Supreme Vehicle.

When a person with a defiled mind is touched by [an object], or gives rise to attachment through mutual regard for one or two bhikṣus,

One should know that the methods for repentance according to the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna are each distinct; nevertheless, since the current discourse on *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight) extensively discusses the maintenance and violation of precepts, it is also necessary to have a brief understanding of the terminology regarding such maintenance and violation. Thus, Nanshan said: "Regarding 'stopping-maintenance' (*zhi-chi*):

through skillful means and right mindfulness, one protects what was originally received in the prohibitions, preventing the body and speech from committing various evils; this is termed 'stopping. By stopping, one does not contravene the precepts."

When the substance [of the precepts] is pure and compliant with what was originally received, it is called "retention" (*dhāraṇa*). To speak of "active retention" (*kriyā-dhāraṇa*): since evil has already been abandoned, one must cultivate goodness;
this necessitates diligent exertion in the three karmas to practice and train in the observance of the precepts. When goodness arises and provides protection, it is termed "active retention.
The meaning is as previously stated. Regarding "active transgression": among the five groups of renunciants, the three poisons are present within.
To cast oneself into the embrace [of desire] and cause the body and speech to agitate, creating objects that contravene the principle, is called "acting" (*kṛta*).

To act while contravening what was originally undertaken is called "offense" (*āpatti*). Regarding the cessation of offenses: it refers to the mind of delusion and indolence, wherein conduct contravenes what was originally undertaken;
because one feels aversion toward various superior activities and fails to cultivate and study them, this is called "cessation. To cease while contravening [the precepts] is likewise an offense.
Because he accepted that vow, it is called a transgression; this meaning is explained in detail in the *Vinaya-śīla-viniścaya* (Lüchāo).
Furthermore, the subsequent text states: "If one's *śīla* is pure, *samādhi* will manifest. If we follow the *Dhyāna-pāramitā*, this is analyzed through four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*):
first, one who has broken the precepts may give rise to concentration, while one who maintains the precepts does not; this is because their past roots of goodness were profound and mature.
First, although one may have violated the precepts in this life, it is by virtue of the conditions of present cultivation that one is able to give rise to concentration.
Second, if one did not plant the seeds of meditative concentration in the past, then even if one maintains the precepts in this life, one will not give rise to it.

Third, those who break the precepts do not give rise to concentration, whereas those who maintain the precepts can give rise to it. Fourth, those who both maintain and violate the precepts can also give rise to concentration.
Regarding those who both maintain and violate [the precepts] without generating [transgressions], one may understand this through reflection by applying established analogies.
"Tǒu" (黈) is pronounced with the *tiān* (天) and *kǒu* (口) initials; it means to universally manifest or bring forth.
In the *Cūḍāpanthaka-sūtra*, it is simply stated: "It is like a person with a festering sore who applies ghee and parched flour and wraps it with a cloth;
because the sore has healed, he scatters medicinal powder over it. One should view the body as a sore, and thus cover it with clothing, seeking [only] to prevent the leakage from the nine orifices."
Regarding the character *yǔ* (飲食) in the current text, it is homophonous with *yù* (愈). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it means "the recovery from illness.

The *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states that among the five hundred disciples, there were two Subhūtis:
one of royal lineage and one of long-standing preceptual lineage; this Deva Subhūti was of royal descent.
Regarding the lineage of those who speak of "heaven": for five hundred lifetimes they are constantly born in the heavens, manifesting in response to śrāvakas and descending into royal palaces;

their blessings and sustenance are natural and never lacking. When the Buddha returns to his native land, he commands them to leave the household life, to restrain themselves and maintain their integrity, wearing coarse garments, eating poor food, using straw mats as beds, and taking both excrement and urine as [their only] resources.
At that time, when the householder Subhūti heard the Buddha’s earnest instruction, he wished to withdraw and return home.
Then, as the Buddha accepted the invitation of King Prasenajit, Subhūti went before the Buddha to take his leave and return. Ānanda said to him, "Sir, please stay for one night.
Subhūti replied, "How can a practitioner stay in a house? I shall go to the residence of a layperson."
Having stayed at the house for one night, he was to return home the following morning. Ānanda informed him, saying, "Please stay; we shall now prepare everything.
He then went to the king's residence, where various seats, banners, flowers, and scented oils were all prepared and adorned.
Deva Subhūti stayed overnight there, and as his mind became tranquil, he attained meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and contemplated the Four Noble Truths. Until—
Later in the night, he immediately attained Arhatship. Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, "The deva Subhūti has already attained Arhatship and is flying in the void.
The Buddha said to Ānanda, "There are two kinds of clothing: those that may be associated with and those that may not.
If wearing fine clothing increases one's resolve for the Path, it may be associated with; if it diminishes the resolve for the Path, it must not be associated with."
Now, there are six types of Arhats who are "liberated by occasion" (*samaya-vimukta*): first, obtaining fine robes; second, obtaining fine food;
third, obtaining fine bedding; fourth, obtaining a favorable location; fifth, obtaining a teacher who speaks well; and sixth, obtaining fellow students.
One who must wait for these six conditions is called an Arhat liberated by occasion. Subhūti of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven is such a person, according to the Sarvāstivāda school.
It is said that this person came from the sixth heaven to be born among humans; he was delivered according to his original habits.
Bhikṣu Māṇava (Face-King) was originally of the Śākya clan. At the time of his birth, there were extraordinary divine signs.
When his mother first became pregnant, she summoned a Brahmin to divinate his fortune. The Brahmin prophesied: "Upon this child’s head there is..."
His mother heard that he had the mark of a celestial crown (*devamakuṭa-lakṣaṇa*) and was glad, yet she was not joyful. She said, "The mark of a celestial crown is the sign of a sovereign.
How could there be two sovereigns within a single kingdom? I fear that if the state learns of this, it will bring about harm and distress;
therefore, I am not joyful. Furthermore, she reflected: "If this son truly possesses the marks of a sovereign..."
Naturally, there must be a deity who protects him; why worry that he will not succeed? Therefore, my heart was filled with joy.
When the months were complete, she gave birth to a son whose head bore the marks of a celestial crown. Furthermore, I requested a brahmin to establish a name for him, but the brahmin replied twice:
"Since his head already bears the marks of a celestial crown, he possesses the characteristics of a king; it would be improper to give him another name."
Because he was distinct from others in this appearance, they established a name for him; thus he was called "Face-King" (Mukharāja).
Later, he left the household life and attained the fruit of the Way. He wore tattered and coarse clothing without any sense of shame; the Bhikṣu Face-King was foremost among them.
The *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish* states that because he once offered a piece of fine cotton cloth (*karpāsa*) to a Pratyekabuddha, he was white-skinned throughout five hundred lifetimes.
He was born wrapped in a woolen cloth; as he grew, his body grew large, and there was the character for "king" (王) on his face.
Fearing that the king might harm him, he entered the monastic life... [and so forth]. Regarding the permission to possess heavy objects, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:

"After my parinirvāṇa, those bodhisattvas who protect and uphold the True Dharma shall, through the power of skillful means, allow those who have broken the precepts and merely bear the name [of a monk] to receive and possess [such items]."

When all impure things are shared equally by the Saṃgha in their use, at that time the Bodhisattva, seeing one who has violated the precepts, shall go to that person’s place and respectfully prostrate and provide the four kinds of offerings.
For this purpose, he should keep eight kinds of impure items. Why? Because this person acts to discipline wicked bhikṣus. Furthermore, it is said that if...
When my disciples have no donors to provide their necessities and food and drink are difficult to obtain during times of famine,
for the sake of establishing and upholding the True Dharma, I permit my disciples to accept and keep slaves,
gold, silver, vehicles, fields, houses, grain, and rice, and to trade for whatever they require. Although I permit them to accept and keep such things, they must certainly be pure.

Regarding the practice of giving with sincere faith, the *Nan-shan yun* (Clouds from the Southern Mountain) states that if one intends to give wealth as a pure gift (*viśuddha-dāna*) to another, the Vinaya texts permit this;

furthermore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* also states: Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, "When a Bodhisattva has not yet dwelled in the Immovable Ground (*acalā-bhūmi*), is it possible for them to break the precepts due to certain causes and conditions?
The Buddha replied, "When a Bodhisattva has not yet dwelled in the Immovable Ground, there are indeed causes and conditions [by which they may do so]."
Therefore, it is possible to break the precepts. Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying, “What is this?
The Buddha told Kāśyapa, “If there is a bodhisattva who knows that by the cause and condition of breaking the precepts, they can cause others to receive, uphold, love, and delight in Mahāyāna sūtras;
and can further cause them to read, recite, master, copy the scrolls, and extensively explain them to others without falling back.”
Because awakening is such as this, even a Bodhisattva who has violated the pure precepts should at that time form this thought:
"I would rather fall into the Avīci Hell for one kalpa, or even slightly less than a kalpa, than allow this person to regress from awakening.
Mañjuśrī said to the Buddha: "If there is a Bodhisattva who takes up and protects such a person, they shall not regress from awakening."
"If it were possible for [a person] to fall into hell, such a thing would not exist. The Buddha praised Mañjuśrī, saying, "Excellent, excellent! It is just as you have said.
Furthermore, in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, it is said that Cunda asked the Buddha: "What is the meaning of what was spoken regarding 'breaking the precepts'?
The Buddha told Cunda: "If one commits the four grave prohibitions or the five heinous crimes, or slanders the True Dharma—such persons as these..."
The one named Cunda, who had broken the precepts, asked again: "Can such a breaker of the precepts be delivered? The Buddha told Cunda:

"There is a cause and condition by which he may be delivered. If, though wearing the dharma-robes, he has not yet abandoned them and remains far from [evil], and his heart constantly harbors fear and shame, reproaching himself, saying: 'Alas! Why have I committed such a grave offense?'"

Having given rise to a mind of repentance and protection for the Dharma, desiring to establish the True Dharma, [the text] states: "Wherever there are those who protect the Dharma, I shall make offerings to them," and so on, up to:
"I say that such a person is not called one who has broken the precepts. One must understand the reason why this is cited.

the thirteenth is constant sitting (*nityakotika*), for this represents the stage of heroic vigor. Furthermore...

The fact that the front and back legs of a *bèi* (a solitary wolf) differ in length is intended to convey the meaning of its flickering and erratic movements.

When the Great Sage granted permission for the three grades [of robes] to be universally opened, if one were to keep the "one hundred and one" items in memory, some say that if one adds the *kṣepaka* (extra) robe, it should be combined with the two other grades when discussing the *śuddhi-vyavahāra* (purification through declaration). Therefore, it is said that there are "one hundred and one essentials."

When discussing the three grades of *śuddhi* (purification), [the former tradition] held that possessing only the three robes constitutes the superior grade, possessing the "one hundred and one" items constitutes the middling grade, and possessing extra items constitutes the inferior grade;
this is based on the Vinaya and differs slightly from the present [tradition], which follows the Great Being of the Snowy Mountains (*Himavat*) for its system of *śamatha-vipaśyanā*.

Regarding the statement that "the three grades are now opened together because of the superior grade": since one who keeps the "one hundred and one" items must necessarily possess the three robes, and one who keeps the "extra" robes must necessarily have possessed the former, it is said that the three grades are opened together. Regarding the discussion of the two grades combined:

this refers to combining the middle grade (keeping the one hundred and one) and the lower grade (keeping the extra) within the superior grade; however, this applies only to those of inferior faculties.
The *Zhiguan* states: "The one hundred and one essential items for sustaining the body must be declared as pure (*shou jing*); this is because these two categories are discussed together.
Thus we know that if one keeps the one hundred and one items, it suffices to merely keep them in mind as one kind;

however, if one does not keep them in mind, one must apply the ritual procedure (*jia fa*). Therefore it says: "If one keeps the one hundred and one items in mind, there are those who say the procedure must be applied."

This refers to the practice of receiving and maintaining [the items] through formal ritual (*dhāraṇā*). If one keeps extra items (*atireka-pariṣkāra*), one must perform the rite of "purifying by declaration" (*śuddhivācanā*);

hence it is said, "if one keeps extra items, one must declare them pure," and so forth. Nanshan states that the "one hundred and one requisites for the body" are to be received and maintained, while extra items and other things are to be kept after declaring them pure.
The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* states that regarding the "one hundred and one items," one may keep up to one hundred and one of each kind.

All external items are superfluous possessions; if they resemble "treasures," they must be included within the category of the "one hundred and one items" (*ekāśata-dharmas*) and need not be formally purified (*viśuddhi*).
As for all other vessels, whether they are standard utensils or otherwise, all external items should be made pure. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:

"My disciples are fully provided with the three robes (*tricīvara*), which suffice to ward off the suffering of cold. If one’s nature cannot endure the cold, one may wear old clothes over them as one pleases."
The Sarvāstivādins asked: "Is this method of pure giving (śuddha-dāna) real or provisional? Answer:

Among all ninety-six kinds of non-Buddhist paths, there is no such method of pure giving. It is through the power of the Buddha’s great compassion and skillful means (*upāya*) that he taught and commanded pure giving;
it is a gift of skillful means, not a true gift. It is intended to allow his disciples to possess surplus wealth.

[The interlocutor] asks: "Since they do not violate the precepts, why does the Buddha not simply allow them to keep surplus wealth, but instead forcefully establishes the precepts and provides these skillful means?
Answer: The Dharma of the Buddha takes few desires as its foundation; therefore, the precepts are established to prohibit the keeping [of such wealth].
However, the faculties and natures of sentient beings differ, and their modes of awakening and entry vary. Thus, as in the past, there were times when [the rules] were relaxed.

If one possesses an extra robe (*atireka-cīvara*) that has not been formally purified (*apariśuddha*), and for the sake of purifying it, gives it to a Venerable One so that it may be transferred through a formal purification (*parivartaka-pariśuddhi*), the recipient who accepts the request should say: "Venerable One, please attend to me with a single mind. You have this extra robe which has not been purified;

for the sake of purifying it, I give it to you, and I now accept it. You [give] this robe to [Name]; [Name] already possesses it.
For the sake of [Name], you should carefully guard, maintain, wear, and use it according to the circumstances—whether as medicine, a bowl, or otherwise."
Accordingly, this *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Although one may listen to, receive, and keep [these robes], they must be received through pure giving from a donor of sincere faith.
A *dānapati* is translated here as "donor" (*shizhu*).
These include the *antarvāsaka*, the *uttarāsaṅga*, and the *saṃghāṭī*.
Mount Nanshan says: Regarding these three robes (*tricīvara*), there is no direct translation for them among the various schools; they are now translated according to their meaning.

The *Bodhisattva Hui Shang Jing* states that the five-strip robe is called the "middle-wearing robe," the seven-strip robe is called the "upper robe," and the great robe (*saṃghāṭī*) is called the "robe for when the assembly gathers.

if in terms of usage and name, the five-strip robe (*pañcaka-kaṣāya*) is called a "low-grade robe" when entering the assembly; and if in terms of usage and name, it is called a "robe for miscellaneous tasks while walking on paths within the monastery precincts.
If one calculates according to the number of strips, they are nineteen, seventeen, down to seven or five strips, as prescribed in the Vinaya.

This is also fully set forth in the *Lüchao* (Commentary on the Vinaya).
Receiving food and receiving medicine are prohibitions based on the gravity of their nature; carrying the alms bowl and wearing the robes are the foundations for preventing censure and suspicion.
Speaking in general terms, medicine is indeed food; thus, Master Nanshan said: "To sustain one's life, do not exceed the limits of medicine.
Although the term "medicine" is used broadly, it must be divided into four categories: First, *kālika-bhaiṣajya* (timely medicine), which may be consumed from dawn until midday.

According to the holy teachings, its consumption is permitted as it accords with the Dharma and does not give rise to karmic transgressions. Second, *vikālika-bhaiṣajya* (non-timely medicine), such as various fermented syrups (*mantha*) and the like. Regarding this...

When one is ill and prepares medicine, there is no violation of the external limits for taking it; by adhering to the three-week limit for medicinal substances, one can fulfill the requirements of the Dharma to its full extent.

The method for receiving *kāla-bhaiṣajya* is as detailed in the thirty-ninth precept of the ninety precepts, "the precept against receiving food [without being invited]," where the Nanshan [Zongjing] extensively analyzes it according to one of its ten sections.
1. The Intent of the Regulation; 2. The Ability to Receive Food; 3. The Objects Received; 4. The Food Received; 5. The Place of Receiving Food; 6. The Method of Receiving Food; 7.
The Contemplation Required for Food; 8. The Method of Eating Food; 9. The Loss of the Method of Receiving; 10. Explanation According to the Text. First, regarding the Intent of the Regulation:
Before the Buddha had established the regulation, the bhikṣus each received food without formal acceptance, and laypeople criticized them, saying: "I..."
To eat food without receiving it from one who wears robes of a dyed color (kasāya) that one does not wish to see is considered taking what is not given (*adattādāna*).
According to the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, there are five reasons for this: first, to sever the causes and conditions for theft; second, to serve as a witness; third, to stop slander;
fourth, to fulfill the practice of having few desires and knowing contentment; and fifth, to inspire faith in sentient beings.
Regarding the remaining nine gates, they shall now be briefly indicated. First, concerning the sixth gate, the method for receiving food:

the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* states that there are three ways to reach the edge [of the vessel]. First, reaching the edge of the body (*kāyapārśva*), which means placing an object into the hands of a bhikṣu.
Second, reaching the edge of the object (*vastupārśva*), which means when a layperson carries an object and causes the bhikṣu to take it by his own hand reaching the edge of the object.

Third, regarding receiving [medicine] at the edge of the vessel: when one places the medicine in a vessel and hands it to a bhikṣu, who receives it by grasping the vessel, both body and mind are engaged in mutual correspondence.

Fourth, for single-minded reception without mutual correspondence, as detailed in the *Shouji Biaojue* (Manual on Receiving and Purifying), there are specific methods for each of the four types of medicine:
non-timely medicine, seven-day medicine, and lifetime medicine, all as fully described in the *Lüchao* (Vinaya Commentary) under "Receiving and Purifying the Four Medicines."

In this chapter, the rules for receiving food and medicine are established to sever the causes and conditions of theft; therefore, they constitute the basis for their classification as offenses of grave nature (*gurutara*).

Thus, the *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary on the *Zhiguan*) states: "Regarding the reception of food and medicine, one must consider the methods [taught] in the *Sukhāvatīvyūha*. Furthermore, the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra-śāstra* states:
"If one prepares food with one's own hands and consumes it without having received it, it defiles the monastic protocol and is termed 'impure' (*aśuci*). [The following concerns] the three robes.

These twenty-two mental factors associated with wholesome states arise together with ten universal factors, ten great wholesome factors, and sometimes with vitarka and vicāra. [In the case of] unwholesome minds, they may also increase with remorse (*kaukṛtya*).
Twenty [mental factors] consist of the ten universal (mahābhūmika), the ten great afflictive (kleśa-mahābhūmika), the two great unwholesome (akuśala-mahābhūmika), and the two—vitarka and vicāra.

Twenty-one include the four afflictions such as anger (krodha) and so forth, along with regret (kaukṛtya). Eighteen are obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta), and twelve are admitted to be non-obscured-unspecified (anivṛtāvyākṛta), as previously stated in the section on mental states;
whichever of these are present, one [additional factor] is added.
The *Abhidharmakośakārikā* states: "Because desire-realm existence possesses vitarka and vicāra, within the category of wholesome minds there are twenty-two mental factors;
at times, regret (*kaukṛtya*) is added. In unwholesome minds, there are twenty-four when associated with the unique [unwholesome roots] or views;

twenty-one when associated with the afflictions such as anger (*krodha*) and so forth, excluding regret; eighteen when associated with the obscured-unspecified; twelve when there is no necessity; and sleep (*middha*) is universal."
According to the *Ekottarāgama*, there are five categories of mental states (*citta*) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*): first, the wholesome (*kuśala*), which is of one type;
second, the unwholesome (*akuśala*), which is of two types, namely that associated with non-common ignorance (*āveṇikī avidyā*) and that associated with other afflictions (*kleśa*);
and third, the neutral (*avyākṛta*), which is of two types, namely the obscured-neutral (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) and the unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*). Now, regarding the mind of the desire realm...
Because concentration necessarily involves vitarka and vicāra, a category of wholesome mind (*kuśala-citta*) must invariably arise with twenty-two mental factors (*caitasika*).

These consist of the ten universal ground-factors (*mahābhūmika*), the ten wholesome ground-factors (*kuśalamahābhūmika*), and two indeterminate factors—namely, vitarka and vicāra. It is not the case that all wholesome minds possess these;
at times, when unwholesome conduct (*akuśala-karman*) increases, the number reaches twenty-three. What is "unwholesome conduct"? It refers to unwholesome actions (*akuśala-kṛtya*).
One should know that the essence of *kaukṛtya* (remorse) is designated as such because it takes unwholesome actions as its object;

that is to say, it is the nature of mental regret directed toward what has been done. In an unwholesome state of mind that is not shared (*āveṇika*), there must necessarily be twenty mental factors arising simultaneously:
the ten universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*), the six universal defiled mental factors (*kleśamahābhūmika*), and the two universal unwholesome mental factors (*akuśalamahābhūmika*).
The factors (dharma) together with the two indeterminate states—namely vitarka and vicāra—are as follows. What is called the "exclusive mental complex" (asādhāraṇa-cittapakṣa)?

It refers to this mental complex which possesses only ignorance (avidyā) and lacks any other afflictions such as greed; it is the same as what was previously described regarding the "exclusive category.

Furthermore, in the mental complex associated with unwholesome views, there are likewise twenty mental concomitants (caitta) that arise simultaneously, and their names are exactly as stated in the section on the exclusive category.

Regarding the statement "a mind associated with unwholesome views," this refers to a state of mind in which there is either false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), or adherence to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
Within this category of unwholesome minds consisting of greed, hatred, pride, or doubt, twenty-one mental factors arise simultaneously;
these are the twenty [factors] common to all unwholesome states, plus one of the following—greed and so forth—as an additional concomitant. As for the aforementioned...
Regarding the category of secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) associated with anger (*krodha*) and so forth, there are likewise two types.
In the mental state associated with one of the ten [secondary afflictions] such as anger, twenty mental factors arise together, just as in the case of the non-common [mental states].

Furthermore, in the mental state associated with the unwholesome *kaukṛtya* (remorse), twenty-one mental factors arise together; that is, the eleven [factors] common to the neutral and obscured-unwholesome [states], plus *kaukṛtya* itself as the twelfth.
In the category of the mind, there are only eighteen mental factors that arise simultaneously:
namely, the ten universal ground-factors (*mahābhūmika*), the six universal affliction-ground-factors (*kleśamahābhūmika*), and the two indeterminate factors, namely vitarka and vicāra.

As for the obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) minds of the desire realm—referring to those associated with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of grasping at extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*)—it should be understood that the [additional] views do not increase [the count] therein.
The previous explanation maintains that in other indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and non-obscured (*anivṛta*) mental states, only twelve mental factors arise together:
namely, the ten universal ground-factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*) along with the two不定 (indeterminate) factors of vitarka and vicāra.

It should be understood that *middha* (sleep/drowsiness) is not incompatible with any of the aforementioned categories of mind, as it is compatible with the wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate natures; therefore, whenever any such category occurs, [middha may be present].
Regarding the increase mentioned here, it refers to the count rising from twenty-two to twenty-three, or from twenty-three to twenty-four;

cases of the unwholesome (*akuśala*) and the neutral (*avyākṛta*) may be understood by analogy. "Obscured" (*nivṛta*) means that defiled phenomena (*kliṣṭa-dharma*) can obstruct the Noble Path and further veil the mind so that it is not pure;
therefore, they are called "obscured. This consciousness is not defiled, and thus it is called "unobscured" (*anivṛta*). "Indeterminate" (*avyākṛta*) means...

Wholesome and unwholesome states possess fruits that are either desirable or undesirable, as well as a distinguished essential nature; because they can be definitively distinguished, they are termed "determinate" (*vyākṛta*).

Because they are neither wholesome nor unwholesome, they are termed "indeterminate" (*avyākṛta*). They are also called "recording" (*vyākaraṇa*), meaning "to record," "to remember," and so forth. The remaining characteristics of phenomena and their definitions will be analyzed in detail below.

The thief of the fetter of sleep is not yet extinguished and its harm remains unremoved; it is like staying in the same room with a venomous snake, or like standing amidst the white blades on a battlefield.
At such a time, how can one sleep? Sleep is a great darkness in which nothing is seen; day after day it encroaches upon and deceives, robbing one of clarity.
When the mind is shrouded by sleep, there is no discernment. Such a great loss—how can one afford to sleep?
