Regarding the phrase "the middle and upper streams each have three types," as cited in the *Shi qian* (Sub-commentary on the Profound Meaning): The *Fu xing* states: "The middle and upper streams each have three types, as cited in the *Shi qian*. [End of Volume Fourteen]

According to the *Abhidharmakośa*, these are generally categorized as nine types: that is, each of the three [types of *antarāparinirvāyin*] is further divided into three—namely, those who attain parinirvāṇa upon being born (*upapadyaparinirvāyin*), those who attain it while moving toward the goal (*anabhisamskāraparinirvāyin*), and those who attain it after being born in the realm of form (*ūrdhvastrotas*). Both those who attain parinirvāṇa with exertion (*sābhisamskāra*) and those without exertion (*anabhisamskāra*) are included within the category of "attaining parinirvāṇa upon being born" (*upapadyaparinirvāyin*). Regarding the three sub-types of the "upon being born" category, they are:
the swift, the non-swift, and the long-delayed; these three meanings can be understood by reflecting on the analogy of a flying spark.

Furthermore, regarding the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), the categories of "swift" and so forth have been discussed. Regarding birth, there are three types: first, established based on swiftness;
second, established based on non-swiftness with movement (*sābhisaṃskāra*); and third, established based on non-swiftness without movement (*anabhisaṃskāra*) and enduring for a long time.

Having thus discussed the swift and so forth for those born in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), we now discuss the three types of "Upstreamers" (*ūrdhvasrotas*): first, the "Total Leaper" (*pluta*), established based on swiftness; and second, the "Half-Leaper" (*ardhapluta*), established based on non-swiftness.

The three types of "disappearance after three lifetimes" (tribhavāntara-parinirvāyin) are established based on their duration; from the beginning of the form realm to its end, these three types of persons remain distinct throughout.

Thus, there are three sets of nine, arising from the differences in karma, afflictions, and faculties. Regarding the difference in karma: one who performs karma conducive to the present life attains the intermediate state parinirvāṇa;
one who performs karma conducive to the next birth attains the birth-state parinirvāṇa; and one who performs karma conducive to a subsequent life [attains the upper-stream parinirvāṇa].

Because they achieve the "Upstreamer" (Urdhvasrotas), it is said that there are three types of afflictions: the lower-grade afflictions lead to the "Attainer in the Intermediate State" (Antarāparinirvāyin);

the middle-grade afflictions lead to the "Attainer upon Rebirth" (Upapadyaparinirvāyin); and the upper-grade afflictions lead to the "Upstreamer. Regarding the distinction of faculties: those with superior faculties are Attainers in the Intermediate State;
those with middling faculties are Attainers upon Rebirth; and those with inferior faculties are Upstreamers. The *Samyuktābhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* states: "The Anāgāmin is either..."

There are five, seven, or eight [types of *antarāparinirvāyin*]. The "five" refers to those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), upon being reborn (*upapadya*), with effort (*sābhisamskāra*), without effort (*anabhisamskāra*), and those who go upstream (*ūrdhvasrotas*).
The "seven" refers to further dividing the one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state into three types, like the metaphors of a flying spark;

the "eight" refers to adding to the five those who attain parinirvāṇa upon arrival (*abhisamaya-parinirvāyin*), those who attain parinirvāṇa in the formless realm (*ārūpya-parinirvāyin*), and those of indefinite timing (*aniyata-parinirvāyin*). Although the name "indeterminate parinirvāyin" is cited in the *Shiqian*, there are few who understand it as referring to a person still in training (*śaikṣa*).
Regarding the meaning: when I read the *Vibhāṣā*, I first encountered this explanation.

The *Mahāvibhāṣā* states that there are also those who attain parinirvāṇa in the indeterminate [category], either attaining parinirvāṇa in the desire realm, or in the form realm, or in the formless realm.
Furthermore, these are subsumed within the seven types of non-returners (*anāgāmin*). If...

In the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), it is called "manifesting *prajñā*"; in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), it is the five types of non-returners (*anāgāmin*); and in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), it is "formless *parinirvāṇa*" (*ārūpya-parinirvāṇa*).
Karma created in this life that ripens in this very life is called "karma to be experienced in the present life" (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya-karman*).

Karma created in this life that ripens in the second life is called "karma to be experienced in the next life" (*upapadyavedanīya-karman*). Karma created in this life that ripens sequentially from the third life onwards is called "karma to be experienced in subsequent lives" (*aparaparyāyavedanīya-karman*).
That which has ripened is called "karma to be experienced in subsequent lives.
Regarding the five cessations and the four foundations of mindfulness, one should briefly consult the *Xuanwen* and its commentary, the *Shiqian*, as they have been explained there;
since there is no significant difference from what is commonly taught here, I shall not cite them now.
In the first twelve [sections], there are eight;
the practices of the first stage consist of ten matters: first, the firmness of the profound mind, because it is unobtainable;
second, equanimity toward all sentient beings, because sentient beings are unobtainable; third, the mind of relinquishment given to others...
1. Because one cannot apprehend a recipient; 2. because one draws near to spiritual friends yet does not exalt oneself; 3. because one seeks the Dharma yet all dharmas are unapprehendable; 4.
because one constantly leaves the household life yet the state of leaving home is unapprehendable; 5.
because one loves and delights in the Buddha’s body and its marks and signs yet they are unapprehendable; 6. because one expounds the teachings of the Dharma yet all dharmas are unapprehendable.
Ninth, because conceptual discrimination cannot be apprehended; tenth, because the dharma that destroys pride and the arising of wisdom cannot be apprehended;
eleventh, because true speech and all other forms of speech cannot be apprehended. On the second stage, one constantly contemplates eight dharmas:

first, purity of ethical discipline; second, knowing gratitude and repaying kindness; third, abiding in patience; fourth, receiving joy; fifth, not abandoning sentient beings; sixth... [text fragment].
1. Entering the mind of great compassion; 2. Reverently receiving instruction from teachers of the seven levels of faith; 3. Diligently seeking all the *pāramitās*; 4.
Practicing the five dharmas within the thirteen stages of the three, four, and five existences; 5. Never being weary of extensive learning; 6. Purifying the giving of the Dharma, and furthermore—
1. One does not exalt oneself while adorning the Buddha-fields. 2. One does not exalt oneself while undergoing the hardships and sufferings of the world. 3. One does not become weary of them. 4.
One abides in a state of shame and modesty, and while dwelling in the fourth stage, one does not abandon ten dharmas:

i. Not abandoning the forest hermitage (āraṇya). ii. Having few desires and being content. iii. Not abandoning the merits of the dhūta practices. iv. Not abandoning the precepts. ... [and so forth] ... x. Not abandoning the wisdom of the Tathāgata.
1. Grasping the characteristics of the precepts; 2. The five impurities and evils of sensual desires; 3. The mind of world-weariness; 4. Relinquishing all that one possesses; 5.
A mind that does not sink into despair; 6. Not giving rise to the two bases of consciousness; 7. Not being stingy with any object whatsoever.
In the fifty-second, sixty-sixth, and sixty-fifth stages, one remains far removed from twelve things: first, being far removed from laypeople; second, being far removed from bhikṣuṇīs;
third, being far removed from stinginess regarding others' households; fourth, being far removed from useless conversation; and fifth, being far removed from anger.
Sixth, distancing oneself from self-conceit; seventh, distancing oneself from disparaging others; eighth, distancing oneself from the ten unwholesome paths of action;
ninth, distancing oneself from great pride; tenth, distancing oneself from self-willfulness; eleventh, distancing oneself from perversion; twelfth, distancing oneself from lust, anger, and delusion.
Within the sixth stage, one is fully endowed with six dharmas, namely the six pāramitās.
In the twenty-eight, five, and seven stages, one does not cling to twenty things: first, not clinging to a self; second, not clinging to sentient beings;
third, not clinging to a life-span; fourth, not clinging to a multitude of persons, up to and including a knower or a seer; fifth, not clinging to the view of annihilationism.
Sixth, not clinging to the view of eternalism; seventh, not forming signs; eighth, not forming views of causality;
ninth, not clinging to name-and-form; tenth, not clinging to the five aggregates; eleventh, not clinging to the eighteen elements;
twelfth, not clinging to the twelve bases; thirteenth, not clinging to the three realms; fourteenth, not making them a place of attachment; fifteenth, not making them an object.
16. Not making a basis of one's own station; 17. Not clinging to views based on the Buddha; 18. Not clinging to views based on the Dharma;
19. Not clinging to views based on the Saṃgha; 20. Not clinging to views based on the precepts.

In the eighth stage, one is fully endowed with these five dharmas, enters in accordance with the minds of sentient beings, sports in the various supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), and contemplates all Buddhas.
The land is as the Buddha-land seen by the one who possesses mastery; that land is as the Buddha-body itself, which is truly observed as being self-adorned.
[This applies to] ninety, twenty, or ten Buddhas.
In the ninth stage, one is fully endowed with twelve qualities: the boundless world of Dharma-love, the portion of those to be delivered,

the Bodhisattva’s attainment of that which accords with his vows, the knowledge of the languages of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and gandharvas and the preaching of the Dharma accordingly, the perfection of the womb, the perfection of birth,
the perfection of the family, the perfection of the lineage, the perfection of the retinue, and the perfection of the manifestation of birth.
One who has achieved the adornment of renunciation, perfected the Buddha-tree, accomplished all virtuous merits,
and fully realized the ten stages of a bodhisattva should be known as being like a Buddha.
The designation "patience" (*kṣānti*) in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* is likewise so.

The treatise asks: "The Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha belong to the Hīnayāna, while the Bodhisattva belongs to the Mahāyāna; why then is it said that the wisdom and abandonment (*jñāna-prahāṇa*) of these two vehicles constitute the Bodhisattva’s patience regarding non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*)?
The answer is: "Because their objects of focus (*ālambana*) are identical—namely, suchness (*tathatā*), the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*), and the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*)."
They are also identical, differing only in the sharpness or dullness of their wisdom.
Upon first hearing the Three Truths, one may only attain the first fruit;
however, according to the Mahāsannipāta Sūtra, when the bhikṣu Aśvajit preached the Dharma for Śāriputra, he said: "Dharmas arise from conditions."
Birth and penetration are the causes; because the causal conditions cease, there is quiescence. The world is suffering (*duḥkha*), and its cause is called origination (*samudaya*).
If one cultivates the Eightfold Noble Path, at the time when the origination of the world ceases, Śāriputra then spoke this verse:
"I have heard the Bhikṣu preach the Four Truths, and immediately transcended the three evil realms. Thus, the Sūtra and the Śāstra differ.
This is merely a difference arising from the specific circumstances [of the audience]. Furthermore, the text below states that "Kumārajīva entered India.

When Kumārajīva was in Jibin, the king provided daily support for five *bhikṣus* and ten *śrāmaṇeras* consisting of a pair of goose carcasses, three *dōng* of rice flour, and six *shēng* of ghee. The current text, however, mentions only five *śrāmaṇeras*.
It refers to humans.
Regarding the *Vajraśekhara-sūtra*, it states that because the Buddha bestows the power of merit and wisdom upon the body of a bodhisattva, it is called "bestowal" (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
Since it is so for the *Pai-p'u-sa* (Bodhisattva-piṭaka), the same should be understood to apply to the two vehicles (*dviyāna*).
The *Kun-le* (Kumbhāṇḍa)—here translated as "Casket Store" (*piṭaka*)—consists of three million two hundred thousand words; it was compiled by Mahākātyāyana during the Buddha’s lifetime.

This was composed by those [who followed him]. After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the lifespan of humans gradually decreased and their power of memory and cognition diminished, such that they were unable to recite the teachings extensively.
Thus, those who had attained the Way compiled them into three hundred and eighty-four thousand words. If a person enters the gate of the *Kun-le* (Saṃghāṭa), their discourse will be inexhaustible;
within it are found various methods, such as the gate of following characteristics (*anulakṣaṇa-mukha*) and the gate of counteracting [afflictions] (*pratipakṣa-mukha*).
Section on the Gate.
Regarding the "Vile Speech" (Durbhāṣita) chapter, the *Fànzhì* (Brahmadharma) states that [the passage] extends up to the *Líyǒuwúděng* (Detachment from Being and Non-being) Sūtra.
The *Jīngyìnyì* (Meaning and Phonetics of the Sūtras) states: "Chānì was originally the name of a horse-herding slave; Jiàndé is the name of the horse."
Chanda, relying on his own status as one who had left the household life from a royal lineage, treated the Tathāgata with contempt while he was still in the world;
he did not follow the laws of the assembly or the monastic community, and during the performance of the Saṃgha’s rites, he would utter words of derision, saying:

"What is there to discuss? It is like fallen leaves driven by a whirlwind, gathered together in one place. Even after the Buddha had passed into parinirvāṇa, he still did not reform himself. The Buddha foresaw this.
It is said that to cause [the offender] to undergo the *brahmadaṇḍa* (Brahma-punishment) to discipline him is called *tūṣṇīmbhāva* (silent exclusion).
Because a separate altar (*maṇḍala*) was established for the method of punishing offenses according to the Brahma-heaven, those who committed the offense were made to enter this altar;

none of the other Brahmās were permitted to speak with them. It is the same in the present case, hence it is called the "Brahma-altar. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that this is from the *Kātyāyanasūtra*.

It is taught that when contemplating the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*), there is no view of non-existence; and when contemplating the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*), there is no view of existence.
This is what is meant by attaining awakening through detachment from the views of existence and non-existence.

However, these two theories—both affirmation and both negation—have not yet reached this region [of China], being mentioned in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (*Dazhidulun*) merely as titles. Furthermore, the preceding text states: "Even if there were authentic teachings..."

Regarding the claim that *śrāvakas* merely attain the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) and thus cede [the realization of] dharmas to Bodhisattvas—those who speak thus of granting and taking away [the realization], the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states:

"The two vehicles realize the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*) but have not yet realized the selflessness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*). Furthermore, the *Bhūmivastu* (or *Dharaṇīśvararāja-paripṛcchā*) states:

"The untainted wisdom of the selflessness of persons belonging to the two vehicles is the wisdom for purifying the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*); the wisdom of the selflessness of phenomena belongs to Buddhas and Bodhisattvas."
Wisdom is the purification of the obscurations to wisdom.
Regarding Guṇavarman’s forty-six verse stanzas—
Guṇavarman means "Armor of Merit" (Gōngdé Kǎi) in Chinese— the forty-six verse stanzas consist of thirty verses.

The "six lines" mentioned here are now said to be forty-six lines, which is likely an error; perhaps there is another source for this, as it was previously cited in the *Xuanjian Bunzhu* (Supplementary Notes on the Profound Commentary).
Harivarman is translated here as "Lion Armor" (Shizikai).
In reverse order, he encountered the Buddhas Vipashyin, Dīpaṃkara, and Ratnaśikhin.
The *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra* states: "I first resolved my mind for enlightenment under Śākyamuni Buddha;
I completed the first asaṃkhyeya-kalpa under Ratnaśikhin Buddha; I completed the second asaṃkhyeya-kalpa under Dīpaṃkara Buddha; and [I completed the third under] Kāśyapa Buddha."
Regarding the completion of the third asaṃkhyeya kalpa, the point where this differs from the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* is reconciled in the *Fayuan*:

"If one speaks in terms of the actual completion [of the kalpa], it occurs during the stage of *vipaśyanā*; if one speaks in terms of having already completed it, it occurs during the time of Kāśyapa.
Thus, the discrepancies between the sūtras and the śāstras each have their own underlying intent."
Regarding the statement that one hundred kalpas are reduced by nine, resulting in ninety-one, this is due to the skipping of nine kalpas.

The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* speaks of "skipping twelve kalpas," and Zhiyi’s commentary explains: "Because the faculties and conditions of beings differ, the Buddha teaches of either an increase or a decrease."
The character "kǎng" (攩) should be changed to the character "dǎng" (黨).
This is as explained in the *Shiqian* regarding the hearing that the Great Nirvāṇa contains the unsurpassed path and so forth.
The *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning) quotes a sutra: "If a bodhisattva hears the Mahāparinirvāṇa, having heard it, they give rise to faith and reflect:
'The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess the unsurpassed path, the great True Dharma, and the correct practice of the Great Assembly;
from this, one establishes their conduct. If one hears of the Mahāparinirvāṇa, this is faith in the fruit and also faith in cessation; there is the unsurpassed path."

That which has already departed is faith in the practice that manifests the fruit; the unsurpassed path is faith in wisdom; the existence of the Great True Dharma is faith in meditative concentration;
and the correct practice of the great assembly is faith in precepts—and so on, as explained at length in the original text.
The meaning may be understood by following the commentary in the *Shiqian* (Explanatory Notes), so there is no need for me to cite it here exhaustively.
"Hui" (禾*會) is pronounced with the initial *kū* and the final *-fú*; it refers to coarse bran. It means reckless or thoughtless.
Zhuangzi said: "What you, Master, consider to be reckless words, I consider to be the practice of the wondrous Way.
(The character *mèng* is pronounced as in *páng-mèng*; *làng* is read according to its original pronunciation, or alternatively as *lì-dàng*.
*Mèng-làng* signifies being diffuse and lacking a point of departure or destination; it also describes a state of lack of refinement and essentiality, and carries the meaning of being cursory.)
Also: *huò* (with the ancient pronunciation *guó*). That which receives the string is called the *huò*.
This differs from the Sarvāstivāda position regarding the nature of offenses.
The *Vibhāṣā*, *Abhidharmakośa*, *Nyāyānusāra*, and other treatises all state that karma enters the past; thus, the *Nyāyānusāra* says:
"The differentiated activity of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) in the stage prior to its arising is termed 'future'."
That which has just arisen is called "present," and that which has already ceased is called "past.
Furthermore, the passage from the following section stating, "This illness of mine is neither real nor existent," refers to the text on the contemplation of subduing (*vinaya*) within that sutra.
Here, in the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*, the author himself cites that sutra, acting as a physician-king; this is for the purpose of providing consolation according to the *Madhyamaka-hṛdaya*.
Because this is a metaphorical illustration, there is no need to cite passages such as "neither true nor existent.

Furthermore, regarding the citation from *Zhuangzi* in the subsequent text—"The ancients who attained their ambitions..."—it states: "Carriages and official robes upon one's person are not one's nature or destiny;

they are things that arrive by chance as temporary lodgings. As lodgings, their coming cannot be warded off and their departure cannot be stopped; therefore, one does not regard them as carriages [or robes]."

"Mian" means to let one's will run free; it refers to being unconstrained by poverty or convention, remaining detached from external affairs, and encountering things unexpectedly—this is called "tàng. Regarding the "fisherman Zheng Hong":
Zheng Hong, who later served as the Grand Marshal (Taishou) of the Han dynasty, once gathered firewood and found a stray arrow. Shortly thereafter, someone came looking for it;
when they encountered Hong and asked what he desired in return, Hong recognized that the person was a divine being and replied, "I have long suffered from the waters of Ruoye Creek..."
"Carrying firewood is difficult; I wish for a south wind in the morning and a north wind in the evening. Later, it was indeed so.
As for the "Fisherman," some say he was Fan Li (the father is pronounced *fǔ*; there is a chapter titled "The Fisherman" in the *Zhuangzi*).

In the *Yijing sanmei jing* (Sutra on the Samādhi of the Bequeathed Teaching), it is said that because the bhikṣu Rāhuṇeyya failed to obtain almsfood, the Buddha ordered the Sangha to be divided into five sections to test the merit of the community;
this was done prior to the division into the five schools after his parinirvāṇa.
The *Luo xunyu jing* (Rāhuṇeyya Sūtra) states: "At that time, whenever the monks of the five schools went out to beg for food, Rāhuṇeyya would always be present."
The group returned with empty bowls to the Buddha. The Buddha commanded the bhikṣus to distribute [the food] and give it to them;

thus, they returned empty-handed one after another. Maudgalyāyana thought to himself: "If even this community of bhikṣus cannot obtain food for themselves, why have all these others returned empty-handed?
If I had traveled together with them, I might still have obtained something. The Buddha, knowing his thoughts, sent Śāriputra along with him and dispatched Maudgalyāyana.
Accompanied by Rāhuṇeyya, they each formed their own separate faction. The Buddha said to Maudgalyāyana, "Wherever I am, you must not go.
Maudgalyāyana then set out with Rāhuṇeyya; just as they were about to arrive at their destination, they saw the Buddha and Śāriputra standing at his gate.
Thus they traveled through ten billion lands, yet [the Buddha] remained there.
Regarding the failure to obtain food: because Rāhuṇeyya failed to practice charity during the time of the Buddha Vipaśyin, he is unable to obtain food wherever he goes today.
As stated in the lower fascicle of the *Yaojiao Sanmei Jing* (Sutra on the Samādhi of the Bequeathed Teaching):
"When the Buddha was in the world, the community of monks wore only robes made from discarded rags; consequently, when Rāhuṇeyya went out for alms, he returned empty-handed."
Knowing their past karmic conduct, he had the community of monks divide the Vinaya into five sections and established five types of monastic robes.

He ordered them to follow one section of the practice each day, thereby instituting ritual regulations so that each group might exercise its particular strengths; he designated the colors of these robes as follows:
the Dharmaguptaka school, which masters the flavor of principle and provides guidance and benefit, should wear red-colored robes; the Sarvāstivāda... [text continues].
The Kāśyapīya school, being broadly learned, versatile, and sagacious, guides others through the transformation of the Dharma; they should wear robes of blackish-purple.
The Mahīśāsaka school, being diligent, courageous, and swift, protects and sustains sentient beings; they should wear robes of madder-brown.

The Sarvāstivāda school, entering into subtle meditation and thoroughly elucidating the profound and mysterious, should wear robes of blue. The Mahāsāṃghika school, diligently studying the multitude [of teachings]...
The sūtra explains that the principle of the meaning requires one to wear yellow robes; from that time onward, one would obtain food in great abundance.
According to this school, it is identical to the Vinaya of the Sarvāstivāda and other five schools following the Parinirvāṇa; please examine this further.
Dharmagupta is the name of the Vinaya Master; his Dharma-name is *Sifen* (Four-Part). The *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* states:

"After my parinirvāṇa, my disciples shall receive, uphold, transcribe, read, and recite the twelve divisions of the Tathāgata’s scriptures, yet they will misunderstand their meaning in a distorted manner."
The person who proclaimed [the teachings] by concealing the treasury of the Dharma through inverted explanations is named Dharmagupta; this is translated as "Dharma-secrecy.
A sutra states that "concealing" (gupta) carries the meaning of "secrecy" (mi), and it is also called "Dharma-treasury," where "treasury" (kosa) carries the meaning of "secrecy."

*Sarvāstivāda* is translated here as "All-Exists. This school maintains that the three time periods exist substantially and that the three natures are all real; they fully accept the dharma of receiving the precepts.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "Furthermore, one may read, recite, and transcribe non-Buddhist scriptures, yet one accepts the existence of the three time periods..."
Because they can skillfully debate and refute non-Buddhists both internally and externally, explain all natures, enable everyone to receive the precepts,
and are able to answer all challenges and inquiries, they are called Sarvāstivāda.
The *Mahīśāsaka Sūtra* states:
"Not forming the perception of earth, nor the perceptions of water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness—this is called Mahīśāsaka.
*Mahīśāsaka* is translated here as "not adhering to the contemplation of existence or non-existence. The Dharma is called the Five-Part Vinaya (*Pañcavargika*).
The *Vātsīputrīya-sūtra* states:
"They all teach that there is a self and do not speak of the characteristic of emptiness; they are like children, hence they are called Vātsīputras.
*Vātsīputra* translates as "Calf-son" (*Gòzǐ*). In ancient times, there was a seer who became infatuated with a calf and fathered a son by it; this [name] is derived from that lineage.
A name is established by means of a clan; this school maintains that the self is neither identical to the aggregates nor does it exist as a real self apart from the aggregates.
The textual passages of their Vinaya have not yet reached this region.

The *Kāśyapaparivarta Sūtra* states that there is no self (*ātman*) nor any experiencer (*vedaka*), and that the transformation of the various afflictions (*kleśa*) is like a corpse; this is called the *Kāśyapīya*.

*Kāśyapa* here refers to the "contemplation of the layered emptiness" (*guru-śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*). The followers of the Sāṃkhya school of heterodox teachings (*tīrthika*) cling to the existence of a real self.

To experience sensory objects is called "the experiencer" (*vedaka*); this is like casting off [the body], and is therefore metaphorically likened to a corpse. This Dharma is named "Liberation" (*vimukti*).
Its precept manual (*śīla-mūla*) is largely identical to that of the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, with some similarities to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* and the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*.
The Sūtra states that one who has extensively and universally studied the five divisions of the scriptural canon is called a Mahāsāṃghika;
*Mahāsāṃghika* translates as "Great Assembly. The introductory commentary to the Vinaya text of this school states: "There are six divisions of the *Sāṃghika*, both general and specific.

These [others] are the general category, while the preceding five are the specific ones. This *Sāṃghika* school is characterized by its broad and pervasive understanding, which gives rise to no biased attachments and universally accords with all things."
Because the five views are common to all [schools], it should be understood that this is a general [classification].
One must know the characteristics in which the Mahāsāṃghika differs from the Mahāsāṃghika [as distinct from the Sthavira]: the Mahāsāṃghika is indeed the Sthavira school.

This refers to the fact that within the Kūṭāgāraśālā at the Piṇḍava Cave, the Sthaviras such as Kāśyapa and five hundred arhats who were free from doubt and liberated through realization held a council; thus, it is named the Sthavira school.

The Mahāsāṃghikas state that at that time, several hundred thousand people among the assembly—both those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)—who were not included among the five hundred followers of the Elder Kāśyapa, spoke to one another outside the cave, saying: "While the Tathāgata was in the world, we studied under the same teacher;
now that the Dharma King has entered parinirvāṇa, he has excluded us from his company. To repay the Buddha's kindness, we ought to..."
When the Dharma-piṭaka was compiled, both ordinary beings and sages gathered together, and the foolish and the wise assembled in full.
They compiled the Sūtra, Vinaya, Abhidharma, as well as the Miscellaneous Collection (Kṣudraka-piṭaka) and the Dhāraṇīs, organizing them into five distinct Piṭakas.
Because this compilation was attended by both ordinary beings and sages, it was consequently called the Mahāsāṃghika (Great Assembly School). Thus, this Mahāsāṃghika...
While Kāśyapa’s great assembly was outside the cave, [the Buddha] was within the cave;
thus, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* translates [the term] as "great assembly" (*mahāsāṃghika*) to distinguish it from the Mahāsāṃghika school. The *Nanshan Jieshu* states that there are four aspects:
first, regarding the two groups, as in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, when the first council was held, five hundred people were selected—these were those inside the cave.
The Sthavira school is also [known as] "the rest," which is not counted among the others; it is named Mahāsāṃghika, that is, the Bahirdeśaka (Cave-dwelling) school.
This is because the Sthaviras and Mahāsāṃghikas were the original divisions at the site of the First Council; thus, the *Mañjuśrī-paripṛcchā-sūtra* states:
"The two fundamental schools are these very ones. Second, the five schools are as listed in the preceding annotations of this text.
These are the five schools. The *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* states that although the five schools differ, they do not obstruct the three aspects of the Buddhas' dharma-realm and nirvāṇa.

Regarding the eighteen schools, as transmitted by the Tripitaka masters of old, it is said that two hundred years after the initial division of the five schools, four schools branched out from the Sarvāstivāda;
these are the Vātsīputrīya, [the Dharmaguptaka, the Mahīśāsaka, and the Kāśyapīya].
The Dharmottarīya school, the descendants of the noble Dharma, constitutes the sixth division. From the Kāśyapīya school, two branches emerged: first, the Saṃmatīya; second, the Sāmmitīya.
Within the Mahīśāsaka school, one branch was further divided, namely the Antarvyavahārika. Four hundred years later, six schools branched out from within the Mahāsāṃghika:
first, the Lokottaravāda; second, the Gokulika; third, the Prajñaptivāda; fourth, [the Bahuśrutīya]; fifth, the Caitika; and sixth, the Pūrvaśaila.
Vīta (5), Śaila (6), and Upaśaila (7). Only the Mahīśāsaka school does not differentiate [these].
The above, including both the root and the branches, constitute eighteen schools; these emerged from within the cave-dwelling schools (*lena-vāsin*).

If one follows the "Section on Differentiation" in the lower fascicle of the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra*, it says: "The two fundamental schools are: first, the Mahāsāṃghika school; second, [the Sthavira school]."
The Vibhajyavāda school, in its first *saṃghī* division, is distinguished into seven:
(1) the Vātsīputrīya, (2) the Lokottaravāda, (3) the Gokulika, (4) the Bahusrutīya, (5) the Caityaśaila, (6) the Pūrvaśaila, and (7) the Aparaśaila.
Within the Vibhajyavāda school, there are further eleven divisions: (1) the Sarvāstivāda, and so forth.

1. Haimavata (Snowy Mountain), 2. Traidaṇḍika (Three Calf), 3. Dharmottarīya (Fourfold Dharma Superior), 4. Bhadrayānīya (Five Virtuous Division), 5. Saṃmitīya (Sixth, Honored by All), 6. Ṣaṇṇagarika (Seventh, Grass-Mound Division), 7.
Mahīśāsaka (Eighth, Great Unruly), 8. Dharmaguptaka (Ninth, Dharma Protector), 9. Kāśyapīya (Tenth, Kāśyapa-Clan), 10. Sautrāntika (Eleventh, Sūtra-Phrase).
These above constitute the twenty schools from beginning to end; this is discussed collectively according to the interior and exterior of the caves. (IV, V)
The *Śataśāstra* states that after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, five hundred different schools heard of ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*) and felt as if their hearts were pierced by knives.
Furthermore, one should know that the characteristics of the twenty schools are largely identical to those in the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra*, as described in the *Saṃayabhedoparacanacakra*.
In the second century, from within the Mahāsāṃghika school, three sub-sects emerged: the Prajñaptivādins, the Bahuśrutīyas, and the Caitikas.

Regarding the two schools: first, the Lokottaravāda (School of Those Who Proclaim the Supramundane); second, the Kṣaṇikavāda (or Saṃmatīya) School; and third, the Prajñaptivāda (School of Provisional Designation).

Master Paramārtha states that this school maintains that mundane and supramundane phenomena lack any substantial reality and exist merely as provisional designations; thus, they are called "Provisional Designation.
As for those who "Proclaim the Supramundane," this school explains that mundane phenomena arise from inversion and are entirely false, and therefore [they are not real].
All that exists substantially is merely a conventional designation; supramundane dharmas do not arise from inversion.
The two objects of emptiness—the path and its fruit—are real, and the wisdom of the two emptinesses is likewise real.

Because the real object can give rise to real wisdom, and real wisdom can penetrate the real object, they are called "real" and are termed "supramundane. As for the term *kīṭa* (chicken-egg), it refers to the aforementioned... [text fragment ends].
In ancient times, there was a seer who dyed his rooster; because its offspring were born with that color, he took it as his name.

The *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra* states that this was the clan name (*gotra*) of the Master of the Vinaya. Next, in the second century, another school emerged from the Mahāsāṃghika called the Bahuśrutīya.
Because the founder of this school was thoroughly versed in the Tripiṭaka and had deeply realized the intent of the Buddha’s teachings, he was called "Much-Hearing" (*bahuśruta*).
Next, two hundred years after the *Śrāvaka* [tradition], another school emerged from within the Mahāsāṃghika named the Sautrāntika.
Master Ji said that this school is so called because they teach that worldly phenomena (*loka-dharma*) are both provisional and real.

Next, when two hundred years were complete, there was a renunciant of non-Buddhist origin who abandoned heterodoxy to return to the Right Path; he was named Mahādeva. This is not [the case with the Sautrāntika].
This Mahādeva, who had committed a heinous crime (ānantarya), went forth from the Mahāsāṃghika school and received the precepts.

Being learned and diligent, he resided on Mount Caitya. Due to a dispute over five matters concerning the causes and conditions with the monks of that school, they were subsequently divided into three sects:
first, the Caitīya school; "Caitya" here is translated as "Spiritual Shrine," referring to the place of his initial birth.
This is because there are spirit temples at all four locations—where he attained enlightenment, where he turned the wheel of Dharma, and where he entered nirvana—to offer worship.
Second, the Haimavata school resides to the west of Mount Caitya; thus it is named the Western Mountain Dwellers (Haimavata). Third, the Uttaraśaila school is located to the north of Mount Caitya;
thus it is named the Northern Mountain Dwellers (Uttaraśaila). When the fundamental and derivative schools are explained separately, they constitute nine schools in total.
Regarding the one called Mahādeva who committed the heinous crimes (*ānantarya*):

more than a hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, there was a king of Magadha named Aśoka who ruled over Jambudvīpa and brought harmony to both humans and spirits. At that time, the Saṃgha of the Buddha’s Dharma became divided.
It is said that this Mahādeva, before his ordination, had committed three of the heinous crimes—namely, killing his father and killing his mother.
Having killed an Arhat and committed three other heinous crimes (*ānantarya*), he was deeply overcome with remorse and sought to extinguish his transgressions.

Just as he encountered the assembly of the Mahāsāṃghika monks gathered outside a cave, they—unaware of his commission of these heinous acts—ordained him and conferred upon him full ordination (*upasampadā*).
Subsequently, because of his intelligence, he came to be revered by King Aśoka; later, however, he fell out with the Sthaviras.

Regarding the dispute over Mahādeva: when settling a legal case (*adhikaraṇa*) by means of the "decision of the majority" (*yadbhūyaś-cīrṇa*) as prescribed in the *Prātimokṣa*, although the number of venerable elders (*sthavira*) within the faction of the Sthaviras was very small, the total number of people was extremely large.
Because King [Mahāsena] considered Mahādeva to be in the right, the two schools proceeded in opposition. As for the two Sthavira schools... [the text continues].
At the beginning of the third century after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, Kātyāyanīputra extensively propagated the Dharma of the Single Flavor among the ordained elders;

however, because he propagated the Sūtras and Vinaya with less emphasis, they diverged from the original school's intent and were subsequently divided into two schools. The first is the Sarvāstivāda, which itself has two branches:

first, those who maintain that conditioned phenomena exist throughout the three periods of time; second, those who maintain that unconditioned phenomena transcend the three periods of time—namely, space and analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).

The essence of non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) exists in all [dharmas]; it is also called the Sarvāstivāda (the School of Proclaiming that All Exists), which refers to the fact that this school establishes its tenets by extensively producing their underlying reasons.
Among the ten schools held by the aforementioned five schools, the *Daśabhāṇavāra* (Ten Recitations) is the primary authority for this school.
Second is the Sthavira school, which later changed its name to the Haimavata (Snowy Mountain) school; the disciples of the Sthavira originally propagated the teachings of the Sūtras.
Because the Sautrāntika school produced many great masters of Abhidharma who were well-versed in its principles, the Sthaviras were suppressed;
consequently, the Sthavira school grew weak, and [the Sautrāntikas] moved into the Snowy Mountains to avoid them, taking their place of residence as their name.
In the third century after the passing [of the Buddha], a school named Vātsīputrīya emerged from the Sarvāstivāda school, adhering to the first five [categories].
Within these schools, the Vātsīputrīya school constitutes the primary sect. Three hundred years later, four schools branched out from the Vātsīputrīya:
first, the Dharmottarīya, so named because they hold that there is a "dharma" (a self) which can ascend; second, the Bhadrayānīya, named after its founder;
"yāna" (胄) carries the meaning of lineage or progeny, referring here to the descendants of the Arhats.

"Descendant" (*vaṃśa*) refers to the lineage of the virtuous. Third, the Saṃmitīya school is so named because its masters weigh, judge, and establish [the teachings], calling them "valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*);
being free from error, it is called "correct" (*saṃmita*). This is the primary authority for the *Vinayavibhāṣā-śāstra*.
Fourth, the Giriśaila school is so named because the mountain forests where the leaders of this school reside are lush and densely wooded. This is the three hundredth [entry].
From the Sarvāstivāda school, another school emerged named the Mahīśāsaka. Its founder was formerly a king whose transformative influence permeated the land and its people;

later, he abdicated the throne, left the household life, and cultivated supernatural powers (*abhijñā*). He was named after his original status as a "sovereign of the earth" (*mahī-īśvara*), hence the name Mahīśāsaka.
Among the aforementioned five schools, they take the Mūlasarvāstivāda as their primary tenet. This is the third [section].
One hundred years after [the Buddha's passing], from the Mahīśāsaka school emerged a branch named the Dharmaguptaka, also called the Dharmaguhya or Dharmarakṣita.
This arhat was a disciple of Maudgalyāyana; after Maudgalyāyana’s demise, Dharmarakṣita compiled what his teacher had taught into five piṭakas:
first, the Sūtra-piṭaka; second, the Vinaya-piṭaka; third, the Śāstra-piṭaka; fourth, the Mantra-piṭaka; and fifth, the... [text ends].
Within the Bodhisattva-piṭaka of the Mahīśāsaka school, there is a sub-sect that establishes its own Piṭaka separately, named the Dharmaguptaka school;
it holds the four branches among the aforementioned five schools to be its primary tenets.
At the end of the third century [after the Buddha’s passing], a school named the Kāśyapīya emerged from the Sarvāstivāda; in ancient times, there was...
Because the radiance of the Rishi’s body was so exceedingly magnificent that it eclipsed all other lights so they no longer appeared, this present master of the school is his descendant;
he takes the Vimuktimārga (Path of Liberation) from among the previous five schools as his primary tenet.
Then, at the beginning of the fourth century, another school emerged from the Sarvāstivāda named the Sautrāntika. This school...
Based on the sūtras as their authority and not on the Vinaya or Abhidharma, they take the sūtras as the proof for all meanings they interpret;

therefore, they are called the Sautrāntika school. Originally and subsequently, they formed eleven distinct branches, which, together with the nine branches of the Mahāsāṃghika, constitute twenty schools in total.
Although within the Sthavira school there were eleven different divisions, each...
Within each of these schools, all five schools' tenets are contained;

however, among them, the Sarvāstivāda school specifically adheres to the *Sarvāstivāda* as its tenet, the Mahīśāsaka school specifically adheres to the *Mahīśāsaka* and the five divisions as its tenet, the Vātsīputrīya school specifically adheres to the *Vātsīputrīya* as its tenet, and the Kāśyapīya school specifically adheres to the *Kāśyapīya* as its tenet. This is the Dharma.
The Tibetan schools are particularly biased toward the *Dharmaguptaka* as their primary tenet;
one must therefore understand that these twenty schools are not merely redundant or unnecessary for those of shallow understanding.
Furthermore, the meaning of [the correspondence] with *Tiwai* differs slightly;
according to the *Guangming wenju*, which cites the *Tiwai jing*, it correlates the five classics with the five precepts as follows: "No killing" corresponds to the *Shangshu*;
"No stealing" corresponds to the *Chunqiu*; "No lust" corresponds to the *Lili*; "No false speech" corresponds to the *Shijing*; and "No drinking alcohol" corresponds to the [Five Classics].

These correspond to the Ten Wholesome Actions (*daśa-kuśala-karmapatha*). Among them, killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct constitute the three bodily [precepts]; false speech subsumes the four verbal [precepts]; and drinking alcohol subsumes the three mental [precepts].
Since worldly people are unable to guard their speech, they briefly establish a single restraint: non-false speech.
Therefore, it is said that binding the ten wholesome actions is precisely the five precepts (*pañca-śīla*). The character *jīng* (矜) is pronounced "lián" (蓮).

The character for "nǎo" (獶) is correctly written as "níáo" (獿), pronounced with the initial *n* and final *-ao* (乃刀切); it refers to a macaque (*míhóu*). This means that the dancers were merely performing like macaques, thereby confusing the distinctions between men and women and between the noble and the humble.
This passage originates from the "Yueli" (樂記) chapter of the *Liji* (禮記). Furthermore, [the commentary] states: "The one wearing the *duānmǐn* (端冕) was Zheng..."
The Master’s commentary states: "Dark and profound" refers to black robes. When speaking of ancient music, one refers to the orthodox music of the former kings.
Zixia said: "The music of Zheng is licentious and excessive, corrupting the will; the music of Song is that of wanton women, drowning the will; the music of Wei is hurried and rapid, vexing the will;
the music of Qi is arrogant and deviant, making the will haughty. These four types of music all lead to excess in carnal desire and harm virtue; for this reason..."
It is not used in sacrificial rites.
The character "疹" (zhèn, with the radical "疒" and the phonetic "忍") is incorrect; the character should be written as "疢" (chèn, with the radical "疒" and the phonetic "恥").
The *Jùnjié qūlǐ* states: "The gentleman is reverent and respectful, exercising restraint and moderation. Here, *jùn* (撙) is synonymous with *qù* (趨); *qù* means to approach.
Thus, it signifies that one approaches others with reverence and respect, exercising due measure and control.
*Ni* (劓) is an instrument for cutting off the nose; *fei* (剕) [is an instrument for cutting off the kneecap].
"Fu" (符) and "fei" (沸) form a compound meaning to cut off the feet; "yue" (刖) is pronounced like "yue" (月).
"Mo" (墨) refers to carving the forehead and staining it black; "sang" (顙) means the brow. "Mo" is also called "qing" (黥); one first carves the face with [an instrument]...
The "branding with ink" punishment involves carving a wound upon the forehead and filling the wound's cavity with ink to change its color.
The "palace" punishment is a form of sexual mutilation: for men, it consists of castration; for women, it consists of confinement in a secluded chamber.
"Great execution" (dàpì) refers to capital punishment; "execution" (pì) refers to a crime deserving death. Thus, those of great guilt die.
The "Lǚxíng" chapter of the *Shàngshū* clarifies these five punishments, which have existed since the times of Táng and Yú. When did they first originate in the High Antiquity?
The five sciences consist of the inner five sciences and the outer five sciences. The outer five sciences are: first, grammar; second, medicine; third, the arts and crafts;
fourth, incantations and rituals; and fifth, seals and talismans. The inner five sciences are the aforementioned four sciences [plus the fifth].
The fifth [of the five sciences], *hetuvidyā* (Logic), is identical to those of the outsiders. Furthermore, some say: the first three are identical to the outsiders;

the fourth is *hetuvidyā*; and the fifth is *adhyātmavidyā* (Inner Science). To briefly explain their meanings: the interpretation of glosses and the definition of characters, as well as their various classifications, is called *śabdavidyā* (Grammar).

Technical arts, mechanical devices, the five elements, and calendrical calculations are called *śilpakarmasthānavidyā* (Arts and Crafts). The mastery of prohibitions and incantations... [is called *vidyāsthānavidyā* (Knowledge of the Sciences)].

The study of medicinal herbs, minerals, acupuncture, and moxibustion is called the science of medicine (*cikitsāvidyā*). The examination and determination of the heterodox and the orthodox, and the investigation and verification of the true and the false, is called the science of logic (*hetuvidyā*).
The thorough exploration and elucidation of the subtle principles of cause and effect within the five vehicles is called the inner science (*adhyātmavidyā*).

Regarding the five spiritual powers (*pañcābhijñā*) and the *dhyānapāramitā*: the "five spirits" are merely alternative names for the five consciousnesses; they are, in fact, the conscious spirit (*vijñāna*).

This is because at the moment of the union of the parents, the physical constituents of semen and blood provide a locus upon which consciousness is entrusted. At that time, there are the three factors of body, life-force, and mind.
When consciousness is fully present within that interval, there is the nature of the five consciousnesses.

The six arts—namely, ritual, music, archery, charioteering, writing, and mathematics—are called the "six arts. As stated in the duties of the Great Minister of the Interior (*Dàsītǒu*) in the *Zhou Lǐ*:
By means of three categories of instruction, the myriad people were taught and promoted for office: first, the Six Virtues—knowledge, benevolence, sagacity, righteousness, loyalty, and harmony;
second, the Six Conducts—filial piety, fraternal duty, harmony with kinsmen, affection for neighbors, trustworthiness, and compassion;
third, the Six Arts—rites, music, archery, charioteering, writing, and mathematics. Rites consist of the principles of the Five Rites; music consists of the singing and dancing of the Six Musics.

"Archery" refers to the five methods of archery; "charioteering" refers to the five regulations of charioteering; "writing" refers to the categories of the six scripts; and "calculation" refers to the reckonings of the nine numbers.
Furthermore, the subsequent passage states: "Suffering and Accumulation are different; [this refers to] the Truth of Accumulation (*samudaya-satya*).

That which is the accumulation within the house of suffering is called the 'accumulation of suffering' (*duḥkha-samudaya*). This text is likely erroneous. Why? Because in the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*, it simply says "knowing."

The fact that the afflictions (*kleśa*) of all sentient beings—their views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*)—are accumulated differently is known from the text of the "Origin" (*samudaya*), for there is no character for "suffering" (*duḥkha*) therein.

It is likely that the Master of the Record (*ji-zhu*) mistakenly took the character for "affliction" (*nǎo*) to be the character for "suffering" (*kǔ*), and thus interpreted it as "the origin of suffering.
Furthermore, the phrase "those who exclusively travel and study" in the passage below is an error. The tradition states: "One name is Fǎngyóuxué; Xú Shì..."

The commentary states that "fǔ" is pronounced like "fú. It further says that "understanding the divisions of the mind" (*xīn jiě fēn jì*) refers to the *Chuán* (Tradition) stating that one's mental consciousness distinguishes weights down to the *fēn* and *zhū*.
Bian Que was a physician from Yue; the *Shìjì* (Records of the Grand Historian) states he was a native of Zheng in Bohai Commandery, surnamed Qín and named Yuèrén.
In his youth, he served as the head of a lodging house for guests, where the guest Chang Sangjun transmitted a secret medical formula to Bian Que. Yang... [text fragment].
The *Fayan* (Discourse on the Law) states: "Bian Que was a man of Lu. The commentary says: "He was a man of Lu in Taishan.
The preface to the *Eighty-one Difficulties of the Canon* (*Nanjing*) states: "Because he resembled Bian Que of the time of Xuanyuan, he was styled 'Bian Que.
He originally resided in the state of Lu, and thus he was a man of Lu. The character *nìng* (儜) is pronounced *nǚgēng* (女耕); it means weak and frail.
Even now, the intent of the *Xiǎngfǎ juéyì miàoshèngdìng jīng* (Sūtra on the Sublime Samādhi for Resolving Doubts during the Semblance Dharma) cited by our present school is likewise.
An Shìgāo’s *Ěrjiào lùn* (Treatise on the Two Teachings) states: "The *Fǎxíng jīng* (Dharmagati Sūtra) has no one to translate it;

although it is included in the category of 'doubtful' texts, it does not harm the grand purport [of the teaching]. The *Xiǎngfǎ juéyì jīng* in one fascicle, the *Rǔguāng jīng* in one fascicle, and the *Chūjiào jīng* [are also such]."

The *Jiǔshíliù dào jīng* (Sūtra of Ninety-Six Paths) in one fascicle, the *Qīngjìng fǎxíng jīng* (Sūtra on the Practice of Pure Dharma) in one fascicle, the *Miàoshèng dìng jīng* (Sūtra of the Wondrous Supreme Samādhi) in one fascicle, the *Jìngtǔ sānmèi jīng* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of the Pure Land) in three fascicles, the *Tíwèi jīng* (Sūtra of Tiwei), the *Zhànchá jīng* (Sūtra of the Divination Board), and others were listed in the old catalogs as either "doubtful" or "spurious.
From the Tang dynasty onward, some were included among the orthodox canon; these [decisions] were all based on personal preferences for inclusion or exclusion.

The *Ēryāpata-sūtra* (Scripture on the Practice of Pure Conduct) and the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-samādhi-sūtra* (Sūtra of the Sublime and Victorious Samādhi), which were formerly listed in the old catalogs as spurious, were ordered by imperial decree during the first year of the Wansui era of the Great Tang Empress Wu to be collated and included among the authentic scriptures by the śramaṇa Mingquan and others of the Foshouji Monastery; they are now appended to the authentic canon as the *Jingtu sanmei jing* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of the Pure Land). The *Ear-Listening Sūtra* (*Er ruzhan cha jing*) was likewise collated and included among the authentic scriptures by the śramaṇas Mingquan and others of the Foshouji Monastery by imperial decree in the first year of the Wansui era of the Empress Wu reign.
