the commentary states that it extends from east of the Ji River to the Ji River. East of the Ji River is called Xuzhou; the commentary states that it extends from east of the Ji River to the sea. North of the sea is called Youzhou;
the commentary states that it extends from the Yi River to the northern barbarians. Qi is called Yingzhou; the commentary states that it extends from Mount Dai.
To the east it reaches the sea.
Regarding the "Nine Yi," the *Erya* states: "The Nine Yi, Eight Di, Seven Rong, and Six Man are called the Four Seas. The commentary notes that these are the Nine Yi.
Regarding those in the east, the eight Di; in the north, the seven Rong; in the west, the six Man; and in the south, the four Huang:
these are the four regions beginning with Guzhu. The *Erya* states: "Guzhu, Beihu, Xiwangmu, and Riyia are called the Four Huang. The commentary notes that Gu... [text truncated]
Zhú is in the north, Běihù is in the south, Wángmǔ of the West is in the west, and Rìxià is in the east;

these are all the states of the bordering regions (*hūn huāng*). Next are the four extremities (*sì jí*), namely the nine *yí* tribes and others. Next are the four wildernesses (*sì huāng*). Regarding the four extremities:
to the east they reach Tàiyuǎn, to the west Bīnguó, to the south Pǔlián, and to the north [the region of] ... (the text ends).
Zhūlì refers to the four extremities, meaning the most distant lands in the four directions. Bīn is pronounced *bīn* and Pǔ is pronounced *bǔ*.
Gū is pronounced *gū*. When old and new bamboo grow together yet do not see one another, it is called *gūzhú*.
Its bamboo produces only one shoot (*sǔn*) every three years; once the shoot has become a mature stalk, the "mother" bamboo dies.

The higher fetters (*ūrdhvabhāgīya*) consist of five items, yet only four are listed here, lacking one: the "taint of the formless" (*ārūpyarāga*). This is merely due to an omission during transcription. As for the taints of the realm of form (*rūparāga*) and the formless (*ārūpyarāga*), they pertain exclusively to the higher realms;
although restlessness (*auddhatya*), conceit (*māna*), and ignorance (*avidyā*) also extend to the lower realms, they cannot pull one downward [into rebirth there]. Therefore, it is so stated.

The "upper-tier" (*ūrdhva-bhāgīya*) fetters consist of the form and formless realms; because they exist above the desire realm, they receive the name "upper. Although greed (*rāga*) extends to these upper realms, it is not exclusively an upper-tier fetter;

hatred (*dveṣa*), however, is exclusively lower and does not extend to the upper realms. The view of self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*), the clinging to views (*dṛṣṭi-parāmarśa*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*) encompass all delusions of view;
although they also extend to the upper realms, they are able to pull one down [to the lower], and are thus called "lower-tier" (*avara-bhāgīya*). The desire realm exists... [in the lower tier].

Because the form and formless realms are inferior, they receive the designation "inferior"; thus it is said that by two [fetters] one does not transcend the desire realm, and by three one returns to the lower [realms].

Therefore, even if one has severed craving and so forth up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), one may still return to the desire realm due to the view of a self-entity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and other such fetters.
If one clings to provisional treatises and the like—

specifically this doctrine of "three non-existences and two existences" (sanwu eryou) which Ci'en [Kuiji] followed— and exclusively relies on the provisional teachings of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* and other texts that take the ultimate quiescence as the definitive standard,
asserting that there is never the attainment of Buddhahood, yet remains ignorant of the sūtras concerning the arising and ceasing [of the Tathāgatagarbha].

In the passage "Transcending conceptions" (*duxiang*) and in that where it says "those of the Two Vehicles who have attained fixed nature all obtain the field of quiescent extinction of the One Vehicle" within the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*,
these two texts can dispel emotional attachments to specific doctrinal schools. If one is well-versed in the provisional and the ultimate, this will become manifest,
as has been analyzed in the supplementary notes on the preceding textual passages.
Niang (釀): the initial radical is "woman" (女) and the phonetic is "liang" (亮). It refers to leavening agent.
*Kǔ* (古孝切) means the leaven for brewing wine;
*cǎn* (慘) means the seventh tone.
Zǐ (觜) is pronounced with the initial *wěi* (委) and the final *qiè* (切). It means to obstruct and ruin.
The character "阻" (zǔ) is likely an error; it should be "沮" (jǔ). "沮" is pronounced *cí lǚ* (as in *cí lǚ*) and also *jiāng yù* (as in *jiāng yù*).
This is fully explained in the first fascicle under the section "Distinguishing Existence and Non-existence.

The single character [in the original] is likely erroneous. It was previously clarified within the "Inconceivable Realm" (*acintya-viṣaya*) during the explanation of the "Ten Suchnesses" (*daśa-tathatā*). — Ancient Record.

This *Zhiguan* is the fifth fascicle. Furthermore, the passage below stating, "The *yòu-yīn* (cause of realization) is neither identical with nor separate from consciousness (*vijñāna*), etc.," is likely an error;
it should read, "The *yòu-yīn* is neither identical with nor separate from consciousness and perception (*saṃjñā*);

the *yuán-yīn* (causal condition) is neither identical with nor separate from sensation (*vedanā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and the self (*ātman*). Therefore, the *Zhiguan* states: "Transforming form (*rūpa*) results in the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*); the Dharma-body is eternal."

Delight in the transformation of consciousness (*vijñāna*) into *prajñā*, wherein *prajñā* is itself purity; in the transformation of feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and formations (*saṃskāra*) into liberation (*vimukti*), wherein liberation is itself the self (*ātman*).

Furthermore, based on the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), one transforms consciousness into permanence, feeling into bliss, perception and formations into self, and form (*rūpa*) into purity.
Moreover, as for the passage in the subsequent section stating, "The analogies and the corresponding texts regarding the wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*) and so forth are all missing," if...

According to the *Jingming shu* (Commentary on the Vimalakīrti Sūtra), it states: "The foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) serve as the seeds; the right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*) serve as growth; the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) serve as the sprouts;

the five faculties (*indriya*) are like the stem; the five powers (*bala*) are like the branches and leaves; the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) are the flowers; and the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*) is the fruit. Furthermore, the subsequent passage states:
"'Pure' (*chun*) means simple and honest, and also implies soaking or nourishing. It appears that the character "soaking" (*zi*) here may be an error and should [be corrected].
The character *qing* (清) is read as *wu* (沃) and means "gentle" (*rou*).

The character *lang* (儢) has the phonetic value of *lü* (呂) and is glossed as "to reject," meaning the mind does not wish to act. What is now called "the mind is not vigorous" (*xin bu li*) is likely a corruption or abbreviation.

The *Zhiguan* (Cessation and Contemplation) states: "Whether facing [the object], turning [the mind], combining both, or regarding the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), the commentary has already clarified this;
now it shall be further elucidated. Although this is not the primary intent of the current text, it may nonetheless serve to manifest broad knowledge through this discussion.
Thus, the *Chanmen* (Gate of Meditation) says: "There are five types of unskillful means: first, vitarka and vicāra..."
Greed is threefold, anger is fourfold, and delusion is fivefold; these five evil karmas each have three types. Regarding the first three:

the first is the mental application (*vitarka*) and discursive investigation (*vicāra*) within a clear and sharp mind; the second is the mental application and discursive investigation within a mind that is half-clear and half-obscured;

the third is the mental application and discursive investigation within a mind that is entirely obscured and deluded. Regarding the second set of three: the first is external greed; the second is internal...
The third [category] consists of three types of external desire for sensual pleasure that pervade all places: first, irrational anger; second, anger that conforms to reason;

and third, anger arising from contention. The fourth [category] consists of three types: first, the calculation of annihilationism and eternalism; second, the calculation of existence and non-existence;

and third, the calculation of the primordial nature of the world (*pradhāna*). The fifth [category] consists of three types: first, the obscuration of dullness and mental darkness; and second, unwholesome reflection.
Regarding the obstacles to the three spheres and the obstacles of oppression, there are six types of treatment for these five and three [obstacles]:

first, direct treatment (*pratipakṣa*); second, transformative treatment; third, non-transformative treatment; fourth, combined treatment; fifth, combined transformative and non-transformative treatment;
and sixth, treatment that is neither direct, nor transformative, nor combined. "Direct treatment" refers to the medicinal remedy applied to the object of the disease.
One treats [the afflictions] by observing their opposites. Regarding the shifting treatment, there are three types: first, both the illness and the remedy shift;
second, the illness does not shift while the remedy shifts; and third, as for the first principle, for example, when a mind of greed is impure, one treats it with its opposite.
Once the treatment is established, one develops aversion toward the previous object and consequently gives rise to anger; at such a time, one should apply the mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
To treat anger means that both the affliction is transformed and the method is transformed. Regarding the second meaning:

when it is simply desire (*rāga*), one transforms the previously practiced method of the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) and instead cultivates the contemplation of loving-kindness (*maitrī-bhāvanā*) to treat the object of desire;
this is called "the affliction is not transformed, but the method is transformed. As for using loving-kindness to treat anger, the Brahmajāla Sūtra Precepts state: "All men are..."
"My father is the father of all women, and my mother is the mother of all women; since they are my parents, I should love and cherish them—how could I further give rise to lustful desire toward them?
Regarding the non-transformation of treatment, there are also two meanings: first, neither the illness nor the method transforms;
second, the illness transforms but the method does not. As for the first meaning, it is like the case of the illness of lustful desire.
If it is not purified by means of the contemplation of impurity, one need not change the visualization;
rather, one should purify it by cultivating the perception of pus, rot, and so forth, and it will naturally depart. Regarding the second meaning:

just as when treating greed, hatred may arise, one simply increases the visualization of impurity and the hatred will naturally be eliminated. As for the combined treatment: if there is both greed and [hatred],...
Regarding hatred (*dveṣa*), one should treat it with the meditation on impurity and the mind of loving-kindness (*maitrīcitta*).

As for "treating both simultaneously" and "not treating both simultaneously," these meanings are the same as those explained regarding "treating by turning" and "treating without turning. That which is neither opposed, nor turned, nor treated simultaneously is the ultimate principle (*paramārtha*).
As for what is called "obstruction by the pressure of objects," it refers to when, during the cultivation of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the body may suddenly experience pain.
One sees various external objects appearing headless, handless, or footless; garments torn and ruined; being sunk into the earth; or being burned by fire;
or seeing oneself falling from a high precipice. Such obstacles oppress the practitioner with evil thoughts.
As for the obstacle of "delusion," it refers to the thought of committing the ten non-virtuous actions, the four grave offenses, returning home, and so forth, which causes one to become dazed.
Those obscured by deep darkness and ignorance—indeterminate, dull-witted, and lacking discernment—erroneously speculate on the nature of the world, thinking:
"Because of the existence of subtle atoms (*paramāṇu*), there exist real dharmas; because of the existence of real dharmas, there are the four great elements (*mahābhūta*);
and because of the four great elements, there exists the conventionally designated sentient world. Based on such reflections, they exclusively practice false paths.

Those who speculate on existence and non-existence wonder whether the self and the aggregates (skandhas) and so forth exist or do not exist; likewise, up to those who speculate on neither existence nor non-existence.
Those who speculate on annihilationism and eternalism inquire: "Do past phenomena cease to exist? Do present phenomena not cease to exist?
When they investigate the three periods of time, they argue that if they cease, there is annihilation, and if they do not cease, there is eternity. Such contentious debate is attachment to anger.
One's own dharma refers to the dharma of others; it is said that affliction does not arise from this [external] non-conformity.
Regarding one who is angry at what accords with principle: even when an outsider comes to cause you affliction, you then give rise to anger;

likewise, as there are the three poisons in a pure land, regarding one who is irrationally angry, anger arises spontaneously without others coming to cause affliction. This applies everywhere to all forms of craving and desire.
Those who are attached to internal and external sensory objects and conditions give rise to craving and desire in all places. Regarding those with internal and external lust:
they take as their object the physical forms of men and women externally, and further, the bodily features internally. As for external lust:
if one is a man, one takes a woman as an object; if one is a woman, one takes a man as an object, becoming consistently muddled.
Regarding those who are deluded by *vitarka* and *vicāra*: although their minds are obscure and resemble sleep, within this state of profound stupor they intensely cling to objects of perception.
When half-lucid and half-obscured, for one with *vitarka* and *vicāra*, lucidity involves clinging to objects while obscurity constitutes the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

Now, in this case, it is merely a matter of these two being present in equal measure. As for *vitarka* and *vicāra* within a mind that is clear and sharp, one does not perceive any wholesome dharmas at all.
It merely involves clearly discerning the objects of perception (*ālambana*).
As for the "Teaching" and "Practice" sections of the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary), their presence or absence is fully detailed in the *Fahua Xuanyi*, the *Weimo Xuanyi*, and other commentaries;

since ancient times until the present, everyone has made this claim. Therefore, the current confusion regarding Chan stems from the ignorant masses who assert that the School of the Lineage (*Zongmen*) possesses no teachings.
To claim that the teachings of our school are merely a matter of "seeing" and "hearing" is, alas, a profound error! The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:
"For example, a treasure in the darkness cannot be seen without a lamp; so too, if the Buddha-dharma is not explained by someone, even the wise cannot comprehend it.
How can you say it is merely a matter of seeing and hearing? Furthermore, consider the case of those who conflate Chan with the scriptures.

How could any school ever have existed without verbal expression? Even if one were to simply raise a hand or brandish a whisk, one would still not escape the fault of being within the realm of conditioned activity (*saṃskṛta*).

How, then, can you recklessly claim that there is "speaking" and "non-speaking" to distinguish between different schools and teachings? Now, the Master [Jiashan] broke this down, saying: "The Teaching (*śāsana*) is that which expresses;
the School (*siddhānta*) is that which is expressed. There must be a School for there to be a Teaching, and there must be a Teaching for there to be a School."
Therefore, the doctrine cannot exist in isolation; if there were no doctrine, how could one know the truth of that which is expressed?
Furthermore, in the subsequent passage, the character "ru" (入) in "next, introducing the sūtra" is an error and should be "da" (大).
Moreover, where it says "entering the non-dual extreme," it should read "not entering the two extremes. Finally, regarding the phrase "feeding sugar to a tiger," [the character] is "yi" (飴).
The character "dang" (當) should be "si" (飼); the character "yi" (飴) is pronounced as "zhi" (之).

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "one who sacrifices their body to complete the person," the character "ren" (人) should be "ren" (仁), as this passage appears in the *Lunyu* (Analects). Moreover, the *Zhi guan* (Śamatha-vipaśyanā) states that "shu pi" (輸皮)—here, "shu" (輸) means "exhaustion."
The *Wuming baoyang xianyu jing* (Sūtra on the Nourishing of the Wise and Foolish through Ignorance) refers to ignorance as a precious elephant; it is because of this that [the teaching] is earnest.
The character "yin" (因) is likely an error; it should read "kùn" (困). [The character for] "shū" (抒) is pronounced with the second tone and the initial "qie" (切).

*Tuo* (with the phonetic component *dou* and *gai*) and also *ta* with *la*: it means to strike with the hand; it is also a variant of *nie*. In the sutras, it is written as the character *cuo* (with the phonetic component *ce* and *jiao*), which is also written as the character *zhuo*.
"Lu" (pronounced lǚ).
There are those who claim that what is subject to outflows (*sāsrava*) is sufficient, and so forth.
The treatise states: It is said that by collecting the mind one can give rise to true wisdom; yet some who merely attain meditative concentration (dhyāna-samādhi) consider this sufficient.

Therefore, the Buddha declared, "This is not sufficient. One should rely upon this concentration to further seek the superior Dharma—namely, the exhaustion of all outflows (āsrava)—and for this reason it is called a reliance.
Regarding the arising of the eight noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*) and the discourse on generating revulsion:
it is said that viewing [the aggregates] as a disease, an abscess, an arrow, a torment, impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self constitutes the eight noble lineages.
Question: Are the seven perceptions identical to the seven supports?
The treatise states: "The question is why the Buddha spoke of the seven supports as the 'seven perceptions of meditative concentration' (samādhi-vimokṣa); therefore, this was said.
This is as in the case of the Elder Vyūḍha.

The following passage uses the character "xuǎn" (select) as its standard, whereas other versions of the sutra use the character "zhuàn" (compile); this may be due to differences in the original manuscripts of the *Huashou jing* (Sutra of the Flower Hand).

The *Huashou jing* states: "There are seven repositories, namely: the wind-repository, the raw-repository, the cooked-repository, the cold-repository, the heat-repository, the vision-repository, and the desire-repository.
Among these repositories, the desire-repository is the most solid; it relies upon nasal mucus, saliva, the flanks, the stomach, excrement, and urine. At that time...
In the assembly there was a lay follower named Vyavahāra. Vyavahāra had a wife named Rūpavatī, who was beautiful and possessed of a handsome countenance;
the lay follower Vyavahāra was deeply attached to her. Upon hearing what the Buddha had said, he immediately addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Do not speak thus! How can you say that the mind of lust arises from excrement and urine? Why is this? Because my wife is upright and magnificent."
The Buddha knew that the householder’s defilement of greed was deep and profound.
He immediately manifested a beautiful woman of exquisite form and entered the assembly. Upon seeing her, the householder asked, "Why have you come?
The woman replied, "I have come to listen to the Buddha preach the Dharma. The householder then pulled her onto his own seat. The Buddha [intervened].
By means of his supernormal power, he caused the woman’s excrement to soil her clothes; the householder, unable to bear the foul odor, covered his nose with his hand.
Then, Bhadanta said to the householder, "Why do you cover your nose? The householder replied, "This place is foul and filthy;
the Buddha, by means of his supernormal power, has caused this woman to discharge excrement and soil my residence."
While the householder was putting on his clothes, Upananda said to him again, "Behold what your wife has done; she is foul and filthy.
The householder replied, "My wife is pure and clean; her body is free of all filth. I believe it is you who are foul and filthy.
Upananda said, "You have no sense of shame! Who calls you a 'householder'? He then seized him by the hand.
At that time, the layman felt a sense of revulsion and clearly perceived the many impurities of women;
desiring to leave the household life, he said to the Buddha, "Welcome. Immediately, the *kāṣāya* robe appeared upon his body and his hair and beard fell away naturally.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for him, and he attained the stage of *srotāpanna*.

Because the space-element (*ākāśa-dhātu*) is empty, food can pass through it. According to the *Vibhāṣā* and the *Abhidharma*: Question: What is the difference between "space" (*ākāśa*) and the "space-element" (*ākāśa-dhātu*)? Answer: Space is non-material (*arūpa*), whereas the space-element is material (*rūpin*).

Space is invisible, whereas the space-element is visible. Space is non-obstructive (*anidarśana*), whereas the space-element is obstructive (*sanidarśana*). Space is non-resistant (*apratigha*), whereas the space-element is resistant (*sapratigha*).

"Emptiness" refers to the unconditioned empty realm (*asaṃskṛta-ākāśa-dhātu*) and the conditioned empty realm (*saṃskṛta-ākāśa-dhātu*). The conditioned empty realm refers to the limit of form (*rūpa-paryanta*) and derived form (*bhautika-rūpa*), such as the emptiness of the eye, the emptiness of the ear, the emptiness of the nose, the emptiness of the mouth, and so forth.
These are explained in detail in the "Excellence of the Object" (*viṣaya-prakarṣa*) section of the *Xuanyiwen* (Profound Meaning).

If one kills a living being with a mind of greed, that which is associated with it is delusion; the volition associated with it is ignorance; the mind associated with it is formative action (*saṃskāra*);
the arising of consciousness is consciousness; the production of the activity of existence is name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*); the manifestation of these various factors is birth (*jāti*);
the transformation of these various factors is aging (*jarā*); and the disintegration of these various factors is death (*maraṇa*).
*Sī* (with the phonetic *xī*) means to employ or to nourish.
*Jiá*.
*Zi* (子) is pronounced with the *xie* (恊) and *qie* (洽) finals;
it means "to harmonize. *Sao* (臊) and *ji* (鰺) both have the *su* (蘇) and *zao* (遭) finals.
Fáng (with the initial rhyme of liáng) [variant character for "fat"].
[Su] and [gan] form a compound.

According to the Sarvāstivāda school, they establish "acquisition of acquisition" (*prāptiprāpti*) and so forth, up to stating that within the Sarvāstivāda system, when karma enters the past, its acquisition reaches the future;
thus, at the time of death, the acquisition ceases.
The *Mahāvibhāṣā* states: "What meaning is intended here by the term 'attainment' (*prāpti*)?

It refers to acquisition and accomplishment. How is this known? The *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra* says: 'What is attainment? It is acquisition and accomplishment. What is acquisition? It is the obtaining of accomplishment.
What is accomplishment? It is what is obtained. Although the terms 'attainment,' 'acquisition,' and 'accomplishment' differ in expression," [they refer to the same thing].
In meaning there is no difference, yet the categories of the dharmas obtained are of eleven kinds. In the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there are four:

namely, the wholesome, the unwholesome, the obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*), and the unobscured-unspecified (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*). In the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), there are three, excluding the unwholesome.

In the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), it is likewise. Furthermore, there are the untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas. Within the desire realm, the wholesome, the unwholesome, and the unobscured-unspecified [each...]

Those possessing the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) that are obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) possess only four aggregates; those in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) each possess all three [types] with five aggregates; those in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) each possess only four aggregates.
Uncontaminated phenomena (*anāsravadharma*) possess five aggregates, as do cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).

Space (*ākāśa*), being an unconditioned phenomenon (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), is excluded, as it is not included among "that which is acquired" (*prāpti*). Question: What is the distinction between acquisition (*prāpti*) and non-acquisition (*aprāpti*)? Answer: [As follows:]... [The text continues with the definition of these two.]

Acquisition (*prāpti*) pertains to both the outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*) and the outflow-free (*anāsrava*), whereas non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) is exclusively outflow-tainted. Furthermore, acquisition pertains to the wholesome (*kuśala*), unwholesome (*akuśala*), and indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), while non-acquisition is exclusively indeterminate.
According to the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, in the "Gate of Emptiness" (*śūnyatā-mukha*), karma reaches the future;

in the "Gate of Existence" (*astitva-mukha*) of the *Abhidharma-piṭaka*, karma enters the past. The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states that this distinction has been handed down from ancient masters of the Sarvāstivāda school.
There are four different [theories]; the Venerable Dharmatrāta speaks thus: "The three time periods differ due to a difference in mode (*bhāva*).
He maintains that when dharmas move through the time periods, although their modes differ, their substance (*dravya*) has no distinction.
Just as when milk transforms into curd, it abandons its taste and potency (*śakti*), but does not abandon its visible color (*varṇa*), so too do these dharmas move through...
Regarding the periods of time: from the future they come to the present, and from the present they enter the past.

It is only the acquisition of their *jāti* (generic character) that is relinquished or acquired, not the substance itself. Conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) in the state where their specific activity has not yet arisen are called "future";
as soon as this has arisen, they are called "present"; and once this has ceased, they are called "past. Thus say the two Venerable Ones.
Ghoṣaka asserts that the three time periods differ due to the distinction of their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).

He maintains that when dharmas proceed through the time periods, a past dharma is conjoined with the characteristic of the past and is not said to be separated from the characteristics of the present and future—just as when a man is currently attached to one wife, he is not said to be free from passion for other women. This is the view of the Venerable [Ghoṣaka].

Vasumitra states that the three time periods differ due to differences in their states (*avasthā*). He maintains that when dharmas move through the time periods, they receive different designations as they reach various states;
because there is a distinction in state, there is no distinction in essence (*svabhāva*). It is like a counting-stick:
when placed in the units place it is called "one," in the hundreds place it is called "one hundred," and in the thousands place it is called "one thousand. This is the fourth master’s view.

Buddhadeva speaks thus: "The distinction between the three time periods arises from their mutual dependence. He maintains that when phenomena proceed through the time periods, they are established with different names based on their prior and posterior relations;
it is not that there is a difference in their substance (*dravya*), category (*jāti*), or characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).

It is just as a single woman is called a 'daughter' in relation to her predecessor and a 'mother' in relation to her successor, according to the sequence [of her relations]; so it is with these [phenomena]."
When the Dharma functions in the world, it is called "past" when awaiting the present and future; it is called "future" when awaiting the past and present;
and it is called "present" when awaiting the past and future. Therefore, the Abhidharmikas maintain that the three time periods exist substantially:
a wholesome dharma of the past does not perish, being bound by the cord of acquisition (*prāpti*); and although a dharma of the future does not yet exist, it arises when its time arrives.

Because the accomplishment of present wholesome dharmas resides within the mind, they all exist. Regarding the acquisition of *vijñapti* (informative) and *avijñapti* (non-informative) action, it is held that they coexist with the physical form;

according to the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, there are eight types of *avijñapti*. As for the simultaneous occurrence of *avijñapti* with the performance of action, this refers to the two types of karma—wholesome and unwholesome—performed through bodily or vocal action.

When one performs an action together with another, both produce the non-informative (avijñapti) karma; likewise, when there is no action, as in the case of the virtuous or unvirtuous restraints (saṃvara), the restraint is lost when the physical form ceases.
These three factors reside in the non-informative: first, the object given does not perish, and the non-informative constantly follows;

Vocal karma gives rise to vocal non-informative action (*avijñapti*), and bodily karma gives rise to bodily non-informative action. There are six types of auxiliary non-informative action:

Therefore, according to the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra*, there are fourteen types of dissociated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*):

first, acquisition (*prāpti*); second, non-acquisition (*aprāpti*); third, homogeneity (*sabhāgatā*); fourth, the state of non-conception (*asaṃjñika*); fifth, the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*); and sixth, the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).

The seventh is life-force (*jīvita*), the eighth is birth (*jāti*), the ninth is subsistence (*sthiti*), the tenth is change (*anyathātva*), the eleventh is cessation (*anirodha*), the twelfth is the name-body (*nāmakāya*), the thirteenth is the phrase-body (*padakāya*), and the fourteenth is the syllable-body (*vyañjanakāya*).
An explanation of their meanings is roughly as at the beginning of this volume. As the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states:

"These various phenomena are dissociated from the mind (*cittaviprayukta*), are not of the nature of form (*arūpa*), and are subsumed within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*). 'Acquisition' (*prāpti*) refers to attainment (*lābha*) and possession (*samanvāgama*). It is not [form].

There are two types of acquisition (*prāpti*) that are the opposite of non-acquisition (*aprāpti*): first, obtaining what was previously unobtained or already lost; second, having obtained it, not losing it and thus achieving its possession. Non-acquisition is established as the opposite of this acquisition. Regarding acquisition and non-acquisition, they are established in mutual opposition. However, such [dharmas] each have three types of acquisition (prāpti) regarding the present and future: first, the three acquisitions of the wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate;

second, the four acquisitions consisting of those bound to the three realms and those that are unbound and untainted (anāsrava). This is because it is maintained that these acquisitions mutually establish one another.

Thus, when a dharma arises, three dharmas arise simultaneously with its own substance: first, the primary dharma itself; second, the acquisition of that dharma; and third, the acquisition of that acquisition.

The "acquisition of acquisition" (*prāpti-prāpti*) is so called because, when an acquisition arises within the continuum, it brings about the accomplishment of both the primary dharma and its own acquisition.
Since the acquisition of acquisition brings about the accomplishment of that [primary] acquisition, there is no fault of infinite regress (*anavasthā*) here.
Thus, whether they be wholesome or defiled dharmas, at the very moment each individual entity first arises, together with its own entity...
In the second moment, six factors arise together: namely, the three primary factors and their three acquisitions (*prāpti*), along with the three acquisitions of those acquisitions (*prāpti-prāpti*).

In the third moment, eighteen factors arise together: namely, there are nine acquisitions of the various factors produced in the first and second moments, as well as nine acquisitions of those acquisitions. In this manner, these acquisitions increase progressively in each subsequent moment.

All past and future afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), as well as innate virtues (*upapattilābhika-kuśala*), possess at every moment both associated (*samprayukta*) and co-existent (*sahabhū*) acquisitions (*prāpti*) that are without beginning or end throughout the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*). These acquisitions are infinite;
for instance, within the single continuum of birth and death of even one sentient being, infinite acquisitions arise at every moment, and it is the same for all sentient beings.
Within each individual continuum, an infinite and boundless number of acquisitions (*prāpti*) arise simultaneously at every single moment;
since even the acquisition of a single sentient being cannot be contained within space, how much less so a second?

If, according to the Sautrāntika school, "acquisition" (*prāpti*) is merely a provisional designation, they would simply say that karma is formed through the conjunction of the mind with body and speech.

However, the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states: "Acquisition" refers to the accomplishment of dharmas for the sake of sentient beings. When a sentient being accomplishes the present five aggregates, it is called "acquisition.
Furthermore, regarding wholesome and unwholesome karma from past lives that has not yet received its fruit of retribution...
It is said that sentient beings accomplish this Dharma, and furthermore, that karmic actions such as transgressions and merits exist only as provisional designations (*prajñapti*).
Why is this so? Because transgressions such as killing and merits such as abstaining from killing are both not substantially real. Question: What is meant by "provisional designation"? Answer:

It refers to the conceptual differentiation based upon the aggregates (*skandha*). For example, it is because of the five aggregates that one speaks of a "person"; it is because of form, odor, taste, and touch [that one speaks of objects].
Because it is said that there are things such as jars, the Dharmaguptakas maintain that two time periods do not exist [as substantial entities]:
the past, because its real dharmas have already ceased and thus do not exist, being merely nominal acquisitions whose retribution is not lost; and the future, because it has not yet arisen.
The present, however, exists because wholesome dharmas are accomplished and reside within the mind. Furthermore, the *Abhidharmakośa* states: "Such accomplishment is only..."
The *Vibhāṣā* masters maintain that [possession] is real (*dravya*) and not merely nominal (*prajñapti*).
Since both of these two positions are well-expounded and do not contradict reason, and because they are the tenets of my own school, the *Mahāvibhāṣā* cites the Dārṣṭāntikas as saying:
"Sentient beings are said to 'possess' those factors (*dharma*) without being separate from them; this [possession] has no real entity (*dravya*), it is merely..."
It is conceptually designated through dependence and discrimination, just as five fingers joined together are called a "fist," yet when separated they are no longer a fist;

therefore, it does not exist substantially. Likewise, a sentient being is said to be "endowed" with those phenomena when not separated from them, but when separated, one is no longer endowed with them;
thus, its essence does not exist substantially. Question: For what reason is this treatise established? Answer: It is based upon the sūtras.
As it is said in the Sūtra: "There is a Wheel-turning King who possesses the seven jewels.
If this possession were a real entity (*dravya-sat*), he would have to possess the bodies of others as well as things not classified as sentient beings (*asattva-saṃkhyāta*).

That is to say, if that Wheel-turning King possesses the wheel-jewel, then since the Dharma is both classified as a sentient being and not classified as a sentient being, we know [that possession is not a real entity].

The statement that "attainment (*prāpti*) is not substantially existent" is intended to refute that school's position and to demonstrate that the essence of attainment is indeed substantially existent.

For if the essence of attainment were not substantially existent, it would contradict the scriptural teaching: "Just as those in training (*śaikṣa*) possess the eight limbs [of the noble path], and Arhats who have exhausted their outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) possess the ten limbs.
Furthermore, there is the fact that one possesses the past and future [limbs] and also possesses non-possession (*aprāpti*).

Thus, we know that the *Abhidharmakośa* specifically expounds upon the *Sūtras*, the *Prakaraṇapāda* specifically expounds upon the *Vinaya*, and the various *Vibhāṣās* specifically expound upon the Buddha’s Abhidharma;
therefore, the claims of the *Vibhāṣā* are established as being "substantially existent" (*dravyasat*).
What is discussed by the Sautrāntikas, however, is established as being merely "provisionally existent" (*prajñaptisat*) and not substantially real, as in the case of the *Abhidharmakośa*.
In the treatise, it is stated that there are two types—provisional names (*prajñapti*) and substantial existence (*dravya*), which are not one-sided. Furthermore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* says:
"Next, what is meant by 'attainment' (*prāpti*) and 'accomplishment' (*siddhi*)? To speak briefly, the causes that bring about birth, provide sustenance, and cause increase are called 'attainment.
By this principle, attainment is a provisional existence. The sub-commentary on the *Śata-dharma-vidyāmukha-śāstra* also states this: "Attainment and accomplishment [are so named]."
This is what is called "attainment.

Furthermore, the term "karma" applies to the preliminary (prayoga), the fundamental (maula), and the subsequent (pṛṣṭha) stages; here, however, the name "karma" is established in reference to the fundamental stage.
As the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states: "Among the unwholesome [actions], first consider the karma of killing, such as when a sheep-slaughterer is about to carry out the act of killing."
At that time, having first conceived the intent to kill, one rises from the bed, takes the payment, goes to the market where sheep are sold,

pays the price, seizes the animal, leads it back, feeds and waters it, and brings it into the slaughterhouse; while holding a knife or staff, whether striking or piercing it before its life has ended—
this is called the preliminary application (*prayoga*) of killing, for the preliminary application is indeed the means (*upāya*).
Therefore, the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya* states: "The preparatory effort (*prayoga*) is the root;

when this manifest karma (*vijñapti-karman*) follows [the intent] and the victim actually dies, at that very moment the manifest and unmanifest karma (*vijñapti-avijñapti-karman*) constitute the fundamental path of action (*mūla-karmapatha*) of killing.

After this moment, the unmanifest karma of killing continues to follow without interruption, which is called the 'subsequent arising' (*pṛṣṭha*) of killing, as well as the subsequent acts of skinning, cutting, dressing, and washing."
Whether weighing, selling, boiling, or eating, the momentary informative action (*vijñapti-karma*) that extols its excellence is likewise called the "subsequent arising" (*pṛṣṭha*) of killing.
Since this is the case for killing, it should be understood accordingly for stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, and so forth;
as it is with unwholesome actions, the same applies by analogy to wholesome ones.

If, within the Mahāyāna, the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) contains and sustains [seeds] until the next life—as the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* quotes from the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, stating: "In the cycle of birth and death among the six destinies, the bodies of various sentient beings—born from eggs, wombs, moisture, or by transformation—arise;
therein, at the very beginning, the mind-consciousness containing all seeds matures and evolves."
It increases, expands, and grows through two types of appropriation (*upādāna*): first, the appropriation of the material sense-faculties and their bases;
second, the appropriation of the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of signs, names, conceptual discrimination, and verbal proliferation (*prapañca*).

Within the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), this consciousness possesses both types of appropriation; within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), it does not possess these two. This consciousness is also called *ālaya*.
For what reason is that consciousness also called the *ālayavijñāna*? Because this consciousness follows along with and maintains the body.
For what reason? Because this consciousness appropriates, stores, and hides within the body, sharing its welfare and peril.

The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states that the *ālayavijñāna* is also called the "fundamental consciousness" (*mūlavijñāna*), as it is the locus for all seeds of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*).
Because it is the basis, it is also called the "dwelling consciousness" (*ālaya-vijñāna*), for it is the place where all seeds reside.
Because it is the locus where all seeds are hidden and concealed, it is also called the "storehouse consciousness" (*ālaya-vijñāna*).

Furthermore, among the eight consciousnesses, this is termed the storehouse consciousness because it is able to contain and maintain the seeds of wisdom without losing their essence; its substance is non-extinguished ignorance (*avidyā*).

"Present-life [retribution], subsequent-life [retribution], and so forth" refers to karma that ripens in the present life (*drstadharma-vedanīya*), karma that ripens in the next life (*upapadya-vedanīya*), and karma that ripens in subsequent lives (*aparāpariya-vedanīya*). Karma created in this life that is experienced in this very life is called "karma to be experienced in the present life.

Karma created in this life that is experienced in the second life is called "karma to be experienced in the next life. Karma created in this life that is experienced in the third... [life] is called "karma to be experienced in subsequent lives."
That which is experienced sequentially after birth is called "subsequent" (*anantarya*);

Yan Zhitui, Court Gentleman for the Palace Gate of the Northern Qi, was a man of superior learning and abundant talent who composed a work in seven volumes consisting of twenty chapters, titled the *Yanshi Jiaxun* (Family Instructions of the Yan Clan). This was intended primarily to instruct his own descendants.
Within these twenty chapters, the second, "Instruction of Sons," cites a popular proverb which says: "Instruct a wife when she first arrives; instruct a son while he is an infant."
Truly profound are these words! Furthermore, in the eighth chapter, "Exhortation to Study," a proverb is cited:
"Accumulating wealth of ten million taels is not as good as having a slight skill within one's person; among skills that are easy to learn and yet precious, none surpasses reading books.

In the tenth chapter, "Returning the Heart," it says: "The matters of the three periods of existence are true and have manifest proof; do not treat lightly the returning of your family’s affairs to the heart [of the Dharma]."
The subtle principles within this [teaching on] pride are fully contained in the various sūtras and śāstras; I shall not attempt to praise or describe them here even slightly.

I fear, however, that you may still lack firm resolve, and thus I urge and exhort you once more briefly: Trace back the origin of the four elements and five aggregates to analyze the existence of form;
employ the six vessels and three vehicles to transport all sentient beings; let the myriad practices return to emptiness, and enter goodness through the thousand gates.
How could his eloquence and wisdom be merely the breadth of the Seven Classics or the Hundred Schools? It is clear that they were beyond the reach even of Yao, Shun, the Duke of Zhou, and Confucius.
He then extensively refuted the slanders and criticisms of the common world, as fully recorded in that text; there is no need to cite them here at length.
The twentieth and final section of the *Zhi pian* (Chapter on Final Regulations) states: "This year I am old and ill; may I suddenly pass away. Let me simply bathe and be done with it."

Regarding the merits of our inner scriptures, one should act according to one's capacity; whether it be to repay boundless gratitude or to express sorrow for the passing of parents like the falling frost and dew, there are times when offerings of vegetarian feasts are made.
Thus, by being loyal and faithful, one does not bring shame upon their kin—this is what I hope for in you.
The Yan family greatly honors our teaching, and for this reason, I have used it as a means to lead them forward.

it should rather say "sixty kalpas. For śrāvakas, sixty kalpas [are required], and for pratyekabuddhas, one hundred kalpas. Could it be that by analogy with those cases, this is acceptable?

As fully described in the *Avataṃsaka*, there are ten kinds of the six sense organs:
first, the flesh eye; second, the deva eye; third, the wisdom eye; fourth, the dharma eye; fifth, the Buddha eye; sixth, the clear eye;
seventh, the unimpeded eye; eighth, the universal eye; ninth, the eye that transcends birth and death; and tenth, the wisdom eye. These are the ten eyes.
Regarding the ear: first is hearing the sound of praise, and so on up to the tenth, which is hearing all sounds throughout the worlds of the ten directions.

Regarding the nose: first is smelling a foul odor and observing that it is not putrid, and so on up to the tenth, which is smelling the fragrance of the realm of the wisdom of all Buddhas, never ceasing the conduct of a Bodhisattva. Regarding the tongue: first... [the text continues].
These ten kinds of tongues are: first, the tongue that analytically understands the inexhaustible practices for liberating all sentient beings;

and so on, up to the tenth, the tongue that causes all sentient beings to reach nirvana. The ten kinds of bodies are: first, the human body; and so on, up to the tenth, the untainted *anāsrava* dharma-body.
The ten kinds of minds are: first, the foremost mind; and so on, up to the tenth, the mind deeply entered into meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Furthermore, the subsequent passage explains the two vehicles’ *aṣṭau vimokṣāyatanāni* (eight bases of mastery). It states: “*Vimokṣa* means abandonment; *āyatana* means understanding;

and *ādi* (‘etcetera’) refers to what is said in the *Dhyānapāramitā*: ‘If, by means of the *abhibhvāyatanas* (bases of mastery), one exhausts the afflictions, then one knows that the false aggregates and sense-bases are all extinguished.
At that time, the *abhibhvāyatanas* change their name to the eight *vimokṣāyatanas*.”

Regarding the first two categories of the path-factors (*mārgāṅga*), since their teaching clarifies that the characteristics of their causes, activities, and fruits are only slightly superior to those of a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*), they are not considered extraordinary.
For example, one who obtains copper cannot see their reflection; though both may obtain a mirror, if it lacks the quality of the dharma-realm, no images will appear.

The latter two chapters on the Path are the dharmas that constitute the characteristics of cultivation; thus the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says that the dharma-body is endowed with marks. If one realizes the Middle Way, one is immediately endowed with these marks.
It is like obtaining a mirror: the myriad forms must necessarily manifest within it.
In the first two [stages], one attains the true image of the dharma-realm that is without phenomena; yet one does not see that the nature of the mind inherently possesses the three thousand realms.
This is like the great void, which is devoid of all forms, or like a crystal bead that cannot rain down jewels. Therefore, it is said that obtaining copper cannot reflect one's face;
this refers to the principle of emptiness, which does not possess existence. In the latter two [stages], within the attainment of the middle, one is able to possess the marks.
Therefore, it is said that when a mirror reflects the myriad images, they must necessarily have form; likewise, the wish-fulfilling jewel rains down jewels inexhaustibly.
This is used to manifest that the Middle Way’s true reality (dharmatā) and wondrous emptiness possess the provisional nature of all phenomena as a wondrous existence.
Thus, in both the *Wenju* and the *Miaoxuan*, the subtle, pure Dharma-body is paired with the Dharma-body endowed with the thirty-two marks.
Regarding the response-body (nirmāṇakāya): is the response-body not the function of wondrous existence? Is the dharma-body not the essence of the Middle Way?

Since the essence must possess function, is it not the case that true emptiness inherently possesses wondrous existence? Just as a bright mirror manifests images—is the manifestation of images not wondrous conventionality?
Is the clarity of the mirror not prajñā? Is the substance of the mirror not the dharma-body? Thus, they are categorized accordingly.
Although they are united, they are ever more distinct; thus, True Emptiness and Wondrous Existence are brilliantly non-confused.

Since Siming did not understand this, he claimed that the Three Truths are identical to the three—emptiness, the provisional, and the middle—and that the three bodies and four lands are perfectly manifest in their respective forms.
How could he have understood that the bright mirror of the Middle Way is fundamentally devoid of all characteristics? As for that which is without characteristics...
One who discusses these characteristics should reflect upon this: they are themselves the wondrous existence inherently present within true emptiness.

This serves to verify that the oceans of marks discussed in these three sūtras are all the *Zhunti* (Exalted and Distinctive) marks; for the person of the Perfect Teaching knows that the entire Dharma-realm constitutes the thirty-two [marks].

Regarding the two [sets of marks], the eighty thousand, and the pores, because they possess these characteristics, all three types of marks may be called "oceans" and are termed "extraordinary physical features" (*viśiṣṭa-lakṣaṇa*). The *Wenju* (Textual Commentary) states, regarding the empty seat as a warning: "One must not see it as lowly and thereby forget its majestic dignity. The *Ji* (Record/Notes) states:

"The body is characterized by form (*lakṣaṇa*), while principle (*li*) is wondrous emptiness (*śūnyatā*); relying on emptiness, one transcends form and characteristics. These all refer to the principle of the wondrous emptiness of the Middle Way;
they do not mean that the absence of form and characteristics constitutes majesty or something extraordinary. It does not mean that— [the passage ends here].
The inferior form of sixteen feet is the superior "exalted special" (zuntè) manifestation; it is named for its majesty and extraordinary nature.

Although the large and small, the honorable and the humble—such as the inferior sixteen-foot form and the superior exalted special form—differ in scale and status, they are all characterized by form (*sanimitta*) and are not the signless state based on emptiness (*animitta*).

Therefore, one cannot allow the Dharma to be treated as a uniform whole simply because the names are identical; one must necessarily distinguish them through principle so that their meanings are clarified.
Is it not the case that the distinction [between the two bodies] is not so? Furthermore, in the subsequent passage explaining the realm of dhyāna-samādhi, it states:

"A profound understanding of the ocean of marks refers only to the boundless marks and excellences of the form body (*rūpakāya*), which are designated as an 'ocean'; it does not refer to the inconceivable ocean of the reward body (*vipākakāya*).

If one were to claim that all three grades [of the response-body] may be called an "ocean" and are thus termed the "Exalted Special Body" (*zhunti*), why did Jingxi [Zhanran] specifically exclude the form body?

Since the ocean of marks is not the ocean of marks of the *saṃbhogakāya*, we know that both the *paricchinna-rūpakāya* (the segmented physical body) and the *dharmatā-saṃbhogakāya* (the reward body of the nature of phenomena) are identical to principle (*tattva*), and thus their essence is the same.
Therefore, the depth, breadth, and boundlessness of the ocean are used as a metaphor for the depth, breadth, and limitlessness of that which is identical to principle.

Although they are the same in being identical to principle and as deep and vast as the ocean, when viewed from the perspective of phenomena (*dharma*) and their functions (*vṛtti*), they do not [conflate].
Because they may be confused with one another, the ocean of marks of the *rūpakāya* (form body) is distinguished from the ocean of marks of the *saṃbhogakāya* (reward body).
The inconceivable ocean of marks of the *saṃbhogakāya* refers to the ocean of marks within the lotus-flower pedestal that contains as many worlds as atoms.

The ocean of marks of the *rūpakāya* refers to the segmented birth-body (*prādeśika-janma-kāya*) of sixteen feet tall with the thirty-two marks; it is called an "ocean" by way of its principle (*li*), and it also includes the realm of shared residence (*sahāloka*).
The Pure Land of Amitābha is the supreme response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) of sixty million *yojanas*, possessing eighty-four thousand marks;

this is the ocean of names that accord with principle. While the segmented birth-body (*pariccheda-janma-kāya*) possesses only these names that accord with principle but lacks the ocean of marks as vast as the atoms within the sublime and distinct *dharmatā*-body of non-alteration (*asaṃskṛta-dharmatā-kāya*), whether it be according to principle or according to phenomena, they constitute the essence and function of both principle and phenomenon.
All these qualities, being all-pervasive, are called the "Ocean of Marks" (*lakṣaṇa-samudra*).

If one were to establish the physical body (*rūpakāya*)—with its marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*)—as the ocean of the boundless principle, yet limit it to the fixed measure of sixteen feet, by what means could one then clarify the inconceivable ocean of marks of the Reward Body (*saṃbhogakāya*)?
Therefore, one should know that upon merely hearing the term "ocean of marks," one must not immediately assume that they are all [of the same nature].

Regarding the "Exalted and Distinct" (zūntè): if one claims that a person of perfect capacity (yuánrén) knows the entire Dharma-realm as manifesting the thirty-two marks, the eighty thousand minor marks, and the clouds of dust-like characteristics, why must these necessarily all be termed "Exalted and Distinct"?
If they are all equally "Exalted and Distinct," for what reason is it said that their essence is identical while their functions differ?
If their essence is identical, is it not the case that both are the Dharma-realm? If their functions differ, is it not the case that the superior and inferior are clearly distinguished?
However, if this were not the case, how could the master and disciple of the *Lotus Sūtra* (Dharmapada) not be the entire body of the Dharma-realm manifesting itself?

For what reason, then, would one call them "those whose bodies are both base and inferior," or describe them as wearing the garments of silent patience and the *ratnāvalī* necklace while enduring the tattered robes of the defilements of birth and phenomena?
According to the doctrine established by Siming, one ought to revise this and say: "The master and disciple of the *Lotus Sūtra* [are the Dharma-realm itself]."

The body and its accompaniments are both superior; though the dharmas of birth are hidden, they are like coarse, shabby, and soiled garments, yet the necklaces and precious ornaments of tranquil patience are revealed.
It is not merely these words and records that clarify the *Lotus Sūtra*; the master and disciple [Zhiyi and Guanding] are those who wear such soiled garments.

The *Miaofa Lianhua Jing Xuan Yi* (Profound Meaning) and *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary) clarify that the opening of the soiled garments reveals the inner body as the "Necklace Elder"—this is what my ancestor [Guanding] explained.

Does the fact that Master Zhi calls it "adhering" (*zhu*), Master Yun "superior" (*sheng*), and Master Jingxi "inferior" (*lie*)—and thus their differing views on superiority and inferiority and their divergent expositions on the manifestation of existence—constitute the slander of establishing a distinction between the heavens?
Furthermore, the *Commentary on the Contemplation Sūtra* states: "When wisdom merges with the essence, it can give rise to great function;
the body is both the body and not the body," and so forth. Herein, superiority and inferiority are clearly manifest; how can one claim that the entire Dharma-realm constitutes the thirty [realms]?
The two marks, the eighty thousand treasuries, and the motes of dust all constitute the two functions of the *vairocana-kāya* (the majestic form) in their entirety;
how can one exclusively speak from the perspective of the *vairocana-kāya* alone? Could it be that the inferior sixteen-foot body does not possess the full function of the entire *dharmadhātu*?
"Ji" (棘) is pronounced with the *yù* and *yuán* finals (*yuè-yuán*), meaning to join or to draw forth; it is also pronounced with the *wáng* and *juàn* finals (*wáng-quàn*).
The *Fǔxíng* (輔行) states: "The name is universal while the meaning is perfect; the name is distinct while the meaning is perfect."
The Sūtra states: "We are now true Arhats. While the names here are the same as those in the *Samdhinirmocana* (Pitaka of the General Teachings), their meaning lies in the Perfect [Teaching].
This is like how the fifty-two stages share names with the Distinct Teaching, yet their significance is perfectly subtle. Regarding the ten points: first, distinguishing the names and meanings;
second, clarifying the number of stages; third, clarifying the severance and subduing [of afflictions], up to the tenth, which clarifies the stages themselves.

From beginning to end, the fourth section of the *Miaoxuan* (The Profound and Mysterious) clarifies the stages of the Shared Teaching (*tongjiao*). First, it explains the ten stages common to the three vehicles;

second, it distinguishes between names that are distinct while their meanings are shared. This further divides into two parts: first, within the stages common to the three vehicles, the Bodhisattva’s specific designations for the "patience" (*kṣānti*) stages are established, yet their meaning remains shared with the other two vehicles.
Second, using the names of the Distinct Teaching (*biejiao*), the names are distinct while the meanings remain shared. This concludes the *Zhi guan* (Cessation and Contemplation).

To the west of the Pamir Mountains (Congling), all belong to the Brahma lineage; to the left of the Iron Gates, all are called the lands of the Hu.

The Pamir Mountains (Congling) are situated in the central-southern part of Jambudvīpa; they join the Snowy Mountains to the south and reach the Hot Sea to the north, extending eastward to the Wushai region and westward to Persia.
Measuring several thousand *li* in length and breadth, they are firmly established.

With snow accumulating in winter and summer, and ice so severe that steep precipices occupy more than half the terrain, wild onions (*shanchong*) grow abundantly below them; hence they are named Congling. Formerly, people referred to them simply as "Onion" (*cong*).
The "Snow-Clad Ridge" (*Snehasaila*) is the Snowy Mountains (*Himavat*). Master Xuanzang stated: "I have personally witnessed and verified that this is not the Snowy Mountains.

The true Snowy Mountains lie south of the Pamir Range (*Gongling*); stretching east and west across the southern ocean and facing open plains to the south, reaching the dense forests to the north, it is only there that one defines the Pamir Range.
It is bounded by the *Yanye* (pronounced *yan* [level tone] and *xie* [entering tone]) and the *Suoxie* (pronounced *suo* [entering tone] and *hua* [level tone]). Furthermore, it should also..."
The mountain cliffs are known for their lush greenery and are called the Congling Iron Gate.
From this land to Guzang, from Guzang to Dunhuang, from Dunhuang to Gaochang, and from Gaochang to the Iron Gate, one passes through sixteen kingdoms in total.
This Iron Gate is the Iron Gate Pass; it serves as the western bulwark of the Han, and from here one enters the mountains for five hundred li.
On both sides of the valley there are no other paths; a single road leads southward, perilous and impassable.

On either side, stone cliffs rise steeply for thousands of *ren*, their color and appearance like iron, which is why it is named as such. One sees the gate of Han, with one leaf standing upright and the other lying flat;
outside is iron and inside is wood, with bells suspended from them. This pass must surely be closed, for it is truly a natural fortress. To the south, one exits through this gate.
The soil is warm and fertile, and flowers and fruits flourish in abundance; the region is named Tukhāra.

It is over one thousand *li* in length and over three thousand *li* in breadth. To the east it reaches the Pamir Mountains, to the west it borders Persia, to the south lies the Great Snowy Mountains, and to the north it rests upon the Iron Gate.
The great river Oxus flows through its center toward the west. As for Guzang, it belongs to the Longyou Circuit.

To the south of the Snow Mountains, extending for ninety thousand *yojanas* in three directions to the edge of the ocean, lies the realm known as Mahācīna.
This is the center of the earth, the Vajra-maṇḍala, where both mundane and supramundane great kings dwell together in this land.
If one were to tilt toward the remote borderlands, this central mountain of our region would likewise be called the "Central Kingdom" (*Zhonghua*).

The *Erya* says, "The Yellow River originates from Kunlun," which describes its source; this was recorded by Yu.
The statement that the Yellow River originates from the Jizuo (積右) mountains refers to its terminal reaches.
The *Hanshu* claims that Zhang Qian traced the river to the kingdom of Shendu (India), which merely indicates that he traveled along its distant course without exhausting its true origins.

According to the Buddhist sūtras, the four rivers originate from Mount Gandhamādana, where they branch out to flow into the four oceans; thus one knows their beginning and end. As for what the world calls Kunlun, the sūtras refer to it as...

Regarding the present-day Xingzhe River (River of Practice) sought on Mount Gandhamādana: it originates from the Snow Mountains; however, because the Snow Mountains and Mount Gandhamādana are layered and densely intermingled, they are difficult to distinguish.

Since snow accumulates there throughout winter and summer, the path is not accessible to humans. Thus, Guo Pu stated: "The source of the Yellow River emerges from the Mysterious Palace at Mount Tiangu.
Examining these various accounts in detail, Mount Tiangu must surely be the Heart of the Earth (*dharmadhātu*); for if the Heart of the Earth is high, [the source flows forth].

First, it is correct that the four rivers branch out from this single source. Second, it is correct that the Divine Land (China) lies to the southeast of Kunlun, clearly showing that the cardinal directions are distinct.

Third, it is correct that while Heaven and Xia face the sea with their backs to the mountains, the Divine Land is situated in the eastern bend of the southern ocean, whereas such a configuration is unheard of to the west.
Finally, it is correct that whenever a Great Sage-King governs, he must do so from the center of the earth; yet this has not been heard of in this region.
These four are the "Correct" (Zheng). As for this land of the Yellow Emperor where the spirit roamed in Huaxu—Wang Shao and others interpreted this as the country of Daxia;

The Hu originally lived north of the mountains and have long since submitted to Han; now they belong to the Turks. It is not the Heaven of Huaxu.
When the land was first opened, there were yet no people or creatures; a Brahmā King descended to be born in this soil and transmitted his original customs of writing and speech to humanity.
This, then, is the language of heaven and the script of heaven, preserved solely in Da Xia.

In all other foreign lands, the scripts and languages differ from one another; the original script of this land merely depicts the tracks of birds, while its dialects range from the refined to the vulgar.
The distinctions between eras are not the same; how could they be compared to the fixed and eternal standards of Huaxu?

The *Pratideśanā-praṇidhāna* (Vow of Confession) is excerpted from a Mahāyāna sūtra; I shall now briefly cite it. The verses for confession state:
"The Buddhas of the ten directions know all things without exception; before them, I now fully disclose and repent of all my evils.
There are two further verses which I do not cite here in full. The verses for exhortation state: "All Tathāgatas of the ten directions who have currently attained enlightenment..."

I request the turning of the Wheel of Dharma for the peace and happiness of all sentient beings. One verse remains, which I shall not cite in full here; the verse of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*) says:
"Whatever merit there is from giving, from upholding the precepts, and from the practice of meditation," and so on, until:
"May the immeasurable merit of humans and devas, and all such as these, be rejoiced in. The verse of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) says: "All the meritorious deeds that I have performed... [all of them].
The verse on the vow for the correct dedication of merit toward the Buddha-way, made for the sake of delivering sentient beings through harmonious union, states:
"May all sentient beings alike resolve to attain Bodhicitta," and continues until it says, "Clearly perceiving the Buddha-nature, just like Mañjuśrī.
Furthermore, the passage below regarding such texts on long-term repentance also sufficiently fulfills the meaning of the fivefold repentance.
"Thus, 'the following is the confession' refers to the liturgical text for the morning worship;

this is from the *Vinayaviniścaya-sūtra*, now briefly cited as follows: 'May all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, who eternally abide throughout all worlds, look upon me with compassion and pity—whether in this life or in previous lives, from [the beginning]...'"

All the various sins committed since beginningless saṃsāra—whether committed by oneself, incited in others, witnessed being committed, or rejoiced in—including even the five heinous crimes and the ten evil deeds—these karmic obstructions are now all confessed. Next, from the passage "Now, all Buddhas...
onwards, is the dedication. As the Sūtra says: "May the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, bear witness to me and keep me in mind."
I, myself, further speak these words before all the Buddhas: "Whatever acts of giving I have performed in this life or in other lives,
or whatever pure precepts I have observed— even down to giving a single morsel of food to an animal—
may all such roots of goodness be dedicated toward enlightenment, in the same manner as the dedication performed by the Buddhas of the three periods of time."
I also dedicate in this same manner. Next, regarding the removal of the multitude of sins, one verse is repeated as a summary example of repentance;
the remaining three are as stated in the Sūtra: "I repent of all sins, rejoice in all merits, and through the merit of inviting the Buddhas, may I attain supreme wisdom.
Next, one verse is repeated to offer homage and take refuge in the World-Honored One. As for the text: [Sūtra].

The passage beginning with "I take refuge in and pay homage with palms joined to the Buddhas of the past, future, and present, who are the most supreme among sentient beings and an immeasurable ocean of merit" is drawn from the *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā-sūtra*; as these five sections of repentance all originate from that sūtra, they are cited here in full detail.

Regarding the chapter on the "Poisoned Drum," Zhiyan (Zhān'ān) says: "The person represents the Buddha; the poison represents the present teaching; and coating the drum represents attachment to the teaching. He further states: "The person represents this sutra;
although they have no desire to hear it, those who encounter it and hear it will certainly be able to sever their delusions. (From the *Wenju ji*).

Regarding the "Cloud Drum": "Equality" refers to the Dharmakāya; "Poison" refers to unconditioned compassion; "Beating" refers to its arousal; "Hearers" refers to those who are ready to receive the teaching;
"Death" refers to the destruction of ignorance—the destruction of delusions of this life is "near death," while the destruction of delusions of future lives is "far death.
Furthermore, the text below states: "Since their vows, numbers, schools, and views differ, there is no need to reconcile them."
The forty-eight vows of the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* and the twenty-four vows of the *Amitābha-sūtra* likely represent different translations of the same scripture;
thus, the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* was translated by Kang Senghai, while the *Amitābha-sūtra* was translated by Zhi Qian of the Wu kingdom.
Furthermore, the *Wuliang qingjing pingdengjue jing* was translated by Zhi Loujiachen of the Han dynasty.
Kāśyapa Mātanga translated these three sūtras, all of which were preached at Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa in Rājagṛha.
Regarding the Forty-eight Vows, the Twenty-four Vows, the various specific vows, and the Ten Great Vows, their texts are extremely extensive;
it would be difficult to record them in full, so one must seek them out in the sūtras themselves to understand their teachings.
This "illumination" (ming) refers to that which has something to be severed; the character "illumination" (ming) is likely an error and should be "name" (ming).
These four selections are from the *Yuanwen* (Vow Text) of Nanyue.

The postscript to the *Nanyue Yuanwen* states: "Regarding those monastics and laypeople in the world who earnestly request a lecture and provide offerings—even those who forcefully urge one to preach a sutra—all such monastics and laypeople are not virtuous friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), but are evil friends (*pāpamitra*).
Why is this? They are all sent by Māra; at first, they feign earnestness as if they were good."
Immediately after this thought arose in his mind, he reflected: "Both the demons of anger and forgiveness—whether good or evil—are not beneficial matters.
From this day forward, one should not place trust in them; even those who call themselves scholars should likewise be distrusted, for they are like enemies feigning friendship.
Alas, alas! This is inconceivable! All kings and kṣatriyas are likewise thus; one must discern and discern."
"Zhe zhe. (Discriminate, discriminate.

In the *Liji* (Book of Rites), this is written as "hangan" (扞格). "Han" (扞) is pronounced with the initial *hu* and the final rhyme *ban* (*hú bàndiǎn*). It means that the teachings cannot overcome one's emotional desires; therefore—
The "Xueji" (Record of Learning) chapter of the *Liji* states: "The method of the Great Academy is to prohibit [immorality] before it has been aroused; this is called 'preparation.

If one prohibits it only after it has been aroused, then prohibitions will meet with resistance and fail to prevail. If one studies only after the time has passed, then despite diligent effort, success will be difficult to achieve.
The commentary notes: "Before it has been aroused' means that desires have not yet arisen; this refers to the age of fifteen. *Honghong* is the sound of chariots."

Yě (also pronounced hóng) is pronounced with the *qièyùn* "hóng"; xiē (scorpion) is pronounced with the *qièyùn* "gé"; it refers to a silkworm. Dù (woodworm) is pronounced with the *qièyùn* "gù"; tuī (to push) is pronounced with the *qièyùn* "tūn".

Kòu (hard) is pronounced with the *qièyùn* "jué"; jìn (stubborn) means to be firm. Duī (a mound) is pronounced with the *qièyùn* "huí"; it means to fall. The *Zhuāngzǐ* says: "Names are the guests of reality.

Because they resemble dust and consciousness, they lack the three natures;
for that which resembles dust is not real. All things within the entire dharma-realm—such as jars, clothing, and vehicles—are likewise [unreal].
Non-conceptual consciousness (*nirvikalpa-vijñāna*). Conceptual consciousness is precisely the consciousness of consciousness (*vijñapti-vijñāna*).

Conceptual form (*rūpa*) is, for example, as when one says that radiance is itself wisdom. Non-conceptual form is that which is composed of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) of the *dharmadhātu*, and so forth.
Regarding the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), the *Treatise on the Three Natures* (*Trisvabhāvanirdeśa*) states that all phenomena do not transcend [these three].

Regarding the three natures—the first being the nature of conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), the second the nature of dependence on others (*paratantra-svabhāva*), and the third the nature of reality (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*)—the three absences of nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) are taught in reference to these.

Because the nature of conceptualization lacks any objective referent, it is called the "absence of characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa-niḥsvabhāvatā*); because the nature of dependence on others lacks independent arising, it is called the "absence of production" (*utpatti-niḥsvabhāvatā*);

and because the nature of reality lacks a separate substantiality, it is called the "absence of nature" (*svabhāva-niḥsvabhāvatā*). As for the nature of conceptualization, it refers to the intrinsic nature of all phenomena as manifested through names and conventions.
The nature that resembles objects—the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*)—is so called because it manifests the self-nature of phenomena by relying on causes and conditions;
specifically, it refers to the portion of deluded consciousness that arises from internal roots as its causal basis and internal objects as its objective condition.

The true nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) refers to the suchness of phenomena (*dharmatā-tathatā*); this suchness of phenomena means that both the imagined (*parikalpita*) and the dependent natures are, in their suchness, non-existent.

Because they lack substantiality, this is explained extensively in that text. Furthermore, the later passage which cites the *Samantabhadra-dhyāna-sūtra* stating that one gradually sees the Buddhas of the East with the mind’s eye is an error;
it should instead cite the sūtra as saying: "The ear gradually hears sounds beyond obstructions;
the eye gradually sees objects beyond obstructions; the nose gradually smells fragrances beyond obstructions. Thus, the *Zhi guan* says: "If..."

Gradually seeing beyond the enclosure refers to the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*) of the inner ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*). Seeing the ten directions thereafter refers to the partial realization of the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*).
As the *Sūtra* states: "The practitioner immediately sees all immeasurable worlds in the eastern direction, with the ground as level as the palm of a hand;
the worlds of the ten directions are likewise so. Since the *Samantabhadra-dhyāna Sūtra* distinguishes between the true and the semblance [realizations], [the former corresponds to the first stage].
The case of the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging is likewise so; that which is cited in the prediction corresponds to the subsequent passage in the *Sūtra of Similarity*, which further states:
"By preaching this sūtra, one attains these constant eyes and the purification of the faculties of ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind"—this is partial realization (*pradeśa-prativedha*).
