Because the character "diao" (調) is pronounced with the departing tone (*qùshēng*), it is judged that those who abide in the first and second phrases and so forth are ordinary or small-capacity practitioners.
If one follows the scriptural text, the first and second phrases and so forth should be distinguished according to the sequence listed in the *Zhiguan* (Mohe Zhiguan).
Thus, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "A sick bodhisattva should thus subdue his mind, yet not dwell within it."
Nor does he dwell in an undisciplined mind. Why is this? To dwell in an undisciplined mind is the way of fools;
to dwell in a disciplined mind is the way of the Śrāvakas. Therefore, a Bodhisattva should not dwell in either a disciplined or an undisciplined mind.
To be free from these two states is the practice of a Bodhisattva. Now, proceeding from the state of an ordinary person...

Because the stages of the Śrāvaka-vehicle Bodhisattva are divided into four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*), the ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) constitutes the first, the Śrāvaka-vehicle the second, and the Bodhisattva the third;
the fourth proposition is [the remaining case]. The character 佷 is a vulgar form; the correct form is 很 (hěn), pronounced with the initial *hu* and the final *kěn*.
As for the character 戾, it is composed of "dog" (*quán*) and "door" (*hù*); that which emerges from under the door is "crooked" (*lì*). This refers to the body being bent. Now it says:

Regarding the character "da" (大) in the phrase "like the great" (如大): the character "da" should be "cong" (從). If it is written as "li" (戾), that is a vulgar form; the correct form is indeed "li" (戾).
If it is written as "li" (悷), this refers to being "long-li" (龍悷), which implies much wickedness, or alternatively, it means to wail in grief. This concludes the four lines of the preceding text.
Since the second line has been lost, it says "not disciplined" (不調); one should instead say "abiding in the first" (住第一).
Regarding the error in the phrasing, let us examine it more closely: where "residing in these words" (居是言) occurs, it should read "residing in the land" (居土).

Where it says "the meaning is that the dark reality does not come" (義云暗實不來), it should read "the meaning is that the dark comes; the dark reality does not come" (義云暗來暗實不來); the two characters "dark comes" (暗來) have simply been omitted from the text.
Furthermore, regarding "ignorance within the three provisionalities" (三假中無明), the character "provisional" (假) should be "cultivation" (修); this refers to the [first]...

Regarding the threefold cultivation of the Middle Way for refuting [extremes], there is no explicit textual passage; it consists of three sections: first, ignorance; second, the nature of phenomena (dharmatā); and third, true conditions.
There are scribal errors and omissions within the preceding and following passages, which I shall not detail further; one should understand them by reference to this.

In treatises such as the *Abhidharmakośa* and the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, it is stated that there are three modes of continuity: instantaneous (*kṣaṇika*), linked (*prābandhika*), and remote (*dūrasamtānika*).

Here, "instantaneous" refers to the cause and effect proceeding simultaneously in the world, as it is said in the Sūtras: "With the eye and visible forms as conditions, eye-consciousness arises," and so forth; furthermore, it is said:
With the eye and visible forms as conditions, delusion (*moha*) arises; this delusion is itself ignorance (*avidyā*). This delusion that seeks after objects is called craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
That which is manifested by craving is karma-existence (*karmabhava*). Other masters say that within a single moment all twelve links are present, truly arising together;
for example, in the mind that initiates action arising simultaneously with greed, "delusion" refers to ignorance, and "volition" (*cetanā*) is [the link of] existence.
The discernment of objects as they function is called *vijñāna* (consciousness). Consciousness, together with the three aggregates (*skandha*), is collectively termed *nāmarūpa* (name-and-form).

The material sense faculties are called the six bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*). The point of contact associated with consciousness is called *sparśa* (contact). The sensation associated with consciousness is called *vedanā* (feeling). Craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is attachment;
the various entanglements (*paryavasthāna*) associated with it are called *upādāna* (clinging). The two types of action—bodily and vocal—arising from these are called *bhava* (becoming).
Thus, the arising of these various phenomena is called "birth," their maturation and transformation is called "aging," and their disintegration is called "death.

"Continuous bondage" refers to the uninterrupted succession of similar causes and effects arising one after another, as stated in the Sūtras. Regarding the state where ignorance serves as the cause for the arising of the category of defiled craving:
this refers to the uninterrupted succession of the five aggregates within the twelve links throughout three lifetimes, as taught by the Buddha.

Regarding the explanation of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) by way of its stages (*avasthā*): since each member (*aṅga*) contains all five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), for what reason are they designated specifically as "ignorance" (*avidyā*) and so forth?
It is because within these various stages, ignorance and the others are predominant; thus, names are established according to what is most prominent.

That is to say, when ignorance is most predominant in a particular stage, the five aggregates of that stage are collectively termed "ignorance," and this applies likewise up to the stage of old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*).

The Most Victorious One [the Buddha] has designated the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) of this stage collectively as "aging and death" (*jarā-maraṇa*); thus, although their substance is collective, there is no fault in the distinction of their names.
Likewise, the five aggregates of the preceding stage act as conditions to collectively induce the five aggregates of the succeeding stage;

this distant continuity occurs because there exist, across the prior and subsequent limits of existence, karmas and afflictions (*kleśa*) that are to be experienced in subsequent lives or at indefinite times. Therefore, the cycle of rebirth is beginningless.

Regarding the phrase "this very distant continuity from beginningless time, such as karma to be experienced in subsequent lives," this refers to the determinate and indeterminate karma to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*), the next life (*upapadyavedanīya*), and subsequent lives (*aparaparyāyavedanīya*).
These various passages have been fully cited from the *Abhidharmakośa*. Furthermore, the text below states:

"In the fourth set of four propositions, what is called 'principle' (*nyāya*) is that which is 'neither of the two' (*ubhayābhāva*)," and so on, up to the discussion of the following three propositions.

Regarding the statement that "all should be called 'principle' (li)": if one relies solely on *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, it refers only to the first phrase; saying "neither emerging nor not emerging" is what is termed "principle.
The remaining three phrases, however, pertain only to phenomena (*dharma*).

When Guang went to inquire after him, the guest said, "Previously, while sitting here, I received wine from you; however, I saw a snake in my cup, which I found quite loathsome. The guest looked and saw the bow, whereupon his illness vanished. This is called the "hallucination of the drinking vessel" (*guǐyǐng*). It is said that if one’s mind is unsettled, even the walls and earth will appear as if they were moving. Thus, when the mind is agitated, one may perceive things that do not exist. How much more so when one is deluded by external forms! Therefore, the Sage taught that all phenomena are like dreams and illusions. In the *Prakṛtisiddhi-śāstra*, because the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) is identical to the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), it is not established separately; rather, only the retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*) is established as the generative cause (*janaka-hetu*).

Furthermore, the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) is the self-part cause (*svabhāga-hetu*), the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*) is the habitual cause (*abhyāsa-hetu*), and the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*) is the supporting cause (*niśraya-hetu*).

At the initial moment of arising, whether superior or inferior, before it has pervaded the entire body, it gradually diminishes and dissolves;
this is called "decrease. Second, when disturbed movement is triggered, the consciousness-mind and the body are bound by meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and cannot attain autonomy;
or because of this, one enters a false concentration and does not emerge for as long as seven days—this is called [disturbance].
When concentration is disturbed by external stimuli, the mind and consciousness become disordered and fail to remain focused on their objects; this is called "distraction" (*vikṣepa*).
When stimulated during the three levels of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), one perceives no body at all; this is called "attaining the concentration of emptiness" (*śūnyatā-samādhi*).
When stimulated, one perceives the body as solid and rigid, like wood or stone; this is called "existence" (*bhava*). Fourth is the clarity of light and darkness.
When the [feeling of] pain arises, one perceives various external colors and lights such as the sun, moon, and stars;
when the [feeling of] darkness arises, the body and mind become dark and obscured, as if entering a dark room;
when the [feeling of] sorrow arises, the mind is afflicted with feverish distress, becoming haggard and displeased; when the [feeling of] joy arises, the mind is greatly delighted.
One is able to settle oneself regarding the six types of suffering and pleasure: when suffering is triggered, there is physical and mental pain and affliction;

"The stages (*bhūmi*) consist of nine: the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) as one, and the form and formless realms (*rūpa-ārūpyadhātu*) as eight, making nine.

In the three formless realms, the nine paths within each stage all mutually serve as causes for one another. Why is this?
Because these paths abide in accordance with their respective stages, they do not fall under the inclusion of any specific realm (*dhātu*), nor are they grasped as "mine" by the craving of others.

Therefore, although the nine paths of the various stages differ from one another, they function as mutual causes because they are of the same kind (*sabhāga*). However, this applies only to those that are equal in status.

The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 63, asks: "What is the difference between the attainment of cessation and the attainment of non-conception? It answers: "In name..."

The distinction between these two is that the former is called the "attainment of non-perception" (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) and the latter is called the "attainment of cessation" (*nirodha-samāpatti*). Their respective spheres (*dhātu*) are also distinct:

the attainment of non-perception belongs to the form realm (*rūpa-dhātu*), while the attainment of cessation belongs to the formless realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*). The Buddhist sūtras state that the attainment of cessation transcends all states of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).

Why, then, is it said that the attainment of cessation is a phenomenon belonging to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception? [This is because] it is said to transcend all [states] of that sphere.

Regarding the answer concerning the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*): although it is indeed a dharma of that realm, because it is characterized by tranquility, it is described as being "like a village" [in contrast to the wilderness].
The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states that the distinction between the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) and the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) is this:

the former is for the sake of seeking liberation, preceded by the perception of renunciation; the latter is for the sake of seeking a state of peaceful abiding, preceded by the perception of stillness.
The contemplation of cessation (*ānāpāna-smṛti*) comes first. Furthermore, regarding the reference to the "eight arts" and so forth in the subsequent text:

Regarding the passage from the *Mysterious Meaning of the Lotus Sutra* (*Fahua xuanyi*) which states: "When the time for the decay of life arrives, the karma of the unconditioned precepts does not perish, etc., it is pure. It says: "As stated in the Preface to the Precepts: 'Old age and death have arrived nearby, and the Buddha-dharma is about to perish.
Yet the Buddha-dharma is profound and serene; how could it ever truly perish? To speak of its perishing is merely to say so because the lifespan of human beings has come to an end."

If the nine husbands have not yet attained the life of untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) and are unable to uphold the prohibitive precepts, then when the body becomes impermanent, the Dharma of the precepts likewise passes away.
Thus, the fivefold Dharma-body—consisting of morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation—arises dependent upon the physical body (*rūpakāya*).
Once the physical body dies, these five factors also perish; this is what is meant by the extinction of the Buddha-dharma within the body.
If one can diligently advance and truly attain the precepts shared with those who have realized the Path, then through this single reception, one will not regress and shall remain eternally tranquil;

thus, one is fully endowed with the fivefold Dharma-body. Even if such a person undergoes seven more births among humans and devas, or is born in an evil realm, they will not only fail to lose the fruit of Srotāpanna, but will certainly attain the fruit of Arhatship. This, then, is the aggregate body.
Although the Buddha-dharma may perish, the fivefold Dharma-body does not perish; being free from decay, it is precisely this that constitutes the long endurance of the Buddha-dharma.
When the profound meaning of the Mahāyāna clarifies the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, enabling one to attain its boundless and great function, this is what sustains and upholds the Buddha-dharma.

Furthermore, it may also be said that one protects oneself against the commission of offenses, for if one fails to exercise vigilance, one will inadvertently commit transgressions.

If the performance of the various dharmas (*saṃghadharma*) should become somewhat lax, then the "various dharmas" refers to the dharmas of the various practices, and "performance" (*kriyā*) refers to the practice of maintaining [the precepts].

Thus, the various dharmas are themselves the practice of maintenance, such as the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa* and so forth. The details are as previously cited from the *Nanshan Suishu Jiejing* (Nanshan’s *Suiji Jie*).

The *Maming* [Vinaya] classifies the methods of mental recollection (*cittānuvartana*)—namely, mental recollection in the presence of another (*sammukhavinaya*), mental recollection regarding the community (*saṃgha-vastu*), and so forth—by distinguishing between "cessation" (*sthiti*) and "action" (*kriyā*). It states:

"Regarding cessation-maintenance (*sthiti-dhāraṇā*), the *Prātimokṣa* (the Code of Precepts) serves as the primary heading; regarding action-maintenance (*kriyā-dhāraṇā*), the *Karmavācanā* (formal procedures) constitutes the major sections.
This refers precisely to what is now termed "self-protection through cessation and action," as well as the "performance of communal legal acts" (*saṃgha-karma*). Thus it is written.
The text states: "The first two chapters accord with principle and maintain the ultimate precepts; these are also maintained spontaneously through the precepts of the first two chapters.
As for the fourth and fifth chapters, the sutra says that 'one who maintains the precepts' refers to maintaining the precepts without deficiency in matters from the third chapter onward.
The *Wenju ji* (Commentary on the Words and Phrases) states: "The first two..."
Regarding the person of the initial stage, their every thought is constantly present within the four kinds of samādhi; they may tolerate minor transgressions of the rules for the three lower groups.

As for the two categories [of the middle and upper stages], in reality they must also include the third category; therefore, the current text states that the first three categories do not entirely fail to observe them.
If this is so, when it is now said that one "guards oneself" regarding the prohibitions and prescriptions (*śīla*), is this not the spontaneous observance of the precepts?
In the first two sections and other such cases, the communal legal procedures (*saṃghakarma*) for performing the practice do not deviate from the third section;
however, regarding matters of "dual observance" and "dual violation" within the category of "abiding in restraint," these must necessarily be complete.

That is to say, within the "observance through cessation" (*saṃvara*) section of the *Prātimokṣa* itself, there are both the two types of observance—cessation and action—as well as the two types of transgression—cessation and action.

Therefore, within the "observance through cessation" of the *Prātimokṣa*, "observance through cessation" refers to such things as abstaining from sexual misconduct; "observance through action" within that same section refers to such things as performing acts of reverence.

Conversely, if one violates these, it constitutes the two types of transgression. Why? Because engaging in sexual misconduct and so forth constitutes a "transgression through action," while failing to perform [acts of] reverence constitutes a "transgression through cessation."

One should understand that "respect" (*gaurava*) and so forth constitute the cessation of an offense. Regarding the single observance (*ekadhāraṇa*) and the separate offense (*pratyeka-āpatti*): within the performance [of the ritual], there may be no cessation;

or it may be that while the full ordination (*upasampadā*) has not yet been conferred, during the *karmavācanā* (formal act), one observes the single observance while the separate offense is absent during the performance. One should know this regarding the single observance.

"Separate offenses" (pṛthag-āpatti) refer to the absence of restraint within the performance [of an action]; thus, by explaining that there is no restraint within the performance, one clarifies the "single observance" (*ekadhāraṇa*) of separate offenses.

However, since the *śīla-mūla* (root of precepts) already possesses both "restraint through non-performance" (*saṃvara-dhāraṇa*) and "violation through performance" (*vipatti-dhāraṇa*), how could this not also apply to the "performance through ritual" (*karmavācanā-kriyā-dhāraṇa*)?

For example, the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa* and the *Karmavācanā* constitute the "performance through ritual" of the communal dharma, yet they are preceded by the cessation [of unwholesome conduct].
External conditions constitute the "observance through action" (*kriyā-dhāraṇa*) within which there is the "observance through cessation" (*niṣedha-dhāraṇa*).

Now, although there is the recitation of the precepts and the *karmavācanā*, because one has not first severed external conditions, there is no "observance through cessation" within the "observance through action. Since the "observance through cessation" is absent, it conversely constitutes a separate offense;

however, because the "observance through action" alone exists, it is called "single observance" (*ekadhāraṇa*). The term "not yet fully ordained" (*asaṃvṛta*) refers to being deficient; this will be explained in the following text.

It may be that they have not yet fully attained [the precepts]; reflect upon this accordingly. Furthermore, regarding the distinction between abstention (*saṃvara*) and performance (*kriyā*), if one follows the prohibitions in one's own practice, the formal procedures (*vastu*) will certainly not be neglected.

As previously stated, when performing communal rites (*saṃghakarma*), the practice may be somewhat relaxed; however, for those who maintain the rules individually or commit specific offenses (*pratyekāpatti*), it may be that they have not yet fully attained them.

While there may be minor deviations regarding the prescribed rules (*prajñapti*), now, as it is categorically forbidden to commit any transgression, it is said that "matters concerning the prescriptions must certainly not be neglected.

Thus, within the practice of single observance (*ekadeśa-śīla*), one must not separately violate [the rules]; is this not because the communal dharmas (*saṃghadharma*) of mental reflection on what is to be done and what is to be avoided (*cetanā-kṛtyākṛtya*) must also be maintained in both ways?
Only then does it accord with one's own practice and conform to the prescriptive teachings. One should know that the initial passage refers to the communal dharmas.

According to the *Shizong Songzhuan* (Song Biography of the Śāriputra Lineage), Vinaya Master Huaisu was a native of Nanyang. At that time, the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang had just returned from the Western Regions.

Regarding the *Huā sānmèi* (Flower Samādhi), the commentaries on its preceding and succeeding sections are uniquely detailed; this is likely because Dongjia is near Tiantai, and their fundamental tenets share a single spiritual lineage. Recently, while reading at the Jingshe (Study Hall), I often thought to myself that the pursuits of the examination candidates were tedious and wearying. At that time, a monk by the wall was diligently reciting scriptures, his voice never ceasing day or night. When I asked him about the various categories [of the texts], he replied: "I have been reciting them for over thirty years. I then realized that what I had previously called "tedious" was actually the very path to the Way. I sighed deeply and said: "How could I ever compare to you? He replied: "If you truly wish to study the Way, you must first abandon the 'five desires' and 'eight winds. Only then can you hope to attain the Way. I was struck with awe and shame, and from that moment on, I resolved to cast aside my former studies and devote myself entirely to the practice of the Way. I am now seventy-two years old, yet I still feel as though I am but a child. I pray that you will not consider me an ignorant person and will grant me your compassionate instruction. I am deeply grateful. I have written this letter to express my gratitude for your kindness. I shall wait for your further instructions. I respectfully submit this. [Seal] Dharma Master Zhixu of the Jingci Monastery, Hangzhou. The above is a copy of a letter sent to the Reverend Master [Name]. I have transcribed it here to serve as a model for those who aspire to the Way. May all who see it take it to heart and apply themselves to practice. This is the true meaning of "repaying kindness. I have recorded this for posterity so that it may be passed down through generations. May all sentient beings, seeing this, awaken to the Dharma and attain liberation. May this merit be dedicated to the benefit of all beings. May they all realize the Great Enlightenment. [Seal] Zhixu, the humble monk of the Jingci Monastery, Hangzhou.
